# Foreword

This volume deals with the formulation of matrix mechanics by Max Born, Werner Heisenberg and Pascual Jordan in fall 1925, and the immediate applications of this scheme to treat atomic problems (Wolfgang Pauli's triumphant treatment of the hydrogen atom, fall 1925; Heisenberg and Jordan's treatment of the anomalous Zeeman effects by including electron spin, early in 1926; Heisenberg's treatment of the many-body problem and resonance in quantum mechanics, spring 1926). Also treated are the modifications of the matrix scheme by Cornelius (Kornel) Lanczos ('field-like' representation of quantum mechanics) and Max Born and Norbert Wiener's formulation of operator mechanics, both in fall 1925. Matrix mechanics and its modifications, as well as Paul Dirac's work on the fundamental equations of quantum mechanics and the algebra of *q*-numbers preceded Erwin Schrödinger's formulation of wave mechanics.

I had the great privilege of discussing these developments with all the participants involved. Helmut Rechenberg and I have made use of these discussions to weave the human context in the narrative of the physical and mathematical framework of the discoveries in question. We have also drawn upon the rich source materials of the *Archives for the History of Quantum Physics*, especially the interviews with Max Born, Werner Heisenberg and Pascual Jordan (cited here as 'AHQP Interviews').* In addition, we have made use of the scientific correspondence of the principal physicists in question.

I am grateful to Aage Bohr for allowing me complete access to the archives held at the Niels Bohr Institute in Copenhagen. I am indebted to the architects of quantum mechanics and the heirs of their literary and scientific estates for permission to use the source materials pertaining to them.

JAGDISH MEHRA

***

\* An inventory of these sources is contained in: T. S. Kuhn, J. L. Heilbron, P. Forman and L. Allen, *Sources for History of Quantum Physics*, The American Philosophical Society, Philadelphia, 1967.

# Introduction

On 30 August 1925 Niels Bohr delivered an address on ‘Atomic Theory and Mechanics’ to the sixth Scandinavian Mathematical Congress in Copenhagen. In his remarks on ‘an attempt at a rational quantum mechanics,’ which he appended to the original address in November 1925 before publication, Bohr said:

> It will interest mathematical circles that the mathematical instruments created by the higher algebra play an essential part in the rational formulation of the new quantum mechanics. Thus the general proofs of the conservation theorems in Heisenberg’s theory carried out by Born and Jordan are based on the use of the theory of matrices, which go back to Cayley and were developed by Hermite. It is to be hoped that a new era of mutual stimulation of mechanics and mathematics has commenced. To the physicist it will seem first deplorable that in atomic problems we have apparently met with such a limitation of our usual means of visualisation. This regret will, however, have to give way to thankfulness that mathematics, in this field too, presents us with the tools to prepare the way for further progress. (Bohr, 1925b, p. 852)¹

With these remarks Bohr addressed himself to the latest status of atomic theory: the difficulties arising in the usual mechanical interpretation, as well as the progress achieved by Heisenberg’s discovery of the quantum-mechanical scheme and its subsequent mathematical formulation by Born and Jordan. In the latter development Bohr saw a revival of the long-established connection between mathematics and physical theory. Since the days of Isaac Newton, mechanics had always been regarded as a part of mathematics. However, in the twentieth century, with the perfection attained by classical mechanics in Henri Poincaré’s *Les Méthodes Nouvelles de la Mécanique Céleste* (1892, 1893, 1899), on the one hand, and Einstein’s special and general relativity theories (in which, again, the mathematicians like Poincaré, Hermann Minkowski, Marcel Grossmann, David Hilbert, Felix Klein, Curbastro Gregorio Ricci and Tullio Levi-Civita played an important role), on the other, one began to believe that mathematics and physics—of which the Newtonian and relativity mechanics were a completed segment—had no further overlap. Bohr’s reminder to the

---
¹ On 25 November 1925 Bohr wrote to Pauli that, induced by a previous letter of Pauli (Pauli to Bohr, 17 November 1925), he had made a series of changes in his Copenhagen address of August 1925, taking into account the recent progress in quantum mechanics initiated by Heisenberg.

Introduction

mathematicians, that the unsolved problem of atomic theory would still require the use of appropriate mathematical tools, was therefore timely. As proof, he cited the fact that ‘a self-contained theory sufficiently analogous to classical mechanics’ had been formulated by Max Born and Pascual Jordan on the basis of ‘Heisenberg’s quantum mechanics,’ and that this new atomic mechanics employed methods which had been developed in higher algebra (Bohr, 1925b, p. 852).

The quick mathematical formulation of the physical ideas, which Heisenberg had proposed in his paper on the quantum-theoretical reformulation of kinematic and mechanical relations, in a consistent theory came as a great surprise to most physicists who had laboured for years on the problems of atomic theory. A wider dissemination of matrix mechanics was limited, however, by the fact that its mathematical methods could not be handled easily for the purpose of calculating the properties of atomic systems. An important breakthrough was achieved by Wolfgang Pauli, who calculated the energy terms of the hydrogen atom in late October 1925. But it was necessary to extend Born and Jordan’s original matrix scheme to deal with atoms containing more than one electron. Several authors independently provided such extensions: Cornelius Lanczos of Frankfurt University and Max Born and Norbert Wiener, then at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. While Lanczos’ proposal concerning a field-theoretical formulation of quantum mechanics became fruitful only later on in the wave mechanical theory, which Erwin Schrödinger discovered independently, the operator mechanics of Born and Wiener helped Heisenberg, Pauli and Gregor Wentzel to generalize matrix mechanics into a symbolic calculus, which was also applicable to the action and angle variables. The observed properties of complex atoms could still not be accounted for until two further features were introduced into quantum mechanics: first, the electron spin, discovered by George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit in the analysis of multiplet spectra (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925); second, the conception of exchange degeneracy (Heisenberg, 1926b). By incorporating these extensions of the matrix scheme, Heisenberg and Jordan successfully calculated the anomalous Zeeman splittings of complex spectra (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926), and Heisenberg arrived at a qualitative understanding of the energy states of the helium atom (Heisenberg, 1926c). Thus, within a period of less than ten months after the submission of Heisenberg’s first paper (1925c), quantum mechanics developed into a theory which provided a satisfactory explanation of many important problems of atomic physics that had concerned physicists for a long time.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0010 -->

Chapter I  
The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

Heisenberg’s observation that the products of the quantum-theoretical analogues of the classical Fourier series, which were supposed to describe the dynamical variables of atomic systems, did not necessarily commute, led to an obvious conclusion: the calculus used in classical mechanics would not serve as an appropriate tool in atomic theory, and different mathematical methods had to be applied. Max Born discovered that infinite matrices could be used to formulate quantum-mechanical relations consistently. The operations with such matrices had been developed by the mathematicians during the second half of the nineteenth century and brought to some perfection in the theory of linear integral equations by Born’s teacher David Hilbert in Göttingen. Born had not only witnessed Hilbert’s work on that subject, but had himself applied the methods of infinite matrices to physical problems, as for example to the problem of specific heat of solids; hence he was well acquainted with the details of the matrix calculus. In Pascual Jordan he found an able collaborator for the task of formulating matrix mechanics.

**I.1 Max Born’s Interpretation of Heisenberg’s Quantum Condition**

During the summer semester of 1925, Max Born, Professor of Theoretical Physics at the University of Göttingen, had been especially busy. In a long letter to his friend Albert Einstein in Berlin, dated 15 July 1925, he gave an account of the events that had taken place. A number of physicists had visited Göttingen: Paul Ehrenfest from Leyden, who lectured on Bose–Einstein statistics and gas degeneracy, Hendrik Kramers from Copenhagen, Peter Kapitza from Cambridge, and Philipp Frank from Prague. ‘For us,’ Born wrote to Einstein, ‘this is very stimulating, but it is often too much for our wives. So they simply run away; my wife and Mrs. Courant have already left, and Mrs. [Philipp] Frank is due to leave in two days’ time.’^2 Then he continued: ‘But do not conclude from that that your visit is going to be unwelcome! We are greatly looking forward to it! But it ought to be at a quieter time. In July, most of the foreigners are already on holiday,

^2 Hedwig Born had left Göttingen on 13 July 1925, accompanied by the children, to go to Silvaplana in the Engadine, Switzerland. Max Born joined her soon after the end of the semester, i.e., early in August 1925.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0011 -->

6 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

and they descend on us in droves. But you know all this business. There is going to be another rumpus tomorrow; it is the inauguration of [Ludwig] Prandtl’s new hydrodynamic institute, with a guided tour, official dinner and gala concert. It will cost me almost an entire working day’ (Born to Einstein, 15 July 1925).

Besides being occupied with receiving visitors and other social activities, Born was deeply interested in the problems of quantum theory. For example, he reported to Einstein about the exciting discussions on Louis de Broglie’s matter waves that had been taking place in Göttingen at that time, which finally led Walter Elsasser to his explanation of the Ramsauer effect (Elsasser, 1925). He continued: ‘But my principal interest is the rather mysterious difference calculus on which the quantum theory of atomic structure is based. Jordan and I are systematically (though with a minimum of mental effort) examining every imaginable correspondence relationship between classical, multiple-periodic systems and quantum atoms’ (Born to Einstein, 15 July 1925). Indeed, Born hoped that the reformulation of the equations of atomic theory as difference equations would lead to a breakthrough in the description of atomic phenomena, for his previous investigations had pointed in that direction.

Upon concluding that all the advanced methods of celestial mechanics had failed in the helium problem (Born and Heisenberg, 1923b), Born had decided that new mathematical tools, completely different from those provided by the differential calculus and applied so successfully to the problem of physics from Newton to Poincaré, had to be developed for atomic mechanics. The calculus of differences seemed to present a natural method to account for the most important result connecting the frequencies and energies of atomic systems; in this case, the classical relation

$$\nu_{\tau}^{\text{cl}} = \tau \frac{\partial W}{\partial J}, \tag{1}$$

giving $\nu_{\tau}^{\text{cl}}$, the $\tau$th harmonic frequency, as a derivative of $W$, the energy, with respect to the action integral $J$, could be replaced by the difference equation

$$\nu^{\text{qu}}(n, n - \tau) = \frac{1}{h} [W(n) - W(n - \tau)]. \tag{2}$$

Born had then concluded that it was necessary to reformulate all the differential formulae of classical multiply periodic systems as difference equations, and had started to search for appropriate examples (Born, 1924b). Although the mathematical method, the calculus of differences, was available to a certain extent (see, e.g., Nörlund, 1924), Born made only slow progress in his programme of ‘discretization’ of classical mechanical relations. The main difficulty was that it was not altogether clear as to which of these relations should be reformulated at all as difference equations. However, encouraged by the successful procedure employed in dispersion theory (Kramers, 1924a, b; Born, 1924b), Born had arrived eventually at an important prescription concerning the reformulation of

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0012 -->

I.1 Max Born’s Interpretation of Heisenberg’s Quantum Condition 7

mechanical equations in quantum theory. In a paper, submitted together with Pascual Jordan in June 1925, he had proposed to deal only with those classical equations in which all quantities correspond to observable properties of atomic systems (see Born and Jordan, 1925a, especially p. 493). Born referred to that paper in his letter to Einstein with the following words: ‘A paper on this subject [i.e., on the application of the difference calculus in atomic theory] in which we examine the effect of non-periodic [electromagnetic] fields on atoms will appear soon. This is a preliminary study for an investigation of the processes occurring in atomic collisions (quenching of fluorescence, sensitized fluorescence à la Franck, etc.); one can understand, I think, the essential characteristics of what goes on. The different behaviour of atoms depends mainly on whether they have an (average) dipole moment, or just a quadrupole moment, or even a still higher electric symmetry’ (Born to Einstein, 15 July 1925). Born hoped that the long march towards the unknown quantum laws would include as steps his discretization procedure and the use of observable quantities.

Born had barely sent off his letter to Einstein when his collaborator Werner Heisenberg came to see him. He had in the meanwhile ‘pursued some work of his own, keeping its idea and purpose somewhat dark and mysterious,’ as Born recalled later (Born, 1978, p. 216). During the summer semester of 1925 Born had seen less of Heisenberg than in previous times. The two of them had not worked on common projects; actually Born had been absorbed in his official duties and in his collaboration with Jordan on the application of dispersion-theoretic methods to aperiodic atomic systems, while Heisenberg had devoted his efforts to the general questions arising from the problem of calculating the intensities of hydrogen lines, a problem which was not in the centre of Born’s interests. In May and early June 1925, before he went to Helgoland to recover from hay fever, Heisenberg had not discussed his work with Born. As he recalled later: ‘At that time everything was so vague. We may, of course, have talked in a general manner about what one could possibly do, but the only time when I really had discussions about it was when he gave me this book on the Bessel functions’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 269). These discussions had taken place already earlier in May, when Heisenberg had begun by guessing the intensities of the Balmer lines and Born had expected that Bessel functions would play a role in solving that problem. After returning from Helgoland, Heisenberg had communicated exclusively with Wolfgang Pauli by letters; Pauli had thus been the only person who was familiar with the difficulties and successes of the quantum-mechanical scheme prior to the completion of the paper (Heisenberg, 1925c). Heisenberg had even sent the manuscript first to Hamburg, requesting Pauli’s opinion before showing it to anybody in Göttingen. Upon receiving a favourable response from Pauli, he had then completed the paper and gone to see Born.

Born recalled the circumstances of receiving Heisenberg’s paper as follows: ‘He came to me with a manuscript and asked me to read it and to decide whether it was worth publishing. At the same time he asked me for leave of absence for the rest of the term (which ended about [1] August [1925]), as he had an

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0013 -->

8  Chapter I  The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

invitation to lecture at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge. He added that though he had tried hard, he could not make any progress beyond the simple considerations contained in his paper, and he asked me to try myself, which I promised to do’ (Born, 1978, p. 216). In spite of the fact that he ‘felt that something real was in the paper,’ Heisenberg was ‘very uncertain about it’ (Heisenberg, *Conversations*, p. 269). Hence he left the question of whether or not the paper should be submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* to Max Born, and went away from Göttingen without waiting for the final decision.<sup>3</sup>

Born received Heisenberg’s paper on the quantum-theoretical re-interpretation of kinematic and mechanical relations around the middle of July, the time when he wrote the letter to Einstein.<sup>4</sup> Because of his preoccupation with other events—such as the inauguration of Prandtl’s hydrodynamic institute—he delayed studying the new work. Many years later he said: ‘I remember that I did not read this manuscript at once because I was tired after the term and afraid of hard thinking. But when, after a few days, I read it I was fascinated’ (Born, 1978, p. 216).<sup>5</sup> He began to think especially about the meaning of the strange rule, which Heisenberg had given for the multiplication of two quantum-mechanical transition

According to Pascual Jordan’s recollection Born had himself thought about the mathematical process of multiplication in quantum theory even before seeing Heisenberg’s paper. Thus he reminded Born: ‘By the way, I recall with certainty that, following our joint work on absorption [Born and Jordan, 1925a], you considered a symbolic multiplication of quantum-theoretical “transition amplitudes” yourself; at that time we used to discuss together almost every day, and you told me about it. Born discovered the first example of the occurrence of two noncommuting matrices in Heisenberg’s quantum condition (Heisenberg, 1925c, p. 886, Eq. (16)),

By expressing Heisenberg’s $q$, the position coordinate of the periodic system under investigation, as

$$q_{nn'} = a(n, n') \exp[i\omega(n, n')t], \tag{6}$$

and the conjugate momentum $p_{nn'}$ by

$$p_{nn'} = m \frac{dq_{nn'}}{dt}, \tag{7}$$

$$\frac{h}{2\pi i} = \sum_{n'=-\infty}^{+\infty} (p_{nn'}q_{n'n} - q_{nn'}p_{n'n}). \tag{8}$$

It was at about this stage that Born, full of excitement with his discovery about what Heisenberg’s quantum rule of multiplication signified mathematically, travelled to Hanover on Sunday, 19 July 1925, to attend the meeting of the *Gauverein Niedersachsen* (Lower Saxony Section) of the German Physical Society.<sup>9</sup> He recalled afterwards: ‘A considerable number of physicists from Göttingen went there by train; it is about an hour’s journey on the North Express. In the train we met physicists from other universities, among them my former assistant Pauli’ (Born, 1978, p. 218). Born happily ‘joined him [Pauli] in his compartment’ and ‘at once told him about matrices.’<sup>10</sup> Pauli, who had been Heisenberg’s confidant while his new ideas had taken shape, who knew all about his work and had approved it only a week ago, did not respond favourably to Born’s excitement about matrices. When Born asked Pauli whether he would care to collaborate with him on the further development of Heisenberg’s ideas, he gave a ‘cold and sarcastic refusal.’ ‘Yes, I know,’ Pauli retorted, ‘you are fond of tedious and complicated formalisms. You are only going to spoil Heisenberg’s physical ideas by your futile mathematics’ (Born, 1978, p. 218).

Born’s approach to Pauli and the latter’s response were typical of the attitudes of both men, who had been the first to learn about the new quantum-mechanical scheme. Born was happy when he discovered the fact that Heisenberg’s multiplication rule, Eq. (3), was none other than matrix multiplication, an operation well known to mathematicians in the work of Arthur Cayley since the 1850s, for he could now exploit the entire formalism of matrix methods more effectively than he had been able to do, e.g., in his work on electron theory sixteen years previously (Born, 1909b). It occurred to Born that the well-established methods of matrix algebra would probably offer a far better tool in discovering the real quantum laws of atomic mechanics than the calculus of differences, with which he had been stuck for almost two years. Quickly abandoned now was Born’s own correspondence principle, i.e., the formulation of quantum laws by transforming

Wolfgang Pauli, however, did not share Born’s enthusiasm. He had in fact been glad that ‘Heisenberg has learned a little philosophy from Bohr in Copenhagen, and does indeed turn away noticeably from the purely formalistic approach’ (Pauli to Kramers, 27 July 1925). And now Born talked about a well-defined mathematical scheme, whereas he, Pauli, only saw in Heisenberg’s work the first tender green shoots in the barren terrain of the difficulties of atomic physics. No, Pauli was not the right collaborator to work with Born in applying matrix methods to Heisenberg’s scheme. Moreover, he was convinced that the product of the physical quantities, *p* and *q*, had to commute, and Born, in his opinion, just could not be on the right track.¹¹ In any case, Pauli did not wish to interfere with Heisenberg’s thoughts and the manner in which he would develop his theory. As Jordan reported later: ‘To Miss Mensing ... he had mentioned at that time that he wanted to leave the topic to Heisenberg himself for the moment’ (Jordan to Born, 3 July 1948).

Since Pauli had given him a negative answer concerning a collaboration on quantum mechanics, Born turned to Pascual Jordan, his main helper in those days, because he was ‘extremely tired and felt unable to make progress alone’ (Born, 1978, p. 218).¹² Jordan was glad to assist his professor again and, within a short time, achieved important progress in the matrix formulation of Heisenberg’s ideas. Soon Born was able to spread the news about the new theory outside Göttingen. On the way to spend his vacation in Switzerland, he delivered a lecture in Tübingen on 30 July 1925. Alfred Landé still remembered Born’s visit four decades later: ‘I first heard of matrix mechanics when Born was in Tübingen .... He told me something about it; that they [i.e., the Göttingen theoreticians] had a completely new approach to quantum mechanics, and everything [was] dominated by multiplication, [in which] *A* times *B* differs from *BA*. I did not understand a single word about it, and I don’t think that Born and the whole group in Göttingen “understood” much more than the mere formulas’ (Landé, AHQP Interview, 3 July 1962, p. 21). However, the mathematical methods of matrices enabled Born and Jordan to formulate the first consistent theory of quantum mechanics within less than two months.

The development of matrix calculus is a story of convergence from multiple mathematical streams. Here is a transcription of the provided page.

I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus

The concept of matrices and the methods of operating with these objects arose in mathematics from three sources. Perhaps the earliest was the renewed interest in conic sections and the subsequent classification of the latter in the language of algebra, which was basically initiated by the work of René Descartes in the first half of the seventeenth century.¹³ More than a century later Leonhard Euler systematically studied second degree equations in three variables *x*, *y*, *z*, i.e., equations of the form

\[
ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + dxy + exz + fyz + gx + hy + kz = 1, \qquad (9)
\]

with constant coefficients, *a*, *b*, *c*, *d*, *e*, *f*, *g*, *h*, and *k*, which describe surfaces in the three-dimensional space (Euler, 1748).¹⁴ He introduced the transformation from the coordinate system, given by the coordinates, *x*, *y*, *z*, to another system, (*x*′, *y*′, *z*′), through the rotation of the coordinate axes by the three (Euler) angles in such a way that the new coordinate axes coincide with the principal axes of the geometrical object under consideration (cone, cylinder, ellipsoid, hyperboloid, hyperbolic paraboloid, or parabolic cylinder). With this ‘principal-axes’ transformation, he then succeeded in classifying the geometrical objects in space described by the second-order equation (9).

The second development that led to matrices emerged from a purely algebraic consideration, i.e., the investigation of the simultaneous solution of systems of linear equations, which were later written as

\[
x_i = \sum a_{ik} y_k \qquad (i, k = 1, \ldots, n), \qquad (10)
\]

---

¹³Conic sections, such as ellipses and hyperbolae, were already studied in the ancient times, especially by the Greeks, but it was only after the Middle Ages that scientists again became interested in them. For example, Kepler’s recognition that the orbits of planets were ellipses demanded a rational explanation of the latter.

René Descartes was born on 31 March 1596 in La Haye, Touraine. He graduated as a lawyer twenty years later from the University of Poitiers and studied mathematics for a year in Paris in the circle of Father Marin Mersenne (the so-called ‘*Académie Mersenne*,’ a precursor of the *Académie des Sciences*). From 1617 he served in various armies for nine years; then he returned to Paris and learned how to construct optical instruments. In 1629 he moved to Holland, where he found a quiet atmosphere to live and work, until he was finally called to Stockholm (in 1649) to instruct Queen Christina of Sweden. Descartes died there soon afterwards of pneumonia on 11 February 1650.

The foundation of analytical geometry was contained in the appendix on geometry (‘*La Géométrie*’) in his famous book ‘*Discours de la Méthode*’ (1637). There he went beyond the results of the Greeks when he tried to construct, e.g., the curve *y*(*x*) describing an ellipse. Although Descartes’ approach was basically constructive, rather than analytic, he explicitly introduced algebraic equations to represent geometrical figures.

¹⁴Leonhard Euler, born on 15 April 1707 in Basle, studied under Johann Bernoulli at the University of Basle. He worked from 1727 to 1741 and from 1766 to his death on 18 September 1783 in St. Petersburg; in between, from 1741 to 1766, he worked at the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin. He was member of most of the prestigious scientific academies of the day. Euler published a vast number of papers on mathematical and physical problems (about 800 memoirs) and wrote more than ten books.

\(^{15}\)Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz was born on 1 July 1646 in Leipzig. He studied law, mathematics and philosophy at the Universities of Leipzig (1661–1663), Jena (1663–1666) and Altdorf, where he received his doctorate in law in 1666. He served the Archbishop and Elector of Mainz, Johann Philipp von Schönborn, and the Dukes of Braunschweig–Lüneburg. He died in Hanover on 14 November 1716.
Leibniz, who is sometimes referred to as the last universal scientist, worked in diplomacy, law, history, philosophy, mathematics and physics. Together with Newton, he invented the calculus and, besides trying to develop a universal symbolism for logic, he introduced much of the symbols and notation that were later used in mathematics. He wrote many books on philosophy, theology, mathematics, physics and history, as well as hundreds of articles and thousands of letters on scientific topics. Leibniz, a member of the important academies of sciences extant in his time, was instrumental in founding the Prussian Academy of Sciences in Berlin (1700); he also urged Peter the Great to found the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences.

Augustin Louis Cauchy was born on 21 August 1789 in Paris. He received his education at the *École Polytechnique* and served as instructor at the *Collège de France* and at *École Polytechnique* until 1830. Then, because of his adherence to the French monarchy, he left Paris and became professor of mathematical physics at the University of Turin. In 1837 he returned to Paris and to the *École Polytechnique*. He died in Sceaux, France, on 23 May 1857.
Cauchy wrote many books on mathematical and physical topics and over 500 articles. He is especially known for his development of rigorous methods in analysis and for his contributions to the theory of complex functions. In physics he dealt primarily with questions of optics.

I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus 15

remained to James Joseph Sylvester to develop fully the theory of determinants; he devoted fifty years of his scientific career to this subject, which was connected most closely with the origin of matrix theory.$^{17}$

Finally, the third root of matrix methods has to be traced to the efforts to generalize the concept of numbers. In an unpublished paper of 1831 Carl Friedrich Gauss was among the first to consider an extension of complex numbers, the most famous of which are the quaternions of William Rowan Hamilton (1844).$^{18}$ A quaternion, $q$, may be defined as an object of the form

$$q = a + b\hat{i} + c\hat{j} + d\hat{k}, \qquad (13)$$

where $a$ is the so-called 'scalar' and the rest is the 'vector' part, with $b$, $c$ and $d$ representing the Cartesian coordinates of a point in the three-dimensional space, and $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ are unit vectors. The algebraic operations with quaternions, such as the multiplication, exhibit properties which deviate somewhat from the analogous operations with real or complex numbers. Especially, the product of two quaternions, $q_1$ and $q_2$—obtained by observing the rules for the products of imaginary vectors, $\hat{i}^2 = \hat{j}^2 = \hat{k}^2 = -1$, and $\hat{i}\hat{j} = -\hat{j}\hat{i} = \hat{k}$, $\hat{i}\hat{k} = -\hat{k}\hat{i} = -\hat{j}$ and $\hat{j}\hat{k} = -\hat{k}\hat{j} = \hat{i}$—is associative but not commutative.

$^{17}$ James Joseph Sylvester was born on 3 September 1814 in London. After attending schools for Jewish boys in London and the University of London, he went in 1829 to the Royal Institution in Liverpool. Being an excellent student and having won several prizes for solving mathematical problems, he continued his education at St. John's College, Cambridge, from October 1831 to the end of 1833. Illness prevented him from taking the Tripos examination before January 1837, and he stood second on the list. Being Jewish, however, he was not allowed to take a degree or to compete for the Smith's Prize. (He obtained his degrees, B.A. and M.A., only in 1841 from Trinity College, Dublin.) Sylvester then became professor of natural philosophy in the University of London in 1837 and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, U.S.A., in 1841. He returned to England after two years, left his academic career for some time, and became engaged in actuarial work. He was called to the Bar in 1850, where he met and made friends with Arthur Cayley. From 1855 to 1870 Sylvester served as professor of mathematics at the Royal Academy in Woolwich, England, and in 1876 he began to lecture at the new Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore until he was called to the Savilian Chair of Geometry at Oxford University in 1883. He retired in 1894 and died on 15 March 1897 in Oxford.

Sylvester was elected Fellow of the Royal Society already in 1839 because of his work on the theory of optical crystals and the motion of rigid bodies. He contributed many papers to the theory of numbers, theory of equations, pure and analytic geometry, and algebra. He founded the theory of algebraic invariants. Besides his mathematical research, his educational and administrative activity was enormous. In the Woolwich time he edited the *Quarterly Journal of Pure and Applied Mathematics*; in Baltimore he founded the *American Journal of Mathematics*, thus initiating research in pure mathematics in the United States. He was a member of many associations and academies, including the London Mathematical Society (President, 1866–1869) and the *Académie des Sciences*, Paris (elected in 1863). He received numerous honours and prizes, including the Copley medal of the Royal Society in 1880. Sylvester also wrote poetry; he translated Horace and several German poets into English. His style is also reflected by the rich mathematical vocabulary which he created.

$^{18}$ William Rowan Hamilton (1805–1865) invented the quaternions in late 1843 and announced them at the meeting of the Royal Irish Academy. He rated this discovery very highly and wrote two books on this subject. Quaternions became a fashionable issue of debate later in the nineteenth century, without leading to important applications in mathematics and physics as Hamilton had hoped. However, quaternions stimulated the invention of other hypercomplex numbers, and also contributed to the development of vector and tensor methods.

16 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

Around the middle of the nineteenth century the above-mentioned concepts and methods had begun to merge towards a more unified calculus. For example, connections had been found between the problem of solving systems of linear algebraic equations and the problem of obtaining the standard expression for quadratic forms in three and more dimensions. For the latter purpose, Euler, when he discussed the reduction of quadratic forms in three variables, i.e., expressions of the type $\sum a_{ik} x_i x_k$ ($i, k = 1, 2, 3$), to their principal axes, already had used what was later called (by Euler himself) the 'characteristic equation.' This equation,

$$
(a_{11} - \lambda) [(a_{22} - \lambda)(a_{33} - \lambda) - a_{23}a_{32}] - a_{21} [a_{12}(a_{33} - \lambda) - a_{13}a_{32}] + a_{31} [a_{12}a_{23} - a_{13}(a_{22} - \lambda)] = 0, \quad (14)
$$

may be written as a determinantal equation involving a quadratic array with coefficients $(a_{ii} - \lambda)$ and $a_{ik}$ for $i \neq k$. The three roots of the third-order equation in the unknown $\lambda$ represent the lengths of the principal axes of the geometrical object associated with the quadratic form under investigation. Cauchy, in extending Euler's results to more than three dimensions, had shown that the characteristic equations, such as Eq. (14), remain the same whatever linear transformation is carried out with the coordinates $x_i$ (Cauchy, 1826). Again, Sylvester put this result into the framework of a general algebraic theory by developing the theory of 'invariants of quadratic forms,' i.e., of the expressions obtained from quadratic forms that are unaffected by linear transformations of the coordinates (Sylvester, 1851). He quickly realized, for instance, that $\det(a_{ik})$, the determinant of the coefficients, is such an invariant. The theory of invariants became a powerful tool in various branches of mathematics during the second half of the nineteenth century and, a little later, also in the theory of infinite matrices.

The name 'matrix' was coined by Sylvester, who denoted by it an array of numbers (not necessarily quadratic), from which the determinant could be formed (Sylvester, 1850). Although matrices had been implicitly present in mathematics ever since Leibniz had taken up the solution of systems of linear equations (Leibniz, 1693), and Cauchy had introduced the arrangement of their coefficients into arrays (Cauchy, 1815), it was Arthur Cayley who, beginning in 1855, developed matrix theory.$^{19}$

$^{19}$ Arthur Cayley was born on 16 August 1821 in Richmond, Surrey, the second son of Henry Cayley, an English merchant who was engaged in Russian trade at St. Petersburg, and his wife Maria Antonia Doughty. Cayley traced his father's family back to the Normans in the days of the Conquest, and even further to a noble family in Normandy (see Bell, 1937, Chapter 12). In 1829, after spending most of their time abroad, the family returned to England; young Arthur attended a private school at Blackheath and later, from his fourteenth year, King's College School in London, where he showed great talent in mathematics. At the age of seventeen he went up to Trinity College, Cambridge. There he distinguished himself as a mathematician and developed a passion for reading novels. He became Senior Wrangler in the Mathematical Tripos in 1842 and was placed first in the competition for the Smith's Prize; he was elected Fellow of Trinity College and Assistant Tutor for three years

# I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus

17

Arthur Cayley produced a vast mathematical output over a period of fifty-four years: 996 papers, which filled the thirteen volumes of *Collected Papers* (Cayley, 1889–1898). His early work already indicated the fields, which would interest him throughout his life: these included the geometry of plane curves, the geometry of *n*-dimensions, elliptic functions and the theory of invariants. His investigations on algebra had a particular impact. Algebra, an ancient field of mathematics, had been greatly revived in the eighteenth century. However, in 1833 George Peacock of Cambridge University put algebra on a new level by introducing the concept of a ‘symbolic algebra,’ which follows combination laws similar to the ones used in arithmetic (Peacock, 1834).²⁰ Peacock’s extension of algebra to objects other than ordinary numbers simplified the path to new concepts, such as the quaternions of Hamilton or the matrices of Cayley. Also the theory of invariants emerged as a field of algebra, and Cayley’s work on this subject attracted scholars in England (George Boole, George Salmon, Joseph Sylvester), Germany (Alfred Clebsch, Paul Gordan), France (Camille Jordan, Charles Hermite) and Italy (Francesco Brioschi). It then became connected with the ideas of Bernhard Riemann, whose work would eventually prove to be one of the cornerstones of a fundamental physical theory: the general relativity theory.

Cayley’s investigations on invariants cannot be separated from his other contributions to algebra, especially from those to matrix theory. His first paper on matrix theory, written in French and published in a German periodical (Cayley, 1855), already reflected the internationalism which would characterize the later development of this field. In this paper, Cayley introduced a shorthand

(1842–1845), an appointment which might have been renewed had he cared to take the holy orders, but Cayley did not. (Unlike his later friend Joseph Sylvester, who was not a practicing Jew but, being Jewish, was not even allowed to compete for the Smith’s Prize, Cayley was an orthodox Church of England Christian; yet he preferred not to become a parson to keep his job.) At the age of twenty-five Cayley left Cambridge and, being attracted by the study of law, entered Lincoln’s Inn to prepare himself for the Bar. Three years later, in 1849, he was called to the Bar and spent the following fourteen years in the routine of legal business. Though it meant a drudgery for him, it provided him an ample living and some spare time to devote himself to work in mathematics. At the Bar he also became acquainted with Sylvester who shared his interest in mathematics and classical literature. Their mathematical discussions in these years laid the foundations of the theory of algebraic invariants which would become fruitful in many fields of mathematics. In 1863 a new mathematical chair, the Sadlerian professorship, was established in the University of Cambridge, and Cayley, then forty-two, accepted it though it meant a cutback in his earnings. At the same time he married Susan Moline; they had a happy marriage, and had two children, a son and a daughter. His life in Cambridge was devoted to mathematical research and university administration, and he had a most successful career. Only once did he leave his university to spend, at Sylvester’s invitation, six months during 1881–1882 at Johns Hopkins University, where he lectured on Abelian functions. Cayley received numerous honours, including the Royal medal (1859) and the Copley medal (1882) of the Royal Society. He died on 26 January 1895 in Cambridge. (For further details, see the article on Arthur Cayley by J. D. North in the *Dictionary of Scientific Biography*, Vol. 3, 1971, pp. 162–170.)

²⁰George Peacock, born in Denton (England) on 9 April 1791, obtained his B.A. (1812) and M.A. (1816) from Cambridge University. He served as Tutor at Trinity College from 1823, and became Lowndean Professor of Astronomy and Geometry in 1836. He revived mathematical analysis in England and introduced Leibniz’ notation in calculus. He worked and wrote books on calculus, arithmetic and algebra. Peacock died in Ely on 8 November 1858.

The composed matrix appears when one solves connected systems of linear equations, in which the unknown variables $(x, y, z, \ldots)$ are given as linear expressions with coefficients $a, b, c, \ldots$, $a', b', c', \ldots$, $a'', b'', c'', \ldots$, of the variables $x', y', z', \ldots$, and the latter as linear expressions of the type of Eqs. \begin{vmatrix}
a & ,b & ,c & ,\ldots \\
a' & ,b' & ,c' & ,\ldots \\
a'' & ,b'' & ,c'' & ,\ldots \\
\vdots & & & \ddots
\end{vmatrix}\right]^{\wedge} (x, y, z, \ldots). \tag{16}
$$

I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus 19

The coefficients or values of the composed matrix were given by the matrix equation

$$\left| \begin{array}{cccc} \alpha & , \beta & , \gamma & , \dots \\ \alpha' & , \beta' & , \gamma' & , \dots \\ \alpha'' & , \beta'' & , \gamma'' & , \dots \\ & \vdots & & \end{array} \right| \left| \begin{array}{cccc} a & , b & , c & , \dots \\ a' & , b' & , c' & , \dots \\ a'' & , b'' & , c'' & , \dots \\ & \vdots & & \end{array} \right|$$

$$= \left| \begin{array}{ccccc} (\alpha & , \beta & , \gamma & , \dots )^{\wedge}(a, a', a'', \dots ), & (\alpha & , \beta & , \gamma & , \dots )^{\wedge}(b, b', b'', \dots ), \dots \\ (\alpha' & , \beta' & , \gamma' & , \dots )^{\wedge}(a, a', a'', \dots ), & (\alpha' & , \beta' & , \gamma' & , \dots )^{\wedge}(b, b', b'', \dots ), \dots \\ (\alpha'' & , \beta'' & , \gamma'' & , \dots )^{\wedge}(a, a', a'', \dots ), & (\alpha'' & , \beta'' & , \gamma'' & , \dots )^{\wedge}(b, b', b'', \dots ), \dots \\ \end{array} \right|$$

(16a)

where $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \dots )^{\wedge}(a, a', a'', \dots )$ denotes the sum $\alpha a + \beta a' + \gamma a'' + \dots$, etc. (Cayley, 1855, p. 284). Cayley noticed that the matrix notation could also be profitably applied in the theory of quadratic and higher-order functions.

Three years later Cayley presented a systematic treatment of matrices, in which he established the laws governing the operations with matrices in detail (Cayley, 1858). Working almost exclusively with quadratic matrices, i.e., matrices in which the number of rows equals the number of columns, he defined the ‘zero’ and ‘unit’ matrices, the former having only 0 as coefficients or elements, the latter having 1 as diagonal elements and 0 as nondiagonal elements. Cayley also showed that the operation of adding two matrices, which yields a matrix whose elements are the sums of the corresponding matrix elements (at the same position), satisfies the associate and commutative laws.$^{21}$ Cayley introduced two kinds of multiplication operations: a ‘scalar’ multiplication by a constant factor, which implies the multiplication of each matrix element by this factor; and the process of ‘compounding’ two matrices, which leads to the composed matrix on the right-hand side of Eq. (16a). Cayley found that the matrix product was associative but in general not ‘convertible,’ i.e., it was noncommutative. He called two matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ ‘convertible’ if they had identical products $\mathbf{AB}$ and $\mathbf{BA}$; he called them ‘skew-convertible’ if they satisfied $\mathbf{AB} = -\mathbf{BA}$. Then he discussed the repeated compounding of a matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and observed that this operation obeyed the relation

$$\mathbf{A}^{n+p} = \mathbf{A}^n\mathbf{A}^p \qquad (n, p \text{ integers}). \qquad (17)$$

He further defined the ‘inverse,’ $\mathbf{A}^{-1}$, of a matrix $\mathbf{A}$ whose determinant is

20 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

different from zero (evidently, the product $\mathbf{AA}^{-1}$ gives the unit matrix), and proposed a practical method of how to construct it. He also introduced the ‘*transpose*,’ $\mathbf{A}^{T}$, of a matrix, which is obtained from $\mathbf{A}$ by exchanging the rows and columns, i.e., by replacing each element $a_{ik}$ by $a_{ki}$. The transpose of a product of matrices is obtained by multiplying the transpose of the individual matrix factors in the reverse order.

With the results, contained in the memoirs of 1855 and 1858, Cayley not only founded matrix methods but also developed them almost fully. During the following decades the mathematicians applied these methods to new fields and problems. Two major trends arose: on the one hand, abstract algebraic structures were studied by employing matrix methods (predominantly by Cayley and Sylvester) and, on the other, matrix methods were successfully used in problems of geometry dealing with multidimensional spaces. Cayley himself opened up the field of applications by stating an important theorem: The determinant of the difference of a matrix $\mathbf{A}$ minus a diagonal matrix, whose elements are equal to det($\mathbf{A}$), will be equal to zero (Cayley, 1858). He proved this theorem for $2 \times 2$ and $3 \times 3$ matrices. In the first case, for example, he easily found that

$$
\begin{align*}
\det \begin{vmatrix}
a - \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}, & b \\
c, & d - \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}
\end{vmatrix}
& = (ad - bc) \det \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} - (a + d) \det \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} + \det \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix}^2 \\
& = \det \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{vmatrix}.
\end{align*}
$$

(18)

Equation (18) was the first equation involving matrices to be written down, and it says simply that the matrix is a root of its own characteristic equation.

Even before matrix theory was established, William Rowan Hamilton had proved a similar theorem for quaternions (Hamilton, 1853, p. 566). The close connection between many results in the theory of quaternions and matrix theory brought up the question, whether Hamilton’s hypernumbers invented in 1843 had inspired Cayley directly to introduce matrices. To an explicit inquiry of Peter Guthrie Tait, however, Cayley replied: ‘I certainly did not get the notion of a matrix in any way through quaternions; it was either directly from that of a determinant, or as a convenient mode of expression of the equation $x' = ax + by$, $y' = cx + dy$’ (Cayley to Tait, 1894; quoted in Knott, 1911, p. 164). The quaternions were indeed a special type of matrices, as Cayley had noticed rather early. Therefore, the operations with matrices and those with quaternions (and other kinds of hypernumbers) obeyed largely the same rules. But in founding matrix methods, which Sylvester called ‘a second birth of algebra, its *avatar* [incarnation] in a new and glorified form’ (Sylvester, 1884, p. 35), Cayley had in mind Leibniz’ general problem of treating systems of linear equations rather than Hamilton’s favourite mathematical objects, the quaternions.

coordinates. Camille Jordan²⁵ showed further that any quadratic matrix **A** might be brought by a similarity transformation (involving a matrix **P** and its inverse) into a canonical form (Jordan, 1870), i.e.,  

$$\mathbf{P A P}^{-1} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathrm{J}_1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\ 0 & \mathrm{J}_2 & 0 & \cdots \\ 0 & 0 & \mathrm{J}_3 & \cdots \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdots \end{vmatrix}. \tag{21}$$  

The \(\mathrm{J}_i\) denote quadratic matrices with \(l_i\) rows and columns, and have the form:  

$$\mathrm{J}_i = \begin{vmatrix} \lambda_i & 1 & 0 & & 0 \\ 0 & \lambda_i & 1 & & 0 \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & & \lambda_i \end{vmatrix}, \tag{21a}$$  

where \(\lambda_i\) are the \(l_i\)-fold roots of the characteristic equation of the original matrix **A**; this equation may be written as  

$$f(\lambda) = (\lambda - \lambda_1)^{l_1}(\lambda - \lambda_2)^{l_2}\cdots(\lambda - \lambda_k)^{l_k}. \tag{21b}$$  

Of course, the canonical form of a matrix, all roots of which are different, is a diagonal matrix. Thus, Jordan’s procedure proved to be identical, in special cases, with the reduction of bilinear forms to a sum of squares or with the transformation to principal axes.  

Only about twenty-five years after its inauguration by Cayley, matrix theory had reached a state of considerable perfection through the investigations of relatively few mathematicians. It was then treated as a fully developed subject in textbooks, such as Maxime Bôcher’s *Introduction to Higher Algebra* (1907) which,  

²⁵Camille Jordan was born in Lyon, France, on 5 January 1838. A brilliant student, he followed the usual career of French mathematicians from Cauchy to Poincaré: at seventeen he entered the *École Polytechnique* and was an engineer until 1885. He found ample time for mathematical research and wrote most of his 120 papers before he retired as an engineer. From 1873 until his retirement in 1912 he taught at the *École Polytechnique* and (from 1883) simultaneously at the *Collège de France*. He was elected a member of the Academy of Sciences in 1881. Jordan died in Paris on 20 January 1922.  

‘Jordan’s place in the tradition of French mathematics is exactly halfway between Hermite and Poincaré,’ writes Dieudonné. ‘Like them he was a “universal” mathematician who published papers in practically all branches of the mathematics of his time.’ Jordan took an active part in the movement which started modern analysis in the last decades of the nineteenth century. His most famous contribution to topology was to realize that the decomposition of a plane into regions by a simple closed curve was susceptible of mathematical proof and to imagine such a proof for the first time. Jordan was the first to embark on a systematic development of the theory of finite groups and of its applications in the directions opened by Galois. The most profound results obtained by Jordan in algebra were his ‘finiteness theorems.’ His last finiteness theorem was a powerful generalization of the results obtained earlier by Hermite in the theory of quadratic forms with integral coefficients. (See the article on Camille Jordan by J. Dieudonné in the *Dictionary of Scientific Biography*, Vol. 7, 1973, pp. 167–169.)

I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus

23

in turn, served as an authoritative reference book on matrix theory for many years to come. For example, it was cited as such in the relevant chapters of books by Courant and Hilbert (1924) and Erwin Madelung (1925). In the meanwhile, however, another important mathematical development had begun that led to a generalization of the concept of matrices, i.e., to matrices having an infinite number of rows and columns.

The earliest steps in this development go far back into the past. Already since the times of Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, one had considered besides finite systems of linear equations also infinite ones, the latter involving infinitely many coefficients, to obtain the solution of certain differential equations. However, all the systems of equations which the mathematicians had treated in the eighteenth century exhibited a characteristic feature: they could be solved by the method of recursion, i.e., step by step, each step involving only a finite number of equations for a finite number of unknowns. Hence these problems did not really demand the use of infinite matrices and determinants. The situation changed drastically when Joseph Fourier, in his *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* (1822) discussed the equation of heat conduction.²⁶ As is well known, Fourier solved the parabolic differential equation

$$
\frac{\partial^{2} T}{\partial x^{2}}=\kappa \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} \text {, }
$$

(22)

determining the space-time dependence of the temperature $T\left(=T(x, t)\right)$ in a linear rod of length $l$ (which, for convenience, may be normalized to $\pi$), having $\kappa$ as the coefficient of heat conduction, with the help of the following assumption. He represented $T$ by an infinite series, i.e.,

$$
T(x, t)=\sum_{v=1}^{\infty} b_{v} \exp \left(-\frac{v^{2}}{\kappa^{2}} t\right) \sin (v x),
$$

(23)

where $b_{v}$ are the harmonic coefficients. He substituted this series in Eq. (22), thus obtaining an infinite system of linear equations determining the $b_{v}$ ($v=1, 2, \ldots$). Fourier solved it in a bold manner, applying at times methods of questionable rigour, and finally found the result expressing each $b_{v}$ as

$$
b_{v}=\frac{2}{\pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} f(x) \sin (v x) d x,
$$

(23a)

where the function $f(x)$ is identical with $T(x, 0)$, the initial values of the temperature at the space points $x$. He was, thus, the first to deal successfully with

He joined the *École Normale* from its founding in 1795 and soon became professor of analysis at the *École Polytechnique*. He accompanied Napoleon to Egypt in 1798 and was appointed governor of Lower Egypt; after his return to France he was made prefect of the Department of Isère. From 1816 onwards he again settled in Paris and became member (1817) and Permanent Secretary (1822) of the Academy of Sciences. Fourier died in Paris on 16 May 1830.

a genuinely infinite system of equations. However, Fourier’s intuitive manner of handling mathematical methods was viewed with suspicion by his contemporaries, and the following generation of mathematicians tried different approaches to arrive at the same results. Only a century later was it possible to continue, what Fourier had started, with improved and extended methods. The so-called ‘harmonic analysis’ would then be developed, containing a clear formulation of Fourier’s ideas, and its relation to the algebraic methods of infinite matrices would also be recognized.

The factual beginning of the theory of infinite matrices can be traced to the theory of infinite determinants. The early approach to handle these objects was first to study finite sections before one passed over to an adequate infinite limit.$^{27}$ Nearly fifty years after Fourier, Th. Kötteritzsch, an otherwise not well-known mathematician, dealt with infinite systems of linear equations ($n = \infty$) of the type of Eqs. (10) (Kötteritzsch, 1870). He reminded himself of the fact that the solution of the finite system ($n$ finite) can be written as

$$y_k = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{A_{ik}}{A} x_i, \quad k = 1, 2, \dots, n, \tag{24}$$

which is known as Cramer’s rule.$^{28}$ In Eq. (24), $A_{ik}$ denotes the minor of the full determinant, $A$, from which the $i$th row and the $k$th column have been omitted, i.e.,

$$A_{ik} = \det \left| \begin{matrix} a_{11} \dots & a_{1k} \dots a_{1n} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ a_{i1} \dots & a_{ik} \dots a_{in} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ a_{n1} \dots & a_{nk} \dots a_{nn} \end{matrix} \right|. \tag{24a}$$

The addition of another linear equation,

$$x_{n+1} = \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} a_{n+1,k} y_k, \tag{25}$$

containing new variables, $x_{n+1}$ and $y_{n+1}$, to the original system of $n$ equations, Eqs. (10), does not change the formal structure of the result, expressed by Eqs. (24). The latter are then simply replaced by the equations

$$y_k = \sum_{i=1}^{n+1} \frac{A_{ik}}{A} x_i, \quad k = 1, 2, \dots, n+1, \tag{24'}$$

---

$^{28}$ Gabriel Cramer (1704–1752), mathematician and consultant in the fortification of his home-town of Geneva, worked on algebraic curves, on which he also wrote a book (Cramer, 1750). In the appendix to the third chapter of this book he gave the result, Eq. (24), for the cases of $n = 2, 3,$ etc. It was therefore called ‘Cramer’s rule,’ though some special cases of it had already been given by Leibniz and Cramer’s contemporaries.

# I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus 25

with the $A_{ik}$ now denoting the minors of the determinant, which is enlarged by including the coefficients $a_{n+1,k}$ and $a_{i,n+1}$ ($i,k = 1,2, \dots, n+1$). Therefore, in principle, the finite system can be replaced by an infinite system. Kötteritzsch concluded, in particular, that the solution for the variables, $y_k$ ($k = 1,2, \dots, \infty$), of such systems may be expressed by the infinite series

$$y_k = \frac{A_{1k}}{A}x_1 + \frac{A_{2k}}{A}x_2 + \dots, \quad k = 1,2, \dots, \infty, \tag{26}$$

which have the same structure as Eqs. (24), except that one sums on the right-hand side up to infinity and employs infinite determinants, i.e., determinants of infinite matrices and their minors. Remarkably enough for the time—after Cauchy, Riemann and Weierstrass had already established new standards of mathematical rigour—Kötteritzsch did not enter into any discussion of the conditions under which his solution (26) exists. He just tried to approximate the infinite systems in steps, i.e., by first solving the finite $n$th section of it, then the ($n+1$)st section, etc. A similar approach was proposed independently later on by Paul Appell (1885) and, stimulated by him, by Henri Poincaré (1885).

The above method of solving infinite systems of linear equations, the so-called ‘section method’ (‘*Abschnittsmethode*’), did not involve infinite determinants directly but only ratios of them. It remained to the American mathematician George William Hill to deal first directly with infinite determinants in his work on the influence of celestial bodies on the motion of the moon (Hill, 1877, 1886).$^{29}$ Hill investigated in particular the solution of the second-order linear

---
$^{29}$George William Hill, born in New York City on 3 March 1838, received his education at Rutgers University (A.B., 1859, M.A., 1862). In 1861 he joined the staff of scientists working in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on the *American Ephemeris and Nautical Alamanac*. At the *Almanac* office Hill was assigned the task of calculating the American ephemeris. Carolyn Eisele writes:

When Simon Newcomb became director of the *American Ephemeris* in 1877, he undertook the reconstruction of the theories and tables of lunar and planetary motion. Hill was induced to work on the theories of Jupiter and Saturn, known to be exceptionally difficult in the determination of their mutual perturbations. Because the *Nautical Almanac* office had meanwhile been transferred to Washington to be under the more immediate jurisdiction of the Navy Department, Hill resided there for a ten-year period beginning in 1882. His success with the Newcomb assignment represented one of the most important contributions to nineteenth-century mathematical astronomy. The calculation of the effects of the planets on the moon's motion was a particular case of the famous three-body problem, which dates back to Newton (1686).

Hill's "Researches in the Lunar Theory," published in the first issue of *American Journal of Mathematics* (1878), had, through its introduction of the periodic orbit, initiated a new approach to the study of three mutually attracting bodies. F. R. Moulton wrote in 1914 that no earlier work had approached it in practical application and no subsequent work had then surpassed it. The article became fundamental in the development of celestial mechanics.

The memoir of 1877 entitled *On the Part of the Motion of the Lunar Perigee Which Is a Function of the Mean Motions of the Sun and Moon* contains the incontrovertible evidence of Hill's mathematical genius. He was led to a differential equation, now called Hill's equation, that is equivalent to an infinite number of algebraic linear equations. Hill showed how to develop the infinite determinant corresponding to these equations. (*Dictionary of Scientific Biography*, Vol. VI, 1972, p. 399)

G. W. Hill was honoured in his lifetime by the bestowal of advanced degrees and medals and by honorary memberships in the most prestigious professional scientific societies throughout the world: Member, U.S. National Academy of Sciences (1874); President, American Mathematical Society (1894–1896); Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society for his researches on lunar theory (1887); Foreign Member of the Royal Society, the Paris Academy, and the Belgian Academy. He died in West Nyack, New York, on 16 April 1914.

differential equation

$$
-\frac{d^2w}{d\tau^2} = \theta w \tag{27}
$$

for the position coordinate \(w\) (the perigee of the moon) as a function of the time coordinate \(\tau\). The factor \(\theta\) on the right-hand side of Eq. (27) takes into account the action of all (i.e., infinitely many) celestial bodies on the moon, and it is therefore given by an infinite sum

$$
\theta = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{+\infty} \theta_k \zeta^{2k}, \qquad k = 1, 2, \ldots, \infty, \tag{27a}
$$

where \(\zeta = \exp(\tau i)\) and \(\theta_k = \theta_{-k}\). Hill now proposed that the solution for the position coordinate takes the form

$$
w = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} b_k \zeta^{c+2k}, \tag{28}
$$

with an unknown coefficient \(c\). By substituting the right-hand side of Eq. (28) for \(w\) in Eq. (27) and also replacing \(\theta\) by the infinite sum, due to Eq. (27a), he obtained an infinite system of equations for the infinitely many coefficients \(b_k\), i.e.,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dots + [-2]b_{-2} - \theta_1 b_{-1} - \theta_2 b_0 - \theta_3 b_1 - \theta_4 b_2 - \dots &= 0, \\
\dots - \theta_1 b_{-2} + [-1]b_{-1} - \theta_1 b_0 - \theta_2 b_1 - \theta_3 b_2 - \dots &= 0, \\
\dots - \theta_2 b_{-2} - \theta_1 b_{-1} + [0]b_0 - \theta_1 b_1 - \theta_2 b_2 - \dots &= 0, \\
\dots - \theta_3 b_{-2} - \theta_2 b_{-1} - \theta_1 b_0 + [1]b_1 - \theta_1 b_2 - \dots &= 0, \\
\dots - \theta_4 b_{-2} - \theta_3 b_{-1} - \theta_2 b_0 - \theta_1 b_1 + [2]b_2 - \dots &= 0, \\
\end{aligned}
$$

with

$$
[k] = (c + 2k)^2 - \theta_0, \qquad k = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots. \tag{29}
$$

The matrix of the coefficients of the system, Eqs. (29), is symmetric. To solve this system, Hill eliminated all \(b\)’s except \(b_0\) and constructed an inhomogeneous system. For the latter to have a solution, its determinant must be zero; hence there follows an equation which determines the value of the constant \(c\) in Eq. (28). Finally Hill worked out the solution for the infinitely many ratios \(b_k/b_0\) and demonstrated that the motion of the moon’s perigee was indeed periodic.

Hill’s procedure, like Fourier’s, for solving infinite systems of equations, was again very bold and not overly rigorous according to the standards of his time, although he tried to justify it by checking the convergence of the infinite determinant. In particular, he argued: ‘All those determinants must be regarded as having a central constituent; when in computing in succession the deter-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0032 -->

# I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus 27

minants formed from the $3^2$, $5^2$, $7^2$, etc., constituents symmetrically situated with respect to the central constituent, we approach, without limit a determinate magnitude, the determinant may be called convergent, and the determinate magnitude is its value’ (Hill, 1886, p. 26). A similar statement had already been made earlier by Kötteritzsch, but Hill surpassed his predecessor by giving a mathematical condition. ‘In the present case,’ he said, ‘there can be scarcely a doubt that as long as $\sum \theta_k \zeta^{2k}$ is a legitimate expansion of $\theta$, the determinant . . . must be regarded as convergent’ (Hill, 1886, p. 26).

Hill’s argument for the convergence of the infinite determinant was received with suspicion by the mathematicians, except by Henri Poincaré, who became interested in infinite systems of linear equations a second time because of Hill’s work.$^{30}$ Poincaré immediately sought to put Hill’s reasoning on a safer mathematical ground (Poincaré, 1886). To that end he considered the special type of matrices, $(a_{ik})$, whose diagonal elements, $a_{ii}$ ($i = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$), are unity. Then he took the determinant, $\Delta_n$, of finite matrices, consisting of $(n \times n)$ elements, symmetric with respect to the diagonal of the infinite matrix, and calculated the infinite determinant $\Delta$ from a limiting process, i.e., as

$$\Delta = \lim_{n \to \infty} \Delta_n. \tag{30}$$

Poincaré proved that the limit (30) existed, provided the sum of the absolute values of the matrix elements, $|a_{ik}|$, with $i \neq k$, was finite. Finally he concluded that the convergence of the right-hand side of Eq. (30) was not altered if one row of the infinite matrix was replaced by a bounded sequence $x_j$, $j = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$ . These results served to establish an essential part of Hill’s intuitive procedure on firm mathematical grounds.

Hill and Poincaré had, without doubt, carried forward the notion of infinite matrices, although they had only discussed the determinants of the latter. The same is true of some of the next steps in the development. Gösta Mittag-Leffler, the Swedish mathematician, who, by reprinting Hill’s memoir of 1877 in his journal, the *Acta Mathematica* (Hill, 1886), had directed Poincaré’s attention to it, now got his student Helge von Koch interested in infinite systems of linear equations and their applications to various mathematical problems (Koch, 1892).$^{31}$ Von Koch first treated the so-called ‘normal’ determinants, i.e., determi-

***

$^{30}$In introducing a reprint of Hill’s work, Poincaré noted: ‘The solution adopted by Mr. Hill is as original as it is bold . . . Did one have the right to set the determinant of these equations equal to zero? Mr. Hill ventured to do so and it was a very daring thing to do; until then an infinite number of linear equations had never been considered; determinants of infinite order had never been studied; no one even knew how to define them, and it was not certain that it was possible to give a precise meaning to this notion’ (Poincaré, in Hill, 1905, p. xiii).

It is surprising that Poincaré did not refer to the occurrence of infinite systems of linear equations in Fourier’s work on heat conduction. He did, however, know about Kötteritzsch’s paper and stated: ‘But his paper was hardly known in the scientific world and in any case was not known to Mr. Hill’ (Poincaré, in Hill, 1905, p. xiii).

nants having the form

$$A = \det \begin{vmatrix}
1 + a_{11}, & a_{12}, & a_{13}, & \dots \\
a_{21}, & 1 + a_{22}, & a_{23}, & \dots \\
a_{31}, & a_{32}, & 1 + a_{33}, & \dots \\
& \vdots & &
\end{vmatrix}, \tag{31}$$

with the $a_{ik}$ satisfying the condition

$$\sum_{i,k=1}^{+\infty} |a_{ik}| < \infty. \tag{31a}$$

These determinants were slightly more general than Poincaré's (in whose case, $a_{ii} = 0$). He also went beyond Poincaré by studying, besides the determinants, certain subdeterminants obtained from the former by omitting a finite number of rows and columns. Since these subdeterminants or (higher) minors were again normal determinants, von Koch could treat both inhomogeneous systems of linear equations, e.g.,

$$y_i + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_{ik} y_k = x_i \qquad \text{with } |x_i| < \infty, \tag{32}$$

as well as homogeneous systems (with $x_i = 0$), which, in general, have solutions only if the determinant, $A$, equals zero—in which case a (higher) minor of $A$ will be different from zero.

Von Koch's early interest in infinite systems of linear equations was connected with the search for solutions of the Fuchs differential equation. He found that solutions of this equation existed under certain severely restrictive conditions.$^{32}$ In order to remove them he delved deeper into the theory of infinite determinants and proved the following theorem: For the convergence of $A$, an infinite determinant given by Eq. (31), it is sufficient that the coefficients satisfy the conditions

$$\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} (1 + a_{ii}) < \infty \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} |a_{ik}| < \infty, \tag{33}$$

$^{32}$The Fuchs differential equation reads:

$$\frac{d^n y}{dx^n} + P_2(x) \frac{d^{n-1} y}{dx^{n-1}} + \dots + P_n(x) y = 0,$$

where each coefficient, $P_r(x)$, $r = 2, \dots, n$, is expressed as a Laurent series in $x$, i.e., as $\sum_{\lambda=-\infty}^{+\infty} a_{r\lambda} x^{\lambda}$ (valid in an anulus in the complex plane around $x = 0$). The solution, $y$, can again be expanded in a Laurent series, and the substitution of the latter in the differential equation gives rise to a system of linear equations for the coefficients of the Laurent series for $y$.

I.2  The Development of Matrix Calculus                                  29

where $|a_{ik}|$ is the absolute value of the coefficient $a_{ik}$ $(i \neq k)$. Moreover, a convergent infinite determinant of the type (31) may be expanded into subdeterminants (or minors) in exactly the same manner as a finite determinant—that is, the determinant is essentially the sum of all possible subdeterminants. From the latter result it became evident that in the case of an infinite matrix, whose determinant assumes a finite value, the origin (or centre) could be chosen arbitrarily. Finally, von Koch concerned himself with another special type of determinants, the so-called ‘uniformly convergent’ determinants, which were again of the form (31), with the coefficients $a_{ik}$ satisfying the conditions
$$ \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} |a_{ii}| < \infty \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{i,k=1}^{\infty} |a_{ik}|^2 < \infty, \quad i \neq k. \qquad (34) $$
He showed that these determinants assumed finite values and drew certain conclusions for the systems of linear equations having such determinants.$^{33}$

On the whole, von Koch’s work remained rather formal, and he did not consider applications of infinite determinants to mathematical problems other than the solution of the Fuchs differential equation. This task was performed by Erik Ivar Fredholm, another student of Mittag-Leffler’s; he employed infinite matrices and determinants in a new powerful approach to the theory of linear integral equations.$^{34}$ Stimulated by the earlier work of Poincaré (1894, 1895), Fredholm began by attempting to solve the integral equation for the unknown function $\phi(x)$,
$$ \phi(x) + \int_a^b K(x, y) \phi(y) dy = f(x), \qquad a \le x \le b, \qquad (35) $$
where $f(x)$ and the kernel $K(x, y)$ are given functions of the variables (Fredholm, 1900, 1903). He divided the interval of integration into $n$ equal parts at the points
$$ x_1 = a + \delta, \qquad x_2 = a + 2\delta, \ldots, \qquad x_{n-1} = a + (n-1)\delta, $$
$$ x_n = a + n\delta = b \qquad (36) $$
and denoted the corresponding values of the functions $\phi(x)$, $f(x)$ and $\delta \cdot K(x, y)$ at these points by $\phi_i$, $f_i$ and $K_{ij}$. Then he showed that the integral equation (35) was equivalent to a system of $n$ linear equations for the unknown variables,

***

He studied at the Stockholm Polytechnic (1885–1886), the University of Uppsala (1886–1888), and the University of Stockholm (1888–1893). He received his doctorate from Uppsala in 1898 and became a professor of mathematics and physics at the university of Stockholm in 1906. He died on 17 August 1927 in Mörby, Sweden.

Fredholm is known for his work on functional equations, especially integral equations, whose modern theory he inaugurated. He was a member of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences and a corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences, Paris.

$\phi_1, \dots, \phi_n$, in the limit of arbitrarily large $n$. The latter system could be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1 + K_{11})\phi_1 + \qquad K_{12}\phi_2 + \dots + \qquad K_{1n}\phi_n &= f_1, \\
K_{21}\phi_1 + (1 + K_{22})\phi_2 + \dots + \qquad K_{2n}\phi_n &= f_2, \\
\vdots & \\
K_{n1}\phi_1 + \qquad K_{n2}\phi_2 + \dots + (1 + K_{nn})\phi_n &= f_n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{37}
$$

Thus, Fredholm recognized that the theory of infinite systems of linear equations could be used to solve the integral equation (35), provided $A$, the determinant of the system (37), and all its subdeterminants, assumed finite values in the limit of infinite $n$. In particular, he was able to employ the generalization of Cramer's rule, Eq. (24), to infinite systems and to obtain the formal solution $\phi(x)$ as

$$
\phi(x) = f(x) - \int_a^b \frac{A \binom{x}{y}}{A} f(y) dy,
\tag{38}
$$

where $A \binom{x}{y}$ corresponds to the minor of the determinant $A$ (in which the $i$th row and the $j$th column have been dropped).

Fredholm's work on the theory of integral equations not only opened the field of the most important applications of infinite determinants, it initiated an even more important line of development in Göttingen, where Hilbert became interested in this subject.$^{35}$ As it happened to any other field which attracted Hilbert's attention, the theory of integral equations was generalized, fully developed and applied to new problems by him. During the first decade of the twentieth century this subject, especially the theory of infinite bilinear forms into which Hilbert turned the problem, moved into the centre of mathematical interest in Göttingen. Hilbert himself devoted six long memoirs to the theory of integral equations (Hilbert, 1904a, b; 1905; 1906a, b; 1910) and assembled them in a book (Hilbert, 1912c); he also supervised numerous doctoral theses of gifted students in this field. In his fourth communication (Hilbert, 1906a), he established the connection between linear integral equations and the theory of bilinear forms, giving Fredholm's earlier treatment a new direction.

Hilbert's main idea was to make use of the combined algebraic–geometric concepts, which had come into use since Euler's transformation of ellipsoids to principal axes. Hence he worked with quadratic forms, bilinear forms and linear forms of variables, extending the previous results right away to the case of infinitely many variables $x_p$, $y_q$ ($p, q = 1, 2, \dots, \infty$). For these forms he introduced a convenient notation borrowed from the theory of $n$-dimensional spaces, like the scalar product of two linear objects, $(x, y)$, which is defined as the sum

32 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

for any sequences, $x_1^{(\nu)}, x_2^{(\nu)}, \dots$ and $y_1^{(\nu)}, y_2^{(\nu)}, \dots$ ($\nu = 1, 2, \dots$)—that converge quadratically towards the values $x_1, x_2, \dots$ and $y_1, y_2, \dots$—turns out to be completely continuous. For example, a bilinear form $A(x, y)$, whose coefficients $(a_{pq})$ are square summable—i.e., $\sum_{p,q} a_{pq}^2$ exists—is always completely continuous (Hilbert, 1906a, p. 203, Theorem VI).

In his theory of infinite bilinear forms Hilbert tried to generalize the most important results already known from the theory of finite matrices, thereby pioneering the methods of infinite matrices. He particularly concerned himself with the problem of transforming quadratic forms, i.e., the special bilinear forms, $A(x, x)$, to principal axes. He showed that such a form can always be reduced to a sum of terms, $\alpha_1^2 x_1^2 + \alpha_2^2 x_2^2 + \dots$, plus an integral. Hilbert called the $\alpha$'s the 'reciprocal eigenvalues' (nowadays they are defined as the eigenvalues themselves) of the quadratic form; all of them constitute the 'discrete spectrum' of the latter. On the other hand, the path of the integral may be associated with the 'continuous spectrum' of $A(x, x)$ (Hilbert, 1906a, p. 198, Theorem III). He further proved that a completely continuous quadratic form possesses only a discrete spectrum (Hilbert, 1906a, p. 205, Theorem VII).

Hilbert confined himself to establishing the fundamental concepts of the theory of infinite matrices and left the development of details to his collaborators, especially to Ernst Hellinger and Otto Toeplitz.$^{37,38}$ In a series of papers they translated Cayley's familiar operations on finite matrices into the new theory (Hellinger and Toeplitz, 1906, 1910). They noticed, in particular, that sums and differences of infinite matrices could be carried out as in the finite case and that Hilbert's procedure of folding infinite bilinear forms was equivalent to matrix multiplication, the latter being associative but not commutative. Further,

$^{37}$Ernst Hellinger, born on 30 September 1883 in Striegau, Silesia, grew up in Breslau and studied at the Universities of Heidelberg, Breslau and Göttingen. In 1907 he received his doctorate with a thesis entitled 'Über die Orthogonalinvarianten quadratischer Formen von unendlich vielen Variablen' ('On the Orthogonal Invariants of Quadratic Forms of Infinitely-Many Variables'), which was supervised by Hilbert. From 1907 to 1909 Hellinger served as an assistant in Göttingen, and from 1909 to 1914 as *Privatdozent* at the University of Marburg. Then he became a professor of mathematics at the newly founded University of Frankfurt. Being Jewish, he was forced to retire from this position in 1936, and at the end of 1938 he was held for a short time in a concentration camp. Upon his release he managed to go to the United States. He taught at Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois, first as lecturer and later as full professor. In 1949 he took a position at the Illinois Institute of Technology, but fell ill soon afterwards and died on 28 March 1950 in Chicago.

Hellinger worked mainly on the theory of quadratic forms and infinite matrices. He also wrote, together with Otto Toeplitz, the review article on integral equations and systems of linear equations for the *Encyklopädie der mathematischen Wissenschaften* (Hellinger and Toeplitz, 1927). In later years he also became interested in certain topics of the history of mathematics.

$^{38}$Otto Toeplitz, born on 1 August 1881 in Breslau, studied mathematics in Breslau and Berlin and became *Privatdozent* at the University of Göttingen in 1907. Later he became a professor of mathematics at the Universities of Kiel (1920–1928) and Bonn (from 1928) until he was dismissed in 1935 because of the Nazi racial laws. In 1939 he went to Palestine as scientific advisor to the administration of Hebrew University, but died soon afterwards on 15 February 1940.

Most of Toeplitz' papers dealt with quadratic forms of infinitely many variables. Later, he went more and more into the history of mathematics and was chiefly concerned with the mathematical ideas in Plato's work.
