I.2 The Development of Matrix Calculus &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 33

they were able to define the inverse of an infinite matrix and to prove that many theorems that were valid for finite matrices were also valid in the case of infinite matrices.$^{39}$ Erhard Schmidt, another disciple of Hilbert's, proceeded in a different direction.$^{40}$ He started to reverse the trend towards algebrization of mathematics, which, since Descartes, had led to such spectacular success. From his work emerged the powerful concept of 'Hilbert space,' which is built up from normed sequences

$$z = \{z_p\} \quad \text{with } \|z\|^2 = \sum_{p=1}^\infty z_p \bar{z}_p < \infty, \quad (44)$$

where the double bars, $\|z\|$, denote the norm of the vector $z$ with complex components $z_p$, and $\bar{z}_p$ denotes the complex conjugate to $z_p$ (Schmidt, 1908).$^{41}$ The geometric point of view was already present in Hilbert's fourth communication on integral equations (Hilbert, 1906a), but Schmidt extended it considerably. It is interesting to note, however, that Schmidt sought to avoid the geometrical language altogether; e.g., he spoke of 'functions with integer index' rather than of points or vectors. In spite of this, the translation of his concepts into the modern language of Hilbert spaces is obvious. Any infinite sequence, $\{z_p\}$, can be regarded as a vector in an infinite-dimensional space; it can be normalized to unity by dividing each component $z_p$ by the norm, $\|z\|$. Two such vectors, $z$ and $w$, may be linearly dependent or not. A particular case of independent vectors is that of orthogonal ones, i.e., vectors $z$ and $w$, for which the expression $\sum z_p \bar{w}_p$ (in geometrical language, the scalar product) is zero. From any set of $n$ independent vectors one may construct $n$ orthogonal unit vectors with the help of the so-called 'Schmidt orthogonalization procedure' (Schmidt, 1908). The total Hilbert space is finally spanned by a complete set of infinitely many unit vectors.
The methods which Schmidt introduced, and their subsequent geometrization, proved to be very helpful in constructing the solutions of infinite systems of linear equations involving real or complex variables. They, thus, also contributed to the theory of infinite matrices. In 1910 Hellinger and Toeplitz presented what they called an 'axiomatic' treatment of the calculus of infinite matrices; that is, they expressed the theory of the latter in a general form, regardless of its specific application to integral equations or algebraic problems (Hellinger and Toeplitz,

34 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

1910). The mathematical theory of infinite matrices had thus been perfected by relatively few people in less than twenty-five years since Poincaré’s discovery of Hill’s work on the moon’s perigee in 1886. Poincaré had stimulated Fredholm’s investigations on integral equations, and these had brought Hilbert to the scene. Hilbert and his students had worked out the theory in a way that not much seemed to have remained to be done. When in April 1909 Henri Poincaré was invited to deliver the Wolfskehl lectures at the University of Göttingen and announced his intention to devote a part of them to integral equations, the local mathematicians were very surprised that somebody could still say anything new on this subject in Göttingen. Poincaré did, and by his lectures (Poincaré, 1910) he closed a development in which he and his host David Hilbert had played a leading role. In Poincaré’s audience was Max Born, who would profit most from an application of the theory of integral equations, especially in its algebraic version, to problems of theoretical physics.

### I.3 Early Applications of Matrix Methods in Physics

Matrix methods had proved to be very useful in a variety of mathematical investigations: systems of linear equations, linear differential and integral equations, etc. But unlike other mathematical tools invented in the nineteenth century, such as quaternions and vectors, they did not seem to arouse the interest of physicists—notwithstanding Peter Guthrie Tait’s prophecy that ‘Cayley is forging the weapons for future generations of physicists’ (Tait, quoted in Knott, 1911, p. 166). One wonders why this was so; why, for instance, such special objects as the quaternions made their way into the physical literature, but not the more general matrices?^42 After all, since the times of Joseph Louis Lagrange, quadratic forms and their determinants had played some role in mechanics—as, for instance, in the so-called ‘secular’ equation, whose roots serve to describe the slow periodic motions of, say, a system of several celestial bodies. However, there occurred no physical problem in the nineteenth century, in which one sought to make use of the specific properties of matrices, although in retrospect one might think of the possibility of applying them in the description of symmetry properties of crystals. When, towards the end of the nineteenth century, physicists

^42 Hamilton applied his quaternions, for instance, to lunar theory and to light propagation in biaxial crystals. James Clerk Maxwell, in his *Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism* (1873), also referred to quaternions. And Peter Guthrie Tait (1831–1901), the influential British mathematician and physicist, tried to persuade his contemporaries to make use of them. Interestingly enough, however, he did not even succeed with his friend William Thomson (Lord Kelvin), who remarked later:

> We had a thirty-eight year war over quaternions. He [i.e., Tait] had been captured by the originality and extraordinary beauty of Hamilton’s genius in this respect, and had accepted I believe definitely from Hamilton to take charge of quaternions after his death, which he had most loyally executed. Times without number I offered to let quaternions into Thomson and Tait [*Treatise on Natural Philosophy* (1867)] if he could only show that in any case our work could be helped by their use. You will see that from the beginning to the end they were never introduced. (Lord Kelvin to G. Chrystall, 1910; quoted in Knott, 1911, p. 185)

I.3 Early Applications of Matrix Methods in Physics 35

started to pay attention to the transformations of coordinate systems in space and time, Cayley's matrices seemed to offer themselves as *the* tool for a proper mathematical formulation. Still one had to wait much longer until Hermann Minkowski in Göttingen made the first application of finite matrices in physics, and this too only after his friend Hilbert had been interested for several years in developing the methods of infinite matrices.

In his great memoir on the electrodynamics of moving bodies, Minkowski introduced matrix notation and formulated the fundamental equations of electrodynamics in matrix language (Minkowski, 1908, Section 11). He restricted himself to $4 \times 4$ matrices, with the help of which he could express the linear transformations of the four space-time coordinates, $x_1$ ($= x$), $x_2$ ($= y$), $x_3$ ($= z$) and $x_4$ ($= ict$). A linear transformation, $x_h \rightarrow x'_k$, given by the equations

$$x_h = \sum_{k=1}^{4} a_{hk}x'_k, \quad h = 1, 2, 3, 4, \qquad (45)$$

which satisfies the condition

$$x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 + x_4^2 = x_1'^2 + x_2'^2 + x_3'^2 + x_4'^2, \qquad (46)$$

Minkowski identified with a Lorentz transformation. He discovered that in this case the matrix of the coefficients, $\mathbf{A} = (a_{hk})$, obeys the equation

$$\mathbf{A}^T\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{1}, \qquad (47)$$

where $\mathbf{A}^T$ is the transpose of the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{1}$ denotes the unit $4 \times 4$ matrix. In the case of a Lorentz transformation, in particular, the determinant of the matrix $\mathbf{A}$ assumes the value 1. The coefficients $a_{14}, a_{24}, a_{34}, a_{41}, a_{42}$, and $a_{43}$ are purely imaginary and $a_{44}$ assumes a positive value.

Minkowski also formed a $4 \times 4$ matrix from the vector components of the electric and magnetic fields, i.e., $\mathbf{E} = (E_x, E_y, E_z)$ and $\mathbf{H} = (H_x, H_y, H_z)$, namely, the skew-symmetric ('alterniernde') matrix $\mathfrak{f}$,

$$\mathfrak{f} = \begin{vmatrix} 0, & H_z, & -H_y, & -iE_x \\ -H_z, & 0, & H_x, & -iE_y \\ H_y, & -H_x, & 0, & -iE_z \\ iE_x, & iE_y, & iE_z, & 0 \end{vmatrix}, \qquad (48)$$

and showed that under a Lorentz transformation, described by the matrix $\mathbf{A}$, it passes over into $\mathfrak{f}'$, with

$$\mathfrak{f}' = \mathbf{A}^T \mathfrak{f} \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathfrak{f} \mathbf{A}. \qquad (49)$$

He further introduced the nonquadratic $1 \times 4$ matrix of differential operators,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0041 -->

36 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

$|\partial/\partial x_1, \partial/\partial x_2, \partial/\partial x_3, \partial/\partial x_4|$, calling it 'the differential operator "lor",' and rewrote Maxwell's equations for the current, $\mathbf{j} = (j_x, j_y, j_z)$, and the charge density $\rho$ as

$$\mathbf{lor\, f} = -\mathbf{s}, \tag{50}$$

with $\mathbf{s}$ being the $1 \times 4$ matrix,

$$\mathbf{s} = |j_x, j_y, j_z, i\rho|. \tag{50a}$$

(In modern notation, $\mathbf{s}$ is replaced by the four-vector $j_\mu$, $\mu = 1, 2, 3, 4$.) With the help of matrix methods Minkowski was able to apply the formal tools of the algebraic theory of invariants, in which he was a master, to the problems of special relativity theory, thereby deriving the fundamental equations of relativistic mechanics and electrodynamics in a compact and elegant manner.

Minkowski's plea for the use of matrix methods in relativity theory was not accepted in general by people afterwards. Even Arnold Sommerfeld, who was very close in spirit to Minkowski, moved away from these methods in his two papers on relativity theory published in 1910 (Sommerfeld, 1910b, c).$^{43}$ Thus, he pointed out in the very beginning of the first paper: 'I have put special emphasis on formulating the definitions and transformations of vectors as much geometrically as possible. The conceptions and calculations necessary for this purpose, which also provide a complete substitute for the matrix calculus used by Minkowski, are (if one admits imaginary coordinates) immediate generalizations of the conventional three-dimensional vector methods' (Sommerfeld, 1910b, p. 749). In particular, Sommerfeld replaced the skew-symmetric matrix $\mathbf{f}$, defined in Eq. (48), by the concept of a 'six-vector,' which he interpreted geometrically as a rotation in four-dimensional space. And in all cases he sought to establish a close connection between the three-dimensional vector methods and Minkowski's form of relativity theory, thereby eliminating the use of matrix methods completely. Sommerfeld's procedure was followed by later authors, for example, by Max von Laue in his book *Das Relativitätsprinzip* (von Laue, 1911). Among the few persons who occasionally made use of matrices in their papers was Max Born, Minkowski's last collaborator. After Minkowski's death, he tried to continue the latter's work on relativity theory. In particular, he employed matrices in his research on the theory of the rigid electron (Born, 1909b)$^{44}$; so did Gustav Mie in

I.3 Early Applications of Matrix Methods in Physics
37

his memoirs on the foundation of a theory of matter, in which he sought to unify the gravitational and electromagnetic fields (Mie, 1912a, c). Both Born and Mie referred to Minkowski, but they did not use matrix methods beyond what Minkowski had already invoked in his pioneering work of 1908.$^{45}$

To be sure, nobody in Hilbert’s mathematical circle—to which Born belonged—was afraid of applying matrix methods whenever they were needed or seemed to be adequate in the problem under investigation. For example, Ludwig Föppl studied the stability of an atom consisting of $n$ electrons for his doctoral thesis under Hilbert (Föppl, 1912).$^{46}$ In the course of this work he had to solve the following determinantal equation for the unknown quantity $\tilde{D}$:

$$ \det \begin{vmatrix} \tilde{D} & D_1 & D_2 & D_3 & & D_{n-1} \\ D_{n-1} & \tilde{D} & D_1 & D_2 & & D_{n-2} \\ D_{n-2} & D_{n-1} & \tilde{D} & D_1 & & D_{n-3} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ D_1 & D_2 & D_3 & D_4 & & \tilde{D} \end{vmatrix} = 0, \qquad (51) $$

with the $D$’s being given coefficients. Föppl’s problem may be considered as the finite version of Hill’s problem. The latter had treated, as we have mentioned in the previous section, the effect of an *infinite* number of celestial bodies on the motion of the moon (Hill, 1877), while Föppl was interested in the influence of a *finite* number of electrons on each other. As a result, the same type of determinants occurred in both problems.$^{47}$ The special determinant (*Zirkulanten*) in Eq. (51), in which each subsequent row follows the preceding one by shifting the coefficients to the right, may be written as a product of simple factors, $F(\alpha_1)$, $F(\alpha_2), \dots, F(\alpha_n)$. Thus, Eq. (51) assumes the simple form

$$ F(\alpha_1)F(\alpha_2) \cdots F(\alpha_n) = 0, \qquad (52) $$

where the factors $F(\alpha_i)$ are defined as the polynomials in $\alpha_i$,

$$ F(\alpha_i) = \tilde{D} + D_1\alpha_i + D_2\alpha_i^2 + \dots + D_{n-1}\alpha_i^{n-1}, \qquad (52a) $$

$^{45}$This also holds for a later work, in which Born discussed the energy-momentum tensor in Mie’s theory of matter (Born, 1914a).

In 1922 he moved to Munich to succeed his father, August Föppl, in the chair of technical mechanics at the Technical University. He retired from the latter position in 1954, and died in Munich on 23 May 1976.

(51) and the determinant of the system of inhomogeneous equations for the unknowns $b_1/b_0$, $b_2/b_0$, etc., which is obtained by dividing each of Hill’s Eqs. (29) by $b_0$. Evidently, this system possesses a nontrivial solution only if the determinant of its coefficients has the value zero. Hence an equation similar in structure to Eq. (51) has, in Hill’s theory of the moon, infinitely many coefficients.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0043 -->

38 &emsp; Chapter I &emsp; The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

and the $\alpha_i$ ($i = 1, 2, \dots, n$) are the roots of the equation

$$x^n - 1 = 0. \qquad (52\text{b})$$

Ludwig Föppl, in investigating the stability of atoms, regarded the atom as a mechanical system consisting of $n$ electrons; hence he had to consider the action of $n - 1$ electrons on one electron. George Hill, on the other hand, had taken into account the action of infinitely many bodies on the moon. The actual physical situation lies between these extremes. Within an atom, as on the moon, only a finite (though large) number of bodies exert sensible forces. The problems of Föppl and Hill are even related more closely if one reminds oneself of the fact that every atom within matter is always surrounded by many other atoms and, depending upon the physical problem under consideration, their interactions have to be taken into account. The mathematical problems involved in such calculations of systems consisting of many atoms can often be handled only after replacing the finite system by an infinite system. Again it was Max Born in Göttingen who made the first application of infinite matrices to atomic problems.

Born had been acquainted with matrix methods ever since he had learned about them from his teacher Jakob Rosanes in Breslau in the beginning of the century. Rosanes was an expert in algebraic geometry and invariant theory, and he inspired many students, among them Born’s friends Ernst Hellinger and Otto Toeplitz and, later, Richard Courant.$^{48}$ These students, especially the first two, did much to propagate the knowledge of matrices. Born recalled many years later:

> As a student in Breslau, I was much under the influence of Toeplitz, who was my senior by one year, and though my interest in algebra was not great he insisted on my learning matrix calculus properly and occasionally refreshed my knowledge when we were together again as young teachers in Göttingen. This turned out to be an advantage to me, first in developing Minkowski’s form of relativity, then for the study of vibrations in crystals, which are determined, indeed, by a quadratic form of a (practically) infinite number of variables, but decidedly at the birth of quantum mechanics. (Born, 1940, p. 617)

Toeplitz’ help proved to be especially valuable in the theory of crystal lattices, which Born and Theodore von Kármán developed in 1912.

$^{48}$Jakob Rosanes was born on 16 August 1842 in Brody, Austria-Hungary (now in the Ukrainian S.S.R.) and studied at the Universities of Berlin and Breslau (1860–1865), obtaining his doctorate at the latter. Rosanes remained in Breslau for the rest of his life: he became *Privatdozent* in 1870, *Extraordinarius* in 1873 and full professor in 1876. He served as rector of his university during the academic year 1903–1904, retired in 1911, and died on 6 January 1922.

Rosanes was a good teacher, but not an equally good lecturer. As Courant recalled later, it was difficult to follow his lectures, especially since ‘he scribbled equations which his students never quite saw because as he wrote he hid them with his body and as he moved along he rubbed them out with his sponge’ (Reid, 1976, p. 13). At times, however, he could deliver inspiring lectures, such as his rectorial address of 1903 on the characteristic features of nineteenth century mathematics (Rosanes, 1904).

**I.3 Early Applications of Matrix Methods in Physics**  
**39**

In order to determine the proper vibrations of a crystal, Born and von Kármán proceeded in the following way. They first considered a linear chain of *N* atoms and took into account the harmonic interaction (whose strength is given by the force constant α) between two adjacent atoms only (Born and von Kármán, 1912). Hence *u<sub>n</sub>*, the displacement of the *n*th atom (with mass *m*) around its equilibrium position, follows from the equation of motion,

$$m \frac{d^2 u_n}{dt^2} = \alpha (u_{n+1} - u_n) - \alpha (u_n - u_{n-1}), \qquad n = 2, \dots, N-1. \tag{53}$$

Born and von Kármán's task consisted in bringing Eq. (53) into the standard form

$$m \frac{d^2 U_n}{dt^2} + \alpha p_n U_n = 0, \qquad n = 2, \dots, N, \tag{54}$$

for *U<sub>n</sub>*, the so-called 'normal' coordinates of the system, with the products (α*p<sub>n</sub>/m*) denoting the squares of the frequencies of the harmonic motion. For this purpose they had to perform a canonical transformation. They recognized, however, that this transformation was equivalent to solving the system of linear homogeneous equations,

$$-u_{n+1} + u_n(2 - p) - u_{n-1} = 0, \qquad n = 2, \dots, N. \tag{55}$$

This system has a nontrivial solution only if its determinant is zero, that is,

$$
\det \begin{vmatrix}
\dots & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \dots \\
\dots & 0, & -1, & 2-p, & -1, & 0, & \dots \\
\dots & 0, & 0, & -1, & 2-p, & -1, & \dots \\
\dots & 0, & 0, & 0, & -1, & 2-p, & \dots \\
\dots & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \dots
\end{vmatrix}
= 0. \tag{56}
$$

The left-hand side yields a polynomial (of order *N* − 2) for the unknown *p*, whose roots may be identified with the *p<sub>n</sub>* in Eqs. (54).

The atoms at the boundary of the chain do not satisfy an equation of motion of the type of Eq. (53). In order to simplify their treatment, Born and von Kármán considered the limit of an infinite chain and imposed the boundary condition *u*<sub>*n*+*N*</sub> = *u<sub>N</sub>*. They expected this limit to yield a reasonably good physical approximation to their problem. Moreover, it did simplify the mathematical treatment considerably, as it allowed one to make use of the results obtained in the theory of infinite quadratic forms. Let us note that an infinite matrix of the type occurring in Eq. (56) is a special case of the type of matrix which had already occurred in Hill's theory of the moon. More importantly, however, Toeplitz had just recently studied in some detail quadratic forms, whose

**44**

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0045 -->

40 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

matrices possessed the same structure (Toeplitz, 1907b, 1911). He wrote these forms as

$$
L = \sum_{p,q=-\infty}^{+\infty} c_{p-q} x_p x_q,
$$
(57)

with real or complex variables $x_p$ and the coefficients depending just on the differences of the indices.$^{49}$ In case that the $c_{p-q}$ form a symmetric or Hermitian matrix, he had shown that the spectrum had to be real (Toeplitz, 1911, p. 361, Theorem 6). As a result the roots of the infinite determinantal equation (56) had to be real as well. Born and von Kármán calculated them by making use of the factorization property, Eq. (52), and the periodicity condition (which implies the equality of the roots $p_n$ and $p_{n+N}$), obtaining the result

$$
p_n = 4 \sin^2\left( \frac{\pi n}{N} \right), \quad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots.
$$
(58)

The frequency spectrum of the infinite linear chain then followed with the help of the equation

$$
\nu = \left( \frac{\alpha}{m} p_n \right)^{1/2}.
$$
(59)

Although Born and von Kármán could derive their result, Eq. (58), by simply substituting in Eq. (53) the periodicity assumption, $u_n = u \exp(in\phi)$, where $u$ is a constant amplitude and $\phi$ a constant phase which eventually equals $2\pi n/N$, only Toeplitz’ theory of $L$-forms justified the steps in the derivation. It further guaranteed that the spectrum of a finite chain of $N$ atoms was accounted for, in an acceptable approximation, by Eq. (58), even if no periodicity condition (which turns the finite chain into an infinite one) was assumed.

The discussion of the linear atomic chain or one-dimensional lattice served only as a preparation for the treatment of the three-dimensional lattice. With the latter, Born and von Kármán wanted to describe a realistic crystal and its thermodynamic properties. They had discussed it already in their first paper (Born and von Kármán, 1912) and returned to it in detail later (Born and von Kármán, 1913b). Instead of starting from the equations of motion, as we have outlined above in connection with the linear chain, they now preferred another approach: namely, they considered right away the potential energy of a three-dimensional lattice of mass points or atoms, whose coordinates (expressing the displacements from the equilibrium positions) are labelled by the indices $l$, $m$,

$^{49}$Originally, Toeplitz (1907b) had used the $L$-forms to study the properties of Laurent series for functions of complex variables, i.e.,

$$
f(z) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{+\infty} c_n z^n,
$$

by using $c_n$, the coefficients of the latter, as the coefficients $c_{p-q}$ in Eq. (57).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0046 -->

I.3 Early Applications of Matrix Methods in Physics 41

and $n$. This means that the atoms are arranged (in equilibrium) at regular distances determined by multiples of the lattice constants, and the values of these multiples become the subscripts of the position coordinates. The latter are therefore written as $u_{l,m,n}$ (the coordinates in the $x$-direction), $v_{l,m,n}$ (the coordinates in the $y$-direction) and $w_{l,m,n}$ (the coordinates in the $z$-direction), where $l$, $m$ and $n$ assume integral values. $V$, the potential energy of a lattice consisting of atoms of the same mass, may be written as a quadratic form of the position coordinates, i.e.,

$$V = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{l,m,n} \sum_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} \left[ u_{l,m,n} \left( a_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(1)} u_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} + b_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(3)} v_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} + b_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(2)} w_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} \right) \right.$$

$$\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad + v_{l,m,n} \left( b_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(3)} u_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} + a_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(2)} v_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} + b_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(1)} w_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} \right) \tag{60}$$

$$\left. \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad + w_{l,m,n} \left( b_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(2)} u_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} + b_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(1)} v_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} + a_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(3)} w_{\lambda,\mu,\nu} \right) \right].$$

Born and von Kármán had assumed that all other atoms (with position coordinates $u_{\lambda,\mu,\nu}$, $v_{\lambda,\mu,\nu}$, and $w_{\lambda,\mu,\nu}$) exert forces on the atom at the lattice point $(l,m,n)$, as against the assumption of nearest-neighbour interaction that had led them previously to the equation of motion (53) for the one-dimensional chain. The six series of coefficients, $a_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(i)}$ and $b_{l-\lambda,m-\mu,n-\nu}^{(i)}$ ($i = 1,2,3$), now replaced the single force constant $\alpha$ of the former system.

Having set up the expression for the potential energy of the three-dimensional lattice, Born and von Kármán were confronted with the task of bringing it into the special, standard form, where it becomes reduced to a sum involving the squares of the transformed, i.e., so-called normal coordinates, $u'_{l,m,n}$, $v'_{l,m,n}$ and $w'_{l,m,n}$, i.e.,

$$V = - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{l,m,n} \left[ p_{l,m,n}^{(1)} (u'_{l,m,n})^2 + p_{l,m,n}^{(2)} (v'_{l,m,n})^2 + p_{l,m,n}^{(3)} (w'_{l,m,n})^2 \right]. \tag{61}$$

The $p_{l,m,n}^{(i)}$, $i = 1,2,3$, denote the eigenvalues of the quadratic form (60)—similar to the $(\alpha p_n)$ in the linear chain—and they are related to the frequency spectrum of the crystal through the equation

$$\nu^{(i)} = \left( \frac{p^{(i)}}{m} \right)^{1/2}, \qquad i = 1,2,3, \tag{62}$$

in which the indices have been dropped for the convenience of writing. Equation (62) is the generalization of Eq. (59) for the case of the three-dimensional lattice.

Born and von Kármán performed the principal-axes transformation of $V$, Eq. (60) to Eq. (61), by assuming that the coordinates, $u_{l,m,n}$, $v_{l,m,n}$, and $w_{l,m,n}$, are periodic functions, all those belonging to a given lattice point $(l,m,n)$ depending on the same phase angle $\omega_{l,m,n}$. The problem of the principal-axes transformation

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0047 -->

42  
Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool  

of the quadratic form, given by Eq. (60), was then extremely simplified: it was reduced to the separate transformations to principal axes of those quadratic forms which are connected with single atoms (each of which has three degrees of freedom associated with the translational motions along the crystal axes). As a consequence of this simplification Born and von Kármán had to solve—instead of the large system of equations that arises in the process of transforming to principal axes the quadratic form describing the potential energy of the total crystal—a system of three homogeneous linear equations in three variables for each atom in the lattice, that is,  

$$
\begin{aligned}
u(A_1 - p) + vB_3 + wB_2 &= 0, \\
uB_2 + v(A_2 - p) + wB_1 &= 0, \tag{63} \\
uB_2 + vB_1 + w(A_3 - p) &= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$  

The variables $u$, $v$ and $w$ are the amplitudes of the harmonic coordinates $u_{l,m,n}$, $v_{l,m,n}$ and $w_{l,m,n}$; for example, $u$ is the amplitude of the function $u \cos \omega_{l,m,n}$, which is assumed to represent the coordinate $u_{l,m,n}$, etc. The coefficients $A_k$ and $B_k$ ($k = 1, 2, 3$) correspond to the sums  

$$
A_k = \sum_{\lambda, \mu, \nu} a_{\lambda, \mu, \nu}^{(k)} \exp(i \omega_{\lambda, \mu, \nu}), \tag{63a}
$$  

$$
B_k = \sum_{\lambda, \mu, \nu} b_{\lambda, \mu, \nu}^{(k)} \exp(i \omega_{\lambda, \mu, \nu}), \tag{63b}
$$  

involving the coefficients which determine the elastic forces between the atoms in the lattice. Finally, the summations over $\lambda$, $\mu$, and $\nu$ extend to all lattice points in the crystal. The system of equations, (63), yields a nontrivial solution for $u$, $v$ and $w$, provided the determinant of the coefficients is zero. This condition yields three real values for $p$, namely, $p^{(1)}$, $p^{(2)}$ and $p^{(3)}$, and these quantities also occur as the factors multiplying the normal coordinates on the right-hand side of Eq. (61). Evidently, in order to carry out the principal-axis transformation of $V$, one has to solve as many systems of three linear equations as there are atoms in the lattice. However, once all $p^{(i)}$ have been determined, one also arrives at the frequency spectrum of the crystal by applying Eq. (62). This frequency spectrum depends, as in the case of the one-dimensional lattice, on the force parameters, $a_{l,m,n}^{(k)}$ and $b_{l,m,n}^{(k)}$, and on the phase angles, $\omega_{l,m,n}$.  

The question arises whether Born and von Kármán, by using a clever trick, avoided the problem of treating a very large or—in the approximation they used—even the infinite three-dimensional lattice. The answer is no; the reason being that in performing the principal-axis transformation of the quadratic form, given by Eq. (60), one obtains a characteristic equation involving a determinant, which is ‘cyclic’ for each direction of the crystal—i.e., it possesses the form of the determinant of Eq. (56) in three dimensions, except that in each row all coefficients are supposed to be different from zero. In general, such a determi-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0048 -->

I.3 Early Applications of Matrix Methods in Physics 43

nant allows one to make the assumption of periodicity. Since there are three directions in a crystal lattice, the phase angles, $\omega_{l,m,n}$, will be composed of $\phi$, $\psi$ and $\chi$, the phase angles associated with the individual directions, i.e.,

$$\omega_{l,m,n} = l\phi + m\psi + n\chi. \qquad (64)$$

Now, instead of one phase, i.e., $2\pi/N$, as in the case of the linear chain, in the spatial lattice three phases—$\phi = 2\pi/N_1$, $\psi = 2\pi/N_2$ and $\chi = 2\pi/N_3$, where $N_1$, $N_2$ and $N_3$ are the numbers of atoms (or lattice points) along the three lattice directions—play a role.

The use of infinite quadratic forms—especially the compact $L$-forms of Toeplitz—in the lattice theory of solids by Born and von Kármán remained perhaps the only significant application of infinite matrices in physics until 1925. In the years following 1912 Born had continued to develop his theory of the solid state, going beyond the problems he had treated first with von Kármán (i.e., the determination of the proper vibrations in a crystal in order to calculate, say, its specific heat). In the course of this work he occasionally referred again to the methods of infinite matrices. For example, he employed $L$-forms in an investigation of the electrostatic potential of a crystal lattice (Born, 1921). Hence Born was perhaps the only scientist who, ever since he had learned about matrices, was aware of their potential use in physics. It is therefore rather surprising why Born had never applied his favourite algebraic method to problems of quantum theory during the early 1920s. One reason for this neglect lay in Born’s scientific temperament. Whenever he pursued a new subject, as was the case with the theory of atomic structure after 1922, he would first stick to conventional approaches and exploit them systematically before turning to a new method. Now in atomic theory there had been applied for many years the methods of Hamilton and Jacobi, which seemed to be particularly adequate to describe the dynamics of multiply periodic systems. Only after these methods were found to be wanting did Born turn to other techniques. However, the new mechanical description of atomic systems, which made use of the difference calculus, still remained very close to the previous one. It was with this scheme, which Born already called ‘quantum mechanics’ in spring 1924, that he had hoped to make progress. At any rate, in summer 1925 he had not exhausted its possible applications by far.

However, the main reason for the absence of matrix methods in the earlier quantum theory has to be found in two facts. First, it was not known until Heisenberg’s discovery that in the description of atoms quantities, which do not commute, play a crucial role; second, the fact that matrices are noncommuting mathematical objects had not appeared openly in any of Born’s previous applications. Thus, Heisenberg, when he hit upon the noncommutativity property of his quantum-theoretical quantities, did not know that there existed sophisticated algebraic methods, which in fact had been perfected by Hilbert and his collaborators in Göttingen, and which could be adapted to handle his problems. Born, in turn, had mostly used matrices with very special properties—such as the ones occurring in Toeplitz’ $L$-forms—for physical application in his lattice

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0049 -->

44 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

theory. Therefore, when he first read Heisenberg's paper on the re-interpretation of mechanical relations in quantum theory, he reminded himself of the matrices in Rosanes' lectures in Breslau rather than of the infinite quadratic forms of Hilbert's theory of linear integral equations. After this recognition, however, he quickly established the connection between the two; and in doing so he brought into play all his mathematical prowess, his thorough knowledge of infinite matrices, and his experience of the principal-axes transformations of infinite quadratic forms.

To an outsider the progress achieved in the formulation of matrix mechanics by Born and his collaborators from July to October 1925 appears like a marvel. For Born, however, all the steps which he took were an almost straightforward application of the mathematical subtleties with which he had become familiar during the previous decade and a half. That a theoretical physicist like Born, having just the appropriate mathematical formalism at his command, was around at the right place in July 1925 may not have been an entirely fortuitous accident of history. But the fact that Born possessed this knowledge explains how Heisenberg's intuitive quantum-mechanical scheme could be transformed into a full-fledged matrix mechanics within a short three months, when everybody—including Heisenberg—expected years of hard intellectual labour before a rational atomic mechanics would arise.

In spite of his mathematical preparation in matrix theory, Born did not enter into its application to quantum mechanics alone. He knew about the complexity of the calculations involved in such things as the principal-axis transformation of an infinite matrix from his own work in solid state theory, and he also knew that the application of matrix methods to quantum theory would require much more than just calculating the spectrum of eigenvalues. Therefore, he desperately wanted someone with experience both in quantum theory and mathematics to assist him in formulating matrix mechanics. Wolfgang Pauli, whom he met in Hanover on 19 July 1925, seemed to be just the right man for this enterprise, but Pauli refused to collaborate. Born then turned to his second choice, Pascual Jordan, who, though less experienced than Pauli, was interested in mathematical formalism and was willing to study in particular the theory of infinite matrices and its application to quantum mechanics.

**I.4 Born's New Collaborator: Pascual Jordan**

Pascual Jordan was born on 18 October 1902 in Hanover, Germany, as the son of the painter Ernst Pascual Jordan and his wife Eva, *née* Fischer.$^{50}$ The fact that both of his parents were interested in natural sciences influenced his intellectual development. Jordan recalled later: 'My mother knew a good deal about plants, flowers, birds and stars. I learnt from her that light takes eight minutes in coming

$^{50}$Jordan's Christian name was, as he told Born, inherited from his great-grandfather, a Spaniard, who had come to Germany as a soldier in Napoleon's army and settled there for good (Born, 1978, p. 216).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0050 -->

I.4 Born’s New Collaborator: Pascual Jordan 45

from the sun to the earth. She was also interested in numbers and calculation; I learnt arithmetic from her’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 1). His father used to paint landscapes, buildings and portraits and knew a lot about perspective; young Pascual learnt much from him about geometry even before he began to attend school. ‘My father used to read popular books about natural science,’ he recalled, ‘especially the series of *Kosmos* books which was popular at the beginning of this century. Each year several books came out in this series, written by people such as [Wilhelm] Bolsche who was well known as a popular author. All these *Kosmos* books belonged to my first reading in natural science’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 1).<sup>51</sup>

At the age of ten or twelve Jordan thought of becoming a painter or architect, and it was only several years later that he decided to study natural sciences. At first he was attracted by biology. As he recalled later: ‘To be sure, already very early as a small boy I liked animals very much. I often visited the zoological garden, and then I also possessed a collection of pictures of extinct animals like saurians, etc.’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 4). With the passage of time, however, his interests shifted to physics and mathematics. Jordan went to the *Reform Gymnasium* in Hanover, a school which laid emphasis on scientific studies. There, for instance, in mathematics he learned differentiation and binomial series; in physics he learned mechanics and other subjects in an elementary manner.

In science, the larger view of all things attracted him. ‘Rather early,’ he remembered later, ‘that is, at the age of fourteen, I had conceived a plan of once writing a big book about all fields of science’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 5). He liked fundamental philosophical questions, and on these he would try to find books to study. First he turned to biology: A. Pauly’s book on the theories of Charles Darwin and Jean Baptiste Lamarck on the propagation of species (*Darwinismus und Lamarckismus*, 1905) had come into his hands. Jordan was particularly interested in the discussions, which were going on in those days, about neo-vitalism and neo-Lamarckism and the question whether organic life could be understood by purely mechanical or physical means. At the age of fourteen he also read Friedrich Albert Lange’s *Geschichte des Materialismus* (*History of Materialism*) and was deeply impressed by it.<sup>52</sup> At about this time he

<sup>51</sup> *Kosmos*—more accurately, *Kosmos, Gesellschaft der Naturfreunde*—was the name of a German association for natural science. From 1904 this association published a journal called *Kosmos*. (The publication was interrupted in 1944, but renewed in 1946.) The journal was addressed mainly to young and lay readers. To supplement the articles on specific topics, a series of small books dealing with certain fields of biology, astronomy, physics and the development of civilization was added. W. Bolsche (1861–1939), a popular writer in Germany, who propagated the ideas of Darwin and Haeckel on evolution in biology—and supported Haeckel’s philosophical scheme, the so-called monism (‘*Monismus*’)—wrote the first volume, entitled ‘*Abstammung des Menschen*’ (1904) and contributed numerous others.

<sup>52</sup> F. A. Lange (1828–1875), philosopher and writer, edited newspapers in Germany and Switzerland before becoming a professor of philosophy in Zurich (1870) and later in Marburg (1872). As a philosopher he belonged to the founders of the so-called ‘neo-Kantianism,’ i.e., a renewed and altered version of Kantian philosophy; as a political writer he propagated early socialistic demands. He also treated topics of the history of philosophy. His book on the history of materialism, first published in 1866, went through many editions, and was reprinted as late as 1926.

philosophical school of empiricism, which exerted much influence on philosophers in other countries
and helped to create the international movement of logical positivism. Schlick was shot to death by a
demented student on 22 June 1936 as he entered the University of Vienna to give his lecture.

bit difficult, for I had actually not attended the first lecture. Since I had to enroll at the university, I was prevented from doing so; hence I had to learn from a fellow student what he had treated. According to this report I worked out [the details of] the lecture’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 12). In any case, he soon became familiar with the Mathematical Institute of Göttingen. Emil Artin, who was then Courant’s assistant, advised Jordan to take pure mathematics rather than physics as his principal subject, and for a while he actually thought of becoming a pure mathematician.

Through Pohl, Jordan met Max Born. By the time of Jordan’s arrival in Göttingen, Born’s principal scientific interest had turned to a systematic examination of the problems of atomic mechanics, though he was still engaged upon the completion of his article on the dynamics of crystal lattices for the *Encyklopädie* (Born, 1923b). Jordan even gave him some technical help, which Born acknowledged in the foreword.$^{60}$ Together with Born he soon began to concentrate on the study of atomic structure. The two of them would often work together and discuss papers of common interest with each other. For Jordan, who stuttered, this friendly personal contact with Born was very helpful. And this, together with his interest in atomic physics, determined his future scientific career.

Already after finishing the *Gymnasium* Jordan had undertaken the study of Sommerfeld’s *Atombau und Spektrallinien*, which introduced him to the excitement of atomic physics. Now in Göttingen in June 1922, during his first semester, he obtained the opportunity of attending Bohr’s Wolfskehl lectures on atomic theory and of listening to the ensuing discussions, which involved the most outstanding experts in the field, including Arnold Sommerfeld and his brilliant students. Thus, during the *Bohr Festival*, he encountered Werner Heisenberg and Wolfgang Pauli, with whom he became better acquainted later. In the following winter semester, 1922–1923, Jordan attended Born’s Seminar, where perturbation theory was discussed in detail, and together with Heisenberg and Friedrich Hund he studied the methods of Henri Poincaré and Karl Schwarzschild. He found this work satisfying, and it confirmed his decision to pursue physics: ‘This thing is so interesting, I must stay in physics’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963, p. 4).$^{61}$

Before going to Göttingen Jordan had acquired knowledge of classical mechanics by studying the relevant portions of Hermann von Helmholtz’ *Vorlesun-*

doctorate. However, besides theoretical physics, he preferred mathematics most. Jordan took several courses from Courant, and he gave technical assistance during the latter’s writing of the *Methoden der mathematischen Physik* (Courant and Hilbert, 1924). Thus he used to meet Courant almost daily to discuss mathematical problems.⁶⁶ Out of curiosity he went to Edmund Landau’s lectures on number theory. He also attended some of Niels Erik Nörlund’s lectures on difference equations, which he later found useful in his work on atomic theory.

Besides lectures and laboratory courses Jordan completed his education by attending the weekly Physics Colloquium as well as participating in the Born–Franck–Hilbert Seminar on the structure of matter (‘*Struktur der Materie*’), which was held regularly each semester and dealt with atomic theory. Now and then he went to the meetings of the *Mathematische Gesellschaft*, where he made the acquaintance of Emmy Noether; after all, because of his work for Courant, he belonged partly to the mathematical circle.

After helping Born with his *Encyklopädie* article on crystal dynamics, Jordan became his closest student. As he recalled: ‘There were also other students, or junior co-workers who had already obtained their doctorate, who spent much time together with Born for joint work in his apartment. I believe I was closer to him [than anyone else], for I had an extensive collaboration with him, first on the book on lattice theory of crystals and later on quantum-theoretical questions’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963, p. 9). Besides Born, Jordan also discussed theoretical problems with other students, but these discussions were much less intense. Jordan used to report to Born about the progress of his theoretical work, and Born would propose new problems and give the necessary advice. On completing the *Encyklopädie* article Born, for a while, became deeply involved in the theory of molecules, a subject tied both to the theory of the solid state and to atomic theory. When Jordan was looking for a problem to treat in his dissertation, Born tried to interest him, too, in molecular theory. But Jordan did not warm up to the idea, for the physics involved was not to his liking. His preference was for more fundamental problems. Now, in 1923, there existed such a problem: in connection with the Compton effect, the problem of the light-quantum and how to fit it into quantum theory was much discussed. The quantum physicists, in particular Niels Bohr, had raised many objections against Einstein’s old conception of light-quanta (Einstein, 1905b). On the other hand, Wolfgang Pauli treated the interaction between electrons and radiation consistently by taking into account the light-quantum properties of radiation (Pauli, 1923b). Then Albert Einstein and Paul Ehrenfest generalized Pauli’s treatment in a further article (Einstein and Ehrenfest, 1923). That Einstein concerned himself again with the light-quantum problem set Jordan moving. Later on he reconstructed his reaction as follows: ‘I believe, I became interested in this work [of Einstein and Ehrenfest] because I had also read Pauli’s paper earlier and had now found this paper of Einstein and Ehrenfest, which I found to be very

⁶⁶ Jordan worked at least as much to help Courant on his book as he did for Born’s review article on lattice dynamics. Courant thanked him in his foreword as one among a long list of ‘true helpers.’

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0056 -->

I.4 Born’s New Collaborator: Pascual Jordan 51

interesting. Then, I think, I announced on my own that I would like to give a talk on it sometime' (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 20 June 1963, p. 21). He thus presented the content of that paper in a seminar, with which Born was satisfied. As Jordan recalled: 'After listening to my seminar on the light-quanta he said that I could take this as my topic if I liked it better. In general one was skeptical [about the light-quanta] and one thought that the problem had to be solved differently, but somehow Born's opinion in this regard was not fixed and he thought that since I had raised the question I might as well pursue it' (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 15).<sup>67</sup> Jordan was glad to have escaped molecular physics, and he turned to the problems arising from the light-quantum hypothesis in atomic physics.

In his thesis Jordan sought to propose a compromise between the extreme positions of the light-quantum theory, as assumed by Einstein, and of the wave theory of radiation, as preferred by Niels Bohr on the basis of correspondence arguments (Jordan, 1924). In particular, he made an attempt to modify Einstein's theory of the interaction between electrons or atoms and radiation (Einstein, 1909a, 1916e) by avoiding an important assumption of the light-quantum theory: namely, the assumption that a light-quantum of energy $h\nu$ necessarily imparts a recoil momentum of magnitude $h\nu/c$ to the electron or atom, where $h$ is Planck's constant, $\nu$ the frequency of radiation, and $c$ the velocity of light. To that end, Jordan assumed that $\sigma(\theta, \phi)$, the distribution of the intensity of radiation scattered from an atom or electron, is not concentrated in one direction in space (denoted by the scattering angles $\theta$ and $\phi$) but varies continuously, taking nonzero values for all $\theta$ and $\phi$. As a result, in Jordan's theory, the momentum of the scattered radiation obtained a value much smaller than Einstein's value $h\nu/c$. And yet, Jordan was able to explain the conclusions derived from the Compton effect concerning the change in the frequency of the scattered radiation and the motion of the recoil electron. His thesis, therefore, sought to bridge the open conflict between Einstein's light-quantum theory and the Bohr–Kramers–Slater radiation theory by offering them a kind of coexistence.

Jordan's work, however, did not persuade his more advanced colleagues. Pauli, for instance, after reading the thesis, simply declared: 'Now I am more

<sup>67</sup>Born himself had not worked on the light-quantum problem before, though he followed the development with interest. On the one hand, his friend Albert Einstein had pioneered the light-quantum hypothesis; he had advocated it over many years against serious objections, and the discovery of the Compton effect seemed to prove that his conception was right. On the other, Niels Bohr—whose guidance Born had followed very closely in atomic theory—refused to believe in the reality of the light-quantum and developed (together with Hendrik Kramers and John Slater in 1924) the counterproposal of a statistical radiation theory. Other physicists were also concerned with the nature of radiation in the early 1920s. Thus Walther Bothe discussed the possibility of deciding the question about the reality of the light-quantum by studying the details of the photoelectric effect (Bothe, 1923c, 1924b). Furthermore he attempted to explain Einstein's fluctuation formula (Einstein, 1909a) and the interaction between radiation and free electrons by assuming the existence of multiple light-quanta having energies $sh\nu$, with $s = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ (Bothe, 1923e, 1924a). Bothe's papers were discussed in Göttingen, especially in the private seminar for students that was arranged from time to time in Hertha Sponer's home (see Hund, AHQP Interview, 25 June 1963, p. 13), and they constituted some of the background of Jordan's interest in light-quanta.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0057 -->

52 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

convinced than ever that Einstein is right' (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963, p. 10). Einstein also studied Jordan's generalization and relaxation of the light-quantum theory and commented on it in a short note to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, where the thesis had been published (Jordan, 1924). He began by saying: 'In the ingenious investigation quoted above, Jordan has tried to disprove the thesis proposed by me, that for each elementary process of emission and absorption a momentum of magnitude $h\nu/c$ is transferred to the emitting or absorbing molecule' (Einstein, 1925c, p. 784). Then he pointed out that Jordan's use of a distribution function $\sigma(\theta,\phi)$, which is nonzero in all space directions $\theta$ and $\phi$, implied that the emitted radiation depended on the direction of the incident radiation in a strange way. Thus, the probability that radiation, which impinges on the atom or molecule from opposite directions with intensities $\rho_{+}$ and $\rho_{-}$, is absorbed, becomes proportional to the square root of the product $\rho_{+} \cdot \rho_{-}$, provided the two incident beams of radiation are not coherent. As a consequence, in the case of radiation coming from one direction—say, with zero intensity $\rho_{-}$—Jordan obtained no absorption at all, evidently in contrast to observation. In addition, Einstein noted that in Jordan's theory an atom or molecule would behave very strangely if exposed to a thermal radiation field and concluded:

> All this is connected with the fact that the author uses a hypothesis, according to which the amounts of radiation taken from rays of different directions are not treated as independent of each other. One must assume this, however, in order not to contradict the most elementary experiences of absorption. If one does so, then one necessarily arrives at the result that in every elementary process of absorption or emission a momentum of absolute magnitude $h\nu/c$ is transferred to the molecule. (Einstein, 1925c, p. 785)

In spite of this criticism Jordan was glad that Einstein took an interest in his work on radiation theory. He continued to work in this field, and some months later he published another paper on the thermal equilibrium between electrons and blackbody radiation (Jordan, 1925d). In it he did not persist in the ideas of his thesis, but followed Pauli's and Einstein and Ehrenfest's treatments of the processes involved. In particular, he showed that thermal equilibrium was still preserved if Planck's law governed the energy distribution in radiation and the free electrons or atoms obeyed Bose–Einstein statistics rather than Boltzmann statistics, as had been assumed previously by Pauli and Einstein and Ehrenfest. In conclusion Jordan thanked 'Mr. Einstein for the kind interest which he has taken in this investigation' (Jordan, 1925d, p. 655). He felt encouraged to continue to make further contributions to the fundamental problem of radiation.

In his student years at Göttingen, Jordan showed no particular eagerness to produce many publications, which was quite unlike Pauli and Heisenberg who were only slightly senior to him. This may have been due to his reticent character and the fact that he began to study physics seriously only in summer 1922. Furthermore, he quite early became involved in the laborious projects of other

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0058 -->

I.4 Born’s New Collaborator: Pascual Jordan 53

people, such as Born’s article for the *Encyklopädie* and Courant’s *Methoden der mathematischen Physik*, from which he did not earn great merit or rewards. Afterwards, when he was ready to attack problems of atomic theory, he did not treat such problems as molecular structure, on which it seemed easier to write papers, but selected the difficult question of light-quanta for his research. So it happened that Jordan’s first publication dealt with the results of his thesis. In this respect Jordan’s scientific career resembled that of an average student, and yet he was considered to be a great talent by his professor. Thus, Born wrote to Einstein in summer 1925 about Jordan and his thesis:

> As regards your objections against Jordan’s paper, I still feel very unsure of myself; but as I am now coming to grips with these things from my own somewhat complicated point of view, I will understand them one of these days. On the whole, you are certainly right; though Jordan’s opinion is based on somewhat different considerations, as he allows coherent bundles of rays, whereas you only mention incoherent ones. Even if Jordan is mistaken in this, as I now think is highly probable, he is still exceptionally intelligent and astute and can think far more swiftly and confidently than I. (Born to Einstein, 15 July 1925)

He thought that Jordan was an able collaborator, who would make his way as a theoretical physicist.

It is surprising, however, that Born did not draw Jordan immediately into his research projects. After completing his doctorate in fall 1924, Jordan studied spectroscopic problems under James Franck. ‘Franck engaged me to help him with the preparation of the book *Anregung von Quantensprüngen durch Stöße* [Franck and Jordan, 1926], and I learnt a great deal from this activity. I had to study a whole series of papers and take notes of their contents in order to collect the material. Later on we wrote it together’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963, p. 7). Again he became involved in a laborious project, which took a long time. This time, however, he acted as a junior collaborator on equal terms, not just as an anonymous helper.$^{68}$ This work also led to certain publications. Jordan thus submitted his first paper on a spectroscopic problem already on 23 February 1925 (Jordan, 1925a), which was based on an experimental observation reported by Karl Meissner of Zurich University in the January issue of *Annalen der Physik* (Meissner, 1925a). While observing the absorption of light by excited neon

54   Chapter I   The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

atoms, Meissner noticed that there occurred two types of transitions, connected with strong and weak absorption, respectively; from this he concluded that the so-called $1s_3$ and $1s_5$ states of neon had a long lifetime, and the $1s_2$ and $1s_4$ states had a short lifetime. Born was interested in Meissner's investigation, which seemed to imply that the ground state of neon was a $p$-state, and he asked Jordan to examine the question on the basis of known theoretical principles.$^{69}$ In his short paper, Jordan tried to organize the terms according to the 'branching rule' of Landé and Heisenberg (1924), but he found that the regularity of the periodic system of elements required certain restrictions upon this rule. Wolfgang Pauli, his former critic, agreed with his result. As he recalled later: 'Pauli, who saw this manuscript [Jordan, 1925a], was very interested in my observation, as he had just then written his paper on the exclusion principle. His paper was ready in manuscript, but not yet published, and he noticed that my remark touched upon his subject' (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 15). Jordan, like Pauli, had used Stoner's classification of stationary states in atoms (Stoner, 1924) and concluded that the ground state of the neon atom must be a $p$-state (with the principal quantum number 2). He thereby predicted the existence of two strong lines, which should arise in transitions from the states $1s_2$ and $1s_4$ to this ground state, and they were discovered a couple of months later by Gustav Hertz experimentally (Hertz, 1925). Jordan was happy with the result of his excursion into spectroscopy and continued to work on similar questions. In July 1925 he published a further note on atomic structure (Jordan, 1925c), in which he attempted to clarify the relation between the spectroscopic terms of atoms and the configurations of the series electrons beyond what had been given previously by Pauli (1925b) or Heisenberg (1925b). Because of these contributions to spectroscopy, Born praised Jordan together with Heisenberg and Hund in a letter to Einstein: 'On the whole, my young people, Heisenberg, Jordan and Hund, are brilliant. I find that merely to keep up with their thoughts demands at times a considerable effort on my part. Their mastery of the so-called "term zoology" is marvellous' (Born to Einstein, 15 July 1925).

In spite of this success Jordan did not become a spectroscopist, but left these matters to his older colleague Friedrich Hund. Instead, Born engaged Jordan to collaborate with him on more fundamental aspects of atomic theory. In November 1924 Born had turned his attention to the problem of the width of spectral lines, for as he reported at the time: 'I am trying to obtain the finite width of the terms by associating with each state a finite lifetime and then applying perturbation theory to it via a Fourier integral' (Born to Heisenberg, 26 November 1924).

56 Chapter I The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

arbitrary structure [in time] that exists only in a finite period of time, say from $t_0$ to $t_1$. The field is represented mathematically by a Fourier integral

$$\mathbf{E}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} \mathbf{e}(\omega) \exp(2\pi i\omega t) d\omega, \quad (65)$$

where $\mathbf{e}(\omega)$ is a vector denoting the Fourier amplitude associated with the frequency $\omega$. The classical part of the problem consisted in applying perturbation theory; that is, one treated the external field as a perturbation of the original system and calculated the change of its properties in some approximation, usually keeping terms up to second order. For their joint work, Born contributed the basic physical ideas and relied on Jordan to carry out the details of the calculation and the mathematical proofs. Thus, Jordan, in a separate paper (Jordan, 1925b), investigated convergence questions; for example, he studied the first-order correction, $S_1$, to the action function, i.e., the expression

$$S_1 = \frac{i}{2\pi} \mathbf{A}_{\tau} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{\mathbf{e}(\omega)}{\nu\tau + \omega} \exp[2\pi i(w^0\tau + \omega t)] d\omega, \quad (66)$$

where the vectors $\mathbf{A}_{\tau}$ denote the Fourier components (labelled $\tau$, which assumes integral values) of the electric moment of the unperturbed system with angle variables $w^0$ and harmonic frequencies $\nu$.${}^{71}$ Evidently, for the integral to exist one had to avoid that the path of $\omega$-integrations should go through a point which makes the resonance denominator disappear. As a proper procedure to do so, Jordan suggested to replace the right-hand side of Eq. (66) by the expression

$$S_1 = - \sum_{\tau} \mathbf{A}_{\tau} \exp(2\pi i w^0\tau) \int_{t_0}^{t} \mathbf{E}(t') \exp[-2\pi i \nu \tau (t - t')] dt', \quad (66')$$

which contained no resonance denominator, and he managed to handle expressions similar to the one for $S_1$ in the same consistent manner (Jordan, 1925b).

Once they had established the exact classical formulae, such as the ones for the energy absorbed by the periodic system or the fluctuation of the energy, Born and Jordan had to translate them into quantum formulae by using Born's discretization prescription, i.e., by replacing certain classical differential quotients (with respect to the action variables) by the corresponding difference quotients. In this task also Jordan assisted Born effectively because he was well acquainted with the methods of difference calculus. Thus, the two of them developed a systematic method of writing the difference expressions occurring in their theory in close agreement with the ones occurring in mathematical literature, especially in Nörlund's book (Nörlund, 1924), which allowed them to carry out calculations in a consistent manner. They used their formalism to demonstrate some of the

---

Since the system is multiply periodic, $w^0\tau$ and $\nu\tau$ stand for a sum of terms, each associated with one degree of freedom.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0062 -->

I.4 Born’s New Collaborator: Pascual Jordan 57

previous results of dispersion theory and to extend the dispersion-theoretic treatment to study the influence of aperiodic fields on atoms. An important example of the latter case occurs when charged particles (electrons or $\alpha$-particles) are scattered by atoms. In order to account for, say, the angle of deflection of the charged particles, Born and Jordan took the classical formula and replaced in it the classical frequencies and amplitudes by the corresponding quantum-theoretical ones. The result appeared to be in agreement with physical observation, and the authors concluded that the reformulation scheme with the difference calculus worked whenever it could be applied in a correct mathematical way.

Born and Jordan were, of course, aware that their work would develop only slowly into the scheme which Born had already called ‘quantum mechanics.’ However, they thought that they were marching along the right path for two reasons. First, they were convinced that the difference calculus represented the most adequate mathematical tool to express quantum laws. Second, they believed that they had rediscovered an important guiding principle, which helped them to select that restricted class of previous relations of atomic theory that could be taken over into quantum mechanics: this was the principle of using relations employing only observable quantities. For example, on the basis of this principle, equations containing the unmeasurable phase differences between electron motions of different atoms made no sense; hence one had to average over the phases in such equations before translating them into quantum theory. Jordan liked this principle because it provided a justification for an otherwise arbitrary step in atomic theory. After all, this principle could be traced back to his favourite philosopher Ernst Mach; moreover, it had already been applied successfully by Albert Einstein in developing relativity mechanics and, maybe, it would now help in creating a new atomic mechanics. However, in summer 1925, it was neither Jordan nor Born who took the next step towards the discovery of quantum mechanics, but Werner Heisenberg. And this step was contained in the manuscript which Heisenberg gave to Born in the middle of July to do with it what he saw fit, and which Born forwarded for publication to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Heisenberg, 1925c).

Jordan had heard of Heisenberg’s new ideas on the quantum-theoretical reformulation of kinematic and mechanical relations in private discussions.$^{72}$ He certainly found them interesting, not only because he respected Heisenberg as a successful senior colleague (whose results had guided him in his own work on spectroscopy), but also because Heisenberg had applied consistently the principle of avoiding nonobservable quantities in equations of quantum theory. However, he did not think of working along the lines suggested by Heisenberg. Born, on the other hand, was intrigued by the discovery that Heisenberg’s ideas required the use of matrices. He quickly wanted to get on with the formulation of

$^{72}$ Friedrich Hund recalled that in July 1925 he attended a private seminar, which Heisenberg gave to a small circle of students and friends at Hertha Sponer’s home before he left Göttingen to visit Leyden and Cambridge.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0063 -->

58  Chapter I  The Rediscovery of a Mathematical Tool

quantum mechanics with the help of matrix methods. Upon Pauli's refusal to collaborate, he immediately asked Jordan to help him again. Even more than in the previous work on the extension of dispersion theory and difference methods he needed assistance in the new task, which was not only difficult but seemed to require lots of technical labour.

The first thing which Born asked Jordan to do was to prove a guess. Heisenberg’s quantum condition, Eq. (5), had fixed the diagonal elements of the product **pq** – **qp**, with **p** and **q** denoting the infinite matrices representing the quantum-theoretical momentum and position variables of a (periodic) system of one degree of freedom. Immediately after his discovery of the possibility of formulating quantum-mechanical equations with matrices, Born tried to rewrite the quantum condition as a matrix equation having the form

$$\mathbf{pq} - \mathbf{qp} = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{1}, \tag{67}$$

where $h$ denotes Planck’s constant and $\mathbf{1}$ the infinite unit-matrix. Equation (67) thus constituted the first equation of the new theory and Born was proud of it. ‘But this was only a guess, and my attempts to prove it failed,’ he recalled later. ‘Jordan . . . after only a few days brought me the solution of the problem’ (Born, 1978, p. 218).

In order to establish Eq. (67), Pascual Jordan turned to the example of the one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator, whose equation of motion may be written as

$$\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \omega_0^2 \mathbf{q} + \lambda \mathbf{q}^n = 0, \quad n = 2, 3, \dots, \tag{68}$$

where $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}$ denotes the second time derivative of the position coordinate **q**, $\omega_0$ the frequency constant and $\lambda$ the parameter of anharmonicity. By multiplying Eq. (68) with $m\mathbf{q}$ ($m$ being the oscillating mass) from the right and from the left, respectively, he obtained two equations whose difference yielded the matrix-equation

$$m(\ddot{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q}\ddot{\mathbf{q}}) = 0, \tag{69}$$

where $\mathbf{0}$ is the infinite zero-matrix. Now the first term on the left-hand side of Eq. (69) could be expressed as the difference of $d(m\dot{\mathbf{q}}\mathbf{q})/dt$ and $m\dot{\mathbf{q}}^2$, where $\dot{\mathbf{q}}$ denotes the first time derivative of the position coordinate; similarly the second term could be expressed as the difference of $d(\mathbf{q}m\dot{\mathbf{q}})/dt$ and $m\dot{\mathbf{q}}^2$. Hence Jordan concluded that Eq. (68) was equivalent to the equation

$$\frac{d}{dt} (\mathbf{pq} - \mathbf{qp}) = 0 \tag{69a}$$

because $m\dot{\mathbf{q}}\ (= \mathbf{p})$ represents the momentum variable of the oscillator. Now the nondiagonal elements of any matrix describing a property of the anhar-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0064 -->

I.4 Born’s New Collaborator: Pascual Jordan 59

monic oscillator contain the exponential time-dependent factor, $\exp[(2\pi i/h) \times (E_n - E_m)t]$, where $E_n$ and $E_m$ are the (different) energies of different states denoted by the indices $n$ and $m$. Hence the nondiagonal elements of the matrix $\mathbf{pq} - \mathbf{qp}$ must be zero, otherwise they could not be constant as required by Eq. (69a). Jordan thus proved Eq. (67) for the case of the one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator.

Jordan’s quick performance pleased Born, and they agreed to develop the new theory of matrix mechanics together. After a careful study of Heisenberg’s paper Born sent it off to *Zeitschrift für Physik* by the end of July 1925 and left for vacation in Switzerland. Jordan stayed behind in Germany to work on the joint enterprise. Fortunately, he had no difficulty in using matrix methods, because he had—in connection with the assistance he gave to Courant in the writing of *Methoden der mathematischen Physik*—once consulted (‘a little bit’) Maxime Bôcher’s *Einführung in die höhere Algebra* (1911), the German translation of a book in which (finite) matrices were discussed in some detail (Bôcher, 1907). Thus, his mathematical background was just of the right kind for him to become Born’s successful principal collaborator in the formulation of matrix mechanics.$^{73}$ A year later Born described his qualities as follows: ‘[Jordan is] perhaps not so productive as far as practical results are concerned, but [he is] very philosophically minded and mainly interested in fundamental questions. Besides Heisenberg and Pauli, I consider him to be the most gifted of the younger colleagues’ (Born to Bohr, 18 December 1926).

$^{73}$ Jordan’s initial familiarity with matrix methods should not be overestimated. As he himself said about it: ‘I knew a little bit, not very much . . . Something on this was contained in Courant’s book [Courant and Hilbert, 1924]. And there is [a book on] *Algebra* by [Maxime] Bôcher’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 17 June 1963, p. 29).

# Chapter II
## Matching the Tools and the Task

Werner Heisenberg had concluded his paper on the quantum-theoretical reinterpretation of kinematic and mechanical relations by recommending ‘a more intensive mathematical investigation of the method which has been very superficially employed here’ (Heisenberg, 1925c, p. 893). He had given the completed manuscript to Max Born, expecting that he would look into it cursorily and, if he did not find some serious mistake, send it off for publication. Although Born had not followed Heisenberg’s work during the previous several weeks, he soon became absorbed in his results, especially after recognizing the presence of a well-defined mathematical scheme behind them. Towards the end of July 1925 the following situation developed in Göttingen: While Heisenberg was visiting Leyden and Cambridge, his suggestion for the investigation of the mathematical method underlying the reinterpretation of kinematic and mechanical relations was taken up by Born. Born, in turn, recruited Jordan to help him in this investigation, especially in the application of the algebra of matrices to formulate a consistent atomic mechanics.

The prospect of using the advanced methods of matrix algebra made Born happy. Not only did he enjoy mathematical formalism for its own sake, as he had shown often enough in his scientific career, he had actually expected for some years that the solution of problems in atomic physics would require the use of a new mathematical tool. Now he realized that the new mathematical tool was the matrix calculus, and he even happened to be acquainted with it. Born’s familiarity with the use of matrices considerably facilitated his task of formulating Heisenberg’s ideas in a consistent mathematical language. Indeed, it soon became clear that the quantum-mechanical theory, for which physicists had searched for many years, would be achieved faster than expected. To that end, as a first step, one had to express Heisenberg’s quantum-theoretical concepts and relations in term of matrices; then one had to attempt to cast all other dynamical relations into matrix form. Thus, in July 1925 Born proposed the programme of matrix mechanics, i.e., of a reformulation of the complete scheme of classical mechanics (including the dynamics of the electron) as a matrix scheme.$^{74}$

***

$^{74}$ The name ‘matrix mechanics’ never appeared in the papers of the Göttingen physicists in 1925 and 1926. They always spoke about the ‘new mechanics’ or ‘quantum mechanics.’ Other people referred to the matrix scheme of Born, Jordan and Heisenberg as ‘Heisenberg’s mechanics’ or ‘Göttingen mechanics.’ Even Erwin Schrödinger, who invented the alternative formalism of wave mechanics, followed this nomenclature. However, in fall 1925 some mathematicians in Göttingen denoted the new quantum-theoretical approach with the word ‘*Matrizenphysik*’ (‘matrix physics’), as

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0066 -->

62 Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task

Together with Pascual Jordan, he carried it out during the following two months. By the end of September they submitted a paper to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, in which they presented the new matrix mechanics (Born and Jordan, 1925b).

## II.1 The Programme of Matrix Mechanics

At the outset of their paper, ‘Zur Quantenmechanik’ (‘On Quantum Mechanics’), which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 27 September 1925, Born and Jordan stated their programme as follows:

> ‘The theoretical approach of Heisenberg [1925c] recently published in this Journal, which aimed at setting up a new kinematical and mechanical formalism in conformity with the basic requirements of quantum theory, appears to us of considerable potential significance. It represents an attempt to render justice to the new facts by setting up a new and really suitable conceptual system instead of adapting the customary conceptions in a more or less artificial and forced manner. The physical reasoning which led Heisenberg to his development has been so clearly described by him that any supplementary remarks appear superfluous. But, as he himself indicates, in its formal, mathematical aspects his approach is but in its initial stages. His hypotheses have been applied only to simple examples without being fully carried through to a generalized theory. Having been in an advantageous position to familiarize ourselves with his ideas throughout their formative stages, we now strive (since his investigations have been concluded) to clarify the mathematically formal content of his approach and present some of our results here. These indicate that it is in fact possible, starting with the basic premises given by Heisenberg, to build up a closed mathematical theory of quantum mechanics which displays strikingly close analogies with classical mechanics, but at the same time preserves the characteristic features of quantum phenomena. (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 858)

At the start of their investigation Born and Jordan found themselves in a somewhat difficult situation because Heisenberg, who had initiated the physical ideas, was away from Göttingen and therefore unavailable for discussions. They could not even ask him whether he agreed with their continuation of his work or whether he would prefer to proceed alone in a different direction. Born was conscious of this situation, especially since Pauli had warned him to keep his hands off and not spoil Heisenberg’s physical ideas by mathematical formalism. On the other hand, he could, with clear conscience, point to the fact that Heisenberg had given him a finished paper in which he had written down all his results and that this paper would be published before long; hence every physicist

---

After 1927 the notion of ‘matrix mechanics’ became standard in the literature (see, e.g., Allen, 1927, p. 78, or Thirring, 1928, p. 405). Later, even Born and Jordan used it in their book *Elementare Quantenmechanik* (1930).

II.1 The Programme of Matrix Mechanics                                                                                       63

had the right to pick up the ideas and elaborate on them. Why should one blame him, Max Born, for using the advantage of having seen Heisenberg's results first? Moreover, he was convinced that the recognition of the possibility of rewriting quantum-mechanical relations in the language of matrices would take atomic theory a great step forward. Thus, it made no sense to await Heisenberg's return, especially since he would not come back to Göttingen immediately after his summer vacation, but spend a few weeks in the fall at Bohr's Institute in Copenhagen. Finally, his absence did not really prevent Born and Jordan from going ahead in late July 1925, for they believed that they had a well-defined programme of their own.

Immediately after Jordan proved Born's conjecture about the matrix formulation of the quantum conditions as Eq. (67), their collaboration on the new theory began in earnest. As Jordan recalled: 'Born explained something about Heisenberg's ideas to me . . . I realized that the [matrix] multiplication which Born had already recognized constituted the fundamental idea, and that one could use this multiplication in order to formulate equations involving [Heisenberg's] patterns of observable [quantum-theoretical] quantities. Since this idea convinced me at once, it determined already fully the programme of our joint collaboration' (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963, p. 19). However, Born and Jordan did not spend many days together working on the matrix formulation of mechanical relations. After a few days they had to interrupt their work: Born left for Tübingen to deliver a lecture on 30 July, and from there he went on to Switzerland for his vacation. 'I was so tired out that I had a little breakdown and was compelled to keep quiet,' Born remembered later (Born, Conversations). However, the elaboration of matrix mechanics continued, for as Jordan reported:

During Born's stay at Silvaplana I was in Hanover at my parents' house, and there I thought about a part of the material that was then treated in the paper of Born and myself. I exchanged letters about it with Born, to whom I reported, of course, my progress. I still recall that, after some time, he considered it desirable to interrupt the exchange of correspondence, since the double strain of a fatiguing sanatorium cure and our discussion through letters on this exciting subject did not agree well with him. (Jordan to van der Waerden, 8 October 1964)75
