II.2 Operations with Matrices 65

quantum laws corresponding to *all* the fundamental equations of classical mechanics and electrodynamics, including even relativistic considerations. For this purpose they had to examine carefully the existing matrix methods and see whether they were adequate to do the job. In Hamiltonian mechanics, for example, all the dynamical variables of a system of $n$ degrees of freedom may be expressed as functions of $q_k$, the generalized position coordinates, and $p_k$, their conjugate momenta, with $k = 1, \dots, n$. Hence Born and Jordan, in their re-interpretation, had to consider rather general functions of matrices $\mathbf{q}_k$ and $\mathbf{p}_k$ denoting the dynamical variables in matrix mechanics. In principle, the mathematical tools for doing so were available in matrix algebra, which they adapted for their purposes. The reformulation of the equations of mechanics and electrodynamics in the language of matrices required two other operations which did not seem to be available and had to be defined: these were the differentiation of a dynamical variable (expressed as a matrix) with respect to time, and the differentiation of a matrix function with respect to one of its (matrix) variables. By introducing both of these differential operations Born and Jordan completed the formal tools necessary for the reformulation of the dynamical laws in matrix form.

When Born returned to Göttingen soon after 15 September 1925 he found that Jordan had most of the material ready for their joint paper. All he had to do was to give it, during the following week or so, the finishing touch and to submit it to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, where it was received on 27 September 1925 and published the following November.$^{77}$ We shall discuss the essentials of this paper in the following.

**II.2 Operations with Matrices**

In Maxime Bôcher’s *Algebra* (1911), the book which Jordan consulted for mathematical questions, a quadratic matrix was defined as an array consisting of an equal number of rows and columns, which was framed on both sides by vertical double bars. Born and Jordan did not follow this notation; rather they took over the one from *Courant-Hilbert* (see Chapter 1, Section 1.2 of Courant and Hilbert, 1924), thus replacing the double bars by round brackets.$^{78}$ They represented an infinite matrix by a bold letter, say $\mathbf{a}$, in order to distinguish it from other quantities, and denoted its coefficients or elements by $a(nm)$, where

---
$^{77}$ This was confirmed by Jordan, for he remarked: ‘It might indeed have been so . . . that when we [i.e., Born and Jordan] met again [in September 1925 in Göttingen], I had already written down to a large extent the first draft of the paper. (To be sure, I do not any longer have more accurate recollections concerning the details associated with it.) I think it is probable that the date of reception, i.e., 27 September 1925, represented entirely correctly the arrival of our manuscript at the journal’ (Jordan to van der Waerden, 8 October 1964).

$^{78}$ Arthur Cayley had written the arrays of coefficients between single vertical lines (Cayley, 1855, p. 282). Later, this notation became standard for determinants (see, e.g., in *Courant-Hilbert* and in Bôcher’s book).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0070 -->

66 Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task

the indices $n$ and $m$ referred to the $nth$ row and $mth$ column, respectively, with $n$, $m = 0, 1, 2, \dots. ^{78a}$ Thus, the matrix $\mathbf{a}$ could be written as

$$\mathbf{a} = (a(nm)) = \begin{pmatrix} a(00) & a(01) & a(02) & \dots \\ a(10) & a(11) & a(12) & \dots \\ a(20) & a(21) & a(22) & \dots \\ \vdots & & & \end{pmatrix}. \tag{70}$$

By putting the indices within round brackets instead of using lower indices as in mathematics (e.g., in Bôcher’s book or in *Courant–Hilbert*), Born and Jordan not only wished to indicate the relationship of their matrix elements with Heisenberg’s transition amplitudes, but also to retain the freedom of adding further (upper and lower) indices to the matrix itself should it be necessary—as, for instance, in describing systems having several degrees of freedom.

After introducing this notation they turned to the operations of addition

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0071 -->

II.2 Operations with Matrices 67

product with an arbitrary matrix is identical with that matrix), and the inverse, $\mathbf{a}^{-1}$, of a given matrix $\mathbf{a}$.

To achieve their goal of reformulating the laws of classical mechanics in terms of matrices, Born and Jordan also needed the concept of a function of matrices. This notion had already been considered by Arthur Cayley in his fundamental memoir on matrix methods. For example, in *Courant–Hilbert* such matrix functions $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{a})$ were considered as are polynomials of a given matrix, i.e., a sum of powers $\mathbf{a}^0 (= 1), \mathbf{a}^1, \mathbf{a}^2, \dots, \mathbf{a}^n$, where each term is multiplied with a constant coefficient. Even the exponential of a matrix was defined there as

$$\exp(\mathbf{a}) = \sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \frac{\mathbf{a}^\nu}{\nu!} = 1 + \mathbf{a} + \frac{1}{2!} \mathbf{a}^2 + \dots \qquad (71)$$

Thus, for the purpose of quantum-mechanical theory, Born and Jordan felt justified in admitting the use of the most general 'matrix functions' of matrices, $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_m)$, depending on $m$ matrix variables, $\mathbf{x}_k$ ($k = 1, \dots, m$), which can formally be represented as a sum of a finite or infinite number of products of powers of the $\mathbf{x}_k$ weighted by numerical coefficients. However, the functions $f(x_1, \dots, x_m)$, with $x_k$ ($k = 1, \dots, m$) known variables, do not describe the most general situation either in conventional analysis or in classical mechanics. Frequently one finds that the dependence of the unknown variables $y_l$ ($l = 1, \dots, n$), on the known variables $x_k$ is given only by a set of equations involving both the $x_k$ and $y_l$. Therefore, Born and Jordan had to re-interpret the functional dependence given by these equations in terms of matrices. Hence they also defined the functions $\mathbf{y}_l(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_m)$ through the equations

$$\mathbf{f}_1(\mathbf{y}_1, \dots, \mathbf{y}_n; \mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_m) = 0,$$

$$\mathbf{f}_n(\mathbf{y}_1, \dots, \mathbf{y}_n; \mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_m) = 0. \qquad (72)$$

They argued that such matrix functions made sense because of the following reason: if one assumes that the $\mathbf{y}_l$ ($l = 1, \dots, n$) can be expressed as a series of products in increasing powers of the $\mathbf{x}_k$ ($k = 1, \dots, m$), each term multiplied with an unknown coefficient, then one obtains the coefficients by inserting the power series *Ansatz* into Eqs. (72). They noted, however, that in the above procedure there was formally a difference with respect to classical theory in the manner of calculating the coefficients of the products of powers of $\mathbf{x}_k$:

> Naturally the number of equations and unknowns exceeds that which would ensue from applying the method of undetermined coefficients in the normal type of analysis incorporating *commutative* multiplication. In each of the equations [(72)], upon substituting the series for the $y_l$ and gathering together correlated terms, one obtains not only a summation term $C'x_1x_2$ but also a term $C''x_2x_1$ and has therefore to bring both $C'$ and $C''$ to vanish (not just only $C' + C''$). This is, however, made

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0072 -->

68 Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task

possible by the fact that in the expansion of each of the $\mathbf{y}_l$, two terms $x_1x_2$ and $x_2x_1$ appear with two available coefficients. (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 862)$^{79}$

The discussion of (matrix) functions of matrices signified much more than merely a technical point in the work of Born and Jordan. The development of classical mechanics from Newton to Hamilton had yielded the fundamental result that every dynamical variable of a given dynamical system could be expressed as a function of the sets of generalized position and momentum coordinates, $q_k$ and $p_k$ ($k = 1, \ldots, n$), where $n$ is the number of degrees of freedom. These functions representing the dynamical variables have the general form of series of products of powers of the $q_k$ and $p_k$. In formulating the new quantum mechanics rationally, Born had decided to stay as close to Hamiltonian mechanics as possible. Hence the recipe he and Jordan followed was to reinterpret all the classical dependences of dynamical variables, say $y_l$, on the canonical variables, say $x_k$ (i.e., the set of all $q_k$ and $p_k$ of the system under consideration), whose matrix form could be expressed by Eqs. (72). The important result of their investigation was that the reformulation could be achieved by taking into account the fundamental property of matrices, i.e., their noncommutativity, which had been known since the work of Cayley. The noncommutativity had been first discovered by Heisenberg to hold for dynamical variables in atomic systems. Born and Jordan went beyond Heisenberg by asking the principal question: Given any classical dynamical variable, is it possible to obtain the corresponding matrix expression by means of well-defined operations? In order to answer this question they had to go beyond the known rules of matrix algebra because the classical laws relating physical quantities or variables also involve other mathematical processes, such as the differentiation with respect to a parameter or a variable. What corresponded to such operations in the matrix theory?

One of the most important, if not *the* most important, parameters in classical dynamics is the time variable. Born and Jordan assumed that it plays the same role in quantum theory as well, and that time derivatives of matrices correspond to time derivatives of classical variables. They defined the time derivative of a matrix $\mathbf{a}$, just as in classical theory, by the equation

$$\frac{d\mathbf{a}}{dt} = \dot{\mathbf{a}} = \lim_{\tau \to 0} \frac{\mathbf{a}(t + \tau) - \mathbf{a}(t)}{\tau},$$ (73)

where $\mathbf{a}(t + \tau)$ and $\mathbf{a}(t)$ denote the matrices for neighbouring values of the time parameter, $t$ and $t + \tau$, respectively.$^{80}$ Then, by definition of the matrix product,

---
$^{79}$In their paper Born and Jordan did not go into the problem of convergence of infinite power series of matrices, which, for instance, was discussed in *Courant-Hilbert* (Chapter I, Section 2) in connection with the series $\sum_{\nu=0}^{\infty} \mathbf{a}^\nu$.

$^{80}$The definition of the derivative of a matrix with respect to a parameter can be copied from the definition of the derivative of a vector with respect to a parameter. Hence, although it was not contained in the books on matrix algebra, which Born and Jordan consulted, they had no difficulty in writing down Eq. (73).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0073 -->

II.2 Operations with Matrices **69**

Eq. (70a), its time derivative follows the usual rule of differentiation, that is,

$$ \frac{d}{dt} (\mathbf{ab}) = \dot{\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{b} + \mathbf{a}\dot{\mathbf{b}}. \tag{74} $$

With these relations one can easily define the time derivative of a matrix function, which is expressed as a finite or infinite sum of terms, each of the latter being a product of powers of matrices $\mathbf{x}_k$ ($k = 1, \dots, n$). In other words, the time derivative of an arbitrary analytic matrix function—i.e., a function which can be expanded, at least in certain domains of its variables, in power series—obtains a well-defined meaning. Evidently, the derivatives of matrices and matrix functions with respect to parameters other than the time may be handled in the same manner.

While the differentiation of matrices with respect to a parameter presented no difficulties (because one could proceed in conformity with the usual method of analysis), the differentiation of a matrix with respect to another matrix appeared to be a different matter altogether. For this purpose, Born and Jordan introduced ‘symbolic differentiation,’ noting right away that ‘only in a few respects does this process display similarity to that of differentiation in ordinary analysis. For example, the rules of differentiation of a product or of a function of a function no longer apply here in general’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 862). Only in case that all matrices, which occur in the expressions whose derivative one wants to obtain, do commute with one another, the rules of conventional analysis should still hold. Born and Jordan explicitly considered the differentiation of a product of matrices,

$$ \mathbf{y} = \prod_{m=1}^{s} \mathbf{x}_{l_m} = \mathbf{x}_{l_1}\mathbf{x}_{l_2} \dots \mathbf{x}_{l_s}, \tag{75} $$

with respect to one of its factors. In Eq. (75), the indices $l_1, \dots, l_s$, may denote any of the indices $1, \dots, n$, of a set of $n$ matrices $\mathbf{x}_k$; that is, the function $\mathbf{y}$ is a general product of powers of the matrices $\mathbf{x}_k$, embracing also products of the type $\mathbf{x}_1^2\mathbf{x}_2\mathbf{x}_1\mathbf{x}_3$. The partial derivative of $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}_k$ is then defined as

$$ \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} = \sum_{r=1}^{s} \delta_{l_r,k} \prod_{m=r+1}^{s} \mathbf{x}_{l_m} \prod_{m=1}^{r-1} \mathbf{x}_{l_m}, \tag{76} $$

where $\delta_{jk}$ is the Kronecker symbol, which is unity for identical indices ($j = k$) and zero otherwise ($j \neq k$).^81

^81 At first sight, the definition of the matrix differentiation of a product, given by Eq. (76), looks unnecessarily complicated. One could surely imagine—as the theoreticians did invent later—a different and simpler definition. This definition was probably due to Jordan, for as Born remarked: ‘This was certainly merely an invention of Jordan. Perhaps I helped, but I had the feeling that doing such things was not in my line’ (Born, Conversations, p. 38). In inventing the symbolic matrix differentiation, Jordan was also motivated by physical considerations, as we shall discuss in connection with the formulation of the variational principle.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0074 -->

70 Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task

The complicated prescription according to Eq. (76) follows the usual rules of differentiation in analysis only if the product **y**, Eq. (75), has a special form; e.g., if **y** is simply a power of one variable, say $\mathbf{x}_1^s$. Already in the case that **y** is a product of powers of two variables, say $\mathbf{x}_1^n \mathbf{x}_2^m$, the rule leads to the result

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}_1} (\mathbf{x}_1^n \mathbf{x}_2^m) = \mathbf{x}_1^{n-1} \mathbf{x}_2^m + \mathbf{x}_1^{n-2} \mathbf{x}_2^m \mathbf{x}_1 + \dots + \mathbf{x}_2^m \mathbf{x}_1^{n-1}, \quad (76\text{a})$$

which is different from the result $n \mathbf{x}_1^{n-1} \mathbf{x}_2^m$ that would be expected from the usual analysis with commuting quantities. However, for a sum of matrices the usual differentiation rule holds; in particular,

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} (\mathbf{y}_1 + \mathbf{y}_2) = \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}_1}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{y}_2}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k}, \quad (77)$$

where $\mathbf{y}_1$ and $\mathbf{y}_2$ are any two products of the form given by Eq. (75).

The two rules of symbolic matrix differentiation, stated in Eqs. (76) and (77), uniquely determine the derivative of the most general analytic matrix function. Born and Jordan pointed out that the apparently complicated rules can be expressed in a simple way by using the concept of the 'diagonal sum,' i.e., of the trace of a matrix, which is defined as the sum of all diagonal elements of a matrix, that is,

$$D(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} y(nn), \quad (78)$$

where $y(nn)$ denote the diagonal elements of the matrix **y**. Then the matrix element in the *mth row and nth column* of the derivative $\partial \mathbf{y} / \partial \mathbf{x}_k$ becomes identical with the derivative of $D(\mathbf{y})$ with respect to the element $\mathbf{x}_k(nm)$ in *the nth row and mth column* of the matrix $\mathbf{x}_k$, or

$$\frac{\partial \mathbf{y}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} (mn) = \frac{\partial D(\mathbf{y})}{\partial x_k(nm)}, \quad n, m = 0, 1, \dots . \quad (79)$$

Born and Jordan proved this result with the help of the multiplication rule, Eq. (70a), for matrices having the product form given in Eq. (75); it may easily be extended because of the sum-rule, Eq. (77), to all analytic functions. The definition of the matrix derivative through Eq. (79) not only looks more compact than the equivalent definition through Eqs. (76) and a subsequent application of Eq. (77); it also possesses two further advantages. First, it helps occasionally in actual calculations on account of the special properties of the trace. For example, the trace of a product of two matrices, $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$, has the following property: if $D(\mathbf{x}_1 \mathbf{x}_2) \left(= \sum_{n,k} x_1(nk)x_2(kn)\right)$ assumes a finite value, then this value does not depend upon the order of the factors $\mathbf{x}_1$ and $\mathbf{x}_2$—because in that case the two sums over $k$ and $n$ in the trace of the matrix product may be exchanged, which

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0075 -->

II.2 Operations with Matrices                                                             71

implies the identity of $D(\mathbf{x}_1 \mathbf{x}_2)$ and $D(\mathbf{x}_2 \mathbf{x}_1)$. A similar property holds for the trace of a product matrix $\mathbf{y}$ having the form given by Eq. (75); $D(\mathbf{x}_{l_1} \mathbf{x}_{l_2} \dots \mathbf{x}_{l_s})$ does not change its value if the factors in the matrix product are permuted cyclically, i.e., $D(\mathbf{x}_{l_1} \mathbf{x}_{l_2} \dots \mathbf{x}_{l_s})$ is equal to $D(\mathbf{x}_{l_r} \mathbf{x}_{l_{r+1}} \dots \mathbf{x}_{l_s} \mathbf{x}_{l_1} \dots \mathbf{x}_{l_{r-1}})$, $r = 1, \dots, s$. Hence the partial derivative of the product matrix $\mathbf{x}_{l_1} \mathbf{x}_{l_2} \dots \mathbf{x}_{l_s}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}_k$ remains the same if one permutes the factors in a cyclic manner. The second advantage of the definition of the derivative through Eq. (79) lay in the fact that it allowed Born and Jordan to formulate the variational principle of classical mechanics in a simple and compact way also in quantum mechanics.

Besides concerning themselves with the symbolic matrix differentiation and some of its implications, Born and Jordan drew attention to another important property

72  
**Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task**

# II.3 Dynamical Laws and Energy Conservation

In order to formulate quantum mechanics in matrix form, Born and Jordan first assembled the known facts of matrix algebra and added a few new definitions, such as the one concerning matrix differentiation.⁸² With the help of these purely mathematical concepts and methods they then proceeded to develop matrix mechanics. As a first step, they looked for the proper expressions for Heisenberg’s ideas in matrix language; after that they generalized these results. They discovered immediately that, instead of using the Newtonian equations of motion as Heisenberg had done, they could equally well start from the Hamiltonian scheme of dynamics. They showed, in particular, that the quantum dynamical laws followed, like the corresponding classical ones, from a fundamental variational principle. Moreover, they found that one of the basic conservation laws of classical mechanics, the one ensuring energy conservation, also held in quantum mechanics, and that the quantum-theoretical frequency condition followed automatically from their matrix scheme.⁸³

Of these steps, the translation of Heisenberg’s ideas about transition amplitudes, the multiplication rule, etc., came about most easily. Born and Jordan started right away from the concept of transition amplitudes, i.e., the assembly of terms occurring in the quantum-theoretical analogue of classical Fourier series describing multiply periodic systems. According to Heisenberg these terms could be written as \( q(nm) \exp[2\pi i \nu(nm)] \) (\( n,m = 0, 1, 2, \ldots \)), where the quantum-theoretical frequency \( \nu(nm) \) is associated with the transition from the stationary state of the system denoted by the index \( n \) to the stationary state denoted by \( m \).⁸⁴ Heisenberg had further required that the coefficients, \( q(nm) \) and \( q(mn) \), which describe the amplitudes of the transition and its inverse, are complex conjugates of each other, and their absolute values, \( |q(nm)| \) and \( |q(mn)| \), should be the same. Born and Jordan now recognized that Heisenberg’s arrays of quantum-theoretical amplitudes could be written in matrix form as

\[
\mathbf{q} = \left( q(nm) \exp\left[2\pi i \nu(nm) t\right] \right). \tag{82a}
\]

The matrix \( \mathbf{q} \) was thus supposed to represent the position coordinate of a quantum-mechanical system. Similarly, the canonically conjugate momentum variable had to be given by a matrix \( \mathbf{p} \), where

\[
\mathbf{p} = \left( p(nm) \exp\left[2\pi i \nu(nm) t\right] \right). \tag{82b}
\]

They noted that ‘the matrices have to be Hermitian, i.e., on transposition of the

---

II.3 Dynamical Laws and Energy Conservation 73

matrices, each element is to go over into its conjugate complex value, a condition which should apply for all real $t'$ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 866). With these words they introduced into physics a new concept, that of Hermitian matrices. What Born and Jordan called Hermitian matrices go back indeed to Charles Hermite, who introduced in the theory of quadratic forms certain substitutions in order to reduce, say, a quadratic form of $n$ variables to a sum of squares (Hermite, 1854).⁸⁵ In case the coefficients of these substitutions are real, the related matrix becomes identical with its transpose; in case the coefficients are complex quantities, the real part constitutes a symmetric matrix and the imaginary part an antisymmetric matrix. Hermitian matrices or Hermitian (quadratic or bilinear) forms of finitely many variables had been applied in the second half of the nineteenth century to various problems of mathematics, especially in the theory of invariants and in number theory. Later, David Hilbert, in the last section of his fourth communication to the theory of linear integral equations, had also discussed quadratic Hermitian forms of infinitely many variables (Hilbert, 1906a, Section XII). He had proved, for instance, that compact forms of that type—i.e., Hermitian forms whose real and imaginary parts are separately compact—possess a discrete spectrum of eigenvalues and can be reduced to a sum of squares. Now in quantum mechanics Hermitian forms, or the related matrices or operators, would find their most important application and become known to all theoretical physicists. Born and Jordan observed that many quantum-theoretical facts fitted naturally into their matrix scheme. For example, the empirical frequency sum-rule

$$\nu(jk) + \nu(kl) + \nu(lj) = 0, \tag{83}$$

which expresses the fact that the frequencies associated with transitions from a given stationary state (index $j$) via intermediary states (indices $k$ and $l$) back to the initial state add to zero, could be obtained by considering the diagonal elements of a product of three matrices of the type of Eq. (82a). Further, they incorporated the frequency condition

$$h\nu(nm) = W_n - W_m, \tag{84}$$

⁸⁵Charles Hermite, born in Dieuze, Lorraine, on 24 December 1822, received his education at the *Lycée Louis-le-Grand* in Paris (1840–1842) and at the *École Polytechnique* (1842–1843), but graduated only in 1848 from the latter because he did poorly in examinations. After holding minor teaching positions at the *École Polytechnique* and at the *Collège de France*, he finally became professor at the *École Normale* in 1869 and at the Sorbonne in 1870. Hermite retired in 1897 and died on 14 January 1901 in Paris.

Mathematically productive since the age of twenty, Hermite was one of the principal developers of the theory of algebraic forms, especially quadratic forms, and he contributed importantly to the theory of elliptic and Abelian functions. He was a master of elegant methods and his proofs had artistic quality. He succeeded in giving the solution of a general quintic equation by means of elliptic modular functions, and in showing that the number $e$ (the base of natural logarithms) is transcendental. Hermite was a generous man, who encouraged many young mathematicians in their first work. He was honoured by a foreign membership of the Royal Society (1873) and election to the Academy of Sciences, Paris (1892).

II.3 Dynamical Laws and Energy Conservation 75

motion under the influence of magnetic fields. For in this latter case, the function H cannot in a Cartesian coordinate system any longer be represented by a sum of two functions of which one depends only on the momenta and the other on the coordinates. (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 868)

In treating such systems a difficulty arises because the symbolic matrix differentiation, as defined by Eq. (76), seems to spoil the Hamiltonian scheme completely. For a given matrix H, it yields equations of motion which have a different structure from the ones in classical theory, although in the correspondence limit the quantum-theoretical equations would approach again the classical ones. The difficulty could be traced, of course, to the noncommutativity of the matrices p and q, which leads to an ambiguity in the products consisting of factors p and q. And yet, the differentiation rule (76) from which the ambiguity arose also provided its resolution, and it was for this reason that Born and Jordan invoked their 'correspondence argument.' In particular, they referred to the fact that in classical dynamics the equations of motion of a given system can be derived from an action principle, i.e., the condition that the time integral L, the Lagrangian function of the system, assumes an extremum when the actual path during the time interval between t₀ and t₁ is taken, or

$$\int_{t_0}^{t_1} L dt = \int_{t_0}^{t_1} (p\dot{q} - H(p, q)) dt. \tag{88a}$$

To reformulate condition (88a) in quantum mechanics, Born and Jordan introduced the Lagrangian matrix function L, which is defined formally as in classical theory. They further argued that in the case of a sufficiently large time interval, t₁ - t₀, only constant terms of L contribute to the integral. Hence they suggested that the integration condition (88a) could be replaced by the summation condition

$$D(L) = D(p\dot{q} - H(p, q)) = \text{extremum}, \tag{88b}$$

where D denotes the diagonal sum and the matrices p and q have to be varied for fixed frequencies ν(nm) of the system. This variational principle in quantum mechanics then yielded immediately the Hamiltonian equations of motion. Since the derivatives of D(L) with respect to any element of the actual matrix variables, p and q, of the system must be zero, the equations

$$2\pi i \nu(nm) q(nm) = \frac{\partial D(H)}{\partial p(mn)} \tag{89a}$$

and

$$2\pi i \nu(mn) p(nm) = -2\pi i \nu(nm) p(nm) = \frac{\partial D(H)}{\partial q(mn)} \tag{89b}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0080 -->

76 Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task

followed for all indices $n$ and $m$ $(= 0, 1, 2, \dots)$. By referring to the matrix differentiation rule, Eq. (79), Born and Jordan immediately noticed that Eqs. (89a, b) led to the usual equations of motion of the Hamiltonian scheme, even for the matrix variables $\mathbf{q}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ of quantum-mechanical systems that have arbitrary Hamiltonian matrix functions $\mathbf{H} (= \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}))$. That is, the equations of motion assumed the canonical form,

$$ \dot{\mathbf{q}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial \mathbf{p}} \tag{90a} $$

and

$$ \dot{\mathbf{p}} = - \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial \mathbf{q}}, \tag{90b} $$

provided the variational principle, Eq. (88b), held.

That a variational principle should be valid also in matrix mechanics seemed evident to Born and Jordan. Indeed, the need for variational principles to govern the laws of physics was clearly recognized by Born throughout his work on atomic problems, although David Hilbert had already held this belief before him.$^{86}$ Even when Born had encountered serious difficulties concerning the validity of the application of classical mechanics to such problems of atomic theory as the calculation of the helium states, he nevertheless had continued to think that ‘the real quantum mechanics must retain the [complete] Hamiltonian formalism’ (Born, *Conversations*, p. 40). It was from this point of view that he had written his *Vorlesungen über Atommechanik* (Born, 1925), which contained, so he believed, those parts of the old atomic theory which had the possibility of surviving in a future theory. And the variational principle was the very foundation of the Hamiltonian formalism; hence Born believed that the most satisfactory formulation of the new quantum theory of atoms would start from a variational principle. Now he was glad that, with Jordan’s help, he had succeeded in expressing the variational principle in matrix mechanics in the simple form of Eq. (88b), and he regarded the derivation of the Hamiltonian equations of motion, Eqs. (90a, b), as a triumph of the variational methods. However, one might argue that the existence of the variational principle is not a *necessary* prerequisite of the dynamical equations in quantum mechanics, for one could just as well postulate the Hamiltonian equations of motion as the foundation of the theory.$^{87}$

***

$^{86}$ David Hilbert had discussed the application of the variational principle to various problems of physics, especially to the theory of gravitation and matter (Hilbert, 1915, 1917). Also in his lectures on the foundations of quantum theory in winter semester 1922–1923 (see footnote 63), he had attributed a leading role to the variational principle in atomic theory.

$^{87}$ The preference for deriving the dynamical relations from a variational principle was very much connected with Hilbert and his school in Göttingen and was not shared by theoreticians in general. Thus, Wolfgang Pauli, in his *Encyklopädie* article on relativity, already had criticized Hilbert’s derivation of the field equations of gravitation by means of postulating a variational principle (see Pauli, 1921b, p. 705, footnote 277). In 1925 he attributed Born’s insistence on a variational principle in quantum mechanics to what he called ‘Göttingen’s deluge of formal learning’ (‘*Göttinger Gelehrsamkeitsschwall*’, Pauli to Kronig, 9 October 1925).

II.3 Dynamical Laws and Energy Conservation 77

Quantum mechanics was, of course, not determined completely by reformulating the equations of motion of the corresponding classical theory in matrix form. In addition, the dynamical matrix variables, **q** and **p**, of a quantum system (with one degree of freedom) had to satisfy the re-interpreted quantum condition, Eq. (67). This matrix equation, which they called the ‘sharpened’ (*verschärfte*, Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 871) quantum condition, yielded important information about the structure of matrices which represent the variables in quantum mechanics. By taking the trace on both sides of Eq. (67), Born and Jordan showed that the matrices **p** and **q** could not be finite because for two finite matrices the difference of the traces $D(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})$ and $D(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p})$ must be zero. Even more, the matrix products did not even have finite traces and the same held for their difference. Hence Born and Jordan concluded that ‘they do not belong to the class of “bounded” infinite matrices hitherto almost exclusively investigated by mathematicians’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 870, footnote (1)). This observation confronted the physicists with serious mathematical difficulties because they were not allowed to take over the well-known mathematical results of the theory of infinite matrices—such as Hilbert’s (1906a)—but had to examine carefully the theorems used in each case separately. Their situation resembled somewhat the one which G. W. Hill had encountered fifty years earlier in dealing with infinite determinants in lunar theory; and, like Hill, Born and Jordan had now to justify their mathematical procedure by pointing to the reasonableness of the physical results obtained therewith. In the early steps of the matrix formulation of quantum-mechanical relations, they could only hope that their methods would be justified *a posteriori*. Their lack of caution in running around the minefield of the theory of infinite matrices, picking and choosing what might be useful, only enhanced their confidence as pioneers in the new theory of quantum mechanics.⁸⁸

While Born and Jordan did not concern themselves with a detailed justification of their mathematical methods, they were eager to derive consequences from their quantum-theoretical scheme. As one of the most important they considered the proof of energy conservation, in particular of the fact that the Hamiltonian matrix of a mechanical system (whose analogue in classical theory was a conserved quantity) did not change in time. For this purpose they first restricted themselves to a periodic system having one degree of freedom, described by the Hamiltonian H,

$$
\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{H}_1(\mathbf{p}) + \mathbf{H}_2(\mathbf{q}), \tag{91}
$$

where the first term on the right-hand side depends on the momentum variable **p** and the second on the position coordinate **q**. The functions $\mathbf{H}_1(\mathbf{p})$ and $\mathbf{H}_2(\mathbf{q})$ were assumed to be power series of their variables, say $\sum_s a_s \mathbf{p}^s$ and $\sum_s b_s \mathbf{q}^s$, with constant coefficients $a_s$ and $b_s$. Many systems in mechanics indeed possess such a

78
Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task

Hamiltonian function, which is called a ‘separable’ Hamiltonian. A particular example of such a system was the anharmonic oscillator treated by Heisenberg: in that H₁ had the form $(1/2m)\mathbf{p}^2$, $m$ being the oscillating mass, and H₂ was either $(m/2)\omega_0^2\mathbf{q}^2 + (\lambda/3)\mathbf{q}^3$ or $(m/2)\omega_0^2\mathbf{q}^2 + (\lambda/4)\mathbf{q}^4$, with $\omega_0$ the frequency constant and $\lambda$ the parameter of anharmonicity.$^{89}$ All Hamiltonians of the type (91) share the property that differentiation with respect to the dynamical variables can be carried out easily because only one of the terms, H₁ or H₂, has to be considered and the differentiation rule of classical theory holds.
For the purpose of proving energy conservation Born and Jordan proceeded as follows. First, they showed that the Hamiltonian equations of motion, Eqs. (90a, b), can be replaced by the equivalent algebraic equations,

$$
\dot{\mathbf{q}} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathrm{H}\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q}\mathrm{H})
$$

(92a)

and

$$
\dot{\mathbf{p}} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathrm{H}\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}\mathrm{H}),
$$

(92b)

involving only the differences of the products of the variables $\mathbf{q}$ and $\mathbf{p}$ with the Hamiltonian matrix. They derived these equations by replacing the partial derivatives, $\partial\mathrm{H}/\partial\mathbf{p}$ and $\partial\mathrm{H}/\partial\mathbf{q}$, by the terms $\partial\mathrm{H}_1(\mathbf{p})/\partial\mathbf{p}$ and $\partial\mathrm{H}_2(\mathbf{q})/\partial\mathbf{q}$, and taking into account the relations

$$
\frac{\partial\mathrm{H}_1(\mathbf{p})}{\partial\mathbf{p}} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} \left[ \mathrm{H}_1(\mathbf{p})\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q}\mathrm{H}_1(\mathbf{p}) \right]
$$

(93a)

and

$$
\frac{\partial\mathrm{H}_2(\mathbf{q})}{\partial\mathbf{q}} = -\frac{2\pi i}{h} \left[ \mathrm{H}_2(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}\mathrm{H}_2(\mathbf{q}) \right],
$$

(93b)

which followed from repeated application of the quantum condition, Eq. (67). For separable Hamiltonians the right-hand sides of Eqs. (93a, b) do not change if H₁ and H₂ are replaced by the full Hamiltonian matrix H; thus Eqs. (92a, b) follow at once.
From the new equations of motion, Born and Jordan concluded that for any analytic function $\mathbf{g}\;(= \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}))$ of the momentum and position variables, the time derivative is also given by the equation$^{90}$

$$
\dot{\mathbf{g}} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathrm{H}\mathbf{g} - \mathbf{g}\mathrm{H}).
$$

(94)

$^{89}$It is reasonable to assume that Jordan first proved energy conservation in the case of the anharmonic oscillator and reported about it to Heisenberg in late August 1925. (See Heisenberg to Jordan, 10 September 1925.)
$^{90}$Born and Jordan introduced the notation $\begin{Bmatrix} \mathrm{H} \\ \mathbf{g} \end{Bmatrix}$ for the difference of the matrix products, $\mathrm{H}\mathbf{g} - \mathbf{g}\mathrm{H}$ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 872). Just a few weeks later, Paul Dirac in Cambridge made a fundamental use of this difference, identifying it—up to the factor $h/2\pi i$—with the quantum-theoretical analogue of the classical Poisson bracket (Dirac, 1925d).

II.3 Dynamical Laws and Energy Conservation  
79  

Finally, if they substituted the Hamiltonian matrix **H**, Eq. (91), for the variable **g** in Eq. (94), they obtained the equation  

$$\dot{H} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (HH - HH) = 0.$$ (95)  

Thus, energy conservation was proved to be satisfied *for all quantum systems whose Hamiltonian matrix is separable*. Moreover, Born and Jordan had succeeded, almost without any calculation, in what Heisenberg had attempted to show in the case of the one-dimensional anharmonic oscillator in perturbation approximation. Since, according to the definition of Hermitian matrices (see Eqs. (82)), the Hamiltonian **H** must then be a diagonal matrix, they derived from Eqs. (92) the relations  

$$h\nu(nm) \quad q(nm) = [H(nn) - H(mm)]q(nm) \tag{96a}$$  

and  

$$h\nu(nm) \quad p(nm) = [H(nn) - H(mm)]p(nm). \tag{96b}$$  

A similar result holds for any dynamical variable because of Eq. (94). Thus, Born and Jordan also arrived at another important goal: a proof of Bohr’s frequency condition, which assumed the form,  

$$h\nu(nm) = H(nn) - H(mm), \quad \text{for } n,m = 0,1,2,\dots,$$ (97)  

in matrix mechanics.<sup>91</sup>  

What was still lacking was the treatment of systems described by a Hamiltonian function which is not separable in the variables **p** and **q**, i.e., it contains such products as **p**<sup>s</sup>**q**<sup>r</sup>. Born and Jordan did not succeed in proving that such a Hamiltonian must always be a diagonal matrix in their scheme. Instead they proposed the following procedure. For an arbitrary nonseparable Hamiltonian, say **H***, they constructed another matrix, **H**, which contained, say, instead of a term **p**<sup>2</sup>**q**, the symmetrized sum $\frac{1}{3}(\mathbf{p}^2\mathbf{q} + \mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q}\mathbf{p}^2)$. Then, by direct calculation, they proved the theorem: ‘*To each function* **H*** = **H**(**p**, **q**) *there can be assigned a function* **H** = **H**(**p**, **q**) *such that as Hamiltonians* **H*** *and* **H** *yield the same equations of motion and that for these equations of motion* **H** *assumes the role of an energy which is constant in time and fulfills the frequency condition*’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, pp. 872–873).  

Born and Jordan had thus absorbed all the necessary physical conceptions, including the re-interpreted quantum conditions, into their scheme of matrix mechanics. Moreover, they had been able to state explicitly the fundamental

postulates of the new theory: such as the use of Hermitian matrices for representing dynamical variables; the existence of a time-independent, i.e., diagonal, Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}$; and the fact that the matrix which expresses the difference of the products $\mathbf{pq}$ and $\mathbf{qp}$ in the dynamical problem (whose momentum and position variables are $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$) should be diagonal simultaneously with $\mathbf{H}$. By giving these formal requirements, which had to be satisfied in treating any dynamical problem—at least any which possessed one degree of freedom—Born and Jordan had replaced Heisenberg’s intuitive approach by a systematic method which was applicable generally.

## II.4 An Example of Discrete Mechanics: The Oscillator

In formulating matrix mechanics Born and Jordan had embarked upon the ambitious goal of ‘constructing an entirely self-contained theory, without the need to invoke assistance from classical theory on the basis of the correspondence principle’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 876). This meant in particular that for calculations with quantum systems one had to rely entirely on the matrix reformulation of the dynamical equations and the ‘sharpened’ quantum condition—at least as long as the matrix reformulation involved no ambiguity. Any further reference to the analogous classical system, which had previously been used again and again together with correspondence arguments, should be superfluous because the real content of Bohr’s correspondence principle had already been fully absorbed in the reformulation prescription. Born and Jordan chose the anharmonic oscillator to illustrate how the matrix methods worked in a simple practical example. They proceeded in two steps: first, they constructed the sequence of energy states of the harmonic oscillator; then they developed a matrix mechanical perturbation method for obtaining the energy states of the anharmonic oscillator.

The Hamiltonian matrix of the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator, whose mass is normalized to unity for convenience, may evidently be written as

$$H = \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{p}^2 + \frac{1}{2} \omega_0^2 \mathbf{q}^2, \qquad (98)$$

where $\omega_0$ is a parameter determining the strength of the restoring force. The momentum matrix, $\mathbf{p}$, is given by the time derivative of $\mathbf{q}$, the position matrix, and the equation of motion becomes

$$\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \omega_0^2 \mathbf{q} = 0. \qquad (99)$$

This *matrix equation* is equivalent to *infinitely many algebraic equations* for $q(nm)$, the infinitely many elements of the Hermitian matrix $\mathbf{q}$, which have the form given by Eq. (82a). Each of these equations, or explicitly,

$$\left[\nu^2(nm) - \nu_0^2\right]q(nm) = 0 \qquad (99a)$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0085 -->

II.4  An Example of Discrete Mechanics: The Oscillator 81

(where $\nu_0 = \omega_0/2\pi$ is a constant of the Hamiltonian describing the system, and $n, m = 0, 1, 2, \dots$) involves one particular matrix element $q(nm).^{92}$ Thus it follows that either this matrix element is zero or the absolute value of the transition frequency connected with it, which is assumed to be related to the energy states through Eq. (84), is given by the constant value $\nu_0$. However, from the application of quantum condition, Eq. (67), it follows that not all matrix elements $q(nm)$ can be zero. In the case of finite $q(nm)$, then, Eq. (99a) implies a strict condition for the absolute value of the energy differences, $W_n - W_m$, of the harmonic oscillator that can be stated as follows: For each index $n$ (denoting a row in the infinite matrix representing a quantum-mechanical variable) there must exist a corresponding index $n'$ (denoting a column) such that $q(nn') \neq 0$ and

$$|W_n - W_{n'}| = h\nu_0. \quad (100)$$

Assuming further that *all energy eigenvalues are different*, or $W_n \neq W_m$ if $m \neq n$ —which appears to be reasonable since the classical one-dimensional harmonic oscillator is a nondegenerate system—one may in fact conclude that, for a given $n$, there are in general two indices, $n'$ and $n''$, which satisfy Eq. (100). That is, for any given $W_n$ exactly two different values, $W_{n'}$ and $W_{n''}$, satisfy Eq. (100), and the corresponding transition frequencies are

$$\nu(nn'') = - \nu(nn') = \nu_0. \quad (101)$$

Turning now to the elements of the Hamiltonian matrix (98), written as

$$H(nm) = 2\pi^2 \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} q(nk)q(km) [\nu_0^2 - \nu(nk)\nu(km)], \quad (102)$$

one can see that, in view of Eqs. (99a), only the diagonal elements, $H(nn)$, are different from zero. Each of these diagonal elements, that is,

$$H(nn) = 4\pi^2 \nu_0^2 [|q(nn')|^2 + |q(nn'')|^2], \quad (103)$$

consists of two terms at most, both of which are larger than or equal to zero. Hence the Hamiltonian matrix of the harmonic oscillator is positive definite, and the energy eigenvalues, $W_n$ $(= H(nn))$, have at least a lower bound zero. Moreover, since Born and Jordan had assumed all energy eigenvalues to be different, there had to exist one *uniquely defined lowest or ground state*, say $W_{n_0}$.
The existence of the lowest energy state could be used for two purposes: first, to calculate—as Heisenberg had proposed previously (Heisenberg, 1925c)—the absolute values of the transition amplitudes $q

*order* of the elements in the infinite matrix **q**. The key for doing so was provided by the quantum condition (67) which, in the case of the harmonic oscillator, assumed the form of equations

$$|q(nn')|^2 - |q(nn'')|^2 = \frac{h}{8\pi^2\nu_0} . \tag{104}$$

For the index $n_0$, associated with the ground state, the second term on the left-hand side of Eq. (104) becomes zero because the state $n''$ is supposed to have a lower energy than the state $n$ which is excluded. The value of $|q(n_0n'_0)|^2$ is then substituted in Eq. (103), yielding the energy $\frac{1}{2}h\nu_0$ for the ground state. Born and Jordan now denoted $n'_0$ by $n_1$ and obtained from the quantum condition the equation

$$|q(n_1n'_1)|^2 - |q(n_1n''_1)|^2 = \frac{h}{8\pi^2\nu_0} . \tag{104a}$$

The second term on the left-hand side of this equation was already known to be equal to $|q(n_1n_0)|^2$ ($= |q(n_0n'_0)|^2$); hence it was possible to calculate the value of the first term, and with it the energy value of the first excited state. Next, denoting $n'_1$ by $n_2$, etc., Born and Jordan continued this procedure and obtained the general formulae for the absolute square of the matrix elements,

$$|q(n_k, n_{k+1})|^2 = \frac{h}{8\pi^2\nu_0} (k+1), \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots, \tag{105}$$

as well as for the energy terms,

$$W_{n_k} = h\nu_0(k + \frac{1}{2}), \quad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots . \tag{106}$$

Equation (106) gives a clear order to the energy states of the harmonic oscillator. Any state $n$ must be contained in the set of states $n_k$, the reason being that the energy states $W_{n_k}$ are nondegenerate and $W_{n_0}$ is uniquely fixed. 'This proves,' Born and Jordan concluded, 'that the indices $0, 1, 2, 3, \dots$ can be arranged into a new sequence $n_0, n_1, n_2, n_3, \dots$ such that the formulae [(105)] and [(106)] apply' (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 878). With these new indices the solution for the matrix **q** assumed the form

$$q = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & q(01) & 0 & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ q(10) & 0 & q(12) & 0 & 0 & \dots \\ 0 & q(21) & 0 & q(23) & 0 & \dots \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \ddots \end{pmatrix}, \tag{107}$$

which Born and Jordan called the 'normal form.' In this standard arrangement

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0087 -->

II.4 An Example of Discrete Mechanics: The Oscillator 83

of indices the energy values, $W_n (= H(nn))$, increase with increasing $n$. 'If inversely, one requires that $W_n = H(nn)$ should always increase with $n$,' they noted, 'then it necessarily follows that $n_k = k \dots \dots$. But thereby only the notation becomes fixed and the calculation more transparent: nothing new is conferred *physically*' (Born and Jordan, 1925b, pp. 878–879).

Thus, two facts made it possible to bring the elements of the matrix $\mathbf{q}$ (and thereby also the elements of the matrices representing other dynamical variables like $\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{H}$, etc.) into the 'normal form': the quantum condition, Eq. (104), which ensured the discreteness of the states, and the positivity of the Hamiltonian matrix elements, Eq. (103), leading to the existence of a ground state. No further postulates were necessary to establish the matrix $\mathbf{q}$, Eq. (107), which had been obtained earlier by Heisenberg by guessing from classical theory, and the full solution of the harmonic oscillator, especially its stationary states, could be calculated. Born and Jordan summarized the achievements of their new matrix scheme as follows:

> Therein lies a profound difference between this and the previously adopted semi-classical determination of the stationary states. The classically calculated orbits merge into one another continuously; consequently the quantum orbits selected at a later stage have a particular sequence right from the outset. The new [quantum] mechanics presents itself as a truly discontinuous theory in that herein there is no question of such a sequence of quantum states defined by the physical process; rather the quantum numbers are indeed no more than distinguishing indices which can be ordered and normalized according to any practical standpoint whatsoever (e.g., according to increasing energy $W_n$). (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 879)

In the solution of the harmonic oscillator problem Born and Jordan demonstrated the conceptual differences between a consistent quantum theory and the earlier semiclassical recipes. After this demonstration of principles they were able to deal with more sophisticated systems, especially the anharmonic oscillator.
In the case of the anharmonic oscillator, described by the equation of motion,

$$\ddot{q} + \omega_0^2 q + \lambda q^2 = 0, \tag{108}$$

where $\lambda q^2$ is a small perturbation term, Born and Jordan obtained the solution in the following way. They expanded the position matrix $\mathbf{q}$ in a series of terms multiplied by increasing powers of the parameter $\lambda$, which implied the subsequent expansions of the matrix elements $q(nm)$, that is,

$$q(nm) = q^{(0)}(nm) + \lambda q^{(1)}(nm) + \lambda^2 q^{(2)}(nm) + \dots, \tag{109a}$$

and of the related transition frequencies $\nu(nm)$, that is,

$$\nu(nm) = \nu^{(0)}(nm) + \lambda \nu^{(1)}(nm) + \lambda^2 \nu^{(2)}(nm) + \dots \tag{109b}$$

They did the same with the second time derivative, $\ddot{q}$, and $\mathbf{q}^2$, the square of the

$$q^{(1)}(n, n - 1) = 0, \tag{112b}$$

The latter yielded the finite transition amplitudes $q(n, n - 3) (n = 4, 5, \dots)$, as well as the corrections to the amplitudes $q(n, n - 1) (n = 1, 2, \dots)$ and to the related frequencies $\nu(n, n - 1)$.
With one exception all first- and second-order contributions to the position matrix of the anharmonic oscillator thus calculated were expressed in terms of the known quantities of the harmonic oscillator solution. The exception occurred in the matrix element $q(n, n - 1)$, whose second-order correction, that is,

$$q^{(2)}(n, n - 1) = \frac{11}{18\omega_0^4} (Cn)^{3/2} \exp(i\psi_{n-1}), \tag{113}$$

included a phase $\psi_{n-1}$ which was not related to the phase $\phi_{n-1}$ of the harmonic oscillator occurring in Eq. (110). Born and Jordan expressed the hope that this arbitrariness—because the extra phase seemed to have no explanation—would be removed in the next order of approximation (which they did not calculate). However, at this point they noted: ‘We have to leave this question open here but we should like to indicate its significance as a point of principle in regard to the completeness of the entire theory. All questions of statistics invariably depend finally upon whether or not our supposition that of the phases of the $q(nm)$ one in each row (or each column) of the matrix remains undetermined be valid’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 881). In other words, the problem of determining the phases $\psi_n$ had to be solved later on by means of a systematic perturbation theory.$^{94}$
Assuming for the moment the identity of $\psi_n$ and $\phi_n$, Born and Jordan had arrived at the matrix mechanical solution of the anharmonic oscillator problem up to terms of order $\lambda^2$; they had calculated the elements of the position matrix $\mathbf{q}$

This matrix was in the normal form from the zeroth-order approximation onwards because it appeared evident that the perturbation term did not change the order of the states as obtained for the harmonic oscillator. The energy matrix, which is of course diagonal, could be calculated from q and the canonically conjugate momentum p ($= \dot{q}$) by adding a term $(\lambda/3)\mathbf{q}^3$ to the Hamiltonian (98). The diagonal elements $W_n (= H(nn))$ were then given by the expression  

$$W_n = \frac{h\omega_0}{2\pi} \left( n + \frac{1}{2} \right) - \lambda^2 \frac{5}{3} \left( \frac{h}{4\pi\omega_0^2} \right)^2 \left[ n(n+1) + \frac{17}{30} \right]. \tag{114}$$  

This result deviated, as Born and Jordan realized immediately, from the one obtained from the second-order perturbation calculation in the previous semi-classical theory; in the latter, the first term was proportional to the quantum number $n$ and the second to $n^2$, with the same order of factors as in Eq. (114). Formally it was possible to remove the discrepancy between the old and the new mechanics by introducing half-integral quantum numbers in the old theory, provided one neglected a constant term of order $\lambda^2$ in the energy. However, with the advent of quantum mechanics such tricks could be dispensed with. For the purpose of comparing the new results with the known ones, Born and Jordan just pointed out that the quantum-mechanical frequencies, $\nu(n, n-1)$, of the anharmonic oscillator—at least in the second-order approximation—agreed with the corresponding classical frequencies, i.e., with $(1/h)(\partial W_n^{(\text{cl})}/\partial n)$. Finally, they showed that the frequencies $\nu(n, n-1)$ satisfied the frequency condition.$^{95}$ This, together with the observation that the quantum-mechanical energy expression, Eq. (114), might also be obtained with the help of the previously reformulated classical perturbation scheme (in agreement with the correspondence principle—see Born, 1924b), concluded Born and Jordan’s quantum-mechanical treatment of the anharmonic oscillator.  

In spite of the limitation of their success to a simple example, Born and Jordan felt very encouraged by their results. They were convinced that in the matrix scheme they had formulated a quantum theory that surpassed the shaky guesswork of earlier years. The new theory indeed seemed to contain all the requirements which one had tried to establish in atomic theory by a careful application of correspondence arguments to specific problems. These requirements were guaranteed by the very fact that the classical Hamiltonian scheme as well as the quantum condition for multiply periodic systems were taken over in the matrix language. But matrix mechanics signified much more than a clever

Born and Jordan therefore firmly believed that the matrix scheme could and should be applied also to problems that had not been treated before: as, for example, radiation theory. In the last part of their paper (Chapter 4) they went on to deal with this problem.

## II.5 Preliminary Remarks on Radiation

Born and Jordan’s first goal had been to give a mathematically secure foundation to the concepts of quantum theory. Among the fundamental assumptions in his paper on the reformulation of kinematic and mechanical relations, Heisenberg had proposed to interpret $|q(nm)|^2$, the square of the transition amplitudes associated with the position coordinate of a periodic system, as the probability for a quantum jump in the system (Heisenberg, 1925c, Section 1). In quantum mechanics this assumption meant, of course, a bold step which required justification. In classical theory the emission of radiation from an accelerated electron could be calculated according to the laws of electrodynamics. Especially, there existed a well-defined relation between the quantities characterizing the motion of the electron and the electromagnetic fields characterizing the intensity of the emitted radiation. In the new quantum-mechanical formalism classical quantities, such as the acceleration of an electron, were simply represented by the corresponding matrix quantities. Was one permitted to perform the same reformulation with the variables of the electromagnetic field? Born and Jordan answered this question in the affirmative, but they immediately added that ‘the considerations advanced here have only a provisional character’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 883).

One of the main reasons for their cautious attitude was the fact that, in early September 1925, they did not know how to formulate the quantum condition for systems having several degrees of freedom. For the moment they bypassed this difficulty by restricting themselves to free cavity radiation, which may be treated as a system of uncoupled oscillators, each possessing a fixed frequency. As they argued:

> There is hardly any doubt as to how to treat this system. For this purpose the fact, that the fundamental equations of electrodynamics are linear (superposition principle), is of special significance; because from that it follows that the substitute (“*Ersatz*”) oscillators [representing the cavity radiation] are *harmonic*, and just in the case of harmonic oscillators—in contrast to other systems—energy conservation is valid independently of the quantum condition . . . One would therefore expect that one may similarly obtain the integral theorems of the electrodynamics of vacuum (energy and momentum conservation) quite generally by solely reformulating Maxwell’s equations in matrix language, without taking into account the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0092 -->

88 Chapter II Matching the Tools and the Task

quantum condition. By demonstrating this we simultaneously gain the means of justifying Heisenberg’s assertion about the significance of $|q(nm)|^{2}$. (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 884)$^{96}$

In order to formulate Maxwell’s equations in matrix language, the meaning of the operations with vectors had to be redefined. For instance, it was necessary to indicate how the scalar and vector products, $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B}$, respectively, of two vector matrices, $\mathbf{A} = (A_x, A_y, A_z)$ and $\mathbf{B} = (B_x, B_y, B_z)$, had to be expressed, because their components would not commute in general.$^{96\text{a}}$ Born and Jordan decided to retain the usual definitions of the products also in matrix theory (i.e., $\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{B} = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z$, and $(\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{B})_x = A_y B_z - A_z B_y$, etc.). Then they wrote for the equations describing the change in time of an electric field matrix $\mathbf{E}$ and a magnetic field matrix $\mathbf{H}$ the matrix equations

$$\text{curl}\, \mathbf{H} - \frac{1}{c} \dot{\mathbf{E}} = 0 \qquad (115\text{a})$$

and

$$\text{curl}\, \mathbf{E} + \frac{1}{c} \dot{\mathbf{H}} = 0, \qquad (115\text{b})$$

where $c$ is the velocity of light *in vacuo*. In composing the (scalar) energy density matrix $\mathbf{W}$, that is,

$$\mathbf{W} = \frac{1}{8\pi} (\mathbf{E}^2 + \mathbf{H}^2), \qquad (116)$$

the question of the commutativity did not arise, because only the products of the same factors (e.g., $\mathbf{E}^2 = E_x^2 + E_y^2 + E_z^2$) occurred. As Born and Jordan noted, this $\mathbf{W}$ satisfied the equation of continuity in matrix form, that is,

$$\dot{\mathbf{W}} + \text{div}\, \mathbf{S} = 0, \qquad (117)$$

with the vector matrix $\mathbf{S}$, where

$$\mathbf{S} = \frac{c}{8\pi} (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{H} - \mathbf{H} \times \mathbf{E}) \qquad (117\text{a})$$

represents the quantum-theoretical analogue of the classical Poynting vector. The vector matrix $\mathbf{S}$ should describe, as in classical electrodynamics, the transport of

---
$^{96}$As we have discussed in Section II.3, the proof of energy conservation (for systems having a separable Hamiltonian) involved the use of the quantum condition. In the case of the harmonic oscillator, however, one can do without it. The Hamiltonian consists of two terms, $\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{p}^2$, where $\mathbf{p}$ is the momentum matrix ($= \dot{\mathbf{q}}$, since the mass is normalized to unity), and $\frac{1}{2} \omega_0^2 \mathbf{q}^2$, where $\mathbf{q}$ is the position matrix and $\omega_0^2$ the force constant. The time derivative of the first term gives $\frac{1}{2} \dot{\mathbf{p}} \mathbf{p} + \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{p} \dot{\mathbf{p}}$, which is identical to $-\frac{1}{2} \omega_0^2 (\mathbf{q} \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{p} \mathbf{q})$. The time derivative of the second term gives $+\frac{1}{2} \omega_0^2 (\dot{\mathbf{q}} \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{q} \dot{\mathbf{q}}) = \frac{1}{2} \omega_0^2 (\mathbf{p} \mathbf{q} + \mathbf{q} \mathbf{p})$. Both time derivatives add up to zero; hence the Hamiltonian matrix is constant in time.

Born and Jordan also went on to prove momentum conservation in matrix electrodynamics, i.e., they succeeded in relating the time derivative of $\mathbf{g}$ to the divergence of the redefined Maxwell stresses.$^{97}$

The equations of vacuum electrodynamics in matrix form involve well-defined operations on the vector matrices $\mathbf{E}$ and $\mathbf{H}$, provided they describe periodic motions: say, $\mathbf{E}$ represents a plane wave moving in the $x$-direction and having the form

$$\mathbf{E} = \left\{ \mathbf{E}(nm) \exp \left[ 2\pi i \nu(nm) \left( t - \frac{x}{c} \right) \right] \right\}, \qquad (118)$$

where $\mathbf{E}(nm)$ is the electric vector amplitude associated with the frequency $\nu(nm)$. Born and Jordan hoped, however, that the matrix equations of electrodynamics would remain valid even if the frequencies $\nu(nm)$ in Eq. (118) were to assume continuous values, so that aperiodic fields could be treated as well. They also did not expect any particular difficulty in casting relativistic equations, such as those describing mechanical and electrodynamic phenomena, into the matrix language. However, for the moment they did not elaborate on these questions; instead they treated the problem of radiation emitted from a Hertzian dipole, especially since it allowed them to answer the question concerning the interpretation of the matrix elements of the position matrix of a periodic system.

In classical electrodynamics an oscillating electron of charge $e$ (which can be considered as a Hertzian dipole), whose position vector is $\mathbf{q}$ relative to the equilibrium position, loses per second the amount of energy

$$- \frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{2}{3} \frac{e^2}{c^3} (\ddot{\mathbf{q}}^2)_{\text{av}}, \qquad (119)$$

through the surface enclosing it; $(\ddot{\mathbf{q}}^2)_{\text{av}}$ denotes the time average of the square of the acceleration vector. Born and Jordan repeated the calculation of the energy loss with matrices: they replaced the vector $\mathbf{q}$ by the vector matrix $\mathbf{q}$ (representing the electron's position in quantum theory) and the time average of $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}^2$ by the diagonal sum of the matrix $\ddot{\mathbf{q}}^2$.$^{98}$ Assuming that the electron oscillates along a

$$-\frac{dW}{dt} = \frac{64\pi^4 e^2}{3c^3} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left[ \sum_{k<n} \nu(nk)^4 |q(nk)|^2 \right]. \tag{120}$$

In this expression, which had been formulated in such a way that the sum included only the spontaneous radiation from a state $n$ of higher energy to a state $k$ of lower energy, the complete analogy to the classical result could be pointed out: in fact, each transition had the intensity corresponding to the one calculated from the classical electrodynamics.$^{99}$

Equation (120) established a direct numerical relationship between the radiation emitted from an oscillating electron (i.e., a quantum-theoretical dipole) and $q(nm)$, the elements of its position matrix. Born and Jordan had thus proved Heisenberg’s interpretation of the $q(nm)$ as transition amplitudes—whose absolute square is proportional to the intensity of the emitted radiation—to be correct.$^{100}$ Their result also provided a secure basis for formulating dispersion theory in matrix mechanics. In spite of this success they were not yet able to give a method for computing the matrix elements $q(nk)$ for electrons bound in atoms; such a calculation seemed to involve the particular coupling between the electromagnetic field and the motion of the electron. Thus, Jordan, looking back on the last part of the matrix mechanics paper, remarked: ‘What is written about radiation in the first paper of Born and myself is not very profound’ (Jordan to van der Waerden, 10 April 1962). However, in September 1925, he and Born were quite content with their preliminary investigation into radiation theory. Since Heisenberg announced that he would join their collaboration, they expected to proceed even faster with their programme of developing a full-fledged scheme of matrix mechanics. The three of them would be able to work out the theory of systems having several degrees of freedom, for as Born and Jordan added a remark in proof to their paper a few weeks later: ‘The extension of the theory to several degrees of freedom, [which we have] announced here, has been carried out meanwhile together with W. Heisenberg and will be published as a continuation of this paper. There we shall also discuss several points, already touched upon here, which have been clarified further in the meantime’ (Born and Jordan, 1925, p. 888). Among these points belonged, besides the treatment of degenerate systems, a detailed discussion of cavity radiation leading to a derivation of Planck’s law from the quantum-mechanical scheme.

$^{99}$Since Einstein’s work on the statistical theory of radiation (Einstein, 1916d), it was well known that including spontaneous radiation alone did not yield formulae which agreed with the classical ones in the correspondence limit. The diagonal sum, $D(\ddot{\mathbf{q}}^2) \left(= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} [2\pi\nu(nk)]^4 \cdot |q(nk)|^2\right)$, correctly includes terms other than those associated with spontaneous emission (i.e., terms with $k < n$). Thus, a factor of two is obtained on the right-hand side of Eq. (120).

# Chapter III
## Completion of the Matrix Scheme

Matrix mechanics was formulated at Göttingen during the University's summer vacation in 1925. Born and Jordan presented the programme of the theory and worked out its most obvious consequences in August and early September; they were then joined by Werner Heisenberg, who, since the end of July, had taken a complete leave from work on physical problems and had spent nearly a month and a half in Munich and on hiking tours in the Alps.<sup>101</sup> In September, Heisenberg did not return to Göttingen; rather he went to Copenhagen, but from there he contributed to the elaboration of the scheme of matrix mechanics in letters to Born and Jordan. Two months later Born, Heisenberg and Jordan submitted a long paper, entitled ‘*Zur Quantenmechanik. II.*’ (‘On Quantum Mechanics II’), to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, which covered fifty-nine pages of its volume 35 (Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926; abbreviated as BHJ, 1926, in the following).

It may seem remarkable how this long memoir containing the theory in its most general form—including periodic systems of several, even infinitely many, degrees of freedom—could be composed in such a short period of time, especially since the three co-authors spent little more than a week together.<sup>102</sup> However, several circumstances combined to yield fast progress of the work. First, Heisenberg, on hearing about the early success of the matrix methods—such as the proof of energy conservation—became very enthusiastic about applying them himself. With his active participation Born and Jordan's programme received a big push forward, for he immediately thought of using matrix mechanics in those physical problems with which he had been concerned for some time. Born and Jordan were gratified to have Heisenberg on their side, for they could rely on his physical intuition. Second, in extending the matrix scheme to general multiply periodic systems, all three of them were able to make use of their thorough knowledge of the classical theory, especially of the perturbation schemes and the theory of canonical transformations. Hence they experienced no difficulties in searching for the appropriate classical equations that could be

<sup>101</sup>From Zell-am-Ziller, a little mountain village in Tyrol, Austria, Heisenberg wrote to Bohr on 31 August 1925: ‘To be sure, I have not thought at all about physics during the entire past month, and I do not know whether I still understand anything about it.’

<sup>102</sup>Heisenberg returned from Copenhagen to Göttingen around 20 October 1925; his first letter to Niels Bohr from Göttingen was dated 21 October 1925. Born left for his American trip on 28 October 1925 (Born to van der Waerden, 10 July 1962).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0096 -->

92 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

reformulated in quantum mechanics. Third, in studying the matrix theory of canonical transformations, Born discovered that mathematically it became identical with the theory of principal-axes transformations of infinite quadratic forms. Thus, the theory developed by his teacher David Hilbert twenty years earlier provided the clue to solving the most important problem of quantum mechanics: the calculation of the energy states of atomic systems. Moreover, it seemed to remove another fundamental difficulty of the old atomic theory that lay in different treatments of discrete and continuous states.

The endeavours of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan led to the development of the theory of matrix mechanics, which was applicable to all types of multiply periodic systems, to nondegenerate and degenerate ones, and in principle even to aperiodic systems. In addition, the authors realized that the matrix equations had a simpler structure than the corresponding classical equations. Thus, for example, the set of Hamilton–Jacobi partial differential equations of classical mechanics was replaced by a set of algebraic equations; their solution established a unitary transformation of the quantum–mechanical Hamiltonian matrix to a diagonal matrix. Now the discussion of conservation laws also appeared to be considerably more elementary. The three co-authors succeeded in presenting the theory in a finished and compact form. Four years later Born and Jordan took it over unchanged into their book *Elementare Quantenmechanik* (1930). This book reflected on every page the debt to the mathematical foundation of quantum mechanics that Hilbert had provided in his theory of integral equations. But it also emphasized the other, the physical foundation of the new atomic theory, which had come from Niels Bohr’s correspondence approach, for as Born and Jordan remarked in their preface:

> Indeed, we see in the new mechanics the rigorous realization of Bohr’s programme. We believe that the new mechanics does not represent an approximation to classical ideas, nor any departure from Bohr’s conceptions (stationary states, quantum jumps, transition probabilities, etc.), but rather their [i.e., of Bohr’s conceptions] systematic extension to a logically consistent system. We have expressed this by asking the founder of modern atomic theory [i.e., Bohr] to allow us to dedicate this book to him. (Born and Jordan, 1930, p. VI)

On receiving a copy of the book, Heisenberg wrote to his former collaborators: ‘I have been especially happy about the dedication to Bohr. One must at least once publicly emphasize that all the essential ideas of Bohr have also been taken over into the new quantum mechanics’ (Heisenberg to Born and Jordan, 20 January 1930).

### III.1 The Three-Man Collaboration

During his long vacation in summer 1925 Heisenberg had received the news about Born and Jordan’s work on the matrix formulation of the quantum-theoretical ideas contained in the paper which he had completed in Göttingen

93

before leaving for visits to Leyden and Cambridge. He became very excited with the progress achieved by his colleagues and immediately expressed the desire to use the new formalism, too. For this purpose, on 20 August, he asked Jordan for further information about the details of calculations in matrix mechanics; and he repeated the same request three weeks later in a postcard, asking that the material should be sent to him to Copenhagen where he was going. ‘Because,’ he wrote, ‘from the day after tomorrow I shall begin to work on physics again and I do not, of course, want to repeat your considerations all over again’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 10 September 1925). Thus, Heisenberg also began to work on matrix mechanics in Copenhagen and at once reported about his results to Jordan: ‘In the two days that I have been here I have not been able to think about much. However, a very simple derivation of Kramers’ dispersion theory and of the formulae of Kramers and myself has occurred to me on the basis of the new formalism’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 13 September 1925). Evidently, the information, which he had meanwhile received from Jordan about matrix mechanics, enabled him to perform calculations with the new scheme himself. Heisenberg was quite satisfied with his initial results, for he remarked: ‘I am very glad, for after all I have written everything quite correctly in my paper [Heisenberg, 1925c], provided that this theory makes any sense at all; gradually I begin to believe that this is really true’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 16 September 1925).

With this expression of hope and confidence Heisenberg began his work on matrix mechanics. At this stage, however, he had no familiarity with matrix methods. As he confessed later:

> I had not realized that those things which I had used in my paper were matrices. I had never taken a course on matrix theory. Of course, I knew how to solve linear equations in a trivial way as one learns in school, but I had never learnt the general scheme of matrices and I did not know that matrices can represent groups. So when I learnt from Born that what I had done was really an example of matrix multiplication, I was very interested, but it was new to me. Then, of course, I started to read up on it and learnt it. (Heisenberg, *Conversations*, p. 163; also AHQP Interview)<sup>103</sup>

The reason why Heisenberg accepted the unusual matrix formalism at once was that it seemed to provide perhaps the only means of handling the greatest difficulty in his quantum-theoretical scheme: the noncommutativity of the re-

<sup>103</sup>Heisenberg’s own testimony contradicts some of the legends which are told about his mathematical education. Thus, there is the story that, when Heisenberg returned from Copenhagen to Göttingen in fall 1925, somebody said to him: ‘Now what were you doing, sleeping in Hilbert’s lectures?’ (Heisenberg, *Conversations*, pp. 162–163). Jordan recalled another story: ‘Once, later on, I heard in conversations that there was a legend that Heisenberg, in order to be able to do physics, had learned matrix theory from Emmy Noether. But this is not true. Emmy Noether represented [i.e., taught] a kind of mathematics which Heisenberg did not like at all, did not esteem at all’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963).
