94  Chapter III  Completion of the Matrix Scheme

interpreted Fourier series. As he recalled later on:

    In my paper [Heisenberg, 1925c], the fact that [the product of quantum-theoretical variables] $XY$ was not equal to $YX$ was very disagreeable to me. I felt this was the only point of difficulty in the whole scheme, otherwise I would be perfectly happy. But this difficulty had worried me and I was not able to solve it. Only for the example of the anharmonic oscillator that I had worked out was I able to get rid of this difficulty. I had written down the Thomas–Kuhn sum-rule as a quantization rule [see Eq. (5)], but I had not recognized that this was just the $pq - qp$ condition [in matrix mechanics]. (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 163; also AHQP Interview)

Now in September 1925 Heisenberg was glad that he had not abandoned the use of the re-interpreted Fourier series just because he had not known how to handle it. The matrix methods of Born and Jordan provided the tool for dealing with noncommuting quantities, and Heisenberg learned an important lesson: ‘If one finds a difficulty in a calculation which is otherwise quite convincing, one should not push the difficulty away; one should rather try to make it the centre of the whole thing’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, pp. 163–164). In any case, he quickly learned the rules of matrix calculus and turned to physical problems.$^{104}$

The first questions in matrix mechanics that occupied Heisenberg were the proof of the dispersion formulae and the formulation of a perturbation theory for systems of one degree of freedom. He completed both tasks within a few days, reporting his conclusions to Jordan in a letter and a postcard, dated 13 and 16 September, respectively. Then, in a long letter to Wolfgang Pauli on 18 September, he wrote about the calculations in detail: ‘Quantum mechanics, which is now very dear to my heart, has meanwhile, mainly through Born and Jordan, made decisive progress, which I shall report to you in the following, even to get a clear idea myself as to what I should believe. One is now really in a position to prove energy conservation, frequency condition and the dispersion formula in a general way on the basis of the previous assumptions [i.e., the assumptions of Heisenberg, 1925c].’ After sketching the results of Born and Jordan, Heisenberg presented to Pauli a matrix reformulation of the classical perturbation scheme for multiply periodic systems (Born and Pauli, 1922). ‘The equations,’ he concluded, ‘contain both Kramers’ dispersion theory [Kramers, 1924a] and Born’s formula for the energy $W_2$ [i.e., the second-order correction to the energy (see Born, 1924b, p. 389, Eq. (33)] and the formulae established by Kramers and myself [Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925]. I believe that is everything that one can demand for the moment’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 18 September 1925).

$^{104}$For the calculations, which Heisenberg performed in Copenhagen, the information received from Jordan on matrix methods was sufficient. On his return to Göttingen, however, he studied the relevant portions of *Courant & Hilbert* (1924) and the translation of M. Bôcher’s book on algebra (Bôcher, 1911). As he recalled: ‘I must have looked into the library in Göttingen and tried to learn something. I think then I read some textbooks about matrices, and then I tried to figure out myself how matrices worked’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 318). However, already in a letter to Pauli, written on 18 September 1925, Heisenberg mentioned the book of Courant and Hilbert. At that time his knowledge of matrix terminology was not very deep; for example, he said ‘unit determinant’ instead of ‘unit matrix.’

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0099 -->

III.1 The Three-Man Collaboration

95

Heisenberg did not content himself with these results, however he went on without delay to introduce another important generalization of the matrix scheme. In a postcard to Jordan dated 21 September 1925, he stated the quantum conditions for systems of several degrees of freedom described by the momentum coordinates $\mathbf{p}_k$ and the position coordinates $\mathbf{q}_k$, $k = 1, \dots, f$, that is,

$$ \mathbf{p}_k \mathbf{q}_l - \mathbf{q}_l \mathbf{p}_k = \begin{cases} \frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{1} & \text{for } k = l \\ 0 & \text{for } k \neq l, \end{cases} \qquad (121\text{a}) $$

and

$$ \mathbf{p}_k \mathbf{p}_l - \mathbf{p}_l \mathbf{p}_k = 0, \qquad (121\text{b}) $$
$$ \mathbf{q}_k \mathbf{q}_l - \mathbf{q}_l \mathbf{q}_k = 0. \qquad (121\text{c}) $$

He added:

> That these conditions yield the frequency conditions, can be demonstrated easily according to your method ... In case of the separation [of the variables $\mathbf{p}_k$ and $\mathbf{q}_k$], the Eqs. [(121)] reduce to your and Born’s formulae, but in case of non-separability one cannot understand Eqs. [(121)] from the classical theory without further arguments. However, I still believe, because of the frequency condition, that Eqs. [(121)] are also always true for non-periodic systems ... I also believe that, if the conditions [(121)] are correct, the perturbation theory can be taken over word for word in the case of several degrees of freedom; of course, in the case of degeneracy, something completely different results. (Heisenberg to Jordan, 21 September 1925)

The key thus seemed to be provided to deal with a large class of quantum-mechanical systems.

Meanwhile Born had returned from his vacation in Switzerland shortly after the middle of September. He quickly completed with Jordan the joint paper on the formulation of matrix mechanics (Born and Jordan, 1925b). At the same time he learned that not only did Heisenberg agree with their work, but had also started to concern himself with the matrix formalism. He was happy to see that Heisenberg had joined his and Jordan’s efforts and that an intensive collaboration on the new theory was developing. He regretted, of course, that Heisenberg could participate in the work only by mail from Copenhagen. After some time he felt that all of them needed closer contact, and he wrote to Niels Bohr: ‘Now I must ask you not to take it amiss that I have suggested to Heisenberg to come to Göttingen a little earlier, so that we may still be able to work together for a few days. It is unfortunate that I have to go to America just at this time, but I cannot turn down the invitation which I have once accepted ... We want to release a three-man paper: Heisenberg, Jordan, and myself; this I want to complete at least roughly before leaving’ (Born to Bohr, 10 October 1925). Before leaving at the end of October for the United States, where he had accepted to lecture in winter 1925–1926 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Born wanted to

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0100 -->

96 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

discuss the theory in detail with Heisenberg and Jordan. ‘In this way’ he wrote to Bohr, ‘much useless work will be saved and the thing will be advanced’ (Born to Bohr, 10 October 1925).
Born had good reason to request Heisenberg’s presence in Göttingen at that moment.105 It was necessary to coordinate as much as possible the ideas and intentions of the three collaborators. Heisenberg and Jordan had never worked together before; their interests had been different and, when Jordan completed his doctorate under Born in fall 1924, Heisenberg had been away in Copenhagen for a long stay. But even Born and Heisenberg had not collaborated actively for more than a year; the two of them had treated different problems of atomic theory and followed ideas which seemed to go in different directions. Now in fall 1925 the situation had changed: Born discovered that Heisenberg’s and his own ideas in quantum mechanics could be formulated systematically in terms of matrices, and Jordan had proved to be his most able helper in doing so. The success of Born and Jordan had convinced Heisenberg into joining the bandwagon of matrix mechanics. However, in spite of their common interest, the three of them had somewhat different goals in mind. Jordan frequently supported Born’s intention of establishing a quantum-mechanical scheme to replace classical mechanics (augmented by quantum conditions) that would be as complete and general as possible. Born and Jordan thus wished to fulfill the aim of their first paper (Born and Jordan, 1925b), which was to erect the matrix formulation of quantum mechanics on the basis of a minimum set of assumptions and to extend the formalism to include also (nonrelativistic and relativistic) systems of several, even infinite, degrees of freedom. On the other hand, Heisenberg, once his call for a consistent mathematical scheme had been answered, was less interested in the mathematical foundations of matrix mechanics and much more in its applications to actual problems. In doing so he felt that one should not leave for the moment the familiar domain of previously observed and treated quantum phenomena, like the ones connected with the emission and absorption of spectral lines and the dispersion of light by atoms. Apart from verifying old results, such as the Kramers–Heisenberg dispersion formulae, by means of the new formalism, he wanted to move closer to the ambition he had entertained earlier in May of that year: that of working out a theory of the hydrogen spectrum. Thus he remarked to Pauli: ‘To be sure, the most important thing is still missing, namely the actual integration [of the equations of matrix mechanics] in the case of hydrogen’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 18 September 1925). It was for this purpose that he was eager to establish the quantum conditions (121) for systems of several degrees of freedom. Hence he reproached Jordan, who thought of attacking also the problems of electrodynamics—which implied systems of infinitely many degrees of freedom—by writing: ‘As for the matrix

105 Heisenberg’s renewed stay at Copenhagen had already been arranged in spring 1925, when he had returned to Göttingen for the summer semester. The reason was that in September 1924 he had received a Rockefeller Fellowship for nine months, but had remained in Copenhagen for only seven months.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0101 -->

III.1 The Three-Man Collaboration 97

calculation in electrodynamics, I would much prefer that one thinks for the moment only about mechanics’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 7 October 1925).
Indeed, there were many points of disagreement between the collaborators that needed straightening out. These concerned both matters of principle and procedure. Born and Jordan had constructed the new theory by setting up a formal mathematical scheme from which the physical results, such as the conservation of energy, could be deduced. In doing so they had emphasized, in particular, the fundamental difference between their approach and the earlier one based on the correspondence principle. Heisenberg, who had followed the Copenhagen tradition of employing the correspondence principle in his own work, did not fully agree with this attitude. He was convinced that even after the discovery of matrix mechanics one could not dispense with Bohr’s correspondence principle, and he continued to use it in establishing matrix relations. A more specific point, on which Heisenberg disagreed with Born and Jordan, was the question of the differentiation of matrix functions with respect to a matrix variable.
In their paper, Born and Jordan had proposed a seemingly complicated definition for the partial derivative of a matrix function $\mathbf{y}$ with respect to one of its matrix variables, $\mathbf{x}_k$, through Eq. (76). They had, however, argued in favour of this definition because the differential quotient, $\partial \mathbf{y} / \partial \mathbf{x}_k$, could be reformulated in terms of the diagonal sum, $D(\mathbf{y})$, and this alternative definition, Eq. (79), looked much simpler. Moreover, it had enabled them to suggest a variational principle in quantum mechanics, Eq. (88b), from which followed the Hamiltonian matrix equations of motion, similar to the corresponding equations in classical dynamics. Now, in October, Heisenberg raised objections and he wrote to Born:

>I have now thought in more detail about the question of the definition of $\partial \mathbf{f} / \partial \mathbf{q}$ and $\partial \mathbf{f} / \partial \mathbf{p}$, respectively, and I am now convinced that your definition is *not* correct—at any rate, it is not useful. That, by itself, it is a question of suitability as to which definition one chooses, becomes evident from the fact that in the case of Cartesian coordinates—that is, for coordinates in which the problem is defined from the very beginning—the difference between the two definitions does not play a role. However, what appears to me to be a decisive objection against your definition is that with it $(h/2\pi i)[\mathbf{1}] = \mathbf{pq} - \mathbf{qp} = \mathbf{PQ} - \mathbf{QP}$ would *not* represent in general a canonical transformation. For in the case of such a transformation [the Hamiltonian matrix function] $\mathbf{H}$ will, in general, pass over into a complicated function of [the transformed momentum and position variables] $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$, which also contains mixed terms $\mathbf{P} \cdot \mathbf{Q}$, etc.; then, however, the equations of motion are not satisfied. (Heisenberg to Born, 5 October 1925)

Thus, Heisenberg argued that in the case of a Hamiltonian which is a separable function in Cartesian matrix variables—such as the Hamiltonian of the anharmonic oscillator or of the hydrogen atom—a transformation of the variables, which leaves the quantum condition, Eq. (67), invariant, and which he defined as a ‘canonical transformation’ in quantum mechanics, would lead to a Hamilto-

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0102 -->

98 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

nian matrix function $\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}\mathbf{Q})$ that does not satisfy the equations of motion.$^{106}$
Heisenberg did not find this conclusion to be acceptable; hence he went on to prove as the ‘only practical definition’ that one, in which the reformulated canonical equations of motions held for all pairs of dynamical variables admitted in quantum mechanics. This definition was expressed by the equation

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} (\mathbf{x}_1^{l_1} \cdot \mathbf{x}_2^{l_2} \dots \cdot \mathbf{x}_k^{l_k} \dots \cdot \mathbf{x}_s^{l_s}) = l_k (\mathbf{x}_1^{l_1} \cdot \mathbf{x}_2^{l_2} \dots \cdot \mathbf{x}_k^{l_k - 1} \dots \cdot \mathbf{x}_s^{l_s}) \quad (122) $$

rather than by Eq. (76).
Heisenberg’s new definition of the matrix derivative formally came much closer to the usual differentiation procedure. Thus, in the general case of a function $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_1, \dots, \mathbf{x}_s)$, the partial differential coefficient $\partial \mathbf{f} / \partial \mathbf{x}_1$ could be written as

$$ \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_1} = \lim_{\alpha \to 0} \frac{1}{\alpha} \left[ \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_1 + \alpha \mathbf{1}, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_s) - \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \dots, \mathbf{x}_s) \right], \quad (123) $$

where $\mathbf{1}$ is the unit-matrix and $\alpha$ represents a (real) number going to zero in the limit considered. Heisenberg noticed immediately that now the usual rule of the differentiation of a product of two matrix functions, $\mathbf{f}$ and $\mathbf{g}$, i.e., the equation

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} (\mathbf{f} \cdot \mathbf{g}) = \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} \mathbf{g} + \mathbf{f} \frac{\partial \mathbf{g}}{\partial \mathbf{x}_k} , \quad (124) $$

was satisfied. From this rule he derived an important consequence. If $\mathbf{F}$ is a function of $\mathbf{p}_k$ and $\mathbf{q}_k$, the dynamical variables of a quantum-mechanical system—which satisfy the commutation relations (121)—then the differential quotients, $\partial \mathbf{F} / \partial \mathbf{p}_k$ and $\partial \mathbf{F} / \partial \mathbf{q}_k$, are given by the equations

$$ \frac{\partial \mathbf{F}}{\partial \mathbf{p}_k} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathbf{Fq}_k - \mathbf{q}_k\mathbf{F}) \quad (125a) $$

and

$$ -\frac{\partial \mathbf{F}}{\partial \mathbf{q}_k} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathbf{Fp}_k - \mathbf{p}_k\mathbf{F}). \quad (125b) $$

$\mathbf{F}$ may represent any variable of the system, including the Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H} (= \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k))$. Hence the equations of motion assume the particular form

$$ \dot{\mathbf{q}}_k = \frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial \mathbf{p}_k} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathbf{Hq}_k - \mathbf{q}_k\mathbf{H}) \quad (126a) $$

$^{106}$The reason why the Hamiltonian equations of motion for the transformed Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q})$ were not satisfied with Born and Jordan’s differentiation definition, Eq. (76), was that for a complicated function $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q})$ the differential quotients $\partial \mathbf{f}/\partial \mathbf{Q}$ and $\partial \mathbf{f}/\partial \mathbf{P}$ could not be expressed as differences, $\mathbf{HP} - \mathbf{PH}$ and $\mathbf{HQ} - \mathbf{QH}$, respectively. This was demanded, however, by the reformulated equations of motion, Eqs. (90) and (92).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0103 -->

III.1 The Three-Man Collaboration 99

and

$$ \dot{\mathbf{p}}_k = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{H}}{\partial \mathbf{q}_k} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathbf{Hp}_k - \mathbf{p}_k\mathbf{H}). \quad (126b) $$

From these equations Heisenberg deduced immediately the time independence of the Hamiltonian matrix and the frequency conditions for systems having several degrees of freedom. For this purpose one has to observe only that the time derivative of the momentum variable $\mathbf{p}_k$ can be expressed in two ways, that is

$$ \dot{\mathbf{p}}_k = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathbf{Wp}_k - \mathbf{p}_k\mathbf{W}) = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (\mathbf{Hp}_k - \mathbf{p}_k\mathbf{H}), \quad (127) $$

where $\mathbf{W}$ is the diagonal matrix of the energy eigenvalues of the system under investigation. Hence the frequency conditions followed. In addition, the difference of the matrices, $\mathbf{W} - \mathbf{H}$, must commute with all functions, $\mathbf{F}$, of the dynamical variables, in particular with the Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}$ itself. Therefore the difference $\mathbf{WH} - \mathbf{HW}$ must be zero, and this gives the energy conservation due to Eq. (85) which defines the matrix $\mathbf{W}$.
Evidently, Heisenberg had excellent arguments in favour of his new definition of the matrix derivative. Still he was aware of the fact that it did not agree in general with the definition, Eq. (79), involving the diagonal sum, and that this led to a certain disadvantage. Thus he wrote to Born: ‘What appears to me certain from the above is that a nice formulation of the canonical transformations, on one hand, and of the minimum principle, on the other, are not immediately consistent with each other. It would be good if you could perhaps reformulate the minimum principle in such a way that it remains valid when one introduces the new definition of $\partial/\partial\mathbf{p}$’ (Heisenberg to Born, 5 October 1925). However, he added in a postscript: ‘It just occurred to me that the reason, which speaks in favour of your definition of the differentiation is still evidently the minimum principle. Now I must ask: Is the principle valid at all? For, suppose I make an arbitrary transformation of $\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}$, to the $\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q}$, such that $\mathbf{PQ} - \mathbf{QP} = \mathbf{pq} - \mathbf{qp}$, then the equations of motion *do not* hold with your definition of $\partial \mathbf{H}/\partial \mathbf{p}$. This must mean, however, that the minimum principle is not valid in these coordinates (i.e., in $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$). But if this is so, then what does it mean at all?’ (Heisenberg to Born, 5 October 1925). Evidently, Heisenberg preferred to drop the variational principle, which Born and Jordan had been so proud of.
Whether it was the definition of the derivative and the related validity of the Born–Jordan variational principle, or the exact form of the perturbation scheme, all these questions made it necessary that Heisenberg should return to Göttingen, which he did shortly after mid-October.$^{107}$ A tough time began, for as Born

$^{107}$Heisenberg wrote to Jordan on 29 September: ‘I definitely intend to come to Göttingen between 18 and 20 October, in order to be able to work with Born for a week.’ He must have been in Göttingen a few days before 21 October 1925, for on that day he wrote a letter to Bohr, thanking him for his hospitality and mentioning the fact that he was already deeply involved in the work on matrix mechanics with Born and Jordan.

recalled: ‘When Heisenberg came it was rather hectic. I had to leave on 2 November [1925] to America, and I wanted to have the paper finished when I left. Heisenberg was very keen on it, too, and so we worked very hard’ (Born, Conversations, p. 43).108 The work was somewhat simplified by the fact that Jordan had already prepared a preliminary manuscript of a paper which served as the basis for discussion. ‘Heisenberg’s most important contribution, namely the commutation rules for several degrees of freedom, was also contained in this draft’ (Jordan to van der Waerden, 8 October 1964). After some debating, the authors also agreed to present both definitions of the matrix derivative, i.e., the definition through Eq. (123) and the original Born–Jordan definition, Eq. As Jordan remarked many years afterwards: ‘The problem, which we treated first, arose primarily from the fact that we took the complicated form of the derivation. After we dropped the latter, the problem disappeared totally’ (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963).

Besides this point the three collaborators had many more questions to settle.110 At times they became discouraged with the amount of work to be done in the writing of the paper. Heisenberg, especially, disagreed with Born and Jordan’s intention to include too many items, and he complained to Pauli soon after returning to Göttingen: ‘At the moment I am almost exclusively occupied with quantum mechanics, and I have serious doubts as to whether the problem of writing this three-man paper has a solution at all in a finite time’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 October 1925). And yet, the authors finally did agree on what to put into the paper. All three of them contributed their share, which Jordan summarized as follows: ‘The S-transformations [i.e., the canonical transformations] and

101 III.1 The Three-Man Collaboration

their use for perturbation theory was Born’s idea. The generalized commutation rules for several degrees of freedom came from Heisenberg. The angular momentum investigations were mostly carried out by me, with an important supplement from Heisenberg. The considerations concerning radiation theory—the first Ansatz for the later quantization of wave fields—came from me’ (Jordan to van der Waerden, 8 October 1964).111 Each of them concentrated on his part, besides checking the calculations of the others. ‘And the writing down of it,’ Born recalled, ‘we also did in parts and then we put it together like a puzzle’ (Born, Conversations, p. 43). Thus, in spite of Heisenberg’s anxiety, the main part of the work was accomplished within a few days. And Born could leave Göttingen with a good conscience because the joint paper was basically in hand, though it was completed only afterwards by his collaborators. In Born’s absence, Heisenberg became responsible for the final editing. A few weeks later, on 16 November 1925, Zeitschrift für Physik received the paper, entitled ‘Zur Quantenmechanik. II.’ (‘On Quantum Mechanics II’); it was published in one of the issues of February 1926 of Volume 35.

In the three-man paper, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan set out ‘to develop further the theory of a general quantum-theoretical mechanics whose physical and mathematical basis has been treated in two previous papers [Heisenberg, 1925c; Born and Jordan, 1925b] by the present authors’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 557). They summarized the content of the paper as follows: ‘The quantum mechanics developed in Part I of this paper [Born and Jordan, 1925b] from Heisenberg’s approach [Heisenberg, 1925c] is here extended to systems having arbitrarily many degrees of freedom. Perturbation theory is carried through for nondegenerate and for a large class of degenerate systems, and its connection with the eigenvalue theory of Hermitian forms is demonstrated. The results so obtained are employed in the derivation of momentum and angular momentum conservation laws, and of selection rules and intensity formulae. Finally, the theory is applied to the statistics of eigenvibrations of a black-body cavity’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 557).112

After Born’s departure from Göttingen, Heisenberg had to coordinate the

102 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

various sections written by the authors separately, and had to rewrite the introduction.113 As he recalled: ‘It was actually a new introduction which used some older parts which Born had written. Born had written an introduction but he was not too satisfied, so I did write a new introduction’ (Heisenberg, Conversations). Comparing the content of this introduction with the motivation of the earlier paper by Born and Jordan, it is evident how Heisenberg altered Born’s original proposal. He did so especially with respect to the correspondence principle. During Heisenberg’s recent stay in Copenhagen he and Bohr had arrived at a common opinion about the new quantum mechanics. Bohr not only accepted the results obtained by Heisenberg and Born and Jordan as ‘a step probably of fundamental importance,’ but he regarded the whole apparatus of quantum mechanics ‘as a precise formulation of the tendencies embodied in the correspondence principle’ (Bohr, 1925b, p. 852). Even though the emphasis in ‘Quantum Mechanics I’ (Born and Jordan, 1925b) had been to replace the correspondence arguments completely by the matrix formalism, Heisenberg, in agreement with Bohr, now regarded the three-man paper—the first comprehensive exposition of the foundations of modern quantum mechanics in matrix language—as the final culmination of the correspondence principle. He expressed it as follows:

If one keeps in mind the fundamental differences between quantum and classical theory, differences which stem from the basic quantum-theoretical postulates, then the formalism proposed in the two above-mentioned publications [Heisenberg, 1925c; Born and Jordan, 1925b] and in this paper, if proved to be correct, would appear to represent a theory of quantum mechanics as close to that of classical theory as could possibly be hoped under any reasonable circumstances. In this context we merely recall the validity of energy and momentum conservation laws and the form of the equations of motion (Chapter 1, §2). This similarity of the new theory with classical theory also precludes any question of a separate correspondence principle outside the new theory; rather, the latter can itself be regarded as an exact formulation of Bohr’s correspondence considerations. In the further development of the theory, an important task will be to investigate more closely the nature of this correspondence and to describe how the symbolic quantum geometry goes over into the intuitive classical geometry. (BHJ, 1926, p. 558)

While, in the introduction, Heisenberg still expressed a cautious attitude and tried to link the new quantum-mechanical theory as tightly as possible with the erstwhile procedures of Niels Bohr, the main thrust and spirit of the three-man paper were quite different. Especially, in the presentation of the theory of canonical transformations and the perturbation scheme, there prevailed a great optimism concerning the prospects of matrix mechanics. These sections, which

113 As Jordan recalled later: ‘It is my very definite recollection . . . I can say with certainty that the paper, so far as the material it should cover was concerned, was indeed completed before Born’s departure; however, it was finally formulated and put together only after his departure. For the final write-up [and arrangement] Heisenberg was responsible’ (Jordan to van der Waerden, 8 October 1964).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0107 -->

103 III.2 Towards a New Perturbation Theory

formed the principal part of the paper, were mainly contributed by Max Born. His programme and intentions ultimately dominated the content of the three-man paper. As he remarked several decades later: ‘I think the style [of the three-man paper] is essentially mine’ (Born, Conversations, p. 43).

III.2 Towards a New Perturbation Theory

In developing the formalism of matrix mechanics, by means of which actual problems in atomic physics had then to be solved, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan appealed to two guidelines. First, they expected that all results, which had been obtained during the previous year on dispersion and related phenomena by systematic guessing involving the correspondence principle, such as Kramers’ dispersion formula, should now follow directly from the matrix scheme. Second, they believed firmly that the tried and true methods of classical mechanics could be translated successfully into the new formalism. As Heisenberg recalled: ‘The analogy with the classical Hamilton–Jacobi technique was the beginning of all efforts; what we did first was just to try to imitate the old methods as closely as we could’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 284). However, in carrying out this programme of imitation, the collaborators arrived initially at quite different-looking results, caused by their separation from each other and their different attitudes towards quantum mechanics. Born and Jordan in Göttingen studied the fundamental papers of Hilbert and his disciples on the theory of infinite quadratic forms and thought of applying the mathematical methods developed in these papers to matrix mechanics. Heisenberg, by temperament and training, was not so familiar with and less interested in this mathematical background; he still attributed to the correspondence principle a guiding role, and regarded the work on matrix mechanics as only a more systematic formulation of his earlier guesswork in atomic physics that had proved to be so successful. Hence their different approaches to perturbation theory in matrix mechanics provide insight into the respective scientific thinking of the three collaborators.

On receiving information about the matrix methods employed by Born and Jordan, Heisenberg in Copenhagen began to apply them himself: he immediately derived, within the new formalism the dispersion formulae of Kramers and of Kramers and himself (Kramers, 1924a, b; Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925), developing for this purpose a first-order perturbation theory which he sketched in a letter to Jordan (Heisenberg to Jordan, 13 September 1925).114 A couple of days later he announced proudly: ‘Going beyond what I have written in my last letter, I have now obtained a complete perturbation theory for problems with one degree of freedom up to an arbitrarily high approximation’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 16 September 1925). He informed Born and Pauli about the details of his

114 Since Jordan’s letters to Heisenberg, written at that time, are not available, we do not know the details of the information which Heisenberg received on matrix theory. However, we may assume with certainty that they did not go beyond what is contained in the Born–Jordan paper.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0108 -->

104 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

perturbation theory in long letters.$^{115}$ Born had just returned from his vacation to Göttingen and was engaged in completing the final write-up of the first paper on matrix mechanics (Born and Jordan, 1925b). Simultaneously he began to formulate his own perturbation scheme, which appeared to him to be quite different from the one contained in Heisenberg's letter.

Heisenberg, in his formulation of the quantum-mechanical perturbation theory, followed the classical scheme as closely as possible. He considered a periodic system of one degree of freedom, described by the Hamiltonian $H$, such that $H$ is given by a Hamiltonian $H_0$ plus terms proportional to powers of a small parameter $\lambda$, that is,

$$H = H_0 + \lambda H_1 + \lambda^2 H_2 + \ldots . \tag{128}$$

The solution described by $H_0$, the unperturbed Hamiltonian, is supposed to be known. $H_0 = H_0(p_0, q_0)$, where $p_0$ and $q_0$ are the momentum and coordinate variables, respectively, is identical with the constant energy $W_0$, which is a function only of the action variable of the unperturbed system (given by the action integral, $\int p_0 dq_0$, over one period of the motion). In classical theory, then, the energy of the perturbed system, described by the full Hamiltonian $H$, Eq. (128), was obtained with the help of a canonical transformation of its dynamical variables, $p$ and $q$. That is, one had to solve the Hamilton–Jacobi partial differential equation

$$H\left(p = \frac{\partial S}{\partial q}, q\right) = W, \tag{129}$$

where $S$ is the action function and $W$, the energy of the perturbed system, which depends only on $J$, the constant action variable of the system. $S$ is assumed to be a function of $J$ and the position variable $q$; it may be expanded in terms of the perturbation parameter $\lambda$, that is,

$$S = q_0 p_0 + \lambda S_1 + \lambda^2 S_2 + \ldots . \tag{130}$$

Hence it was possible to solve Eq. (129) in successive approximations. For this purpose one expressed also the variables of the perturbed system as power series in $\lambda$, say $p = p_0 + \lambda p_1 + \lambda^2 p_2 + \ldots$ and $q = q_0 + \lambda q_1 + \lambda^2 q_2 + \ldots$, and substituted these expressions, as well as the expansions (128) and (130), into Eq. (129); then one found the zeroth-order approximation by keeping only terms independent of $\lambda$, the first-order approximation by keeping terms proportional to $\lambda$, etc.

In trying to reformulate the classical perturbation scheme, Eqs. (128)–(130), in matrix mechanics Heisenberg observed that, in agreement with the matrix

---

III.2 Towards a New Perturbation Theory 105

differentiation rule (i.e., Eq. (125b) for one degree of freedom), the classical expression $\partial S/\partial q$ had to be replaced—apart from constant factors—by the matrix expression $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}\mathbf{S}$, involving the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ and the canonically conjugate matrix variable $\mathbf{p}$. This fact allowed him to write down a matrix-theoretical perturbation scheme for a quantum system described by a Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}$, which, in analogy with the classical Hamiltonian of Eq. (128), can be expanded as a series involving terms multiplied by increasing powers of $\lambda$ (i.e., $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{H}_0 + \lambda \mathbf{H}_1 + \lambda^2 \mathbf{H}_2 + \ldots$). To begin with, he assumed that $\mathbf{H}_0$, the Hamiltonian of the unperturbed system, was diagonal in the dynamical variables $\mathbf{p}_0$ and $\mathbf{q}_0$. Then he expanded all quantities occurring in the matrix-equation, which corresponds to the Hamilton–Jacobi equation (129), in power series in $\lambda$. He found that the position matrix $\mathbf{q}$ assumed the form

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{q} = \mathbf{q}_0 &+ \lambda (\mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{q}_0 - \mathbf{q}_0 \mathbf{S}_1) \\
&+ \lambda^2 \left[ (\mathbf{S}_1^2 \mathbf{q}_0 - 2 \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{q}_0 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{q}_0 \mathbf{S}_1^2) + (\mathbf{S}_2 \mathbf{q}_0 - \mathbf{q}_0 \mathbf{S}_2) \right] + \ldots , \tag{131}
\end{aligned}$$

and that a similar equation held for $\mathbf{p}$, the momentum matrix. 'You will immediately recognize the law for forming the $\mathbf{q}_i$ and $\mathbf{p}_i$, respectively,' Heisenberg wrote to Pauli. 'One always deals with iterated forms of the type $\mathbf{S}\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{q}\mathbf{S}$' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 18 September 1925). With the help of these equations he found for $\mathbf{H}$ an expression having the same structure as the right-hand side of Eq. (131), except that $\mathbf{q}_0$ was replaced everywhere by $\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{q}_0)$. By substituting the expression for the Hamiltonian matrix into the reformulated Eq. (129)—i.e., the equation $\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \mathbf{W}$—and by equating the terms with equal powers of $\lambda$, he finally obtained the following set of equations:

$$\mathbf{H}_0 = \mathbf{W}_0,$$
$$\mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_0 - \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{H}_1 = \mathbf{W}_1, \tag{132}$$
$$\mathbf{S}_2 \mathbf{H}_0 - \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_2 + \tfrac{1}{2} (\mathbf{S}_1^2 \mathbf{H}_0 - 2 \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1^2) + \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_1 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{H}_2 = \mathbf{W}_2,$$

etc. (All matrices such as $\mathbf{H}_0$, $\mathbf{H}_1$, $\mathbf{S}_1$, etc., in Eqs. (132) depend on $\mathbf{p}_0$ and $\mathbf{q}_0$, the zeroth-order of the dynamical variables of the system under investigation.)

Heisenberg was very happy with the new scheme which, as he confessed to Pauli, imitated exceedingly well the 'famous Born–Pauli model' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 18 September 1925), i.e., the classical scheme which Pauli had worked out together with Born and Göttingen several years earlier (Born and Pauli, 1922).$^{116}$

---

$^{116}$For example, the classical equation corresponding to the second equation in Eqs. (132) was $(\partial H_0/\partial J)(\partial S_1/\partial w^0) + H_1 = W_1$, where $J$ and $w^0$ denote the action variable of the perturbed and the angle variable of the nonperturbed system, respectively (see Born and Pauli, 1922, p. 140, Eq. (7$_1$)). Now, in the first term the differential quotient $\partial H_0/\partial J$ may be replaced by $\nu_0$, the frequency of the unperturbed system, while the differential quotient $\partial S_1/\partial w^0$ becomes identical with $2\pi i S_1$ because $S_1$ is assumed to be periodic in $w^0$. In matrix theory this product, or $\nu_0 \hbar (2\pi i / \hbar) S_1$, then indeed corresponds to the difference, $\mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_0 - \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0110 -->

106 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

As he recalled much later: 'The whole thing was that I wanted to make the ideas of Bohr's correspondence principle more and more precise and, finally, I came out with something which was simpler than classical mechanics. That, of course, was a great surprise and a great encouragement. And the perturbation theory was just a very nice point where it happened' (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 285). His satisfaction, however, was not shared by Born who had meanwhile worked out a different scheme. Born recalled the situation as follows:

> All of us posed the problem [of developing perturbation theory in quantum mechanics]. Then Heisenberg wrote us a letter with the formalism. But before his letter arrived we had already found the transformation of a matrix into another coordinate system [i.e., $\mathbf{f} \to \mathbf{f}'$] as $\mathbf{f}' = \mathbf{S} \mathbf{f} \mathbf{S}^{-1}$. And then I looked at Heisenberg's scheme and thought: "That's pure nonsense; it is so complicated, when all he has to do is to develop [the transformation matrix] $\mathbf{S}$ into a power series with respect to a given function." We did this and it came out beautifully. I remained in the belief all the time that Heisenberg's suggestion was wrong. (Born, Conversations, p. 41)

Already in their initial investigations on matrices Born and Jordan had noticed the possibility that every matrix equation may be invariant if one transforms the matrices involved, say $\mathbf{a}$, into $\mathbf{a}' = \mathbf{b} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{b}^{-1}$, where $\mathbf{b}$ is an arbitrary singular matrix and $\mathbf{b}^{-1}$ is its inverse (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 866). At the same time, however, they had added that this transformation property did not seem to hold always for equations involving matrix differentiation. Now it seemed to be profitable to apply the transformation invariance in the problem of calculating the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{H}$, the Hamiltonian matrix of a given quantum system. All one had to do was to introduce a transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ in such a way that the transformed Hamiltonian became identical with the diagonal energy matrix $\mathbf{W}$, or

$$\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}) = \mathbf{S} \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{q}_0) \mathbf{S}^{-1} = \mathbf{W}. \tag{133}$$

Evidently, Eq. (133) represented the matrix reformulation of the classical Hamilton–Jacobi equation (129), for it served the same purpose: that is, it provided a method of performing a transformation of the dynamical variables, $\mathbf{p}_0$ and $\mathbf{q}_0$ (by which one initially described the system under investigation), to new variables, $\mathbf{p}$ ($= \mathbf{S} \mathbf{p}_0 \mathbf{S}^{-1}$) and $\mathbf{q}$ ($= \mathbf{S} \mathbf{q}_0 \mathbf{S}^{-1}$), in which the Hamiltonian is a constant of the time. The beautiful simplicity of this equation and its connection with the mathematical theory of principal-axes transformation of quadratic forms convinced Born and Jordan immediately that it had to be *the* matrix reformulation of Eq. (129).

Born and Jordan proceeded right away to develop their perturbation scheme from Eq. (133). They expanded the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ as the classical analogue in Eq. (130), and obtained the expansion of the inverse matrix $\mathbf{S}^{-1}$ as

$$\mathbf{S}^{-1} = \mathbf{1} - \lambda \mathbf{S}_1 + \lambda^2 (\mathbf{S}_1^2 - \mathbf{S}_2) + \ldots . \tag{134}$$

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0111 -->

III.2 Towards a New Perturbation Theory 107

On substituting the expressions for $\mathbf{S}$ and $\mathbf{S}^{-1}$ into Eq. (133) they derived, by direct calculation, the following set of equations:

$$\mathbf{H}_0 = \mathbf{W}_0,$$
$$\mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_0 - \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{H}_1 = \mathbf{W}_1,$$
$$\mathbf{S}_2 \mathbf{H}_0 - \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_2 + \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1^2 - \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_1 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{H}_2 = \mathbf{W}_2, \tag{135}$$

$$\mathbf{S}_r \mathbf{H}_0 - \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_r + \mathbf{F}_r(\mathbf{H}_0, \ldots \mathbf{H}_r; \mathbf{S}_0, \ldots \mathbf{S}_{r-1}) = \mathbf{W}_r,$$

etc., where $\mathbf{H}_0, \mathbf{H}_1, \ldots$, are to be taken throughout as having the arguments $\mathbf{p}_0$ and $\mathbf{q}_0$, and $\mathbf{F}_r$ are matrix functions as indicated, with $\mathbf{F}_1 = \mathbf{H}_1$, $\mathbf{F}_2 = \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1^2 - \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_1 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{H}_2$, etc. The perturbation scheme, Eqs. (135), appeared to be simpler than Heisenberg's competing scheme, Eqs. (132); in addition, it turned out to be at least as close to the classical scheme.$^{117}$

From the third equation (second-order approximation) onwards, the Born–Jordan scheme disagreed with Heisenberg's proposal. Since Eqs. (135) had been derived rigorously, Born and Jordan thought that Heisenberg, who was not as familiar with matrix methods at that time as they were, had simply made an error.$^{118}$ At first, Heisenberg was bothered by this disparity. However, he soon discovered that his scheme was not really wrong; it just differed from Born and Jordan's by the assumption he had made for the perturbation expansion of the transformation function $\mathbf{S}$. He wrote to Jordan:

> Initially I was very much ashamed of the "computational error" in my theory of the solution, and I wrote about it to Born—especially, since it was no computational error, but only a wrongly-guessed formula. Meanwhile, however, I have thought it over, and found that my carelessness had not led me astray at all this time, and that

---

$^{117}$In classical theory the first three equations of the perturbation scheme in the case of a periodic system having one degree of freedom and a Hamiltonian $H$ ($= H_0 + \lambda H_1 + \lambda^2 H_2 + \ldots$) were (see Born and Pauli, 1922, p. 140, Eqs. (7$_0$)–(7$_2$)):

$$H_0 = W_0,$$
$$\frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w^0} + H_1 = W_1,$$
$$\frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J} \frac{\partial S_2}{\partial w^0} + \tfrac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial J^2} \left( \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w^0} \right)^2 + \frac{\partial H_1}{\partial J} \frac{\partial S_1}{\partial w^0} + H_2 = W_2,$$

where $S_1$ and $S_2$ are the terms of the action function $S$ ($= J w^0 + \lambda S_1 + \lambda^2 S_2 + \ldots$), $w^0$ is the angle variable (in the zeroth order), and $J$ is the action variable of the system.

### 108 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme  

my formulae were as correct as Born’s (only in Born’s case the justification is much nicer and more transparent, while in my case one must prove something “easily” by complete induction). (Heisenberg to Jordan, 29 September 1925)  

Indeed, if one wrote the expansion of the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ as  
$$\mathbf{S} = 1 + \lambda \mathbf{S}_1 + \lambda^2 \left( \frac{1}{2} \mathbf{S}_1^2 + \mathbf{S}_2 \right) + \dots, \tag{136}$$  
then one arrived at Heisenberg’s perturbation scheme, Eqs. (132).¹¹⁹ However, he frankly admitted that ‘Born’s form for the canonical transformation is almost the high point of the present theory’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 29 September 1925).  

The definition of the transformations, such as those contained in Eq. (133), as ‘canonical’ transformations in matrix mechanics, appears to be rather bold. In classical mechanics, canonical transformations of the dynamical variables are determined by the fact that they leave the (canonical) Hamiltonian equations of motion invariant; that is, these equations hold for all dynamical variables which are related through canonical transformations. If one tried to make use of this definition in quantum mechanics, one had to take into account the fact that the corresponding matrix equations, Eqs. (90), involved matrix differentiation (i.e., the differentiation of matrices with respect to matrices). Hence it was not clear from the very beginning whether—especially for nonseparable Hamiltonians—these equations remained invariant under the transformation of the variables $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ into $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{Q}$, with  
$$\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{S p S}^{-1} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{S q S}^{-1}. \tag{137}$$  

However, if the differential quotients, $\partial H/\partial \mathbf{p}$ and $\partial H/\partial \mathbf{q}$, could be replaced by algebraic expressions—and this was always the case when one used Heisenberg’s definition of the matrix differentiation, contained in Eq. (123)—then the transformation (137) indeed represented a canonical transformation. By the end of September 1925, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan agreed to use the algebraic form, Eqs. (126), of the Hamiltonian equations in matrix mechanics. Hence they were perfectly allowed to consider the transformations (137) as canonical transformations.  

In this context another question arose: namely, whether the transformations (137) represented the most general canonical transformations. The authors approached this question in a slightly different form. They noticed that the transformations (137) left the quantum condition invariant; that is, Eq. (67) remained the same for all sets of variables $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$, related by Eqs. (137). Since the quantum conditions were supposed to play the crucial role in the theory,  


¹¹⁹ Jordan later recalled the following about the discussion concerning perturbation theory: Heisenberg’s original perturbation formula did not yield—in contrast to Born’s, which was based on the canonical transformation $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{S p S}^{-1}$—a procedure which would allow one to find the full power series in the perturbation parameter. Heisenberg’s formula gave only the first and second terms of this power series. While Born first believed that Heisenberg’s formula for the second [-order] term was incorrect, since it did not agree with the corresponding term of his [Born’s] formula, Heisenberg discovered later that the matrix which he denoted as $\mathbf{S}$ was the logarithm of Born’s quantity $\mathbf{S}$. In this sense Heisenberg’s formula still provided the correct second-order approximation. (Jordan to van der Waerden, 23 July 1962)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0113 -->

### III.3 Several Degrees of Freedom and Degeneracy 109  

Born, Heisenberg and Jordan stated a new definition of the canonical transformations.¹²⁰ They said: ‘By a “canonical transformation” of the variables $\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}$, into new variables $\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q}$, we understand a transformation in which $\mathbf{p q} - \mathbf{q p} = \mathbf{P Q} - \mathbf{Q P} = (h/2\pi i)[1]$; for then the same canonical equations apply to $\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{Q}$ as to $\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q}$’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 565). However, with this definition also one could not answer the question concerning the most general form of a canonical transformation. ‘We would surmise,’ the authors stated, ‘that Eq. [(137)] represents in fact the most general canonical transformation’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 565).  

In spite of this uncertainty, the three collaborators accepted and further developed the Born–Jordan transformation theory and the perturbation scheme derived from it. They used it to formulate, especially, the matrix mechanics of systems having several degrees of freedom, both degenerate and nondegenerate. Thus, they provided, at least in principle, the tools to solve the problem of integrating the canonical equations of motion for an arbitrary quantum-mechanical system, which they had recognized to be equivalent to the problem of diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix by introducing canonically transformed variables.  


### III.3 Several Degrees of Freedom and Degeneracy  

In their initial formulation of matrix mechanics Born and Jordan had restricted themselves to systems having only one degree of freedom; they expected, in due course, to generalize the theory to systems having an arbitrary number of degrees of freedom that normally occur in atomic physics. The first step towards such a generalization was taken up by Heisenberg in Copenhagen during the second half of September 1925, at a time when his collaborators in Göttingen were still concerned with writing up their paper (Born and Jordan, 1925b). In a postcard to Jordan he stated the quantum conditions, Eqs. (121), for systems having several degrees of freedom. Although Born and Jordan had also discussed the possibility that similar conditions might apply to these systems, they had not succeeded in deriving them from first principles in matrix theory—as they had done with the quantum condition, Eq. (67)—and therefore remained in doubt about the entire question.¹²¹  


¹²⁰ The definition of canonical transformations with the help of the quantization condition first occurred in Heisenberg’s letters. (See, especially, Heisenberg to Born, 5 October 1925.)  

¹²¹ In his postcard, after giving the formulae (121), Heisenberg remarked: ‘So far as I recall, you wrote similar conditions in a letter to me, but later you raised objections’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 21 September 1925). As we have mentioned in footnote 110 Hermann Weyl, independently of Heisenberg, arrived at the same quantum conditions (Weyl to Born, 27 September 1925). Moreover, as is evident from a letter of Heisenberg to Pauli, dated 24 September 1925, Pauli also obtained them at the same time. There Heisenberg wrote: ‘Your conjecture about the quantum conditions for [systems with] several degrees of freedom is right, of course.’ Finally, Paul Dirac in Cambridge, who worked out the consequences from Heisenberg’s quantum-mechanical ideas independently of the Göttingen physicists, presented Eqs. (121) in his symbolic language in his paper on the fundamental equations of quantum mechanics (Dirac, 1925d, p. 648, Eqs. (10)).

### 110 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme  

However, their doubts and objections did not convince Heisenberg. ‘Your reservations concerning the quantum conditions,’ he wrote to Jordan, ‘do not appear to me really convincing, though I must also admit that I have no compelling reasons for the form [of Eqs. (121)], except only those of formal beauty’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 29 September 1925). And he added the remark: ‘Compare, for example, the bracket symbols (the Jacobians [Heisenberg wrote “die Jakobische”]) of classical mechanics.’ Though with this remark he had hit upon an interesting idea, which was used later in a modified form by Paul Dirac to justify the quantum conditions (121) for systems having several degrees of freedom, he did not elaborate on it further. Heisenberg suggested that for the moment one should not pay particular attention to the question whether or not one could derive them rigorously from the equations of motion, Eqs. (126). This point of view was then adopted more or less by all collaborators; they adopted Eqs. (121) finally as the quantum conditions for systems having several degrees of freedom. In fact they changed their name to ‘commutation relations’ (‘Vertauschungsrelationen’) in their paper (BHJ, 1926, p. 573).¹²² They also agreed to take Eqs. (126) in all cases, i.e., for separable and nonseparable Hamiltonian matrices, as the canonical equations of motion. With respect to the question of deriving the commutation relations they remarked:  

Equations [(121)] would, together with Eqs. [(126)], obviously entail too extensive a set of requirements for the $\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k$, if all these equations were independent of one another. As an interesting mathematical problem must rank the derivation of Eqs. [(121)] using the minimum number of independent and mutually consistent assumptions; nevertheless, this question will not be handled here. We shall content ourselves with mentioning that $d \sum_k (\mathbf{p}_k \mathbf{q}_k - \mathbf{q}_k \mathbf{p}_k)/dt = 0$ is a general outcome of the equations of motion [(126)]. On the other hand, it will be shown that in general the equations [(121)] together with the equations of motion [(126)] ... can be satisfied (apart, of course, from singular exceptions). (BHJ, 1926, p. 575)¹²³

The latter referred, of course, to the particular quantum orbits of the old atomic theory. Actually it would turn out that Eqs. (121) are also compatible with motions which were earlier considered to be not quantized. Hence the new name appeared to be more accurate.  

¹²³ The word ‘commutation’ stemmed from the mathematical language. Hermann Weyl, for example, spoke about the ‘commutator $\mathbf{P Q P}^{-1} \mathbf{Q}^{-1}$ of the two infinitesimal transformations $\mathbf{P} = 1 + \delta \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{Q} = 1 + \epsilon \mathbf{q}$,’ which he found to be equal to $1 + \delta \epsilon [(\mathbf{p q} - \mathbf{q p}) + \dots]$ (Weyl to Born, 27 September 1925). Paul Dirac also introduced the word ‘commute.’ As he recalled:  

Another question of notation—it often happens that $u v = v u$ is a special case. When that is so, the mathematicians who had been handling noncommutative algebra said that $u$ permutes with $v$. It seemed to me that the word “permute” was not really very appropriate. One thinks of permutations as rearranging the order of several quantities, and here we are concerned only with two quantities. So I invented the word “commute.” I do not think it had been previously used in mathematics. I said that, when $u v = v u$, $u$ and $v$ commute with each other. That again is a notation which everyone has accepted since then. (Dirac, 1977, p. 129)

### III.3 Several Degrees of Freedom and Degeneracy 111  

To prove the compatibility of the commutation relations and the equations of motion, the authors had to generalize perturbation theory to quantum-mechanical systems with several degrees of freedom.  

In the formal description of such systems Born, Heisenberg and Jordan again followed the analogy with the previous semiclassical description. In the latter, a multiply periodic system having $f$ degrees of freedom depended on $f$ ‘quantum numbers,’ $n_1, \dots, n_f$. In the matrix theory discussed so far a quantum number of the old theory became associated with a pair of indices denoting the rows and columns of infinite quadratic matrices. When one treats systems of $f$ degrees of freedom according to the same prescription, one has to use matrices characterized by $f$ pairs of indices. In their paper the authors therefore represented dynamical variables in terms of ‘$2f$-dimensional matrices,’ writing the position and momentum matrices as  

$$\mathbf{q}_k = \left( q_k(n_1, \dots, n_f; m_1, \dots, m_f) \right) \tag{138a}$$  

and  

$$\mathbf{p}_k = \left( p_k(n_1, \dots, n_f; m_1, \dots, m_f) \right), \tag{138b}$$  

respectively, $k = 1, \dots, f$ (BHJ, 1926, p. 572). The significance of Eqs. (138) is that, instead of two-dimensional arrays which describe periodic quantum systems of one degree of freedom, one has now to take $2f$-dimensional arrays.¹²⁴  

Although this form of visual representation of the matrices for multiply periodic systems may be considered as being suggestive or convenient in many cases, it is by no means the only possible representation of the variables. In fact, the authors noted explicitly:  

Nevertheless this representation, albeit under certain circumstances very convenient and clear, is by no means essential. Even for several degrees of freedom the fundamental dynamical equations assume the form of matrix equations, but these matrices can as before also be written in two-dimensional form. It became apparent already for one degree of freedom that the sequence of the stationary states, as given by the ordering of the matrix rows, is (in contrast to the erstwhile theory) purely fortuitous and is not governed by any intrinsic property of the system. This  


¹²⁴ Born was accustomed to the representation of systems having several degrees of freedom by multidimensional mathematical objects already from his investigation of three-dimensional lattices of atoms. (See, e.g., Born & von Kármán, 1912.) Note that in Eqs. (138a, b) the matrix elements on the right-hand side consist of amplitudes and periodic factors in time; usually Born, Heisenberg and Jordan denoted only the amplitudes as ‘$q_k(n_1, \dots, n_f; m_1, \dots, m_f)$’.

observation can now be directly transferred to many-dimensional matrices as well; one can carry out any arbitrary rearrangements and, in particular, transform the $2f$-dimensional matrices into two-dimensional ones. The reason is that the basic definitions of addition and multiplication, as also of differentiation with respect to time, are evidently totally independent of any *ordering relations* existing between the basis systems of indices $n_1, n_2, \dots, n_f$, which, if taken *singly*, specify the *states* and, if taken *in pairs*, specify the *transitions*. (BHJ, 1926, p. 573)

The question as to which of the two equivalent representations of quantities (accounting for the properties of periodic systems having $f$ degrees of freedom) to use—the one with $2f$-dimensional matrices or the one with two-dimensional matrices—was then determined only by practical considerations. In the applications made by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan in the three-man paper, no preference was given to one or the other; both were used.

The fundamental problem in quantum mechanics, namely, the determination of the energy states of a Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}$ describing a system of $f$ $(>1)$ degrees of freedom, could now be formulated in the same way as for systems with one degree of freedom. Again the authors called those transformations ‘canonical’ that leave the commutation relations (121) unaltered; that is, if two sets of variables, $\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k$, and $\mathbf{P}_k, \mathbf{Q}_k$, are connected by transformations of the type given in Eqs. (137) involving a transformation matrix, $\mathbf{S}$, and its inverse, $\mathbf{S}^{-1}$—both of which are either $2f$- or 2-dimensional in agreement with the representation chosen for the dynamical variables—then the same commutation rules are satisfied by $\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k$ and $\mathbf{P}_k, \mathbf{Q}_k$. The diagonalization of the Hamiltonian may be obtained in this case by a canonical transformation of the original variables, say $\mathbf{p}_k^0$ and $\mathbf{q}_k^0$, in the matrix $\mathbf{H}$, according to Eq. (133) generalized to periodic systems of $f$ degrees of freedom.

Similarly Born, Heisenberg and Jordan began to develop a perturbation scheme for multiply periodic systems, which would be applicable, provided their Hamiltonian could be expanded in a series of terms multiplied by increasing powers of a small perturbation parameter $\lambda$. They assumed that in the zeroth-order approximation the system consists of $f$ uncoupled systems, each having one degree of freedom, described by the diagonalized Hamiltonians, $\mathbf{H}^{(k)}(\mathbf{p}_k^0, \mathbf{q}_k^0)$, for zeroth-order variables, $\mathbf{p}_k^0, \mathbf{q}_k^0, k = 1, \dots, f$. Hence the zeroth-order energy matrix, $\mathbf{W}_0$, is a direct sum of these individual Hamiltonians, and the perturbation terms give rise to the coupling. In order to diagonalize the total Hamiltonian of the system one can then formally use the same scheme as in the case of one degree of freedom, i.e., Eqs. (135), in which the appropriate matrices for systems of $f$ degrees of freedom are inserted.$^{125}$ Thus, the expectation, which Heisenberg had already expressed in his postcard to Jordan on 21 September 1925, that the perturbation scheme for systems of one degree of freedom could be extended to

$^{125}$ For example, the dynamical variables, $\mathbf{q}_k^0$ and $\mathbf{p}_k^0$, which diagonalize the Hamiltonian, assume the form given by Eqs. (138); the elements $q_k^0(n_1, \dots, n_f; m_1, \dots, m_f)$ are identical with $q_k^0(n_k, m_k)$, the matrix elements of the $k$th uncoupled system, if for all $j \neq k$ the indices $m_j$ and $n_j$ are identical and zero otherwise.

III.3
Several Degrees of Freedom and Degeneracy
113

systems with several degrees of freedom, was fully confirmed, as long as one considered nondegenerate systems.

Everybody, who was familiar with the problems of atomic theory, expected that the so-called degenerate systems had to be treated with special care. As ‘degenerate’ systems one had denoted those systems which, at least in some approximation, exhibited several identical energy states. Only by the action of a small perturbation, usually provided by a not-too-strong external electric or magnetic field (as in the case of the Stark and Zeeman effects of the hydrogen atom) or by the mutual interaction of electrons (as in the case of many-electron atoms), did each degenerate energy state of the system under investigation split into a pattern of slightly shifted terms. In principle, also in systems of one degree of freedom (with an appropriate potential function) can the energy states become identical, but in the usual situations that occurred in atomic physics the degeneracy was, as a rule, associated exclusively with systems having several degrees of freedom. Among the latter it was easy to find degenerate ones. One had just to assume that in the zeroth-order approximation two or more of the decoupled systems were identical: such as the two electrons moving around a helium nucleus, which represents the zeroth-order approximation to the helium problem. Hence Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had to pay particular attention to studying perturbation theory in the degenerate cases, for they quickly realized that their perturbation scheme represented by Eqs. (135) broke down in such cases. This result followed immediately from the calculation of the elements of the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ according to Eqs. (135); for $S_r(nm)$, the elements of the $r$th approximation, one obtained

$$S_r(nm) = \frac{F_r(nm)}{h \nu_0(nm)} (1 - \delta_{nm}), \quad r = 1, 2, \dots, \tag{139}$$

where $F_r(nm)$ are the elements of the matrix function $\mathbf{F}_r$, and $\nu_0(nm)$ is the frequency of transition from the state denoted by the quantum number $n$ to the state denoted by the quantum number $m$. (For systems with $f$ degrees of freedom both $n$ and $m$ are sets of $f$ quantum numbers, $n_1, \dots, n_f$, and $m_1, \dots, m_f$.$^{126}$) These equations became meaningless when the unperturbed system under consideration possessed degenerate eigenvalues because then certain $\nu_0(nm)$ were zero for $n \neq m$. Thus, the problem arose to develop a perturbation scheme for degenerate systems.

In degenerate systems there occurred many characteristic features, and these features were reflected in the matrix treatment. Thus, for example, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan noted the following fact: while one could still derive energy conservation, i.e., the fact that $\dot{\mathbf{H}}$, the time derivative of the Hamiltonian matrix vanished, this did not lead to a diagonal matrix $\mathbf{H}$. Therefore, in this case, they

$^{126}$ To derive Eqs. (139) one observes that $\mathbf{S}$, like the classical action function, has no constant term. Hence all diagonal matrix elements $S_r(nn)$ must be zero. On the other hand, the periodic terms of $\mathbf{S}_r \mathbf{H}_0 - \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_r$ and $-\mathbf{F}_r$ must be identical.

suggested a ‘sharpening of the fundamental equations’ by requiring that: ‘*As the basic equations, one should generally be able to choose the commutation relations and the property H = W = diagonal matrix*’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 577). It was only with the latter requirement that the validity of the frequency condition and the uniqueness of the energy for degenerate systems seemed to be established. However, the authors immediately noted that if the energy is uniquely given, the dynamical variables, $\mathbf{p}_k$ and $\mathbf{q}_k$, in which the Hamiltonian is diagonal, are not uniquely defined, but that either of the sets, $\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k$, and $\mathbf{p}'_k, \mathbf{q}'_k$, connected by a constant transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$, would do the same job.$^{127}$

The situation described above also occurred in the case of nondegenerate systems. However, there the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ (relating different systems of variables) must be diagonal, with matrix elements $S(nn)$ equal to $\exp(i\phi_n)$, where $\phi_n$ denotes a constant phase. The matrix elements of two different sets of dynamical variables, $\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k$, and $\mathbf{p}'_k, \mathbf{q}'_k$, which diagonalize a nondegenerate Hamiltonian matrix, were then related to each other by means of phase differences, that is,

$$p'_k(nm) = p_k(nm) \exp[i(\phi_n - \phi_m)] \tag{140a}$$

and

$$q'_k(nm) = q_k(nm) \exp[i(\phi_n - \phi_m)]. \tag{140b}$$

Hence they could not be determined more accurately than up to a phase.$^{128}$ For degenerate systems, on the other hand, the situation was quite different. In particular, it was not permitted to infer from the constancy of the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ relating two sets of dynamical variables that it is diagonal; hence very different sets of variables could diagonalize the Hamiltonian of a degenerate system. The authors commented on this uncertain situation as follows:

> This indeterminancy seems to lie in the very nature of things. Apparently, degenerate systems possess a *lability* by virtue of which arbitrarily small perturbations can bring about finite changes in coordinates, and this finds its mathematical expression in that in complete absence of perturbations, the solution of the dynamic equations remains partly indeterminate. Naturally, for every single real atom the coordinates which specify the physical properties of the system, in particular the transition probabilities, are always fixed uniquely either by external perturbations or by the previous history of the system. (BHJ, 1926, pp. 578–579)

$^{127}$ The proof of the constancy of $\mathbf{S}$ is straightforward. If $\mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}', \mathbf{q}') = \mathbf{S} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{S}^{-1}$ is identical with $\mathbf{W}$, then $\mathbf{W}$ commutes with $\mathbf{S}$, and $\dot{\mathbf{S}}$ becomes zero.
$^{128}$ Equation (140a) follows immediately from the equation $p'_k(nm) = p(nm) S_{nn} S_{mm}^{-1}$. Since the matrices $\mathbf{p}'_k$ and $\mathbf{p}_k$ are assumed to be Hermitian, one obtains $|S_{nn}| = |S_{mm}|$. This result then leads to Eqs. (140), provided one normalizes all dynamical variables.
The statement contained in Eqs. (140) had been anticipated already earlier by Born and Jordan in connection with the treatment of the anharmonic oscillator (Born and Jordan, 1925b, p. 881). It was independently emphasized by Heisenberg for general systems: ‘As far as the phases are concerned, it is trivial in any case that a phase constant of the form $\phi_{ik} = \phi_i - \phi_k$ *always* remains arbitrary’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 7 October 1925).

Again, as in the classical case, one had to assume, of course, that $\overline{\mathbf{H}}_1$, the time average, was finite.$^{130}$ The transformation of the original variables, $\mathbf{p}_k^0$, $\mathbf{q}_k^0$, to new variables, $\bar{\mathbf{p}}_k^0$ ($= \mathbf{S}_0 \mathbf{p}_k^0 \mathbf{S}_0^{-1}$) and $\bar{\mathbf{q}}_k^0$ ($= \mathbf{S}_0 \mathbf{q}_k^0 \mathbf{S}_0^{-1}$), now brought well-determined quantum variables of the problem in the zeroth-order approximation. $\mathbf{H}_0$ was supposed to remain diagonal in the new variables, assuming the same eigenvalues as before.$^{131}$ After performing this extra transformation, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan could go on to apply their perturbation scheme, Eqs. (135), for nondegenerate systems. That is, the perturbation scheme for degenerate systems (given in BHJ, 1926, p. 579, Eqs. (26)–(29)) differed from the one for nondegenerate systems only by the additional transformation involving the matrix $\mathbf{S}_0$; hence the total transformation in the degenerate case is composed as a matrix product, $\mathbf{S}_0\mathbf{S}$, with the factors $\mathbf{S}_0$ and $\mathbf{S}$, the latter indicating a transformation matrix for a nondegenerate system.

The procedure for solving the perturbation equations for a degenerate system was found to be analogous to that in the classical case. From the first equation, that is,

$$ \mathbf{S}_0 \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_0^{-1} = \mathbf{W}_0, \tag{142} $$

the authors concluded that all matrix elements $S_0(nm)$ were zero, except those for which the associated frequencies $\nu_0(nm)$ vanished. As a result the matrix $\mathbf{S}_0$ reduced to blocks of finite submatrices along the diagonal, the elements outside the blocks being zero. The numbers of rows and columns of these (quadratic) submatrices were determined by the degree of degeneracy of the different eigenvalues of the diagonal matrix $\mathbf{W}_0$; that is, for two identical eigenvalues a $2 \times 2$ submatrix appeared in $\mathbf{S}_0$. The nonzero elements of $S_0(nm)$ now had to be chosen such that the second equation of the degenerate perturbation scheme was satisfied.$^{132}$ As a result of this procedure, however, those elements $S_1(nm)$ of the first-order perturbation matrix $\mathbf{S}_1$ (the matrix $\mathbf{S}$ was assumed to be expanded as $1 + \lambda\mathbf{S}_1 + \lambda^2\mathbf{S}_2 + \dots$), for which $\nu_0(nm)$ vanished, could not be determined by the first-order perturbation equation for degenerate systems.$^{133}$ The authors fixed them only by going over to the second-order approximation in the following way: they took the 'time average' over the third second-order perturbation equation, arriving at the equation

$$ \overline{(\mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1^2 - \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_0 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{S}_1 \mathbf{H}_1 - \mathbf{H}_1 \mathbf{S}_1 + \mathbf{H}_2)} = \mathbf{S}_0^{-1} \mathbf{W}_2 \mathbf{S}_0, \tag{143} $$

where the bar on top of the bracket denotes the diagonal elements of the

### III.3 Several Degrees of Freedom and Degeneracy

117

corresponding matrix and $\mathbf{W}_2$ on the right-hand side is supposed to be a diagonal matrix, yielding the second-order correction to the energy of the system under investigation. After that they solved the full second-order perturbation equation; that is, they calculated those elements $S_2(nm)$ of $\mathbf{S}_2$, the second-order correction to the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$, which lay *outside* the diagonal blocks (i.e., at positions where the matrix $\mathbf{S}_0$ has nonzero elements). Again the other elements of $\mathbf{S}_2$ could be obtained from the next higher-order equation, i.e., by time-averaging over the third-order perturbation equation. The calculation of still higher-order contributions to the transformation matrix could be continued by following the same procedure; i.e., by first evaluating a part of the elements of $\mathbf{S}_3$ by solving the third-order equation, and the rest by solving the time-averaged fourth-order equation, etc.$^{134}$

Having obtained the perturbation scheme for treating degenerate systems, i.e., for systems whose energy matrix in zeroth-order approximation contains identical eigenvalues, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan still had to demonstrate that no contradiction would arise in applying it. 'The difficulty lies in the fact,' they acknowledged, 'that at each order of approximation equations have to be satisfied by matrices which are already fixed to a large extent [e.g., the second-order perturbation equation is used both to determine elements of the matrix $\mathbf{S}_1$ and of $\mathbf{S}_2$ with the same diagonal matrix $\mathbf{W}_2$], so that it is not possible to foresee whether or not these equations will really prove soluble' (BHJ, 1926, p. 580). However, they did not feel too bad about this situation, for the same difficulty existed in classical theory. As in the latter, they did not expect any particular trouble in quantum mechanics, at least not with those systems which became nondegenerate when higher-order perturbations were included because then the calculations could be continued with the perturbation scheme for nondegenerate systems in which no such complications arose.

With their perturbation scheme for degenerate systems the authors had achieved the goal of formulating the fundamental equations of matrix mechanics and the principal methods for solving them, in close parallel to the classical equations. At times they found that the quantum-mechanical equations possessed a simpler structure than the classical ones; the description of quantum systems also turned out to be less complicated. For example, in classical theory *different* perturbation schemes had to be applied to cases involving 'real' degeneracy (see Born and Pauli, 1922) and to those involving 'accidental' degeneracy (Born and Heisenberg, 1923a). In a case of 'real' degeneracy the frequency associated with the degenerate degree of freedom vanished for all values of the action variables, while 'accidental' degeneracy occurred when the associated frequencies were zero only for selected values of the action variables.
