III.4 Born’s *Idée Fixe* and a Letter to Niels Bohr 119

berg, who preferred a more intuitive, physical approach, recognized the superiority of the mathematical methods employed especially by Max Born. He expressed this change in his attitude in a letter to Wolfgang Pauli. After discussing the fundamental problem of quantum mechanics, i.e., the diagonalization of the Hamiltonian matrix, he remarked: ‘The problem is (I shall not write this in greater detail) equivalent to a principal-axes transformation of infinitely many variables, i.e., to a system of infinitely many homogeneous linear equations. The energy values $W_n$ are the eigenvalues of this problem; they may be discrete or continuous. The multiplicity of an energy value represents its statistical weight’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 12 October 1925). With these remarks Heisenberg pointed to a new formulation of matrix mechanics, which could be considered as being most general and complete, transcending even Born and Jordan’s matrix mechanics in its sophistication. This theory formed part of the mathematical tradition of Göttingen and was now made use of by Max Born.

Just when Heisenberg wrote to Pauli from Copenhagen the lines quoted above, Niels Bohr received a long letter from Born. In this letter Born explained in some detail the fundamental mathematical ideas on quantum mechanics that had taken shape in his mind. ‘I am so happy,’ he wrote, ‘that you like Heisenberg’s idea. I am quite sure that it represents a great progress and that the formulation, which Jordan and I have given to it, is perhaps in a certain sense something final, so far as one can say that at all in physics’ (Born to Bohr, 10 October 1925). Born now proceeded to give reasons for his conviction to Bohr, who was anything but a formalist and who did not readily accept mathematical arguments. ‘For me the possibility of this formulation has a very personal attraction,’ wrote Born. ‘Since my student days I have have been haunted by an *idée fixe*, namely, that all essential laws of physics must find their adequate formulation as invariants of linear substitutions.’ Born had acquired this *idée fixe* about the structure of physical laws under the influence of his teachers in mathematics, and he told the story to Bohr:

> When I began to study in Breslau in 1900, I learned—from the old, little known, but very ingenious and stimulating mathematician [Jakob] Rosanes—analytic geometry immediately in the form of a theory of invariants; and I was introduced by him also to the works of Cayley, Frobenius and others, in which matrix calculus constituted the most important formal tool. Then in 1905 I came to Göttingen under the influence of [Felix] Klein, who saw everything from the point of view of the theory of invariants, and of [David] Hilbert, who had then just seized Fredholm’s theory of integral equations and was about to extend it to a theory of the quadratic forms of infinitely many variables. All this strengthened my *idée fixe*. Then, from the side of physics, came relativity theory, which completely fitted into the scheme. (Born to Bohr, 10 October 1925)$^{136}$

---
$^{136}$Actually, Born had gone to Göttingen in 1904. He had witnessed there not only the development of the theory of integral equations in Hilbert’s hands, but also Hermann Minkowski’s steps towards a relativistic electrodynamics along the lines which Felix Klein had conceived many years earlier in connection with the theory of invariants in geometry. Thus, Klein had set up the programme of formulating theories in mathematics and physics in the framework of the algebraic theory of invariants, while Hilbert and Minkowski—whose student Born was primarily—had carried out the programme in practice.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0124 -->

# 120
## Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

In looking back on his student days, Born reminded himself of Hilbert’s work on the generalization of the theory of integral equations, in which Hilbert had employed what he called ‘Hermitian forms of infinitely many variables’ (Hilbert, 1906a). In this work, Hilbert had, in particular, extended to infinite forms a proof given by Charles Hermite that a finite quadratic form \( A(x, x^*) \) (\(= \sum a_{nm} x_n x_m^* \) with \( a_{nm} = a_{mn}^* \)) of the complex variables, \( x_1, \dots, x_k \), can always be reduced by a transformation to new variables, \( y_1, \dots, y_k \), to a sum of squares, \( \sum \lambda_n y_n y_n^* \), each term being weighted by a coefficient which turns out to be the root of the characteristic equation associated with the form (Hermite, 1855). Hilbert’s theory of the principal-axes transformation, developed further by his students Ernst Hellinger (1907, 1909) and Hermann Weyl (1908), had made a deep impression on Born, and he mentioned the consequences in his letter to Bohr by saying: ‘Thus it happened that everything [in physics], which I did myself, e.g., the contributions to the lattice theory of crystals, always ended up in my treating the matter as transformations of quadratic forms or something similar’ (Born to Bohr, 10 October 1925). In his work on lattice theory, Born had already explicitly performed a principal-axes transformation of a quadratic form of infinitely many variables (Born and von Kármán, 1912). Thus, it was not surprising that now, in fall 1925, he reminded himself of this experience and tried to apply it to the problems he was treating in quantum mechanics.

In writing to Bohr, however, the thought crossed Born’s mind that the knowledge of all this mathematical background alone would only help a little, for he said: ‘I am sure that such a one-sided method of viewing things might appear to you as being quite ridiculous, because the formalism is rather secondary for the actual physical relationships. I am, however, aware of the fact that I lack that physical intuition which you and Heisenberg possess; and all that I can contribute to advance the thing consists in putting the physical regularities into a mathematical scheme.’ In spite of this confession of his own shortcomings, Born thought it fortunate that he was well prepared to take up Heisenberg’s ideas and to formulate them in a proper mathematical language. Thus he wrote to Bohr: ‘Therefore I am now so happy that Heisenberg’s rules fit exceedingly beautifully into my *idée fixe*, and that one can express quantum mechanics directly in the form of an eigenvalue problem; thereby one can, it seems to me, perceive all theoretical possibilities quite well. I am very curious how far the presently formulated fundamental theorems will hold out; it may well be that new principles will have to be added. But I am firmly convinced that the basic skeleton of the formulation is reasonable’ (Born to Bohr, 10 October 1925).

During the next eighteen days, until he left for an extended visit to the United States, Born worked on the application of Hilbert’s principal-axes transformation theory to the problems of matrix mechanics, especially the fundamental problem of determining the eigenstates of the energy matrix. Born’s discussion of the connection between the theory of Hermitian forms and quantum theory revealed the great beauty of the intimate relationship between physics and mathematics. In it, he first restated the problem of diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix as an eigenvalue problem of an infinite quadratic Hermitian form. Then he used his

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0125 -->

# 121
## III.5 The Eigenvalue Problem and the Transformation to Principal Axes

formulation and the concept of ‘eigenforms’ (‘Eigenformen’), developed by Hilbert and Hellinger, to throw new light on the treatment of perturbed systems in matrix mechanics. Born’s use of the principal-axes transformation theory for the purpose of solving the quantum-theoretical problem of motion led to an important physical conclusion: in general the infinite matrices, considered in the quantum-mechanical description of physical variables, should possess both discrete and continuous indices and the Hamiltonian matrices, especially, should then have discrete *and* continuous eigenvalues. This result was received with great enthusiasm by Heisenberg and Jordan. They took over without any change Born’s contribution to the ‘connection [of quantum mechanics] with the theory of the eigenvalues of Hermitian forms’ as Chapter 3 of their joint paper.<sup>137</sup>

### III.5 The Eigenvalue Problem and the Transformation to Principal Axes

In order to deal in matrix mechanics with the fundamental problem of calculating the energy states of a system of \( f \) degrees of freedom, described by the Hamiltonian matrix \(\mathbf{H}\), Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had found the following prescription: One may select any special system of matrices \( p_k^0 \) and \( q_k^0 \) (\( k = 1, \dots, f \)), such that the commutation relations (121) are satisfied. The dynamical problem then consists in searching for a transformation to new variables, represented by the matrices \( p_k \) and \( q_k \), which obey the same commutation relations and at the same time reduce the Hamiltonian \(\mathbf{H}(p_k, q_k)\) to a diagonal matrix. It was this particular problem to which Born wanted to apply the mathematical theory of principal-axes transformation of bilinear forms. Thus he remarked: ‘The transformation of the matrices can most easily be grasped if one regards them as a system of coefficients of linear transformations or bilinear forms’ (BHJ, 1926, Chapter 3, p. 582). With these words he not only referred to the fact that the very origins of matrix theory lay in algebraic equations, but especially to the connection between matrix mechanics and Hilbert’s theory of quadratic forms, which he now brought into focus.

The formal relation between the quantum-mechanical problem and the algebraic problem was easily established. With every infinite Hermitian matrix \(\mathbf{a} = (a(nm))\) (where the indices \( n \) and \( m \) assume integral values, starting, say, from zero)—whose transpose, \(\mathbf{a}^T\), equals the matrix \(\mathbf{a}^* = (a^*(nm))\), in which all the elements of the original matrix are replaced by their complex conjugates—Born associated a quadratic Hermitian form, \( A(x, x^*) \),

$$ A(x, x^*) = \sum_{n,m=0}^{\infty} a(nm) x_n x_m^*, \tag{144} $$

<sup>137</sup> Born remarked about the writing of Chapter 3 as follows: ‘I remember darkly that Heisenberg and Jordan were not interested much in this chapter and left it to me. Heisenberg checked everything, but he did not have a deep interest in it’ (Born, *Conversations*, p. 46).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0126 -->

# 122
## Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

of an infinite set of complex variables, \( x_0, x_1, \dots \).<sup>138</sup> Evidently, the quadratic Hermitian forms assumed real values. In his theory of integral equations, Hilbert had considered linear transformations of the variables, especially what he called ‘orthogonal substitutions’ (Hilbert, 1906a, p. 196). His procedure was now taken over by Born, who performed linear transformations of \( x_n \) to new variables \( y_l \), defined by the equations

$$ x_n = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} v(ln) y_l, \quad n = 0, 1, \dots, \tag{145} $$

involving the transformation matrix \(\mathbf{v} = (v(ln))\). With this transformation the quadratic form \( A(x, x^*) \), Eq. (144), could be written as

$$ A(x, x^*) = B(y, y^*) = \sum b(nm) y_n y_m^*, $$

with

$$ b(nm) = \sum_{k,l=0}^{\infty} v(nk) a(kl) v^*(ml). \tag{146} $$

The coefficients of the transformed quadratic form constituted a matrix \(\mathbf{b}\), which was obtained from the matrix \(\mathbf{a}\) through the matrix equation

$$ \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{v} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{v}^{*T}. \tag{147} $$

The matrix \(\mathbf{b}\) again turned out to be Hermitian, as followed at once from its definition and the application of the rule concerning the transposition of a matrix product, that is, \((\mathbf{ab})^T = \mathbf{b}^T \mathbf{a}^T\). The matrix \(\mathbf{v}\) was first called ‘orthogonal’ and later ‘unitary,’ provided the substitution, expressed by Eq. (146), did not change the ‘unit Hermitian form’ (‘Hermitesche Einheitsform’) \( E(x, x^*)\). Evidently, \(\mathbf{v}\) had then to satisfy the equation

$$ \mathbf{v} \mathbf{v}^{*T} = \mathbf{1} \quad \text{or} \quad \mathbf{v}^{*T} = \mathbf{v}^{-1}. \tag{148} $$

As a result, Eq. (147) defined a special transformation, a unitary transformation of the matrix \(\mathbf{a}\).<sup>139</sup>

<sup>138</sup> For the moment the time-dependent exponentials, \(\exp[2\pi i v(nm)t]\), are included in the coefficients of the quantum-mechanical matrices.

<sup>139</sup> Hilbert had first defined ‘orthogonal transformations’ only in connection with quadratic forms possessing real coefficients (Hilbert, 1906a, p. 180, *passim*). Later (in Section XII of the same paper, p. 216, *passim*) he generalized the concept of orthogonal transformations so as to apply also to Hermitian forms with complex coefficients. Later in 1906 he would speak about ‘Hermitian orthogonality’ in this context (Hilbert, von Neumann and Nordheim, 1928, p. 22). In 1925 Born used the same notation as Hilbert, i.e., he called the transformation with the matrix \(\mathbf{v}\), satisfying Eq. (147), an ‘orthogonal’ transformation.

The notion of a ‘unitary substitution’ or a ‘unitary orthogonal matrix,’ on the other hand, had already been used in mathematics two decades earlier (L. Autonne, 1902, p. 108; I. Schur, 1909, p. 489). John von Neumann returned to this concept in 1927 in his first paper on the mathematical

# 123
## III.5 The Eigenvalue Problem and the Transformation to Principal Axes

Born now referred to the well-known mathematical result that it is always possible to reduce a Hermitian form of finitely many complex variables by a unitary transformation to a sum of squares, of which each term is multiplied by a real coefficient (Hermite, 1854, 1855). In matrix language this result meant that for any matrix \(\mathbf{a}\) there had to exist a ‘unitary’ (or ‘complex orthogonal’) transformation involving a matrix \(\mathbf{v}\) satisfying Eq. (148), such that

$$ \mathbf{v} \mathbf{a} \mathbf{v}^{-1} = \mathbf{W}, \tag{149} $$

where \(\mathbf{W}\) is a diagonal matrix with elements \(\delta_{nm} W_n\). Hilbert had obtained an analogous result for compact (completely continuous) infinite matrices (Hilbert, 1906a). In agreement with Hilbert’s notation, Born called the \( W_n \)—obtained from the transformation of an infinite Hermitian form \( A(x, x^*) \) to principal axes (the \( W_n \) could also be interpreted as the inverse of the lengths of the axes of the associated geometrical figure)—the ‘eigenvalues’ (‘Eigenwerte’) and their ensemble the ‘mathematical spectrum’ (‘mathematisches Spektrum’) of \( A(x, x^*) \). The spectrum, he noted further, is made up of discrete and continuous parts; he retained Hilbert’s names, i.e., ‘Punktspektrum’ (‘point spectrum’) for the discrete eigenvalues \( W_n \) and ‘Streckenspektrum’ (‘continuous spectrum’) for those eigenvalues which are not separated but continuously connected (BHJ, 1926, pp. 583–584).<sup>140</sup> Hilbert had proved the existence of a continuous spectrum, in addition to a discrete spectrum, for the bounded quadratic forms, i.e., for forms whose coefficients satisfy the condition given by Eq. (42). (See Hilbert, 1906a, pp. 189–190, Theorem II.)

Hilbert had created his mathematical concept of ‘spectrum’ in close analogy to the notion of ‘term spectrum’ in physical spectroscopy. That now proved to

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0128 -->

124 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Chapter III &nbsp;Completion of the Matrix Scheme

have been a genuinely prophetic insight for the purpose of applying the mathematical theory of infinite quadratic forms to matrix mechanics, especially in connection with the fundamental problem of diagonalizing Hermitian matrices describing quantum systems. Born was immediately able to translate Hilbert’s result into the appropriate physical language and conclude that the matrix **S** of Eq. (133), which generates canonical transformations in quantum mechanics, should be a unitary matrix and satisfy the relation (148).

At first sight it appeared that in this manner of transforming **H**, the Hamiltonian matrix of a given quantum system, into a diagonal matrix **W**, little had been gained towards the solution of the dynamical problem beyond what had been achieved already. For example, the uniqueness of the spectrum of eigenvalues for an arbitrary Hamiltonian matrix could be proved also if the transformation matrix **S** was an arbitrary nonsingular matrix having just an inverse.$^{141}$ However, the new mathematical representation soon revealed its advantages, especially when one reformulated the problem of diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix **H** by the equivalent algebraic problem of solving the infinite set of linear equations,

$$Wv_k - \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} H(kl)v_l = 0, \qquad (150)$$

for the unknown variables, $v_k, k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, and the unknown parameter $W$. The $H(kl)$ are to be identified with the elements of the Hamiltonian matrix (including the time-dependent exponentials). If **H** is a finite matrix, the associated set of Eqs. (150) is finite and yields nontrivial solutions (i.e., $v_k \neq 0$) only when the parameter $W$ assumes certain discrete values, $W_n, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$; these $W_n$ are given by the roots of the characteristic equation, $\det[H(kl) - W\delta_{kl}] = 0$. Furthermore, it turns out that these roots are identical with the elements of the matrix **W**, obtained by diagonalizing the matrix **H**. Hence the equivalence of the dynamical problem in quantum mechanics and the problem of finding a nontrivial solution of the set of linear equations is established in this case. However, Hilbert had extended the equivalence proof to include a large class of infinite matrices as well.$^{142}$ This could be verified most easily by assuming that *all eigenvalues, $W_n$, of the Hamiltonian matrix under consideration were nondegenerate*. Then, for each $W_n$, there existed a specific set of variables, $v_k = v_{kn}$

---
$^{141}$The reason for the identity of the resulting diagonal matrices **W** ($= \mathbf{SHS}^{-1}$) and **W'** ($= \mathbf{THT}^{-1}$) for different unitary transformation matrices **S** and **T** lies in the fact that also the matrix product $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{TS}^{-1}$ is a transformation matrix. Because of $\mathbf{W'} = \mathbf{MWM}^{-1}$, there follow the equations, $M(nm)(W'_n - W_m) = 0$, where not all elements $M(nm)$ are zero. Thus, for a given eigenvalue $W'_n$ there exists at least one eigenvalue $W_m$ and vice versa. Moreover, the multiplicity of a given eigenvalue, which determines the weight of the energy state of the system, is uniquely defined, independently of how the Hamiltonian matrix is transformed into the diagonal matrix.

$^{142}$Hilbert (1906a) had especially dealt with what he called ‘completely continuous’ (compact) and ‘bounded’ matrices (see our discussion in Section I.2). His results were slightly generalized and later reformulated by Ernst Hellinger later (Hellinger, 1909), from where Born took them over in quantum mechanics. (However, the reference to Hellinger’s paper in BHJ, 1926, p. 583, footnote 2, is not quite correct.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0129 -->

III.5 &nbsp;The Eigenvalue Problem and the Transformation to Principal Axes &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;125

$(k = 0, 1, 2, \dots)$, which satisfied the equations

$$W_n v_{kn} - \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} H(kl)v_{ln} = 0. \qquad (150a)$$

Evidently, the $v_{kn}$ were determined only up to constant factors by Eqs. (150a), and not all of them should be zero. Two different sets, $v_{kn}$ and $v_{km}$, associated with different energies, $W_n$ and $W_m$, could be shown to be orthogonal; this followed by applying Eqs. (150) for the state $W_n$ and the complex conjugate equations for the state $W_m$. By normalizing the nonzero expression $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} v_{kn} v_{kn}^*$ to unity, Born obtained the orthogonality relations for the sets of $v_{kn}$ ($k, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$), that is,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} v_{kn} v_{km}^* = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } n = m \\ 0 & \text{for } n \neq m. \end{cases} \qquad (151)$$

Hence he identified the $v_{kn}$ with the elements of the matrix **S**, with the help of which the infinite Hamiltonian matrix **H** (whose elements coincide with the coefficients $H(kl)$ in Eq. (150a)) had to be transformed to a diagonal matrix **W**. (See Eq. (133).$^{143}$)

To demonstrate the correctness of this assertion, Born turned to the Hermitian form, $H(x, x^*) \left(= \sum_{k,l=0}^{\infty} H(kl)x_k x_l^*\right)$, and transformed the variables $x_k$ in it to new variables $y_m$ with the help of the $v_{kn}$, i.e., $x_k = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} v_{km} y_m$; thus he obtained the result

$$H(x, x^*) = \sum_{k,l=0}^{\infty} \sum_{m,n=0}^{\infty} H(kl) v_{km} y_m v_{ln}^* y_n^* = \sum_{m=0}^{\infty} W_m y_m y_m^*. \qquad (152)$$

Though the right-hand side of this equation yielded the desired proof, its derivation included an intermediate step which needed justification. Specifically, Born had exchanged the infinite sums over $m$ and $n$ with the infinite sums over $k$ and $l$. Such a procedure was permitted only if the Hermitian form was ‘completely continuous’ or ‘compact’ (see the discussion in Section I.2), which was guaranteed, for instance, when the sum of squares of all coefficients, $\sum_{kl} |H(kl)|^2$, existed. However, the quadratic Hermitian forms arising in matrix mechanics were not compact at all. Hence the result, expressed in Eq. (152), appeared to be very questionable. Still Born, who knew about the difficulty, expected that his result would remain valid for those mechanical systems in which the existence of a discrete spectrum was known empirically; he showed further that if it was so, the initially made assumption of nondegeneracy of the energy states could be dropped.

---
$^{143}$In Hilbert’s theory of quadratic forms (Hilbert, 1906a), the $v_{kn}$ ($k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$) were the coefficients of the so-called ‘linear eigenforms’ $L_n(x) \left(= \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} v_{kn} x_k\right)$. An orthogonal (and complete) system of the latter, denoted by the running index $n$ ($= 0, 1, 2, \dots$), served to reduce a Hermitian quadratic form to principal axes. (See, e.g., Hellinger, 1909, p. 222, *passim*.) This result was taken over by Born in matrix mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0130 -->

126 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Chapter III &nbsp;Completion of the Matrix Scheme

Forgetting about this admitted lack of mathematical rigour in establishing the relation between the algebraic methods employed in the theory of infinite quadratic Hermitian forms and the fundamental dynamical problem of matrix mechanics, one could profitably use Eqs. (150) or (150a) to understand more clearly the already formulated perturbation scheme of quantum mechanics, especially to clarify certain aspects which had been left unanswered before. For this purpose, Born considered a system described by a Hamiltonian matrix $H$, which could be expanded in terms of a small parameter $\lambda$, and substituted its matrix elements $H(kl)$ ($= \delta_{kl} W_l^{(0)} + \lambda H_1(kl) + \lambda^2 H_2(kl) + \dots$) into the algebraic equations (150). He then also expanded the parameter $W$ ($= W^{(0)} + \lambda W^{(1)} + \lambda^2 W^{(2)} + \dots$) and the variables $v_k$ ($= v_k^{(0)} + \lambda v_k^{(1)} + \lambda^2 v_k^{(2)} + \dots$) in terms of $\lambda$ and, by considering the terms of zeroth order, first order, second order, respectively, he arrived at the linear, homogeneous equations

$$v_k^{(0)} (W^{(0)} - W_k^{(0)}) = 0, \qquad (153a)$$

$$v_k^{(1)} (W^{(0)} - W_k^{(0)}) = -v_k^{(0)} W^{(1)} + \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} H_1(kl) v_l^{(0)}, \qquad (153b)$$

$$v_k^{(2)} (W^{(0)} - W_k^{(0)}) = -(v_k^{(1)} W^{(1)} + v_k^{(0)} W^{(2)}) + \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} [H_1(kl) v_l^{(1)} + H_2(kl) v_l^{(0)}]. \qquad (153c)$$

Evidently, Eqs. (153) were completely equivalent to the first three equations of the matrix perturbation scheme, Eqs. (135), for nondegenerate systems. By solving Eqs. (153) and the following equations expressing higher-order approximations, solutions were obtained for the unknown $v_k^{(0)}$, $v_k^{(1)}$, $v_k^{(2)}$, etc. (namely, the values $v_{kn}^{(0)}$, $v_{kn}^{(1)}$, $v_{kn}^{(2)}$, etc.) and the parameters $W^{(0)}$, $W^{(1)}$, $W^{(2)}$, etc. (namely, the values $W_n^{(0)}$, $W_n^{(1)}$, $W_n^{(2)}$, etc.), which turned out to be identical with the solutions found from Eqs. (135) for the elements of the transition matrix **S** ($= \mathbf{S}_0 + \lambda \mathbf{S}_1 + \lambda^2 \mathbf{S}_2 + \dots$) and the elements of the diagonal energy matrix **W** ($= \mathbf{W}^0 + \lambda \mathbf{W}^{(1)} + \lambda^2 \mathbf{W}^{(2)} + \dots$).

Thus far, the algebraic perturbation scheme had achieved nothing new; however, its advantage showed itself in the fact that it allowed one to deal with both nondegenerate and degenerate systems, which the scheme of Eqs. (135) could not do. This was explicitly demonstrated by Born in Chapter 3, Section 2, of the three-man paper in the following way. For systems, whose unperturbed Hamiltonian had $r$-fold degenerate eigenvalues, say $W_n^{(0)} = W_{n+1}^{(0)} = \dots = W_{n+r-1}^{(0)}$, Eq. (153a) yielded the solution $W^{(0)} = W_n^{(0)}$ for the zeroth-order energy. However, for this energy value, $r^2$ nonzero solutions existed in the same (zeroth) approximation for the coefficients $v_k^{(0)}$, these being $v_{nn}^{(0)}, v_{n,n+1}^{(0)}, \dots, v_{n,n+r-1}^{(0)}; v_{n+1,n}^{(0)}, v_{n+1,n+1}^{(0)}, \dots, v_{n+1,n+r-1}^{(0)}; \dots; v_{n+r-1,n}^{(0)}, v_{n+r-1,n+1}^{(0)}, \dots, v_{n+r-1,n+r-1}^{(0)}$. All the

III.5 &nbsp;The Eigenvalue Problem and the Transformation to Principal Axes &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;127

other solutions, namely, $v_{k,n}^{(0)}, v_{k,n+1}^{(0)}, \dots, v_{k,n+r-1}^{(0)}$, where $k \neq n, n+1, \dots, n+r-1$, were zero. This result reflected a general property of Eqs. (150): If an eigenvalue is $r$-fold degenerate, then $r$ linearly independent solutions exist for the set of unknown variables $v_k$; this implies that *the statistical weight of an eigenvalue is determined by the algebraic structure of Eqs. (150)*, which may be called the eigenvalue equations.

In order to arrive at the explicit solutions, $v_{kn}^{(0)}$, for the above-mentioned variables, one had to go—in agreement with the observations made in Section III.3 concerning the perturbation scheme for degenerate systems—to the first-order equation (153b). After substituting in it for the unperturbed energy, $W^{(0)} = W_n^{(0)}$, the right-hand side became zero; then arose $r$ homogeneous linear equations for $r$ unknown variables $v_k^{(0)}$, which had nontrivial solutions only if the matrix of the coefficients was singular. As a consequence, the determinant of this matrix had to be singular; that is, the condition

$$\det \begin{pmatrix} H_1(nn) - W^{(1)}, & H_1(n, n+1), & \dots & H_1(n, n+r-1) \\ H_1(n+1, n), & H_1(n+1, n+1) - W^{(1)}, & \dots & H_1(n+1, n+r-1) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ H_1(n+r-1, n), & \dots & \dots & H_1(n+r-1, n+r-1) - W^{(1)} \end{pmatrix} = 0 \qquad (154)$$

had to be satisfied. Evidently, Eq. (154) allowed one to calculate the $r$ characteristic roots or eigenvalues, $W_n^{(1)}, W_{n+1}^{(1)}, \dots, W_{n+r-1}^{(1)}$, and these values split the $r$-fold degenerate state with energy $W_n^{(0)}$ into states with energies $W_n^{(0)} + \lambda W_n^{(1)}, W_n^{(0)} + \lambda W_{n+1}^{(1)}, \dots, W_n^{(0)} + \lambda W_{n+r-1}^{(1)}$.

Equation (154) possesses the structure of the ‘secular’ equation in classical astronomy and leads to similar consequences: for instance, slow (‘secular’) oscillations appear in the perturbed quantum system with periods—e.g., $(h/\lambda) \cdot (W_n^{(1)} - W_{n+1}^{(1)})^{-1}$—which are large compared to the periods of the unperturbed motion because of the smallness of the perturbation parameter $\lambda$.$^{144}$ Two situations are then possible: either the $r$ roots of Eq. (154) are different or they are not. In the latter case, one must repeat the whole procedure for obtaining the values of $v_k^{(0)}$ in the next higher approximation, as we have discussed already in Section III.3. Thus, again Born’s new algebraic perturbation scheme, Eqs. (153), confirmed the conclusions of the matrix scheme for degenerate systems; in

---
$^{144}$In classical astronomy the motions of certain planets, which have periods that are approximately multiples of a ground period, experience slow oscillations (‘secular’ motions). In atomic physics the same phenomena occur, and again the ‘secular’ frequencies turn out to be many orders of magnitude smaller than those of normal transitions.

Let us recall that Born had come across a similar secular problem earlier in connection with lattice dynamics (Born and von Kármán, 1913b). There he had studied the modes occurring in a three-dimensional lattice; the degeneracy in question had originated because no distinction had been made in the three space directions in the zeroth-order approximation. The degeneracy was removed as soon as anisotropic crystals were considered.

addition it provided elegant and well-established methods for the actual calculation.$^{145}$

The orthogonality relations for the coefficients $v_{kn}$, Eqs. (151), or the corresponding unitarity condition for the matrix $\mathbf{S}$ establishing a canonical transformation, led to an important consequence concerning degenerate systems. Born considered, in particular, a system having an $r$-fold degenerate value $W_n^{(0)}$ in zeroth-order approximation and concluded from the unitarity of the $(r \times r)$-submatrix of $\mathbf{S}_0$, discussed earlier, that the sum of absolute squares of $r$ transition amplitudes, $\sum_{m=n}^{n+r-1} |q^{(0)}(mk)|^2$, with $k \neq n, n+1, \ldots, n+r-1$, had to remain invariant, if the canonical transformation generated by the matrix $\mathbf{S}_0$ was applied to the dynamical variables of the system. Since the sum of absolute squares of the transition amplitudes had been found to be closely related to the total intensities of line multiplets—in the approximation in which the emitting atom may be considered as a degenerate system—one could agree with Born’s conclusion: ‘This result provides a mathematical representation of the so-called spectroscopic stability, which has played an important part in the more recent theories of fine-structure intensities’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 590). Heisenberg, who had contributed extensively to these ‘more recent theories,’ was willing to consider Born’s conclusion as confirming the validity of the application of the theory of principal-axes transformation to atomic theory.

Born had another reason to be pleased with *his* reformulation of the quantum-mechanical transformation theory. ‘The calculations with matrices,’ he said later, ‘seemed to me rather artificial and complicated, while the calculations in the algebraic formalism went on in a straightforward manner’ (Born, Conversations, p. 48). Born was also glad to have taken further steps in emancipating quantum mechanics from the use of semiclassical concepts; the setting up of the new perturbation scheme indeed confirmed the opinion which he had expressed in the introduction to Chapter 3 of the three-man paper. There he had remarked: ‘The treatment of the preceding sections has aimed at solving the basic quantum-theoretical equations in a manner as closely parallel to classical theory as possible. But behind the formalism of this perturbation theory there lurks a very simple, purely algebraic connection and it is well worth bringing it into the limelight’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 581). The algebraic connection thus discovered allowed him, among other things, to obtain just *one* set of perturbation equations, Eqs. (153), which was equally applicable to systems having either nondegenerate or degenerate unperturbed Hamiltonians. However, for this reason alone one might not consider it necessary to employ the advanced mathematical tools of Hilbert’s theory of the principal-axes transformation of infinite quadratic forms. There was another expectation to which Born addressed himself when he said: ‘We shall thus arrive at a new definition of the energy constants (“terms”) which also

***

Hence they may be arranged in a $(r \times r)$-matrix $\mathbf{S}_0^r$, which appears as a finite submatrix of the zeroth-order infinite transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}_0$ of Eq. (141').

remains valid in the case of aperiodic motion, i.e., of continuously varying indices’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 581). Thus, the tools of higher algebra, developed by David Hilbert and his school, seemed to offer for the first time the possibility of dealing with quantum systems, such as the hydrogen atom, having both discrete and continuous energy terms. Born was convinced that this possibility would lead to fundamental progress in the efforts to formulate the quantum theory of atoms and he proceeded to discuss the necessary mathematical methods and their application to quantum mechanics.$^{146}$

### III.6 Continuous Spectra and the Significance of the Transformation Matrix

Around mid-September 1925, on his return trip to Göttingen after the summer vacation in Silvaplana, Born passed through Zurich and reported to Hermann Weyl, then a professor of mathematics at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology (E.T.H.), about the new developments in quantum theory, especially the success achieved by the introduction of infinite matrices. Weyl’s imagination caught fire; soon afterwards he informed Born that ‘your *Ansatz* in quantum theory has made an enormous impression on me,’ and wished him godspeed in the pursuit of his ‘fabulous discovery’ (‘fabelhaften Entdeckung’) (Weyl to Born, 27 September 1925).

Weyl’s enthusiasm about the use of matrix methods in quantum theory, which led him at once to derive a few results himself, had good reasons.$^{147}$ After all, in Göttingen he had participated in the development of the theory of linear integral

***

$^{146}$ Heisenberg explained the reason why the three-man paper contained a repeated discussion of perturbation theory, with matrices *and* with purely algebraic methods, as follows:
In some way we did not feel that we should do it too systematically; but we also thought that it might be of some help for other physicists to show in one part of the paper how similar it [i.e., the matrix perturbation scheme] is to those older things which one had tried. Then we could show that there is a new technique [the algebraic one] which seems to be more powerful and actually deals with the same problem in another way. So we felt, “Why not give everything in the paper?” We did realize that it was a kind of duplication of things, but . . . we did not know what would be the most convenient. We had the impression that there may be other still more convenient mathematical schemes behind it. [We] felt that there [was] a great transformability in the whole thing, but we were not so far ready to write down a general scheme. The canonical transformations were actually in the paper in some way—in the Born part of it—but not in this very special general way in which one would later use it to go over to the Schrödinger picture. (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 283)
Born saw the development as follows:
We were [initially] entirely in Heisenberg’s footsteps. He had the idea that one should take matrices, although he did not know that his dynamical quantities were matrices . . . And when one had such a programme of formulating everything in matrix language, it takes some effort to get rid of matrices. Though it seemed quite natural for me to represent perturbation theory in the algebraic way, this was not a particularly new way. (Born, Conversations, p. 48)

$^{147}$ For example, in his letter to Born mentioned above, Weyl considered some of the mathematical implications of matrix mechanics. In particular, he proposed the commutation relations, Eqs. (121), for systems having several degrees of freedom. Weyl continued to be interested in the development of matrix mechanics and kept contact with Göttingen by exchanging letters with Pascual Jordan (Weyl to Jordan, 13, 23, and 25 November 1925). He also received the proof-sheets of the papers on matrix mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0134 -->

130 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

equations based on infinite matrices. In his doctoral thesis under Hilbert, Weyl had extended his teacher’s methods to deal with integral equations whose kernels can neither be represented by compact nor by bounded infinite matrices (Weyl, 1908). In particular, he had shown that if the difference of two matrices is a compact matrix, then the original matrices have the same ‘continuous spectrum.’$^{148}$

The main outcome of the investigations of Hilbert (1906a), Hellinger (1907) and Weyl’s own on the spectrum of infinite quadratic matrices or forms dealt with what Weyl had called the ‘principal theorem concerning the orthogonal transformations of bounded quadratic forms’ (Weyl, 1909, p. 373). This theorem stated that a bounded Hermitian quadratic form, $K(x, x^*)$, can be reduced to the following ‘normal’ form,

$$K(x, x^*) = \lambda_0 y_0 y_0^* + \lambda_1 y_1 y_1^* + \ldots + \int \lambda d\sigma(\lambda; y y^*), \quad (155)$$

by a unique unitary linear transformation of the original (infinitely many) variables $x_0, x_1, x_2, \ldots$ into new variables $y_0, y_1, y_2, \ldots$ (see Hilbert, 1906a, p. 198, Theorem III). The ‘normal’ form or the principal-axes representation, Eq. (155), contains two terms: first, a discrete sum whose coefficients are called the ‘discrete’ eigenvalues of the spectrum of $K(x, x^*)$; second, an integral over a continuous interval yielding the ‘continuous’ spectrum.$^{149}$ The absolute value of the discrete spectrum of eigenvalues, $\lambda_\alpha$ ($\alpha = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$), is bounded by $M$, which is the bound of the quadratic form $K(x, x^*)$, defined by an equation of the type of Eq. (42) in Section I.2. The integral representing the continuous spectrum has boundaries lying between $-M$ and $+M$; it involves a ‘spectral form,’ $\sigma(\lambda; yy^*)$, which increases monotonically from zero, for $\lambda = -M$, to the sum of all $y_n y_n^*$ ($n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$) for $\lambda = +M$. In the case of a compact infinite quadratic form all eigenvalues can be shown to belong to the discrete spectrum, while in the most general case of an unbounded infinite quadratic form—that is, one in which the bound $M$ in Eq. (42) is infinitely large—the spectrum of eigenvalues has discrete and continuous parts, both of which may extend from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$. $^{150}$

***

$^{148}$ Weyl had continued to work on problems related to his thesis and proved, for instance, the theorem that the spectrum of a bounded quadratic form remained essentially unaltered if an arbitrary compact form was added to it (Weyl, 1909).
$^{149}$ In Hilbert’s original paper the eigenvalues $\lambda$ were the inverse of those defined in Eq. (155).
$^{150}$ Hilbert had illustrated the important point as to how a continuous spectrum of eigenvalues can arise in infinite quadratic forms by discussing the special real unbounded quadratic form, $K(x, x) = x_1x_2 + x_2x_3 + x_3x_4 + \ldots$ (Hilbert, 1906a, pp. 207–208). For any finite section of this form—i.e., if one considers, say, only $N$ variables and breaks off the rest—all eigenvalues are discrete. However, in the infinite case, one has to solve a recursive set of homogeneous linear equations of the type of Eqs. (150) in order to perform the transformation to principal axes. This set of equations yields a continuous spectrum for $\lambda$, extending from $-\infty$ to $-1$ and from $+1$ to $+\infty$.
It should be added that Hilbert had proved the fact that a nonbounded quadratic form can be reduced to the ‘normal’ form, Eq. (155), provided there exists a real number $\lambda'$ which is not an ‘accumulation’ point of the eigenvalue spectrum; that is, $\lambda'$ is neither contained in the continuous spectrum nor does any sequence of discrete eigenvalues converge towards it (Hilbert, 1906a, p. 175, Theorem I). The latter condition is obviously satisfied for the above-mentioned nonbounded form; it would be different for a form exhibiting a continuous spectrum from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$.

III.6 Continuous Spectra and the Significance of the Transformation Matrix 131

Born knew all these results perfectly well and he decided to exploit them in matrix mechanics to treat the fundamental problem of diagonalizing the Hermitian Hamiltonian matrices by means of the principal-axes transformation. In making use of these results, he occasionally assumed that certain theorems, which had been proved by the mathematicians for bounded matrices only, would also hold in the case of the unbounded forms occurring in matrix mechanics.$^{151}$ He had no proof for this essential assumption since even the expert mathematicians, such as David Hilbert himself or Richard Courant, did not know. He had just to rely on his own intuition and on the physical facts; these implied that atomic systems possessed discrete *and* continuous energy states; hence he concluded the same to be true in matrix mechanics.$^{152}$ He remarked: 'The simultaneous appearance of both continuous and line spectra as solutions of the same equations of motion and the same commutation relations seemed to us to represent a particularly significant feature of the new theory' (BHJ, 1926, p. 590).$^{153}$ The question now was how to describe and determine the continuous spectrum of a given Hamiltonian matrix or of the associated Hermitian form.

In classical physics, the continuous spectra of atomic systems had been assumed to be connected with aperiodic motions, and the latter could be treated sometimes by means of Fourier integrals. In the Fourier integral, say for $x(t)$, the

***

$^{151}$Born referred explicitly to the problem of extending the results of the mathematical theory of bounded forms to nonbounded forms in Chapter 3 of the three-man paper. There he remarked: 'Up till now, the theory of quadratic (or Hermitian) forms of infinitely many variables has been developed mainly for a special class ("bounded" forms) (D. Hilbert, [1912c]; E. Hellinger, [1909]). But here we are concerned just with nonbounded forms. We may nevertheless assume that in the main the rules run likewise' (BHJ, 1926, p. 583, footnote 2).

It is easy to see, for example, that the matrices describing the quantum-mechanical harmonic oscillator are not bounded matrices because the discrete spectrum, $W_n = (n + \frac{1}{2}) h\omega_0 / 2\pi, n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, is not bounded by any number $M$.

$^{152}$Pascual Jordan recalled as follows about the mathematical problems involved in the extension of the theory of infinite forms:

> What we needed from mathematics was partially what one really knew about the fundamentals of quadratic forms, etc. What the mathematicians did not know we had to find anyway by ourselves, especially what we wanted for the purposes of quantum mechanics. Born had a reprint of a paper by [Ernst] Hellinger, who, in connection with Hilbert's work, had extended the mathematical tools; he [Born] tried to extract something for us from it. But he did not find much that we could use. What we could use from the paper were results which we knew already anyway, and what went beyond it with respect to fine mathematical details [in Hellinger's paper] did not suit us very much. (Jordan, AHQP Interview, 18 June 1963)

The mathematicians themselves had not yet entered into the problems posed by the physicists in the domain of the new quantum mechanics. However, in winter 1925 Heisenberg gave lectures on the new theory in the mathematical circle of Göttingen, and soon thereafter Hilbert began to take interest in the mathematical foundations of quantum mechanics. Later, John von Neumann developed the general theory of nonbounded matrices (von Neumann, 1927a, b).

$^{153}$The fact that the fundamental equations of quantum mechanics, in particular the quantum condition, did not exclude the treatment of aperiodic systems had occurred to Heisenberg before he learned about the mathematical theory of quadratic forms. (See Heisenberg to Pauli, 18 September 1925.)

Let us also remind ourselves here that David Hilbert, when developing his theory of the eigenvalues of infinite quadratic forms, had had in mind the spectra of chemical atoms, which include both discrete and continuous states. Therefore, bounded quadratic forms had seemed to him especially interesting objects of study.

132 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

position coordinate of an aperiodic system,

$$x(t) = \int \phi(\nu) \exp(2\pi i \nu t) d\nu, \quad (156)$$

the amplitude $\phi(\nu)$ had to be interpreted as the *amplitude density* in the frequency interval $\nu$ and $\nu + d\nu$. Also all the other physical quantities had then to be described by Fourier integrals of the type of Eq. (156) involving amplitude densities in the same sense. Born concluded that:

> We shall have to expect quite similar situations in quantum mechanics. Instead of the quantities $q(kl)$ [i.e., the elements of Hermitian matrices describing the properties of periodic quantum systems] we shall have quantities of the form $q(k, W)dW$ or $q(W, W')dW dW'$, depending on whether one [index $W$, denoting the energy in the continuous spectrum] or both of the two indices [denoting the energies $W$ and $W'$ in the continuous spectrum] lie in the continuous region. (BHJ, 1926, p. 591)

Born further assumed that, similar to the situation in the classical theory, the energy $W$ in the continuous region will have to be a 'total energy' per interval, $dW$, 'since the probability for an atom to have an absolutely definite energy $W$ in the continuous region is zero' (BHJ, 1926, p. 591).

Such an extension of the description of aperiodic motion to the quantum case was natural in the light of earlier considerations. $^{154}$ Even more important for Born, as he reminded himself, was the fact that 'the mathematical theory of continuous spectra which occur in bounded quadratic forms has, starting from the fundamental investigations of Hilbert, been developed in detail by Hellinger' (BHJ, 1926, p. 590). Ernst Hellinger had been Born's friend since their student days together in Breslau, and he had gone to Göttingen with Born to work on a doctoral thesis under Hilbert. Its results now came in handy for Born in trying to extend the matrix methods to include the treatment of continuous spectra.

In his thesis, Hellinger had discussed the problem of obtaining a complete set of 'orthogonal invariants' of bounded quadratic forms of infinitely many variables (Hellinger, 1907). As his main task, he had turned to the analysis of the continuous eigenvalues given by the integral term on the right-hand side of Eq. (155). For this purpose he had introduced what he called the 'linear differential forms' ('*lineare Differentialformen*'), $d\phi(\lambda, y) (= \sum_n d\phi_n(\lambda)y_n)$, of infinitely many variables $y_n$ (Hellinger, 1907, pp. 21, 74); the coefficients of these differential forms, $d\phi_n(\lambda)$, are supposed to be differentials of functions, $\phi_n(\lambda)$, such that the sum of the squares, $\phi(\lambda) = \sum \phi_n^2(\lambda)$, exists and represents a continuous, monotonic function of $\lambda$, the energy eigenvalue in the continuous spectrum. The principal-axes transformation, which gives the continuous part of the eigenvalue spectrum of a quadratic form, $K(x, x) (= \sum_{n,m} K_{nm} x_n x_m)$, is then achieved with the help of

$^{154}$In the case of aperiodic motion, the Fourier integral representation replaced the Fourier series representation, which applied to periodic systems. In their paper, submitted in June 1925, Born and Jordan had discussed this representation in connection with the correspondence principle approach (Born and Jordan, 1925a).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0137 -->

III.6 Continuous Spectra and the Significance of the Transformation Matrix &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; 133

those linear 'differential eigenforms' whose coefficients solve the set of (eigenvalue) equations

$$\lambda d\phi_n(\lambda) - \sum_m K_{nm} d\phi_m(\lambda) = 0 \quad (157)$$

with the eigenvalues $\lambda$. $^{155}$ Since $\lambda$ varies continuously within the interval which lies between $-M$ and $+M$, where $M$ is the bound of the quadratic form, continuously many 'differential eigenforms' *appear* to solve Eq. (157). This, however, is really not so, since only those functions, $\phi_n(\lambda)$, which are continuous in $\lambda$ and the sum of whose squares is a continuous function, $\phi(\lambda)$, are admitted; and of the latter only denumerably, though possibly infinitely, many exist. $^{156}$ Hence only denumerably many differential forms, $d\phi^{(\alpha)}(\lambda, y)$ ($\alpha = 1, 2, 3, \dots$) satisfy Eqs. (157). Different differential eigenforms of a quadratic form are orthogonal to each other and can be normalized. If one generalizes Hellinger's results to Hermitian forms, the continuous terms on the right-hand side of Eq. (155) assume the form

$$\int d\sigma(\lambda; yy^*) = \sum_{\alpha=1}^\infty \int \lambda \sum_n \frac{y_n y_n^* d\phi_n^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) d\phi_n^{(\alpha)*}(\lambda)}{d\phi^{(\alpha)}(\lambda)} , \quad (158)$$

where $\sum_n d\phi_n^{(\alpha)*}(\lambda)y_n^*$ represents the complex conjugate of the linear differential eigenform $d\phi^{(\alpha)}(\lambda, y)$, and $d\phi^{(\alpha)}(\lambda)$, the differential of the function $\phi^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) (= \sum [\phi_n^{(\alpha)}(\lambda) \cdot \phi_n^{(\alpha)*}(\lambda)])$, expressing the normalization. Evidently, this result states the transformation to principal axes for the continuous part of the eigenvalue spectrum.

In summer 1925 Max Born became fascinated by the possibilities offered by Hellinger's complete orthogonal transformation of infinite bounded quadratic forms. He noticed that, in order to deal with the continuous eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix, he had only to adopt the procedure of the mathematicians. Thus he assumed that, 'in analogy with the results for bounded forms' (BHJ, 1926, p. 591), one can reduce the Hermitian form $H(x, x^*)$ associated with the Hermitian matrix to the following 'normal' form:

$$\sum_{k,l} H(k, l) x_k x_l^* = \sum_n W_n y_n y_n^* + \int W(\phi) y(\phi) y^*(\phi) d\phi. \quad (159)$$

$^{155}$For the case of real quadratic forms, $K(x, x)$, see Hellinger, 1909, p. 242, §5, Eq. ($1'$).
Evidently Eq. (157) replaces the corresponding equation (see Eq. (150)) for discrete eigenvalues. In order to see the connection one might just consider a finite interval from $\lambda_1$ to $\lambda_2$ in the continuous spectrum. Then, from Eqs. (157), one obtains the equations $\int_{\lambda_1}^{\lambda_2} \lambda d\phi_n(\lambda) - \sum_m K_{nm} \Delta \phi_m(\lambda) = 0$, where $\Delta \phi_n(\lambda) = \phi_n(\lambda_2) - \phi_n(\lambda_1)$; these have indeed the structure of the discrete Eqs. (150).
$^{156}$If the function $\phi_n(\lambda)$ is analytic in $\lambda$, then it may be characterized by the coefficients of the (in general infinite) power series in $\lambda$. If the function $\phi_n$ is not analytic but still continuous, then one of its derivatives (or a denumerable set of its derivatives) possesses a jump or discontinuity; within a finite interval of $\lambda$, however, only denumerably many jumps of finite height will occur, hence again only denumerably many differential eigenforms exist.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0138 -->

134 &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

All he had done so far was to replace the eigenvalue (i.e., spectrum parameter) $\lambda$ (in Eqs. (155) and (158)) by the energy $W$ (the eigenvalue of $H(x, x^*)$) and to rewrite the expression on the right-hand side of Eq. (158) appropriately. In order to determine the structure of the generalized transformation to principal axes in physics, Born discussed in detail the solution of the eigenvalue equations (150) for continuous values of the energy $W$, referring at each step to the corresponding mathematical investigation of Hellinger.

Born started out with the observation that two solutions, $v_k(W')$ and $v_k(W'')$, whose energy eigenvalues $W'$ and $W''$ lie in the continuous spectrum, cannot be normalized similar to the solutions in the discrete case (see Eq. (151)) because the function of two variables $\sum_k v_k(W')v_k(W'')$, having the property

$$\sum_k v_k(W')v_k(W'') = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } W' = W'' \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (160)$$

would be badly irregular, if it exists at all' (BHJ, 1926, p. 592). $^{157}$ Hellinger had avoided dealing with this function by introducing the concept of differential forms, and Born now followed his lead. Instead of taking $v_k(W)$ as the solutions of Eqs. (150), he took the differential solutions $v_k(W)dW$; from the coefficients $v_k(W)$ he constructed the function $\phi(W)$ according to the equation

$$\sum_k \left| \int v_k(W) dW \right|^2 = \phi(W), \quad (161)$$

the so-called 'basis function' ('*Basisfunktion*,' Hellinger, 1909, p. 246), which allows one to normalize the differential solutions. That is, in matrix mechanics the $v_k(W)dW$, $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, with different values of the continuous energy parameter $W$, act as orthogonal differential solutions of Eqs. (150), normalized by the basis function $\phi(W)$ which corresponds to Hellinger's $\phi(\lambda)$ in Eq. (158). Two solutions, $v_k(W')dW'$ and $v_k(W'')dW''$, are orthogonal in the sense that for two (finite) intervals, $\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_2$, of the continuous spectrum with $\Delta_{12}$ as the common interval (overlap) one finds

$$\int_{\Delta_1} v_k(W') dW' \cdot \int_{\Delta_2} v_k^*(W'') dW'' = \int_{\Delta_{12}} d\phi(W) = \phi(W^{(2)}) - \phi(W^{(1)}), \quad (162)$$

where $W^{(1)}$ and $W^{(2)}$ are the end points of $\Delta_{12}$.

Born considered the fact that it had been possible to construct the transformation matrix generating the principal-axes transformation as the most important consequence of the mathematical theory of Hermitian forms. He wrote this orthogonal matrix as

$$\mathbf{S} = (v_{kn}, v_k(W)dW) \quad (163)$$

$^{157}$In agreement with the mathematical consensus at the time, Born did not consider the object $\sum_k v_k(W')v_k(W'')$ as a function at all. The concept and theory of so-called 'generalized functions' was developed by the mathematicians later, especially after Paul Dirac introduced his delta-function into physics (Dirac, 1927a).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0139 -->

III.6 Continuous Spectra and the Significance of the Transformation Matrix &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; 135

because its elements comprise the totality of discrete values $v_{kn}$ and of values $v_k(W)$ which are discrete in one index ($k$) and continuous in the other ($W$). For quantum systems he represented S schematically as

$$\mathbf{S} = \left( \begin{array}{ccccc}
  & k \to & & & \\
  n \downarrow & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
  & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
  & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot \\
  W \downarrow & | & | & | & | & |
\end{array} \right) \quad (163')$$

because the ordering of the columns and rows in the matrices had been established in such a way that the energy values in the diagonalized Hamiltonian increased with increasing indices, and the continuous spectrum occurred for higher values of the energy than the discrete spectrum. The transformation matrix, therefore, contained two types of rows: first, those with a discrete index, corresponding to eigenforms, $\sum_k v_{kn} x_k$ ($n = 0, 1, 2, \dots$), of the discrete spectrum; second, those with a continuous 'index' and labelled by the (continuous) energy eigenvalue $W$, corresponding to the differential eigenforms, $\sum_k v_k(W) dW x_k$, of Hellinger. $^{158}$ Four sets of equations determine the orthogonality and normalization of the rows of S, namely,

$$\sum_k v_{km} \cdot v_{kn}^* = \delta_{nm}, \quad (164a)$$

$$\sum_k v_{km} \cdot v_k^*(W) dW = 0, \quad (164b)$$

$$\sum_k v_k(W) dW \cdot v_{kn}^* = 0, \quad (164c)$$

$$\sum_k v_k(W') dW' \cdot v_k^*(W'') dW'' = d\phi, \quad (164d)$$

while in the normalization equations for the columns (which have always discrete indices) there occurs a sum arising from the discrete terms and an integral from the continuous terms. $^{159}$ With the help of this unitary transformation matrix one can indeed introduce new variables into the Hermitian form $H(x, x^*)$, those having discrete indices ($y_n$) and others having continuous indices ($y(\phi)d\phi$); in

$^{158}$Note that, in the above definition of the transformation matrix, Eq. (163'), Born did not follow the usual definition, for he used the first index $k$ to denote the columns rather than the rows.
$^{159}$The discrete contribution is $\sum v_{kn} v_{ln}^*$, and the continuous contribution is $\int v_k(W) dW \cdot v_l^*(W)/d\phi$; both add up to $\delta_{kl}$.

Chapter III  Completion of the Matrix Scheme

these new variables the Hermitian form then assumes the normal form, given by the right-hand side of Eq. (159).<sup>160</sup>

As Born found in the example of the momentum variable of a system having one degree of freedom, the elements of the matrices describing the variables of a quantum system having discrete and continuous eigenvalues fell into four classes. Even if one started with a matrix $\mathbf{p}^{(0)} (= p^0(kl))$, which possesses only discrete indices $(k, l = 0, 1, 2, \dots)$, after the transformation by the matrix $\mathbf{S}$—which diagonalizes the Hamiltonian matrix of the system under consideration—the matrix $\mathbf{p}$ would contain the following elements: first, amplitudes $p(mn)$ denoting the transitions between discrete states with energies $W_m$ and $W_n$; second, ‘amplitude densities’ $p(m, W)dW$ denoting the transitions from a discrete state, $W_m$, to a state in the continuous spectrum whose energy lies between $W$ and $W + dW$; third, the amplitude densities $p(W, n)dW$ for transitions from states in the continuous spectrum (energy between $W$ and $W + dW$) to the discrete state $W_n$; finally, the amplitude densities $p(W', W'')dW'dW''$ for the transitions from an energy state between $W'$ and $W' + dW'$ in the continuum to another continuum energy state lying between $W''$ and $W'' + dW''$. Therefore, in matrix mechanics, all matrices corresponding to dynamical variables, $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})$, have the general structure indicated by the following scheme:

$$
\mathbf{f} = \left( \begin{array}{c|c}
\begin{array}{c} n \rightarrow \\ m \downarrow \\ \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \\ \cdot \cdot \cdot \cdot \\ \vdots \end{array} & \begin{array}{c} W'' \rightarrow \\ \rule{0.5em}{0.1pt} \rule{0.5em}{0.1pt} \\ \rule{0.5em}{0.1pt} \rule{0.5em}{0.1pt} \\ \vdots \end{array} \\ \hline
\begin{array}{c} W' \downarrow \\ | \\ | \\ | \end{array} & \begin{array}{c} \text{[shaded area]} \\ \diagup \diagup \\ \diagup \diagup \\ \diagup \diagup \end{array}
\end{array} \right

III.6 Continuous Spectra and the Significance of the Transformation Matrix 137

same fundamental dynamical equations and commutation relations. By Born’s application of the principal-axes transformation, therefore, the formal mathematical structure of matrix mechanics was completed. It was capable of handling all those problems in atomic physics in which *only the libration coordinates appeared*, that is, where the dynamical variables which increased linearly for large times could be avoided.<sup>161</sup> About this, Heisenberg wrote to Pauli: ‘We have now also worked out the problem of continuous spectra from the point of view of this mathematical theory. At first it looks very chaotic; later one realizes that the calculations are not worse than in the case of Fourier integrals’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 October 1925).
By introducing the mathematical tool of principal-axes transformation into quantum mechanics Born had to answer a question of principle. In spite of the fact that the principal-axes transformation acted only as a means of integrating the equations of motion of a given quantum system, he still had to understand what, after all, did the elements of the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ represent, for they did occur explicitly in the equations of perturbation theory, as in Eqs. (135) or (153), and had to be calculated. Following the guiding principle applied hitherto in the formulation of the new quantum theory, namely, that only observable quantities should enter into the equations describing physical systems, one of two conclusions had to be adopted: either the principal-axes transformation itself had no physical meaning, hence one ought to eliminate it from the quantum-theoretical equations; or the matrix elements of $\mathbf{S}$ were observable quantities and their physical significance had to be determined.
Born was inclined to believe that the transformation matrix effecting the principal-axes transformation of the Hermitian form $H(x, x^*)$ possessed a genuine physical meaning, and he set out to ascertain it by considering the formal structure of the eigenvalue equations (150a). In each of these equations, for fixed $n$, there appear only the elements $v_{kn}$ (with $k = 0,1,2, \ldots$), i.e., the elements forming a row of the matrix $\mathbf{S}$ (see Eq. (163), specialized to the situation that only a discrete spectrum is associated with $H(x, x^*)$). Born now assumed that a column or a row of the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$ must have a well-defined physical meaning, and he mentioned it to Heisenberg, who did not respond positively to this assumption. ‘He disliked,’ Born recalled later, ‘having to take a column or row [of a matrix], that is to consider the quantities $v_k$ ($k = 0,1,2, \ldots$) without adding a second index as in $v_{kn}$. He stuck to the argument that [in quantum mechanics] the absolute square of one matrix element $|v_{kn}|^2$, represents the probability of the transition from a state $k$ to another state $n$, hence only the matrix elements, $v_{kn}$, have a physical significance’ (Born, Conversations, p. 47). Born, on the other hand, believed that it made sense to talk meaningfully about

<sup>161</sup>The extension of the scheme to include nonlibrating coordinates was not treated by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan in their joint paper, for they explicitly excluded those variables whose analogues in classical theory could not be described by Fourier integrals. They remarked, however, that ‘the observable effects of an atom (such as radiation, the force upon another atom, etc.) do not in general belong to this type of function’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 595).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0142 -->

138 Chapter III Completion of the Matrix Scheme

the columns of the transformation matrix, but he could not for the moment justify his conviction; therefore he avoided a discussion of this fundamental question in the three-man paper.
However, a trace of the debate between Born and Heisenberg may still be found in the joint paper. In discussing the meaning of the differential $d\phi$ entering Eq. (159), the authors stated: ‘Thence $d\phi$ essentially represents the number of atoms having an energy which lies between $W$ and $W + dW$, or the *a priori* probability that the energy of the atom lies between $W$ and $W + dW$’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 594). Since $d\phi$, according to Eq. (164d), denotes the absolute square of a ‘continuous’ row of the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}$, Eq. (163), the physical significance of this quantity had been found. Similarly, the sum of the absolute squares of the discrete quantities, $\sum_k v_{kn} v_{kn}^*$, was interpreted as the probability that the discrete state, denoted by $n$, has the energy $W_n$. In October 1925 Born did not have the time to investigate the problem beyond these statements. But he continued to pursue his interest in finding the physical meaning of the transformation matrix, especially of its rows and columns. Many years later he recalled: ‘This thought occupied my mind all the time, and that led me much later to the statistical interpretation [of Schrödinger’s wave function]. At that time [in fall 1925] I could do nothing with the discrete method [i.e., matrix mechanics], but when Schrödinger came I saw that the same question could be asked in the wave theory’ (Born, Conversations, p. 44). Thus, Born’s early involvement in this question of principle prepared him to make a fundamental discovery: the statistical interpretation of the wave function.<sup>162</sup>

<sup>162</sup>Born had a further reason to study the meaning of the transformation matrix. According to Heisenberg’s investigation, the squares of the transition elements—such as the square of the elements of the position matrix, $|q(nm)|^2$—yielded the transition probability. Born, however, argued that this was not really so because in dispersion theory the important quantity was rather the dipole moment; hence he asked the question: ‘Why not take the coefficients of the momentum matrix or those of any matrix function $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q})$?’ (Born, Conversations, p. 45). In fall 1925 he was already looking for some general principle that would allow one to calculate transition probabilities.
Incidentally, many years later Heisenberg used another transformation matrix, denoted by the same letter $\mathbf{S}$, in the theory of elementary particles (Heisenberg, 1943a, b; 1944). By definition, this matrix involved only observable quantities. Perhaps Heisenberg wanted to make up for his old mistake of 1925 in having misjudged the importance of the quantum-mechanical transformation matrix.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0143 -->

Chapter IV
The Success of Matrix Mechanics

After the theoretical scheme of quantum mechanics, including the matrix and the equivalent algebraic formulations, had been established by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, it became necessary to deal immediately with two tasks: first, with tests to confirm the consistency of the new theory, especially by comparing its results with those which were considered reliable—such as the results of dispersion theory and radiation theory; second, to extend the application of the new theory beyond the simple examples which it had been possible to treat thus far. In both tasks the Göttingen theoreticians received the help of other physicists who had had close relations with them and had become familiar with their matrix methods and early results prior to publication. It had thus been possible for these physicists to work on quantum mechanics already, say, from October 1925, several weeks before the three-man paper was submitted or the first paper of Born and Jordan (1925b) appeared in print. In checking the consistency of the new theoretical scheme, Hendrik Kramers made an interesting interpretation of the quantum conditions or commutation relations, while Wolfgang Pauli calculated the energy states of the hydrogen atom by employing exclusively matrix methods.
Pauli’s work on the hydrogen atom must be regarded as a real triumph of the matrix methods, especially because he bypassed a major difficulty of the available quantum-mechanical formalism: the obvious impossibility of describing the action and angle variables. Ever since the days of Hamilton and Jacobi, these variables had provided the key to the solution of multiply periodic systems; and to avoid their use seemed to imply that one could not transfer the methods of classical dynamics, including the perturbation scheme, to calculate the energy states of real atoms. Pauli, however, discovered a clever method to solve the hydrogen problem without invoking angle variables. He was thus able to diagonalize the Hamiltonian matrix for one-electron atoms and, in addition, to determine their behaviour in constant external electric and magnetic fields in perfect agreement with the experimental information. ‘It was stupid,’ Born confessed with some envy about Pauli’s success, ‘that we could not solve the hydrogen atom; it was straightforward’ (Born, Conversations, p. 50). However, the procedure, which worked in the case of the hydrogen atom, could not be extended to two- and more-electron atoms. These problems had to wait until an action-angle formalism became available in quantum mechanics, that is, until the matrix scheme was extended to deal with nonlibration variables as well. Before

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0144 -->

140 Chapter IV The Success of Matrix Mechanics

that generalization it was only possible to treat a very selected class of atomic problems, such as the rotational motion of diatomic molecules.

### IV.1 The Treatment of Dispersion Phenomena

The first ‘outside’ contribution to matrix mechanics came from Hendrik Kramers. He had, however, been familiar with the results of this theory for some time. On one hand, he had visited Göttingen in June 1925 and had learned from Heisenberg about his efforts to revise the fundamental concepts of quantum theory; on the other, he had met Heisenberg again in Copenhagen the following September, while the latter was working on matrix theory in collaboration with Born and Jordan. Finally, Kramers spent a few days in November 1925 with Pauli in Hamburg (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 3 November 1925). Shortly afterwards he submitted a note to *Physica*, the Dutch journal, in which he made ‘a few comments on the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg’ (‘*Eenige Opmerkingen over de Quantummechanica van Heisenberg*,’ Kramers, 1925c).<sup>163</sup> In this note he discussed in particular a specific connection between the dispersion formulae (Kramers, 1924a; Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925) and the quantum conditions, Eqs. (121).<sup>164</sup>

After introducing the matrix notation, Kramers started by rewriting the dispersion formula for the electric moment of an atomic system induced by an incident electromagnetic radiation having a frequency $\nu$ and electric field strengths $E^{(1)}$, $E^{(2)}$, $\dot{E}^{(3)}$, in the $x$-, $y$-, and $z$-directions, respectively. He denoted the Cartesian coordinates, describing ‘symbolically the motion of an electron in an atomic system’ (Kramers, 1925c, p. 370), as $\mathbf{q}^{(k)} = (q^{(k)}(mn) = (1/2e)A_{m,n}^k \exp[2\pi i \nu(mn)t])$, where $A_{m,n}^k$ is the amplitude in the $k$ (= 1, 2, 3 or $x, y, z$)-direction of the radiation of frequency $\nu(nm)$, emitted by the atom during

<sup>163</sup>It is of interest to note that Kramers, in the beginning at least, had been skeptical about the prospects of Heisenberg’s endeavours. (In a postcard to Pauli, dated 29 June 1925, Heisenberg mentioned that he was increasingly becoming more convinced of his new ideas, and Kramers therefore accused him of being too optimistic.) Later, after Heisenberg had completed his paper (1925c), Pauli tried to convince Kramers of the importance of the ideas contained in it. He wrote: ‘The “community of true believers” [in Bohr’s faith—meaning, principally, Kramers] would neither gain much honour nor much success by attempting to fight the trend of the present development in quantum theory, which is directed towards an analysis of the concepts of motion and force. For it seems to me that there is great hope of moving forward *positively* along this path. In particular, I have greeted with jubilation Heisenberg’s bold proposals (about which you have certainly heard in Göttingen)’ (Pauli to Kramers, 27 July 1925). Then, while Heisenberg stayed in Copenhagen in late summer 1925 before returning to Göttingen, Kramers learned from him about the matrix formulation of quantum mechanics. He acknowledged this information in a footnote in his paper by stating: ‘I want to express my sincere thanks to Mr. Heisenberg for his kind information about the recent development of his theory by Born, Jordan and himself’ (Kramers, 1925c, p. 369, footnote 1).

<sup>164</sup>Kramers’ paper (1925c) did not constitute his earliest positive response to Heisenberg’s work. Earlier, in his presentation of dispersion theory to the sixth Scandinavian Mathematical Congress in Copenhagen in August 1925, he had mentioned the ‘interesting and promising results’ which had ‘already been obtained in the papers [of Born (1924b) and Heisenberg (1925c)] ..., which contain an audacious attempt of developing a new “quantum mechanics”’ (Kramers, 1925b, p. 153).

Although Pauli had directed Kramers’ attention to this fact, neither he nor Kramers investigated the consequences of the connection between the quantum conditions and the classical Poisson brackets.<sup>169</sup> On the other hand, after reading Heisenberg’s paper on the quantum-theoretical re-interpretation of kinematics (Heisenberg, 1925c), Paul Dirac independently discovered this connection and made it the basis of a complete scheme of quantum mechanics applicable to atomic mechanics in general, far beyond the range of matrix mechanics (Dirac, 1925d).

The Kramers–Heisenberg theory of dispersion had provided the immediate point of departure for the discovery of quantum mechanics. It seemed natural, therefore, to derive the well-known dispersion formulae. This had been done already, as we have mentioned, in September 1925 by Heisenberg. He had succeeded fully and had considered this success of the matrix theory as confirming its validity, for, as he wrote to Pauli: ‘I believe that this [i.e., the derivation of the dispersion formulae] is all that one can demand for the moment’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 18 September 1925). Although he was satisfied for the moment, Heisenberg soon thought of testing whether the matrix methods could also be applied successfully to describe other ‘dispersion’ phenomena, such as the scattering of fast $\alpha$-particles by atoms, or, more generally, all those situations which could be treated as the action of time-dependent external forces on atoms. These phenomena had been discussed in detail during the previous months both in Copenhagen and Göttingen (Bohr, 1925a; Born and Jordan, 1925a), and now people at those places, especially Niels Bohr, were interested in their renewed discussion in terms of quantum mechanics. On 21 October 1925, a few days after returning to Göttingen from Copenhagen, Heisenberg reported to Bohr about the first little progress he had made. He wrote:

> If, in analogy to the classical theory, one investigates the conditions under which it makes sense to talk about “external forces,” that is, to neglect the reactions, then

With the expressions (ab) one denotes the known symbol of Poisson:

$$(ab) = \sum_k \left( \frac{\partial a}{\partial I_k} \frac{\partial b}{\partial w_k} - \frac{\partial a}{\partial w_k} \frac{\partial b}{\partial I_k} \right),$$

where the canonical variables, $I_k, w_k$, are nothing else but the uniformizing variables (the $w$’s are Stäckel’s “angle variables”) which play such a great role in the quantum theory of periodic systems. The quantities $I_k$ in the theory are put equal to integer multiples of Planck’s constant. However, such “quantum conditions” have to be considered out of date from the point of view of Heisenberg’s theory. The methods developed in the paper of Kramers and Heisenberg [1925] yield, when adjusted to Poisson brackets, directly the result that the equations [(121) or (167)] are the fitting quantum-theoretical “re-interpretation” of (classical) bracket expressions.
