144 Chapter IV The Success of Matrix Mechanics

one finds that also in quantum mechanics the computational rules of the *classical* theory are always valid in the same approximation for the periodic functions occurring in the external forces (these forces may be either periodic in time or expandable in a Fourier integral), provided these conditions [i.e., the reactions can be neglected] are satisfied. This appears to me again to constitute a beautiful example of the correspondence-like connection of the new theory with the classical theory. (Heisenberg to Bohr, 21 October 1925).

Heisenberg’s discussion of the dispersion phenomena became the basis of a full section of the three-man paper, dealing with these problems in a systematic way from the point of view of matrix theory (see BHJ, 1926, Chapter 1, Section 5, entitled ‘System for which the Time Enters Explicitly in the “Energy Function”’).
Born, Heisenberg and Jordan formulated the problem of the action of time-dependent forces on atoms in quantum mechanics ‘. . . as the limiting case of interaction between two systems in which the influence of the interaction on one of the two systems (called system A) is so small that the action upon the other (system B) remains unaffected by this influence’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 568). In classical mechanics the total Hamiltonian function describing the two systems is then given by a sum of three terms, say, $H = H_A + \lambda H_B + \lambda \epsilon H_{AB}$, where the first, $H_A$, denotes the energy of free system A, the second, $\lambda H_B$, the energy of the free system B, and the third, $\lambda \epsilon H_{AB}$, the coupling or interaction energy. The third term is supposed to be a correction, which is small compared to the total energy and to the energies $H_A$ and $\lambda H_B$ (i.e., $\epsilon \ll 1$). Now the system A is taken to be known. Then the motion of system B may be determined by the Hamiltonian function $\lambda H_B + \lambda \epsilon H_{AB}$, where the interaction energy term, $\lambda \epsilon H_{AB}$, depends, of course, on the coordinates of the system A. The latter coordinates may be time dependent; however, for a fixed time $t$, only given values of these coordinates (and their conjugate momenta) enter into the classical calculation. If the reaction of the system B on system A may be neglected—say, due to the fact that system B has a much smaller energy than A (or $\lambda \ll 1$)—then the motion of B is completely described by the Hamiltonian function $\lambda H_B + \lambda \epsilon H_{AB}(p_B, q_B; t)$, where the interaction term depends explicitly on time $t$ (which takes into account the dependence on the variables of A). Thus, an adequate classical description of the action of an external time-dependent force on system B is provided.
Born, Heisenberg and Jordan then turned to the discussion of the same problem in quantum mechanics. They began by noting:

> In the quantum-mechanical calculation the situation is just the same, provided we restrict ourselves to first-order perturbations (i.e., terms proportional to $\epsilon$ in the coordinates and momenta, etc., of the system B). It is altogether different, however, for higher-order perturbations, since in evaluating higher-order terms we encounter products of quantities in which more than one implicitly contains the coordinates of A. But this means, according to the quantum mechanical rule of building a product, that it by no means suffices to know the “external forces as functions of time” merely for the *given* values of the constants in A, but these external forces must be known for *all* values of these constants. Thereby, however, the concept of external forces appears in fact to become devoid of meaning. (BHJ, 1926, pp. 568–569)

IV.1  The Treatment of Dispersion Phenomena
145

As mentioned above, the difficulties with the concept of external forces did not show up in the lowest-order approximation; in that case one neglects the reaction of system **B** on **A**, which leads to a change of the variables of **A**, and this change, in turn, induces additional terms of order $\lambda\epsilon^2$ in the variables of **B**.$^{170}$ The latter result even allows one to make a more precise statement concerning the concept of external forces in quantum mechanics. Evidently, it makes sense to talk about external forces if the action of the system **A** on the system **B** can be described in a manner independent of the dynamical variables of **B**. This is especially so when the parameter $\lambda$, which characterizes the influence of the relative magnitude of the system **B** with respect to the system **A**, is very small. The authors noted, however, that ‘in this approximation the quantum mechanical construction of products, and thereby the calculation of the perturbation to higher orders in $\epsilon$ can again be effected. In fact, the rules for this building of products reduce simply to those of classical multiplication, as in this approximation the coordinates, amplitudes and frequencies which enter into $\mathbf{H}_{AB}$ do not depend on the constants in **A**’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 569).
A careful examination of the conditions, under which the concept of external forces had a well-defined meaning in their theory, enabled Born, Heisenberg and Jordan to suggest that certain important problems of atomic physics could perhaps be solved by applying a time-dependent quantum-mechanical perturbation theory. In particular, they argued that:

In this sense one could, for example, treat the action of a strong alternating electromagnetic field on an atom indeed as the influence of an “external force” by neglecting the reaction of the atom [on the incident electromagnetic radiation], since the field energy can be regarded as infinitely large compared with that of the atom. The action of $\alpha$-particles upon the electrons of an atom could also be viewed as an “external force,” as in classical theory, because of the large energy of the $\alpha$-particles; in this approximation, the Fourier expansion in time of the force thereby exerted upon the electrons would also be the same as in classical theory. (BHJ, 1926, p. 569)

On the other hand, the authors were very well aware of the fact that an approach of that kind was not applicable to some other phenomena: for instance, the action of forces due to one atom upon another could not be treated as an operation of external forces (except in the first-order terms) since neglecting the reaction in higher-order terms would lead to wrong results.$^{171}$

$^{170}$System **B** acts on the System **A** via the coupling term $\lambda\epsilon\mathbf{H}_{AB}$. Hence the original dynamical variables of the system **A** might be shifted by terms of order $\lambda\epsilon$. Since system **A** reacts on **B** again via the coupling term $\lambda\epsilon\mathbf{H}_{AB}$, a change of the variables of **B**, $\mathbf{p}_B$ and $\mathbf{q}_B$, is induced, which has the order $\lambda\epsilon^2$, i.e., it is of the second order in the small perturbation parameter $\epsilon$ and of first order in $\lambda$.

$^{171}$In choosing their examples, the authors wanted to draw attention to the fact that their new theory allowed them to deal, in principle, with all the phenomena that Bohr had discussed earlier (Bohr, 1925a). However, the phenomena, which Bohr had not been able to treat either with classical theory or by the then existing perturbation approach, were now identified with situations where one had to apply higher-order time-dependent perturbation theory involving possibly products of non-commuting matrices and difficulties with the concept of external forces.

146
Chapter IV  The Success of Matrix Mechanics

In order to develop their time-dependent perturbation scheme, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan turned to the standard problem of dispersion theory: the scattering of radiation of frequency $v$ by an atom.$^{172}$ For simplicity one may assume that E, the electric field vector of the incident radiation, is parallel to the position vector of the atom; the problem may then be treated in one dimension (having one degree of freedom). In classical theory the interaction with the radiation changes the Hamiltonian of the free atom by a term $eq_0 E \cos(2\pi vt)$, where $E$ is the amplitude of the electric field and $- e$, the charge of the electron, plays the role of a small perturbation parameter; $q_0$ denotes the position of the electron, i.e., its distance from the positively charged nucleus.$^{173}$ In matrix theory one has just to substitute the Hermitian matrix $\mathbf{q_0}$ for the position coordinate $q_0$, and the interaction term becomes accordingly

$$\lambda \mathbf{H}_1 = e\mathbf{q_0} E \cos(2\pi vt). \tag{168}$$

Hence, in case the frequency of the incident radiation is finite, i.e., $v \neq 0$, the perturbation term in the Hamiltonian matrix (describing the atom plus external radiation) shows a time dependence which is not included in the dynamical variables of the atom. It is evident that in this case a perturbation scheme different from the one given by Eqs. (135) has to be used in order to calculate the first-order correction to the position matrix or the induced electric moment of the atom because Eqs. (135) had been derived only for those Hamiltonian matrices which depend exclusively on the dynamical variables $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ of the atomic systems under investigation.$^{174}$

The fact that a time-dependent perturbation scheme was necessary for dealing with time-dependent external forces was already known from classical dynamics.

$^{172}$Evidently, the authors expected to deal later on with other 'dispersion' problems, such as the scattering of $\alpha$-particles by atoms. However, the available matrix formulation prevented them from treating aperiodic motions; only later on would Born return to the scattering problem by using Schrödinger's wave mechanical formulation (Born, 1926a, b, c).

$^{173}$Since the electron's charge $e$ has a dimension, it must be normalized in order to reveal its magnitude. The dimensionless parameter corresponding to $e$ is the square root of Sommerfeld's fine-structure constant $\alpha (= 2\pi e^2 / hc)$, which is smaller than 0.1.

$^{174}$In the problems treated so far by perturbation theory, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had assumed that the position and momentum variables depend periodically on time with the characteristic frequencies, $v(mn)$, of the atomic system. In the dispersion problem, however, the frequency of the incident radiation is, in general, different from any of the frequencies $v(nm)$; hence the time dependence via the exponential function $\cos(2\pi vt)$ must be considered explicitly in the Hamiltonian.
The situation is, of course, different when the external frequency $v$ is very small compared to all frequencies $v(mn)$; the time dependence in Eq. (168) may then be forgotten. After calculating the transformation matrix $\mathbf{S}_1$ according to the second equation (135) and substituting it into the equation for $\mathbf{q}_1 (= \mathbf{S}_1\mathbf{q_0} - \mathbf{q_0}\mathbf{S}_1)$, one finds the matrix elements as

$$q_1(mn) = \frac{E}{h} \left[ \sum_{k \neq m} \frac{q_0(mk)q_0(kn)}{v_0(mk)} - \sum_{k \neq n} \frac{q_0(mk)q_0(kn)}{v_0(kn)} \right].$$

This result was hinted at by Heisenberg in a letter to Jordan, dated 13 September 1925, as reproducing the results of dispersion theory. Evidently, this is true only in the limit of very low frequencies of the incident radiation.

148 Chapter IV The Success of Matrix Mechanics

and

$$e\Delta q(mn, -1) = \frac{Ee^2}{2h} \sum_k \left[ \frac{q_0(mk)q_0(kn)}{\nu_0(mk) - \nu} - \frac{q_0(mk)q_0(kn)}{\nu_0(kn) - \nu} \right] \exp(-2\pi i \nu t).$$ (171b)

If the state of the atom remains unchanged, that is, if only matrix elements with $m = n$ are considered, Eq. (171a) becomes identical with the Kramers dispersion formula for coherent scattering (Kramers, 1924a). On the other hand, the matrix elements with $m \neq n$ reproduce the dispersion formulae for incoherent scattering (Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925, §4). Finally, the authors had no difficulty in considering Eqs. (171) in the limit of very high frequency of the incident radiation, $\nu \gg |\nu_0(mn)|$, and in deriving the classical Thomson formula for the scattering of light by a free electron.$^{177}$ Matrix mechanics was thus able to provide a complete justification for all the dispersion formulae which had been obtained earlier on the basis of correspondence arguments.

Born, Heisenberg and Jordan dealt with a still different approach to problems described by time-dependent Hamiltonians (BHJ, 1926, Chapter 1, Section 5, pp. 570–571). This approach may be applied to all cases in which the Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H}$ depends, besides the dynamical variables $\mathbf{p}_k$ and $\mathbf{q}_k$, on the time $t$ via a periodic function with a frequency $\nu$, i.e., $\mathbf{H} = \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k, \cos(2\pi \nu t))$; moreover, the time dependence may already exist in the unperturbed problem. To treat such problems, the authors suggested the following procedure: One formally introduces the new dynamical variables $\mathbf{q}'$ and $\mathbf{p}'$, where $\mathbf{q}'$ is a diagonal matrix having all its elements identical to $\cos(2\pi i \nu t)$, and $\mathbf{p}'$ the canonically conjugate momentum obtained from the new Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}'$,

$$\mathbf{H}' = \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{p}_k, \mathbf{q}_k ; \mathbf{q}') + 2\pi\nu\sqrt{1 - \mathbf{q}'^2} \mathbf{p}'. \quad (172)$$

The explicit time dependence was thus absorbed into a new, independent degree of freedom, and the previous problem turned into a formally time-independent problem described by the *Ersatz* Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H}'$.$^{178}$

The authors unfortunately did not illustrate the application of the above idea by a practical example, nor did they return to it later; the brief episode was forgotten completely. Still, the procedure involving the introduction of a new pair

$^{177}$For large $\nu$ the authors obtained the matrix formula,

$$e^2\mathbf{q}_1 = - \frac{Ee^2}{2\pi i h \nu^2 m_e} (\mathbf{p}_0\mathbf{q}_0 - \mathbf{q}_0\mathbf{p}_0) \cos(2\pi \nu t),$$

where $m_e$ is the mass of the electron and $\mathbf{p}_0$ the momentum variable. By substituting the commutation relation, this yields the induced moment as $Ee^2 \cos(2\pi \nu t) / (4\pi^2 \nu^2 m_e) \cdot 1$.

$^{178}$Evidently, the introduction of the new variables does not influence the equations of motion for the variables $\mathbf{p}_k$ and $\mathbf{q}_k$.

IV.2 Fluctuations in Cavity Radiation 149

of variables and the *Ersatz* Hamiltonian $\mathbf{H}'$ was certainly interesting, at least in a formal sense: it constituted the first attempt at replacing the time coordinate by a quantum-theoretical variable, in this case a matrix. The attempt to give a quantum-theoretical meaning to time would be made again several times later on, especially by Wolfgang Pauli and Paul Dirac, and would lead to some important consequences.$^{179}$

## IV.2 Fluctuations in Cavity Radiation

In October 1925 Heisenberg reported to Pauli:

Another thing, which Jordan has [especially] done for our paper is [to treat] the statistical behaviour of eigenvibrations, say of a membrane, in the new theory. Jordan claims that one obtains for the interference fluctuations the right result, i.e., both the classical and the Einstein terms, and he believes that he sees an analogy of our calculations with Bose’s statistics. I am a little unhappy about it, for I do not understand statistics enough in order to decide whether there is something reasonable in it, but I cannot also criticize it, because I find the problem itself and the calculation significant. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 October 1925)$^{180}$

The extension of matrix mechanics to systems of many degrees of freedom had provided the necessary tool for investigating the problem of cavity radiation from a fresh point of view. What Heisenberg, at the time, considered a ‘significant problem and calculation,’ Pascual Jordan, the author of this investigation, later on described as his ‘most important contribution to quantum mechanics’ (Jordan to van der Waerden, 10 April 1962).

In his quantum-mechanical treatment of radiation, Jordan developed a consistent ‘wave’ theory of cavity radiation, which was completely in the spirit of Bohr’s ideas and at the same time reproduced the light-quantum effects predicted by Einstein (1909a). In order to understand the progress made by Jordan we must recall how the radiation problem stood in summer 1925.

The theory of radiation was characterized by two distinct approaches whose fundamental assumptions seemed to be in serious conflict with each other. On one hand, Einstein’s quantum theory of an ideal gas (Einstein, 1924c, 1925a, b) made use of his concept of the light-quantum and the statistics introduced by

$^{179}$We shall discuss Pauli’s first attempts to treat time as the variable conjugate to the energy in Chapter V, Section 4, of this volume. Dirac’s treatment of ‘quantum time’ will be discussed in Volume 4, Section V.4.

$^{180}$Pascual Jordan was the expert on radiation theory in Born’s Institute ever since he dealt with this subject in his thesis (Jordan, 1924). In 1925 he had treated the problem of radiation in two papers: first, in the joint work with Born on the quantum theory of aperiodic motion (Born and Jordan, 1925a), where the authors derived dispersion-theoretical expressions for Einstein’s emission and absorption coefficients (§10, pp. 500–503); second, in a note on the thermal equilibrium between atoms and cavity radiation (Jordan, 1925d), where he showed that the results of Pauli (1923b, 1924b) and of Einstein and Ehrenfest (1923) remained unchanged when Bose statistics was used for the atoms rather than the classical (Boltzmann) statistics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0154 -->

150 Chapter IV The Success of Matrix Mechanics

Bose (1924a). In Göttingen and Copenhagen, on the other hand, there was a tendency, as embodied in the theory of Bohr–Kramers–Slater (BKS, 1924), to stick to the wave description of electromagnetic radiation even in considering the phenomena of absorption and emission of light by atoms. One of the basic assumptions of the BKS theory of radiation, namely, that energy and momentum were not strictly conserved in individual interactions between radiation and matter, was proved to be wrong by the experiments of Bothe and Geiger (1925a, b). It was, therefore, a challenge for Bohr’s followers to demonstrate that all phenomena which had been explained hitherto on the basis of light-quanta would follow from a suitable quantum-theoretical reformulation of the classical wave theory.$^{181}$

In summer semester, 1925, Paul Ehrenfest gave a lecture on ‘The Energy Fluctuations in a Radiation Field due to the Superposition of Quantized Eigen-oscillations’ in the Göttingen Seminar on ‘The Structure of Matter.’ When Jordan took up the discussion of the statistics of electromagnetic radiation in matrix mechanics, the content of this lecture—which Ehrenfest also published in *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Ehrenfest, 1925a)—was of great help to him for two reasons: First, Ehrenfest had put his finger precisely on that feature of the classical radiation theory which could not be true in quantum theory, this being the concept of the superposition of statistically independent waves. Second, he had illustrated his arguments by using the simplest model for cavity radiation: a string, fixed at both ends, capable of undergoing elastic (transverse) vibrations. Jordan not only adopted Ehrenfest’s model for the quantum-mechanical treatment; he also found that the latter completely confirmed the failure of the classical superposition property.$^{182}$

$^{181}$The opinion that the light-quantum description did not give the true nature of radiation had been expressed several times during the previous years by Niels Bohr and his collaborators, and they had tried to avoid the light-quantum description completely. Thus, for example, Kramers and Heisenberg, in their joint paper on dispersion theory, had emphasized that the phenomena of secondary radiation—which Adolf Smekal had treated on the basis of light-quantum considerations (Smekal, 1923c)—could be dealt with satisfactorily according to the wave description of radiation (Kramers and Heisenberg, 1925, pp. 685–686, 695–707).

$^{182}$Let us note here that in summer 1925 the problem of the quantum-theoretical wave concept had received particular attention in Göttingen, especially in connection with the idea of matter waves that had been proposed by Louis de Broglie (1924e, 1925). Walter Elsasser, a young student of James Franck’s, had proposed to explain the Ramsauer effect (Ramsauer, 1921b, 1922, 1923) on the basis of de Broglie’s ideas (Elsasser, 1925). De Broglie’s ideas had also been related by Einstein (1925a) to the new statistics governing ideal quantum gases (Bose, 1924a; Einstein, 1924c). During his visit to Göttingen in summer 1925 Paul Ehrenfest helped Born and his collaborators to understand the connection between the matter waves and Bose–Einstein statistics. (See Born’s remark in his letter to Einstein, dated 15 July 1925: ‘*Glücklicherweise erschien Ehrenfest hier und hat uns ein Licht aufgesteckt.*’ ['Fortunately Ehrenfest turned up here and enlightened us.'])
All the physicists in Göttingen had enjoyed Ehrenfest’s visit, which took place in the second half of June 1925. While his lecture had enlightened Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, others did not find much in it. Thus, Frits Zernike, after seeing the published paper (Ehrenfest, 1925a), wrote: ‘[I have] full appreciation of your clear statements—but, apart from the special clarity of the presentation, does it contain anything that had not been calculated by Ornstein and myself?’ (Zernike to Ehrenfest, 1925, undated; reported in Ehrenfest, 1925b, p. 316).

IV.2 Fluctuations in Cavity Radiation 151

In classical theory the vibrations of a one-dimensional string of length $L$ may be described by $u (= u(x, t))$, the lateral displacement, which satisfies the equation of motion

$$\frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \,, \quad (173)$$

if the wave velocity is normalized to unity. With the boundary condition $u(0, t) = u(L, t)$, Eq. (173) admits a periodic solution that can be expressed by an infinite sum of terms, $\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} q_k(t) \sin(k\pi x / L)$, where $q_k(t)$ is a periodic function of time (i.e., $q_k(t) = \sin(\omega_k t + \phi_k)$, $\omega_k = k\pi / L$ being the frequency and $\phi_k$ ($k = 1, 2, \ldots$) the phase constant). The energy of the vibrating string is then given by $H(L, t)$, where

$$H(L, t) = \frac{L}{4} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left\{ \dot{q}_k^2(t) + \omega_k^2 q_k^2(t) \right\}, \quad (174)$$

which is obviously independent of time.$^{183}$ The vibrating string thus appears as a collection of harmonic oscillators with frequencies $\omega_k$ and effective ‘mass’ $L/2$. Ehrenfest had also evaluated the energy of a segment of length $l$ ($\ll L$) of the string and found the result$^{184}$

$$H(l, t) = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{j, k=1}^{\infty} \left\{ \dot{q}_j(t) \dot{q}_k(t) K_{jk} + \omega_j \omega_k q_j(t) q_k(t) K'_{jk} \right\}, \quad (175)$$

where

$$K_{jk} = \frac{\sin\{(j - k)(\pi / L)l\}}{\omega_j - \omega_k} - \frac{\sin\{(j + k)(\pi / L)l\}}{\omega_j + \omega_k} \quad (175\mathrm{a})$$

and

$$K'_{jk} = \frac{\sin\{(j - k)(\pi / L)l\}}{\omega_j - \omega_k} + \frac{\sin\{(j + k)(\pi / L)l\}}{\omega_j + \omega_k} \,. \quad (175\mathrm{b})$$

Ehrenfest’s aim had been to analyze the status of radiation theory and the consistency of its assumptions. In particular, he had asked the question whether the assumption of the statistical independence of waves, which is valid in classical theory, leads to any conflict with quantum-theoretical results. His

$^{183}$Equation (174) is obtained by evaluating the integral, $\frac{1}{2} \int_0^L \{ \dot{u}^2 + (\partial u / \partial x)^2 \} dx$, under the assumption that the length of the string is large compared to each of the wavelengths associated with one of the frequencies, $\omega_k$, of the eigenvibrations.

$^{184}$For calculating $H(l, t)$, the square of the spatial sine functions cannot be replaced by their average values. In the case that $l$ becomes large, i.e., of the order of $L$, the second terms on the right-hand sides of Eqs. (175a) and (175b) can be neglected, and the first terms in both equations become equal to unity; hence Eq. (175) agrees in this limit with Eq. (174).

152                                          Chapter IV   The Success of Matrix Mechanics

calculation of the energy fluctuation in the string had shown that Einstein’s formula for blackbody radiation (Einstein, 1909a, p. 189) could not be derived even if he used Planck’s law for the distribution of thermal energy among the vibrational modes of the string.<sup>185</sup> Since the new statistical approach of Bose and Einstein obviously yielded the right fluctuation formula, Ehrenfest had concluded that a fundamental inconsistency existed in the wave theory of radiation (Ehrenfest, 1925a, p. 362).
Jordan, in fall 1925, had quite a different goal in mind. He started with the conviction that the wave picture *must* yield a consistent treatment of radiation, including the quantum effects. He decided against invoking any reminiscence of the light-quantum concept, such as had been used, for example, by Peter Debye in his ingenious derivation of Planck’s radiation law (Debye, 1910). As he remarked:

> Such a mixture of theoretical wave and light-quantum considerations would seem to us hardly to accord with the real nature of the problem. Rather, we believe it to be consistent to separate the theoretical wave-aspect of the problem completely from the theory of light-quanta, that is, to treat the wave-statistics of black-body radiation throughout by the more general statistical rules applying, e.g., to quantum-theoretical atomic sytems. (BHJ, 1926, p. 607)

Jordan had available a more or less complete quantum-theoretical scheme, namely, matrix mechanics, which, he believed, should be able to determine the validity of the *assumptions* that Ehrenfest, for instance, had used in his analysis: in particular, how the available energy was distributed among the vibrational modes of the string and whether it was justified to talk about statistically independent waves. Moreover, thought Jordan, if matrix mechanics was a valid theory it should also lead to the correct ‘light-quantum term’ in Einstein’s fluctuation formula. He, therefore, started by simply translating Ehrenfest’s classical treatment into the new quantum-theoretical language.
In matrix mechanics, the dynamical variables of the one-dimensional string, such as *u(x, t)*, the lateral displacement entering Eq. (173), and *q<sub>k</sub>*, its Fourier amplitudes, as well as H(l, t), the energy of a segment of the string according to Eq. (175), had to be represented by matrices. On the other hand, the spatial coordinate had now to appear on the same footing as the time coordinate *t*, that is, as a number; the reason being that if a string were replaced by a sequence of mass points connected by elastic forces, then *x* can be represented by the *number* of a mass point multiplied by the lattice constant.<sup>186</sup> Since the summations over *k*

<sup>185</sup> In particular, Ehrenfest had not been able to derive the correct ‘light-quantum’ term (see Ehrenfest, 1925a, especially §§4 and 6).
<sup>186</sup> This treatment of the string was taken over later on into lattice dynamics. It is of interest to note, however, that in 1925 Born did not immediately consider lattice dynamics from this point of view, and he did not indicate any consequences of it in his lectures at M.I.T. (Born, 1926d). The reason probably was that thus far the quantum-mechanical treatment of radiation had only been Jordan’s favourite subject.

The same situation arises when one considers the square, **Δ**<sup>2</sup>, and its time average, <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sup>2</sup></span>, the matrix describing energy fluctuations. The latter matrix may be decomposed into two contributions, (<span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup></span> + <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup></span>) and (<span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>1</sub>**Δ**<sub>2</sub></span> + <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>2</sub>**Δ**<sub>1</sub></span>). Jordan evaluated the first contribution and obtained the result<sup>188</sup>

$$\overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_1^2} + \overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_2^2} = \frac{lL^2}{4\pi} \int_{\pi}^\infty \left( \omega^2 \overline{\mathbf{q}_\omega^2} \right)^2 d\omega. \qquad (178a)$$

In classical theory the second contribution becomes zero when one makes the obvious assumption that the eigenvibrations are statistically independent. Ehrenfest had derived this result explicitly in his lecture at Göttingen in summer 1925.<sup>189</sup> However, *the assumption of statistical independence of the eigenvibrations cannot be taken over into quantum theory*. There the expression <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>1</sub>**Δ**<sub>2</sub></span> + <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>2</sub>**Δ**<sub>1</sub></span> must be calculated explicitly, and Jordan obtained the result

$$\overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_1 \mathbf{\Delta}_2} + \overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_2 \mathbf{\Delta}_1} = \frac{lL^2}{8\pi} \int_0^\infty \left[ (\dot{\mathbf{q}}_\omega \mathbf{q}_\omega)^2 + (\mathbf{q}_\omega \dot{\mathbf{q}}_\omega)^2 \right] \omega^2 d\omega. \qquad (178b)$$

This expression involves products of noncommuting matrices **q**<sub>ω</sub> and <span style="text-decoration: overline">**q**</span><sub>ω</sub>, for the latter (if multiplied by the ‘mass’ of the string, i.e., the factor *L*/2) can be considered as the momentum **p**<sub>ω</sub>. By making use of the commutation relations for **q**<sub>ω</sub> and **p**<sub>ω</sub>, i.e., Eqs. (121), Eq. (178b) can also be written as

$$\overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_1 \mathbf{\Delta}_2} + \overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_2 \mathbf{\Delta}_1} = - \frac{l}{4\pi} \int_{\pi}^\infty \left( \frac{\hbar \omega}{2\pi} \right)^2 d\omega \cdot \mathbf{1}, \qquad (178b')$$

where **1** is the unit matrix.

<sup>188</sup> The derivation of Eq. (178a) presents no difficulties, because the matrices in <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup></span> and <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup></span> all commute. Hence one obtains for (<span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>1</sub><sup>2</sup></span> + <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>2</sub><sup>2</sup></span>) the expression
$$\frac{L^2}{4\pi^2} \int_0^\infty d\omega \int_0^\infty d\omega' \frac{\sin^2[l(\omega - \omega')]}{(\omega - \omega')^2} \left( \omega^2 \omega'^2 \overline{\mathbf{q}_\omega^2} \, \overline{\mathbf{q}_{\omega'}^2} \right).$$
By changing the integration variables ω and ω' to ω<sub>+</sub> = <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub>(ω + ω') and ω<sub>−</sub> = <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub>(ω − ω'), and observing the relation
$$\lim_{l \to \infty} \frac{1}{l} \int_{-\Omega}^{+\Omega} \sin^2 \frac{(l \omega_-)}{\omega_-} f(\omega_-) \, d\omega_- = \pi f(0),$$
one obtains indeed Eq. (178a).

IV.2  Fluctuations in Cavity Radiation                                        155

In order to compare the quantum-mechanical fluctuation matrix <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sup>2</sup></span> with the expression from Einstein’s fluctuation formula (Einstein, 1909a, p. 189), Jordan considered the contribution from a specific frequency ν (= ω/2π), which he reformulated as

$$\overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_\nu^2} = \frac{1}{2l} \left[ \overline{H_\nu(l, t)} \right]^2 - \frac{l}{2} (h\nu)^2 \mathbf{1}, \qquad (179)$$

where <span style="text-decoration: overline">H</span><sub>ν</sub>(*l*, *t*) is the time average of the Hamiltonian matrix H<sub>ν</sub>(*l*, *t*),

$$H_\nu(l, t) = lL(2\pi\nu)^2 \mathbf{q}_\nu^2, \qquad (180)$$

associated with the frequency ν.<sup>190</sup> Apart from a factor 2*l*, H<sub>ν</sub>(*l*, *t*) may be regarded as the Hamiltonian matrix of a harmonic oscillator of mass *L*/2 and frequency ν, whose eigenvalues—given by (*n* + <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub>)*h*ν, where *n* = 0, 1, 2, . . . —all contain <sup>1</sup>/<sub>2</sub>*h*ν, the constant zero-point energy term. H<sub>ν</sub>(*l*, *t*) may, therefore, be expressed as the sum of two terms,

$$H_\nu(l, t) = H_\nu^{th}(l, t) + 2l \frac{h\nu}{2} \mathbf{1}, \qquad (180a)$$

where the first term on the right-hand side represents the ‘thermal’ part of the Hamiltonian, while the second term denotes the constant zero-point energy. After substituting this expression for H<sub>ν</sub>(*l*, *t*) in Eq. (179), Jordan obtained the following result for <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>ν</sub><sup>2</sup></span>:

$$\overline{\mathbf{\Delta}_\nu^2} = h\nu \overline{H_\nu^{th}(l, t)} + \frac{1}{2l} \left[ \overline{H_\nu^{th}(l, t)} \right]^2. \qquad (179a)$$

Thus, the fluctuation matrix, <span style="text-decoration: overline">**Δ**<sub>ν</sub><sup>2</sup></span>, consisted of two terms, which had to be related to the terms in Einstein’s formula (see Einstein, 1909a, p. 189). The latter is

$$\overline{\Delta_\nu^2} = h\nu \overline{E_\nu} + \frac{\overline{E_\nu^2}}{z_\nu V} , \qquad (181)$$

giving the energy fluctuation, <span style="text-decoration: overline">Δ<sub>ν</sub><sup>2</sup></span>, of blackbody radiation in the frequency ν contained in a volume *V*; <span style="text-decoration: overline">*E*<sub>ν</sub></span> denotes the average energy distributed to the frequency ν at a given temperature *T*, and *z*<sub>ν</sub> (= 8πν<sup>2</sup> *d*ν/*c*<sup>3</sup>) is the number of modes. By identifying *l* with the volume *V* in the case of the one-dimensional

$$\overline{H_\nu(l, t)} d\nu = lL(2\pi\nu)^2 \overline{\mathbf{q}_\nu^2} \, d\nu,$$
where **q**<sub>ν</sub> is identical with **q**<sub>ω</sub>, except that the variable ω becomes replaced by ν.

156 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter IV &nbsp; The Success of Matrix Mechanics

string, and putting $z_{\nu}$ equal to 2, Jordan arrived at a complete agreement between the result of his quantum-mechanical calculation, Eq. (179a), and Eq. (181).$^{191}$

Jordan’s result pleased Born and Heisenberg, and the three collaborators concluded that, ‘If one bears in mind that the question considered here is actually somewhat remote from the problems whose investigation led to the development of quantum mechanics, the result [Jordan’s] . . . can be regarded as particularly encouraging for the further development of the theory’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 615). Indeed, by considering waves in matrix mechanics, Jordan had been able to derive the same fundamental result: namely, a formula containing the light-quantum term, which followed from the application of Bose statistics to light-quanta (Einstein, 1925a, p. 8, Eq. (34)), thereby taking, in a sense, the first step towards the quantization of wave fields.

Although this line of investigation appeared to be very promising, it was not pursued further. Jordan recalled that one reason was: ‘Later on Heisenberg explicitly doubted whether this application, which I had made of quantum mechanics to the case of a system of *infinitely many degrees of freedom*, was correct’ (Jordan to van der Waerden, 10 April 1962). To be sure, Jordan’s treatment of wave fields was not without difficulties, as it involved formally divergent expressions, such as the integral in Eq. (178b’). Though, in the three-man paper, the authors avoided any discussion of the complete frequency spectrum of the string extending, in principle, to infinity, they were conscious of the mathematical difficulties presented by the treatment of infinitely many degrees of freedom.

Heisenberg’s doubts, as well as Born’s, were perhaps enhanced by the objections raised by Albert Einstein against the treatment of the vibration of the string in the three-man paper. As Einstein informed Jordan: ‘The thing with the fluctuations is wrong. It is true that one can compute with the zero-point term $\frac{1}{2} h \nu$ the average magnitude of the fluctuations, but not the probability for a very large fluctuation. For weak (i.e., Wien’s) radiation, for example, the probability for finding the total radiation in a fraction $V$ of the total volume $V_0$ is $W = (V / V_0)^{E / h \nu}$. This, evidently, cannot be explained with the zero-point term, although the expression is substantiated on the basis of thermodynamics’ (Einstein to Jordan, 6 March 1926).

In spring 1926 Jordan did not have any good answer to Einstein’s argument concerning the zero-point energy of radiation, and his satisfaction in having derived the fluctuation formula (179a) became muted at the time.$^{192}$ However, he continued his interest in the radiation problem and would later on make important contributions to the quantum theory of wave fields.

Born and Jordan would discuss the implications of this assumption later on and work out the details of the comparison between Jordan’s formula (179a) and Einstein’s formula (181). (See Born and Jordan, 1930, §73.)

IV.3 &nbsp; The Conservation of Angular Momentum &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 157

# IV.3 &nbsp; The Conservation of Angular Momentum

Compared to the detailed formalism of matrix mechanics that had been developed, its applications thus far had been quite poor; they were confined to systems which consisted of harmonic or slightly anharmonic oscillators. For instance, the derivation of the dispersion formulae implied only the use of a harmonic oscillator model in which the transition frequencies of the scattering atoms had been introduced as empirically known constants. However, in a dynamical theory of atomic systems the frequencies and the intensities of the spectral lines should actually be obtained from the equations of motion; hence the appropriate general methods of integrating these equations had to be developed in matrix mechanics. The hope, of course, was that these general methods would then allow one, as in the classical case, to perform the integration for realistic atoms and molecules having one or more electrons. In spite of serious endeavours, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, during their collaboration in fall 1925, did not succeed in solving any such atomic problem. They assembled all the preliminary results obtained in that direction in Section 4.1 of the three-man paper (BHJ, 1926, pp. 595–605). Besides some general remarks on the use of conserved quantities in quantum-mechanical problems, the authors dealt in detail with the properties of angular momentum and a preliminary application of their formalism to intensity problems of complex spectra. The latter parts were worked out entirely by Werner Heisenberg and Pascual Jordan.$^{193}$

In the discussion of conserved properties in quantum mechanics, the authors could rely heavily on the analogous situation in classical mechanics. In the latter, the general properties of $H$, the Hamiltonian describing a given dynamical system, serve directly to integrate the equation of motion. For instance, the conservation of energy can be derived as a consequence of the property that $H$ does not depend explicitly on time (except via the dynamical variables $p$ and $q$). The conservation of momentum and angular momentum can be similarly derived from other properties of $H$, which are also called symmetry properties. If for a system of $f$ degrees of freedom the values of $f$ independent constants of motion are known, then—according to a fundamental theorem of classical mechanics—

______________________________________________________________________________________

$^{193}$Jordan had begun to work on the matrix formalism of angular momentum very early, probably even before the completion of the first paper on matrix mechanics in September 1925. By the time of Heisenberg’s return from Copenhagen to Göttingen in October, Jordan had written a first draft of the three-man paper, which included a section on the angular momentum. Heisenberg had worked independently on this problem in Copenhagen, and it was then decided that he and Jordan should compose the final draft of this section. Jordan later specified the respective contributions as follows: Up to about p. 600 [i.e., the end of the first part of the angular momentum treatment, including the commutation relations for the components of the angular momentum and the polarization rules] the content was from me. The important Eq. (18) [i.e., the formula describing the line intensities] and the consequences derived from it, which led to the selection rule for $j$ [the total angular momentum] came from Heisenberg. However, the formula (24) [i.e., the formula describing the quantization of the total angular momentum], as also (25) [i.e., the formula yielding the relations between certain matrix elements of the angular momentum components], were already contained in the older manuscript of Born and myself. Page 604 [where the intensity formulae for the multiplets are presented] again came from Heisenberg. (Jordan to van der Waerden, 23 July 1962)

158
Chapter IV  The Success of Matrix Mechanics

the motion of the system is completely determined. Born, Heisenberg and Jordan now asked whether to these classical results analogous ones corresponded in quantum mechanics. There were two aspects to this question: first, how to find the conserved dynamical variables for a given quantum system; second, how such properties could be used in order to integrate the equations of motion, which meant specifically how the Hamiltonian matrix $\mathbf{H}$ describing the system could be diagonalized.

To answer the second of these questions, the authors reminded themselves of the fact that in classical mechanics the knowledge of a conserved dynamical variable for a system of $f$ degrees of freedom reduces the integration problem to one in which the system has $(f - 1)$ degrees of freedom.$^{194}$ In matrix mechanics a similar situation existed; that is, there also the conserved quantities could be used to solve the dynamical equations of motion. To demonstrate this point, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan referred to the following argument. A conserved dynamical variable of a quantum system may be represented by a matrix, say $\mathbf{A}$ ($= \mathbf{A}(p, q)$), which is constant in time. If the system is not degenerate, then $\mathbf{A}$ becomes diagonal. Let $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ ($= \boldsymbol{\phi}(p, q)$) be any other dynamical variable of the same system. The difference,

$$\boldsymbol{\phi}\mathbf{A} - \mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{\phi} = \boldsymbol{\psi}, \tag{182}$$

can be calculated with the help of the commutation relations for the $p$'s and $q$'s, the pairs of canonically conjugate dynam

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0163 -->

IV.3 The Conservation of Angular Momentum 159

the matrix $\phi$ by the Hamiltonian matrix $\mathsf{H}$ of the system. Obviously, $\mathsf{H}$ commutes with any conserved quantity $\mathsf{A}$; hence the matrix $\psi$ on the right-hand side of Eq. (182) must have only zero elements. In the case of a nondegenerate system of one degree of freedom the matrix $\mathsf{A}$ is diagonal; so must be, because of Eq. (182), the Hamiltonian matrix $\mathsf{H}$. Then, however, the problem of integrating the equations of motion is solved automatically because the quantum-theoretical Hamiltonian can be expressed as a function of the variable $\mathsf{A}$ analogously to the classical case; in particular, the diagonal elements of $\mathsf{H}$ may be calculated from the matrix elements of $\mathsf{A}$. In the case of systems with several, say $f$, degrees of freedom, the equation

$$\mathsf{H}\mathsf{A} - \mathsf{A}\mathsf{H} = 0 \qquad (183)$$

does not necessarily imply that both matrices $\mathsf{H}$ and $\mathsf{A}$ are diagonal. Even in the case that the system is nondegenerate, different energy states may be associated with one value, $A_n$, of the conserved variable $\mathsf{A}$. However, if one succeeds in obtaining a complete set of $f$ independent conserved variables, $\mathsf{A}, \mathsf{A}', \mathsf{A}'', \ldots$, the integration of the equations of motion of the system would be achieved without difficulty. The reason is that the Hamiltonian $\mathsf{H}$ does not depend on the variables which are canonically conjugate to $\mathsf{A}, \mathsf{A}', \mathsf{A}'', \ldots$; hence it must be a function of the conserved variables alone, and its matrix elements will depend only on the elements of the matrices $\mathsf{A}, \mathsf{A}', \mathsf{A}'', \ldots$. In order to obtain the dependence of $\mathsf{H}$ on the $\mathsf{A}$'s one has to solve simultaneously $f$ matrix equations of the type of Eq. (183). The eigenvalues of the conserved quantities, $A_n, A_{n'}, A_{n''}, \ldots$, i.e., the elements of the diagonalized matrices, $\mathsf{A} = (\delta_{nm}A_n)$, $\mathsf{A}' = (\delta_{n'm'}A_{n'})$, $\mathsf{A}'' = (\delta_{n''m''}A_{n''})$, etc., determine the Hamiltonian matrix $\mathsf{H}$ completely; especially, $\mathsf{H}$ becomes diagonal in $f$ pairs of indices $(nm), (n'm'), (n''m''), \ldots$. In that sense the knowledge of the conserved variables plays a similar role as in classical theory for the solution of quantum-theoretical problems.

The practical question now arose about finding suitable conserved variables of quantum systems. A possible guide for the search was provided by the conserved variables of the corresponding classical systems. In the previous models of atomic structure, angular momentum had played an important role as a conserved quantity; some atomic properties, such as the energy states of diatomic molecules or the intensities of components of complex spectra of many-electron atoms, had been treated by considering the atoms as rotating systems. Heisenberg and Jordan, therefore, discussed in detail the matrices describing the angular momentum of quantum systems. To begin with, they defined the components of the total angular momentum of a system consisting of $N$ particles (electrons and nuclei) by re-interpreting the corresponding classical expressions in terms of matrices. That is, they replaced the Cartesian coordinates, $q_{kx}, q_{ky}, q_{kz}$, and the conjugate linear momentum coordinates, $p_{kx}, p_{ky}, p_{kz}$, of the $k$th particle ($k = 1, \ldots, N$), by the Hermitian matrices, $\mathsf{q}_{kx}, \mathsf{q}_{ky}, \mathsf{q}_{kz}$ and $\mathsf{p}_{kx}, \mathsf{p}_{ky}, \mathsf{p}_{kz}$, describing the analogous variables in matrix mechanics. Thus, they arrived at the following definition of the Cartesian components of the total angular

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0164 -->

160 Chapter IV The Success of Matrix Mechanics

momentum of the system¹⁹⁶:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{M}_{x} = - \sum_{k=1}^{N} (\mathbf{p}_{k y} \mathbf{q}_{k z} - \mathbf{q}_{k y} \mathbf{p}_{k z}), & \quad (184) \\
\mathbf{M}_{y} = - \sum_{k=1}^{N} (\mathbf{p}_{k z} \mathbf{q}_{k x} - \mathbf{q}_{k z} \mathbf{p}_{k x}), & \quad (184\text{b}) \\
\mathbf{M}_{z} = - \sum_{k=1}^{N} (\mathbf{p}_{k x} \mathbf{q}_{k y} - \mathbf{q}_{k x} \mathbf{p}_{k y}). & \quad (184\text{c})
\end{aligned}
$$

The usefulness of the formal introduction of angular momentum in quantum mechanics became immediately evident when Heisenberg and Jordan considered systems, which can be described by separable Hamiltonian matrices. In that case the time derivatives of the angular momentum components, $\dot{\mathbf{M}}_{x}$, $\dot{\mathbf{M}}_{y}$ and $\dot{\mathbf{M}}_{z}$, could be shown to be separable functions of the position and momentum variables of the system; i.e., they were sums of functions, $\phi(\mathbf{p}_{k})$ and $\psi(\mathbf{q}_{k})$, each of which depended only on the momentum ($\mathbf{p}_{k}$, $k = 1, \ldots, N$) or position variables ($\mathbf{q}_{k}$, $k = 1, \ldots, N$).¹⁹⁷ Since all $\mathbf{p}_{k}$ commute with each other, as all $\mathbf{q}_{k}$ commute, an important consequence followed: if in a given classical system a Cartesian component of angular momentum is conserved, the same holds for the corresponding quantum system.¹⁹⁸

The most important property of the matrices $\mathbf{M}_{x}$, $\mathbf{M}_{y}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{z}$, defined by Eqs. (184), is expressed by their commutation relations. The latter were obtained with the help of the commutation relations, Eqs. (121), for systems having several degrees of freedom. Thus Born, Heisenberg and Jordan found¹⁹⁹

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{M}_{x} \mathbf{M}_{y} - \mathbf{M}_{y} \mathbf{M}_{x} = - \frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{M}_{z}, & \quad (185\text{a}) \\
\mathbf{M}_{y} \mathbf{M}_{z} - \mathbf{M}_{z} \mathbf{M}_{y} = - \frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{M}_{x}, & \quad (185\text{b})
\end{aligned}
$$

¹⁹⁶The definition of the angular momentum coordinates by Eqs. (184) agrees with the definition in the three-man paper only up to a negative sign (see BHJ, 1926, Chapter 4, p. 596, Eqs. (1)). The above definition, however, is the same as given by Pauli in his treatment of the hydrogen atom in the case of one rotating particle (Pauli, 1926a, p. 345, Eqs. (26)), and by Born in his lectures on atomic dynamics (Born, 1926d, Lecture 16, Eqs. (3)). We have kept the original notation of BHJ, i.e., $\mathbf{M}_{x}$, $\mathbf{M}_{y}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{z}$, for the components of the angular momentum; Pauli used $P_{x}$, $P_{y}$ and $P_{z}$ instead.

¹⁹⁷The time derivative of, say, $\mathbf{M}_{x}$, contains terms such as $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{k y} \mathbf{p}_{k z}$ and $\mathbf{q}_{k y} \dot{\mathbf{p}}_{k z}$, which may be expressed as $(\partial H / \partial \mathbf{p}_{k y}) \cdot \mathbf{p}_{k z}$ and $- \mathbf{q}_{k y} \cdot \partial H / \partial \mathbf{q}_{k z}$, respectively. Now, if $H$ is a separable Hamiltonian, i.e., a sum of two matrix functions, $\phi(\mathbf{p}_{k x}, \mathbf{p}_{k y}, \mathbf{p}_{k z})$ and $\psi(\mathbf{q}_{k x}, \mathbf{q}_{k y}, \mathbf{q}_{k z})$, then $(\partial H / \partial \mathbf{p}_{k y}) \cdot \mathbf{p}_{k z}$ is a function of the momentum coordinates only and $- \mathbf{q}_{k y} \cdot \partial H / \partial \mathbf{q}_{k z}$ is a function of the position coordinates only.

¹⁹⁸The same statement is true for the total linear momentum of the system, whose components are $\mathbf{p}_{x} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{p}_{k x}$, $\mathbf{p}_{y} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{p}_{k y}$, $\mathbf{p}_{z} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{p}_{k z}$.

IV.3 The Conservation of Angular Momentum 161

$$
\mathbf{M}_{z} \mathbf{M}_{x} - \mathbf{M}_{x} \mathbf{M}_{z} = - \frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{M}_{y}. \quad (185\text{c})
$$

These equations stated the noncommutativity of the Cartesian coordinates of angular momentum in quantum mechanics, and they led to an immediate consequence: either *all three* components $\mathbf{M}_{x}$, $\mathbf{M}_{y}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ are conserved, or *none* of the three components is conserved, or just *one* component is conserved.²⁰⁰ The same theorem holds for classical systems; however, while it is proved easily in matrix mechanics by a few algebraic steps, it takes a long computation to establish it in classical mechanics. The reason is that the dynamical equations, from which the conservation of a given classical variable has to be derived, are very complicated partial differential equations; in quantum theory, on the other hand, the corresponding dynamical equations are purely algebraic equations. The theorem on the conservation of the components of angular momentum in quantum theory, contained in Chapter 4 of the Born–Heisenberg–Jordan paper, thus represented the first example of a general situation: namely, that the conservation laws for dynamical systems can be established much more easily in quantum mechanics than in classical mechanics.²⁰¹

Before applying the matrix formalism of angular momentum to specific systems, the authors studied the general question concerning the possible eigenvalues of the matrices $\mathbf{M}_{x}$, $\mathbf{M}_{y}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{z}$. Since it is sufficient to consider the problem just for one matrix, $\mathbf{M}_{z}$, they proceeded in the following way. They first treated a system whose motion is symmetrical with respect to the $z$-axis. As a result of this symmetry property, $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ must be conserved at least for systems described by Hamiltonian matrices, which are separable in the Cartesian coordinates and momenta of their constituent particles, just as in the classical theory.²⁰² Moreover, the authors assumed that the energy states of the system under investigation are nondegenerate, i.e., $W_{n} \neq W_{m}$ for $n \neq m$. Then the matrix $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ becomes diagonal, or $\mathbf{M}_{z} = (\delta_{mn} M_{z n})$, with the diagonal elements numbered by the same index, $n$, as the energy states. By commuting the position matrices of the constituent, $\mathbf{q}_{k x}$, $\mathbf{q}_{k y}$, $\mathbf{q}_{k z}$, with the matrix $\mathbf{M}_{z}$, Heisenberg and Jordan

To prove the first statement, one first assumes that two components, say $\mathbf{M}_{x}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{y}$, have zero time derivatives. Then it follows from Eq. (185b) that the expression $\mathbf{M}_{y}(\mathbf{H}\mathbf{M}_{z} - \mathbf{M}_{z}\mathbf{H}) - (\mathbf{H}\mathbf{M}_{z} - \mathbf{M}_{z}\mathbf{H})\mathbf{M}_{y}$ must be zero. Since $\mathbf{M}_{y}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ do not commute, it follows that $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ must commute with $H$; hence $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ is also conserved if $\mathbf{M}_{x}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{y}$ are conserved quantities.

²⁰¹Later, especially Hermann Weyl (1928) would discuss the symmetry properties in quantum mechanics in detail.

²⁰²These systems include most of the complex atoms, whether they are free or under the influence of a static electric or magnetic field in a given direction. (In the first case the preferred direction is provided by the direction of the core’s angular momentum in the atomic core–series electron model of complex atoms.) In classical theory the time independence of the $z$-component of the angular momentum follows from the fact that the Hamiltonian of a system (having symmetry around the $z$-axis) does not depend on the angle variable $\phi_{z}$ (canonically conjugate to $\mathbf{M}_{z}$). In matrix mechanics this argument could not be taken over because $\phi_{z}$ had not yet been included among the variables described by Hermitian matrices. By restricting themselves to separable Hamiltonians, however, Heisenberg and Jordan could take over the classical result without involving the existence of the angle variable in matrix mechanics.

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{l x}(n m)(M_{z n} - M_{z m}) = \frac{h}{2\pi i} q_{l y}(n m), & \quad (186\text{a}) \\
q_{l y}(n m)(M_{z n} - M_{z m}) = - \frac{h}{2\pi i} q_{l x}(n m), & \quad (186\text{b}) \\
q_{l z}(n m)(M_{z n} - M_{z m}) = 0, & \quad (186\text{c})
\end{aligned}

where $M_{z n}$ and $M_{z m}$ are two eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}_{z}$. These equations describe the polarization of the radiation emitted by the system; they state in particular that radiation with finite intensity (which is proportional to $|q_{x}(n m)|^{2}$, $|q_{y}(n m)|^{2}$ and $|q_{z}(n m)|^{2}$) occurs only if the value of the angular momentum component $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ changes by the amounts $- h/2\pi$ or zero.²⁰³ As a consequence, all eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ may be ordered in sequences of the form

$$
M_{z n} = \frac{h}{2\pi} (n_{1} + C), \quad n_{1} = \ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots, \quad (187)
$$

where $C$ is a constant, which still has to be determined. Moreover, one is allowed to conclude that all eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ of a system with axial symmetry can be separated into several sequences with different constants, $C'$, $C''$, etc., such that $C'$ is not equal to $C''$ plus an integer; no transitions will occur between the states belonging to different sequences because of the selection rule which states that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ may change only by 0 or $h/2\pi$.

The question must be asked why Heisenberg and Jordan numbered the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ in Eq. (187) by the index $n_{1}$ rather than the index $n$, which characterizes the energy eigenvalues. The reason was that in a physical system many states of different energy may be associated with a given value, $(n_{1} + C) \cdot h/2\pi$, of angular momentum component. Therefore, one should replace the index $n$ by the sum of two indices, $n_{1} + n_{2}$ (both $n_{1}$ and $n_{2}$ are integer numbers, of course), with $n_{2}$ denoting the different energy states which have the same $\mathbf{M}_{z}$-value. This decomposition of the index $n$ allowed the authors to write all matrices describing variables of the axially symmetric system as four-dimensional matrices with two index pairs, $(n_{1} m_{1})$ and $(n_{2} m_{2})$. Thus, for example, the dependence of the matrices $\mathbf{q}_{k x}$ (or $\mathbf{q}_{k y}$) and $\mathbf{q}_{k z}$ on the first index pair may be expressed by the factors $\delta_{1, |n_{1} - m_{1}|}$ and $\delta_{n_{1} m_{1}}$, respectively, and the same holds for the angular momentum components $\mathbf{M}_{x}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{z}$. Since, however, $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ is supposed to be a diagonal matrix, its elements may be simply written, in agreement with Eq. (187), as

$$
M_{z}(n_{1} n_{2} ; m_{1} m_{2}) = \delta_{n_{1} m_{1}} \delta_{n_{2} m_{2}} \frac{h}{2\pi} (n_{1} + C). \quad (187')
$$

IV.3 The Conservation of Angular Momentum 163

While $\mathbf{M}_{x}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{y}$ do not commute with $\mathbf{M}_{z}$, the matrix $\mathbf{M}^{2}$ describing the square of the total angular momentum, i.e., $\mathbf{M}^{2} = \mathbf{M}_{x}^{2} + \mathbf{M}_{y}^{2} + \mathbf{M}_{z}^{2}$, does; hence it will also be diagonal in both index pairs.

Having exhausted the information obtainable from an axially symmetric, nondegenerate system, Heisenberg and Jordan considered systems described by a Hamiltonian $H_{0}$ plus a small perturbation $\lambda H_{1}$. They assumed further that for a vanishing perturbation parameter ($\lambda = 0$) all three angular momentum components are conserved, i.e., $\dot{\mathbf{M}}_{x}^{0} = \dot{\mathbf{M}}_{y}^{0} = \dot{\mathbf{M}}_{z}^{0} = 0$; hence the system described by $H_{0}$ is spherically symmetric, and the perturbation term $\lambda H_{1}$ destroys the symmetry around the $x$-axis and $y$-axis. Then for $\lambda = 0$ the system must be degenerate; in spite of the fact that all matrices are time independent, one can choose only $\mathbf{M}_{z}^{0}$ (and $(\mathbf{M}^{0})^{2}$) as diagonal. However, it is still possible to assume the other components, $\mathbf{M}_{x}^{0}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{y}^{0}$, as being diagonal in the index pair $(n_{2} m_{2})$ discussed above. From the latter representation the authors concluded immediately that the diagonal elements of the matrix $(\mathbf{M}_{x}^{0})^{2} + (\mathbf{M}_{y}^{0})^{2}$ were always positive; the same must be true, of course, of the diagonal elements of the matrix $(\mathbf{M}^{0})^{2} - (\mathbf{M}_{z}^{0})^{2}$.²⁰⁴ Now $(\mathbf{M}^{0})^{2}$, the matrix of the degenerate system, does not depend on $n_{1}$, the index characterizing the eigenvalues of the matrix $\mathbf{M}_{z}^{0}$; as a consequence the number of possible eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}_{z}^{0}$ for a given index $n_{2}$ will be finite. This means that for a fixed value of $n_{2}$ the two-dimensional submatrices of $\mathbf{M}_{x}^{0}$, $\mathbf{M}_{y}^{0}$ and $\mathbf{M}_{z}^{0}$ in the index pair $(n_{1} m_{1})$ must be finite matrices; and these finite matrices still satisfy Eq. (185a). In taking the diagonal sum, $D(\mathbf{M}_{x}^{0} \mathbf{M}_{y}^{0} - \mathbf{M}_{y}^{0} \mathbf{M}_{x}^{0})$, involving the finite matrices, Heisenberg and Jordan noticed that the result was zero; hence they derived the equation

$$
\sum_{n_{1}} (n_{1} + C) \frac{h}{2\pi} = 0, \quad (188)
$$

where the $n_{1}$-sum extends to all possible values $n_{1}$ for a fixed $n_{2}$. Equation (188) implies that the constant $C$ in Eq. (187) can assume only two values, $C = 0$ or $C = \frac{1}{2}$. The authors therefore concluded: ‘If for the angular momentum around the $z$-axis [i.e., $\mathbf{M}_{z}$] we now introduce the notation usually used in the literature, namely, $m(h/2\pi)$ in place of $(n_{1} + C)(h/2\pi)$, we have shown indeed that the selection rule $m \rightarrow (m + 1, m, m - 1)$ applies to $m$ and that $m$ is either “integer” or “half-integer”’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 600).

The fact that the matrix formalism of angular momentum admitted only *integral* or *half-integral* eigenvalues for $\mathbf{M}_{z}$ settled an old argument, which had arisen in connection with the explanation of the anomalous Zeeman effects and the band spectra of molecules in the earlier quantum theory of multiply periodic systems. On occasion, it had seemed necessary to introduce half-integral quantum numbers (see, e.g., Heisenberg, 1922a; Kratzer, 1922). Now this earlier ad hoc assumption was endowed with a firm basis, and at the same time other

In this case the transitions are characterized by the transition in $m$, the eigenvalue (up to a factor $h/2\pi$) of the matrix $\mathbf{M}_z$, and the polarization of the emitted radiation follows from Eqs. (186): i.e., if the value of $m$ does not change at all, then the plane of radiation emitted by the $k$th electron is parallel to the $z$-axis; if, however, the value of $m$ changes by one unit, the amplitude of the emitted radiation parallel to the $z$-axis becomes zero, hence the plane of the emitted radiation will be perpendicular to the $z$-axis (the radiation being circularly polarized in this case). In free atoms such an axis of symmetry, which is fixed in space, does not exist. In the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure, the practice then was to introduce the direction of the total angular momentum (provided the latter was different from zero) as a preferred direction. Evidently, this direction is not fixed in space, for the atoms collide with each other and in the absence of an external field the total angular momenta of different atoms have an arbitrary direction. For the purpose of calculating the properties of the radiation emitted by the $k$th electron in a given atom, it had been found convenient to consider the electron's position coordinate, $X_k$, $Y_k$ and $Z_k$, in a coordinate system whose $Z$-axis was in the direction of the total angular momentum of that atom. Heisenberg and Jordan reformulated these position coordinates of the classical theory in a suitable way as the matrices $\mathbf{X}_k$, $\mathbf{Y}_k$ and $\mathbf{Z}_k$, and they succeeded in establishing commutation relations between these matrices and $\mathbf{M}^2$, the matrix describing the square of the total angular momentum of the atom under consideration. From these relations they then derived the eigenvalues of the matrix $\mathbf{M}^2$, that is,

$$M_j^2 = j(j + 1)\left( \frac{h}{2\pi} \right)^2. \qquad (189)$$

In transitions with finite intensity the value of $j$ changes either by one unit or by zero.${}^{206}$ Moreover, the authors were able to identify the value of $j$ with the *maximum value* of the index $m$, which characterizes the eigenvalues of the

${}^{205}$Kramers and Pauli (1923) had argued previously that quantum numbers other than integral and half-integral ones might occur in the band spectra of molecules. Now Heisenberg was especially happy that besides the integral quantum numbers only half-integral ones were permitted in quantum mechanics (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 12 October 1925).

${}^{206}$In order to derive the commutation relations between $\mathbf{X}_k$, $\mathbf{Y}_k$ and $\mathbf{Z}_k$, and $\mathbf{M}^2$, it was assumed that $\mathbf{M}^2$ was a diagonal matrix with diagonal elements $M_n^2$. Then it was found that $\mathbf{Z}_k$ commuted with $\mathbf{M}^2$, but $\mathbf{X}_k$ and $\mathbf{Y}_k$ did not. As a consequence of the commutation relations the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}^2$ could be written in terms of an index $j$, Eq. (189); moreover, transitions associated with finite elements of the matrix $\mathbf{Z}_k$ involved no change of the index $j$, while transitions associated with finite elements of the matrices $\mathbf{X}_k$ and $\mathbf{Y}_k$ involved a change of $j$ by one unit.

# IV.3 The Conservation of Angular Momentum

angular momentum in a given direction.$^{207}$ Hence $j$ corresponded to what had been called the quantum number of the total angular momentum of an atom in the former theory of atomic structure. In agreement with the values of $m$, therefore, $j$ could also assume either integral or half-integral values.

To some extent the above results confirmed those that had been obtained earlier. For example, the same selection rules, i.e., $j \rightarrow j, j \pm 1$ and $m \rightarrow m, m \pm 1$, came out as in the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems. On the other hand, important differences showed up. From the analysis of spectroscopic data it had been concluded that certain transformations in atoms, such as the transition from a state with $m = 0$ to another state with $m = 0$, was forbidden. In the new theory such exclusions could not be justified at all. As the authors remarked: 'Our result demonstrates further that the exclusion of individual states, such as was, for example, necessary in the earlier theory of the hydrogen atom in order to prevent collisions between the electron and the nucleus, has no place in the theory proposed here' (BHJ, 1926, p. 600).$^{208}$ Another strong point in favour of the new quantum theory was that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}^2$, the square of the total angular momentum of an atom, were given by $j(j + 1)$ in units of $(h/2\pi)^2$, which explained the former ad hoc introduction of 'washed out' (*verschwommen*) values for the squares of the angular momenta in the formulae describing the spectroscopic data. Thus, quantum mechanics offered a genuine chance of deriving, for example, the intensity rules for the components of complex spectra and the associated anomalous Zeeman effects.

The most important test case of the new angular momentum formalism seemed to be the problem of the anomalous Zeeman effects. Early in 1925, Samuel Goudsmit and Ralph Kronig (1925) and Helmut Hönl (1925) had derived formulae for the intensities of Zeeman components on the basis of specific mechanical models using correspondence arguments. A few months later, in June 1925, Heisenberg had indicated that these intensity formulae might be obtained by a quantum-theoretical re-interpretation of the kinematical relations describing the classical rotator (Heisenberg to Kronig, 5 June 1925; Heisenberg, 1925c). Now, in fall 1925, one had to give a consistent and complete derivation of the Goudsmit–Kronig–Hönl formulae. For this purpose Heisenberg and Jordan had just to treat a complex atom with a finite angular momentum and to express the position matrices, $\mathbf{q}_{kx}$, $\mathbf{q}_{ky}$, and $\mathbf{q}_{kz}$, of the $k$th electron in terms of the matrices $\mathbf{X}_k$, $\mathbf{Y}_k$, and $\mathbf{Z}_k$. Thus, for transitions in which the total angular

Then followed the relation, $M_x(j, m - 1; j, m) + iM_y(j, m - 1; j, m) = (h/2\pi)\sqrt{j(j + 1) - m(m - 1)}$. $$

All these results, however, did not go beyond the conclusions of the formulae which had been accepted earlier as representing correctly the available empirical spectroscopic data. The virtue of the matrix derivation of the known results lay in the following: First, it became possible to discard specific models of atoms, which had been employed earlier to deal with the role of angular momentum in the analysis of spectroscopic data. All that seemed to be necessary in matrix mechanics was the basic concept of classically rotating electrons and re-interpretation of this motion in matrix language. Second, the empirically devised quantum numbers and their selection rules, by means of which the data had been organized and ordered, now received a well-defined meaning as being related to the total angular momentum (characterized by the index $j$) and to one of its components (characterized by the index $m$). In the matrix formulation of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan there was no room for arbitrariness, and the question to be answered with all urgency was whether *all* empirical spectroscopic data could be accounted for by their scheme. This question was related to the important dynamical problem: How could the angular momentum of an atomic system, having a well-defined Hamiltonian matrix, be calculated? How was it related to the energy eigenvalues, say in the case of the simplest atom—hydrogen—and what values would the indices $j$ and $m$ assume in this case? The answer to these, and other, questions had to be obtained soon, for then alone would it be possible to decide whether the matrix formulation of quantum theory could deal with realistic atoms.

# IV.4 Wolfgang Pauli’s Conversion

In their meeting in Hanover on Sunday, 19 July 1925, Wolfgang Pauli had rejected Max Born’s invitation to collaborate with him on a consistent mathematical formulation of Heisenberg’s newly discovered rules for the quantum-theoretical re-interpretation of kinematics and mechanics. Pauli had had several reasons in mind for doing so. Psychologically the most important was that in the

course of his investigations of previous years he had arrived at the conclusion that the *real* quantum theory, which would give a coherent account of atomic phenomena, would be born from fresh insights, from the insights of young men such as Heisenberg and himself. Pauli believed that the new quantum theory was again ‘*Knabenphysik*,’ the young man’s game, just as it had been for Einstein and Bohr in its earlier stages. He thought that an ‘oldster’ like Born, forty-three years of age in 1925, would kill the freshness of new ideas by casting them too soon into the framework of an erudite mathematical formalism. Born, Pauli believed, should better stick to his work on crystal lattices and leave quantum theory alone.${}^{210}$

Even during the following months of summer and fall 1925 Pauli did not change his negative attitude towards Born’s involvement in the new quantum mechanics. On 9 October he wrote a long letter to Ralph Kronig, then at Copenhagen, in which he discussed again, as he had done often during the past year, a detailed mechanical model with the help of which he sought to explain the multiplet structure of spectral lines and their behaviour in magnetic fields. Pauli mentioned to Kronig that he would present this matter along similar lines in his article on quantum theory in *Handbuch der Physik*, which he was about to complete within two or three weeks (Pauli, 1926b). He continued:

> I have already a great longing for a reasonable scientific activity! Heisenberg’s mechanics has again given me hope and joy in living. It has not yet brought the solution of the riddle, but I believe that it is again possible to go forward. One must first seek to liberate Heisenberg’s mechanics from Göttingen’s [i.e., Max Born’s] deluge of formal learning (*formalen Gelehrsamkeitsschwall*) and better expose its

${}^{210}$The idea that he was not young enough to contribute really decisive ideas had been mentioned by Born himself in a letter to Pauli written as early as 1919. In this letter Born had talked about the necessity of introducing completely new concepts in order to find a way out of the difficulties of quantum theory, and had remarked: ‘But how one might do that, I don’t have any idea. Though I am not yet old, I am already too old and burdened to arrive at the solution. That is your task; according to what I have heard about you, to solve such problems is your calling.’ And then he continued: ‘However, if you wish to roam around for the moment in the lowlands of conventional physics, then I recommend to you a problem, which is connected with a just published paper of Stern and myself [Born and Stern, 1919], which I am sending you herewith’ (Born to Pauli, 23 December 1919). The problem had been to prove that the surface energy of a cubic sodium chloride (NaCl) crystal is a minimum. Pauli, however, was not interested in the theory of crystal lattices, while Born continued to work in this field over the years.

In my conversations with Pauli during the years 1952–1958 he often referred to the fact that the discovery of and work on the new quantum mechanics and its applications had been ‘*Knabenphysik*’ (‘boys’ physics’), for all the people involved—Heisenberg, Dirac, Jordan, Pauli himself, and the others, except Born and Schrödinger, had been young men. Unlike his teacher Arnold Sommerfeld, towards whom Pauli always showed great respect, he held Born in mild contempt, principally for the latter’s overwhelming interest in mathematical formulations rather than the clarification of physical ideas themselves. In my last conversation with Heisenberg, on 25 February 1975 in Munich, I brought up the question of how sharply Pauli used to treat Born. Heisenberg agreed and said: ‘Yes, he was quite disrespectful towards Born. It would not have occurred to me to treat Born like that; he was my professor. But Pauli was different. He could be very sharp and impatient’ (Conversations with Pauli and Heisenberg, J. Mehra).
