While Pauli was berating Göttingen’s deluge of formal mathematical erudition Heisenberg and Jordan, in one of their contributions to the three-man paper, were developing the methods for treating angular momentum in matrix theory by using a trickle of that erudition. To them it seemed that the specific models that had been employed in the classification schemes of ‘term zoology’—including Pauli’s latest, about which he wrote to Kronig—could now be forgotten. Heisenberg, to whom Kronig showed Pauli’s letter, therefore reacted strongly to the criticism of matrix mechanics and he wrote to Pauli:

With respect to both of your last letters I must preach you a sermon, and beg your pardon for proceeding in Bavarian: It is really a pigsty that you cannot stop indulging in a slanging match. Your eternal reviling of Copenhagen and Göttingen is a shrieking scandal. You will have to allow that, in any case, we are not seeking to ruin physics out of malicious intent. When you reproach us that we are such big donkeys that we have never produced anything new in physics, it may well be true. But then, you are also an equally big jackass because you have not accomplished it either.... (The dots denote a curse of about two-minute duration!) Do not think badly [of me] and many greetings. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 12 October 1925)

Ten days later, the usually good-natured Heisenberg explained to Pauli the reasons for his sudden explosion. He wrote:

The story of this letter which I composed in a fit of rage (on my own stupidity) is this: Concerning your letter to Kronig I wrote to you what I thought about your models [of atomic structure]; that was very little, for I do not wish to think about these questions for the moment. Further I wrote to you about some new results in quantum mechanics. Finally, it occurred to me, in connection with your letter [to Kronig], that I had been thinking for three days about continuous spectra and understood nothing, and that made me write the said [angry] conclusion [of my letter]. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 October 1925)

Indeed, Heisenberg had been struggling hard with the application of matrix methods to actual physical problems. He felt justified in wishing that, instead of playing ‘variations on an old theme’ (‘*Variationen über eine alte Weise*’) with such virtuosity on the ‘organ of Zoology’ (‘*die Orgel der Zoologie*’) and sending forth blasts of sarcasm against the work of people in Göttingen and Copenhagen, Pauli would ‘accomplish something new in physics’ (‘*etwas physikalisch Neues fertig bringen,*’ Heisenberg to Pauli, 12 October 1925).

In the early fall of 1925 Pauli’s scientific attitude was still characterized by a deep liking for Bohr’s correspondence principle as the guide for treating problems of atomic physics. During the writing of his *Handbuch* article on quantum theory (Pauli, 1926b) he had acquired a special mastery in handling the most

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0173 -->

IV.4 Wolfgang Pauli’s Conversion 169

subtle problems of atomic spectroscopy, such as the combination lines of atoms appearing in the presence of an electronic field by means of the correspondence approach (Pauli, 1925d). With this experience Pauli found it even more compelling to adhere to the physical content of the correspondence principle in treating the problems of atomic mechanics. He particularly admired Heisenberg’s success in sharpening the correspondence principle and giving it a more precise meaning by re-interpreting kinematical and mechanical relations. The mathematical formulation which Heisenberg’s discovery received in Göttingen in the hands of Born, Jordan and Heisenberg himself could only mean, in Pauli’s opinion, a fallback to the barrenness of (Born’s) formal techniques.

To Heisenberg, Pauli’s negative attitude towards the use of matrix methods seemed to be unreasonable, especially since all the pertinent features of the correspondence principle had already been successfully incorporated in matrix mechanics. Heisenberg believed that there was no longer room for any doubt about the consistency of the mathematical framework of the new quantum theory; one had only to apply the theory to solve actual problems.

It was not difficult to decide which problem was the most urgent and had to be treated first. For some time Heisenberg had shared Pauli’s view that Bohr’s theory of the hydrogen atom contradicted certain fundamental notions which, on the basis of the analysis of the fundamental problems of atomic physics that had taken place since Bohr’s lectures in Göttingen in summer 1922, one expected *the real* quantum theory should satisfy. The fact that the Balmer spectrum had been obtained from Bohr’s theory appeared to Pauli and Heisenberg, and to Bohr himself, as an ‘accident.’ One of the principal objections was the use, in the atomic domain, of such ‘unobservable’ classical pictures as electron orbits. Now that the notion of orbits had been abandoned in the purely quantum description of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, Bohr’s celebrated derivation of the Balmer formula seemed to have lost its justification entirely. From the beginning of his efforts at re-interpreting kinematical and mechanical relations in quantum theory, Heisenberg had aimed at the solution of the problem of determining the spectrum of the hydrogen atom and the intensities of the transition lines. Would the matrix methods now enable one to arrive at the desired goal?

Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, during their joint work on matrix mechanics, had always been aware of the necessity of treating realistic atomic systems. They hoped that the algebraic methods would indeed enable them to do so. Thus, for example, in introducing the theory of Hermitian quadratic forms they remarked: ‘Thereby we attain the prospect of finding methods for direct calculation of the energy without explicitly solving the problem of motion: methods which correspond to Sommerfeld’s method of complex integration’ (BHJ, 1926, p. 581).<sup>211</sup> However, when it came to displaying the methods explicitly, the authors did not

<sup>211</sup> Heisenberg constantly pressed Born and Jordan to enter into the discussion of practical problems in atomic physics. Thus, in connection with the matrix theory of canonical transformations, he remarked: ‘Born’s form for the canonical transformation [see Section III.2, Eqs. (137)] is almost the high point of the theory; hopefully one would soon succeed in obtaining the methods of integration [of the equations of motion] from it’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 29 September 1925).

present any details, but referred simply in a footnote to the methods of Karl Heinrich Graeffe and Daniel Bernoulli, which one might use for determining the eigenvalues of finite and bounded infinite matrices.<sup>212</sup> Now both methods, cited in the three-man paper, were not applied at all to the solution of problems of atomic physics, for it was not expected that they would be successful in the case of unbounded Hermitian forms or matrices. Heisenberg noted this disparity between the elaborate formalism and the difficulty of using it to calculate the energy states of realistic atomic systems when he wrote to Pauli: ‘The most important part of the paper seems to me to be, in spite of its mathematical character, the principal-axes transformation; it is thought to represent only a method of integration, and up to now it is only of little help, but formally it is still very beautiful’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 23 October 1925). To which Pauli rejoined that ‘for this “in spite of” (“*trotz*”) I could embrace you’ (‘*Für dieses “trotz” könnte ich Sie umarmen*’), for he just did not believe that the mathematical methods invoked by Born would be of any help in actual physical problems.<sup>213</sup> And Heisenberg, more than Born and Jordan, his collaborators in erecting the framework of matrix mechanics, felt the bitterness of the failure, in particular his own, in dealing with the problems of the hydrogen atom, the solution of which would supply the first crucial test of the new theory.<sup>214</sup>

<sup>212</sup> The problem of determining the eigenvalues of a finite quadratic matrix is equivalent to finding the roots of the associated characteristic equation. In the case of an $(n \times n)$-matrix the characteristic equation is an equation of order $n$. One can solve such equations rigorously only for the orders 2, 3, and 4. For higher, but finite orders, Daniel Bernoulli (1700–1782) had proposed the following method (Bernoulli, 1732). Suppose that all the roots of the characteristic equation of order $n$ are different and can be arranged according to their decreasing absolute value as $|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| > \cdots$. Now consider the equations $(\lambda^h)^n - c_1^{(h)}(\lambda^h)^{n-1} + c_2^{(h)}(\lambda^h)^{n-2} - + \cdots = 0$ ($h = 2, 3, \ldots$), having the roots, $\lambda_1^h, \lambda_2^h, \ldots, \lambda_n^h$, $h$ being an integer greater than 1. The coefficients, $c_i^{(h)}$, may be obtained from the corresponding coefficients, $c_i$, in the characteristic equation (i.e., $\lambda^n - c_1\lambda^{n-1} + \cdots = 0$) by using the method of ‘recurrent series.’ Then the largest eigenvalue, $\lambda_1$, may be calculated from the equation $\lambda_1 = \lim_{h \rightarrow \infty} (c_1^{(h)} / c_1^{(h-1)})$, that is, from an approximation procedure involving the evaluation of the coefficients $c_1^{(h-1)}$ and $c_1^{(h)}$. Having obtained $\lambda_1$, one may find the second eigenvalue ($\lambda_2 = \lambda_1^{-1} \cdot \lim_{h \rightarrow \infty} (c_2^{(h)} / c_2^{(h-1)})$), the third eigenvalue, etc., from a similar approximation method. Bernoulli’s method of calculating the eigenvalues of a finite quadratic matrix was extended by Erhard Schmidt to compact matrices (Schmidt, 1905). His method could also be applied to bounded matrices, but in the case of matrices with continuous eigenvalues it made no sense.

Another method for finding the roots of an algebraic equation of finite order (which includes the characteristic equations for $(n \times n)$-matrices) had been proposed by K. H. Graeffe (1799–1873) in a book on the solution of higher-order equations (Graeffe, 1837). His method exhibited some similarity with the one of Bernoulli: again one assumed that the eigenvalues were ordered in a sequence, such that $|\lambda_1| > |\lambda_2| > \cdots$, and one considered equations of the type, $(\lambda^h)^n - c_1^{(h)}(\lambda^h)^{n-1} + \cdots = 0$, but now $h$ had to be an *even* number. Graeffe’s method, which can be extended to obtain the eigenvalues of bounded infinite quadratic matrices, converges faster than Bernoulli’s.

<sup>213</sup> The above remark of Pauli was reported by Pascual Jordan in a letter to van der Waerden, dated 10 April 1962.

I remember that Heisenberg was also quite angry with himself that he had not done it’ (Born, *Conversations*, p. 50). IV.4 Wolfgang Pauli’s Conversion 171

On the other hand, Pauli’s pride was hurt when, on his provocation, Heisenberg had called him a ‘jackass who had not accomplished anything physically new.’ He will show them that such an epithet did not apply to him and decided to beat the *Göttinger Gelehrten* at their own game of matrix theory. He will solve the problem by means of methods, which he had only railed against thus far, thus picking the pearl of physical wisdom out of the chaff of mathematical formalism.

By mid-October 1925 Pauli knew enough about matrix mechanics; Heisenberg had written to him three times from Copenhagen, describing in detail the progress achieved by Born, Jordan and himself.<sup>215</sup> Pauli knew that in order to find the key to the solution of the hydrogen problem, which had escaped Heisenberg and his collaborators, and to carry the calculation through to completion, he would have to make good use of his own considerable formal power and mathematical virtuosity. And, maybe, if matrix mechanics did not yield the energy states of hydrogen correctly, it could still be pronounced wrong.

Less than three weeks after he had been accused of not having ‘accomplished anything physically new,’ Pauli reported to Heisenberg about his successful diagonalization of the Hamiltonian matrix of the hydrogen atom. Matrix mechanics had passed its first crucial test. Heisenberg, with great joy and a touch of envy, marvelled that Pauli had completed the theory so soon (‘*daß Sie diese Theorie so schnell herausgebracht haben,*’ Heisenberg to Pauli, 3 November 1925).

The reason for Pauli’s quick success was that he had recognized at once a major weakness of the matrix theory and had found a way of curing it in the case of the hydrogen problem. In his paper he later on characterized this weakness as follows: ‘The presently known version of the laws of the new quantum mechanics requires that we avoid the introduction of a polar angle $\phi$. Since the latter is not confined within finite limits, it cannot formally be represented as a matrix in the same way as the above-mentioned coordinates [Cartesian coordinates of multiply periodic systems], which execute librations in classical mechanics’ (Pauli, 1926a, p. 345).

The difficulty of re-interpreting classical coordinates, which do not describe *librations* and thus cannot be represented by Hermitian matrices, was certainly the principal obstacle in solving the problem of the hydrogen atom in matrix

Let us recall that the explanation of the hydrogen spectrum (Balmer’s formula) was the first great success of Bohr’s theory [of 1913] and has since remained its keynote. If the new theory failed here it would have to be abandoned in spite of its many conceptual advantages, but, as Pauli has shown, it stands the test successfully’ (Born, 1926d; 1970 reprint, p. 113).

Surprisingly, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had not encountered any difficulty in treating in matrix language the angular momentum, which is the dynamical variable conjugate to \( \phi \), the angle of rotation. In fact, however, they had not cared at all about the angle variable, but had considered the angular momentum by itself and drawn certain important consequences for atomic systems from its conservation. Heisenberg had brought one of these results to Pauli’s attention, when he remarked in a letter: ‘For systems with axial symmetry the angular momentum around the axis is an integral multiple of \( h/2\pi \), such that the possible states lie symmetrically with respect to zero and constitute a sequence free of gaps (with no exclusion of zero being possible), whose members differ by \( h/2\pi \)’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 12 October 1925). This was important information because it implied two observations: first, the angular momentum could be quantized in matrix mechanics; second, the eigenvalues of the \( z \)-component of angular momentum, when described by integral quantum numbers, included the value \( m = 0 \). (See Eq. (188) with \( C = 0 \) and \( n_1 = m \).) Pauli knew that in the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atoms the state \( m = 0 \) had to be excluded at times, and this always caused serious difficulty in the application of the ‘principle of mechanical transformability.’ From Heisenberg’s report it appeared that such a situation did not occur in matrix mechanics, which aroused Pauli’s interest to investigate this question in the case of the hydrogen atom.²¹⁶

In the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory the hydrogen atom had been treated as having two degrees of freedom, with the electron orbiting along a Kepler ellipse in a plane. The integration of the equation of motion of the electron, expressed in polar coordinates, was made possible by determining two constants of motion: for instance, the angular and the radial momenta. This equation could not be genuinely re-interpreted in matrix mechanics because of the difficulty of representing the angle as a matrix. However, Pauli discovered a way out of this difficulty. He recalled that Wilhelm Lenz, his Hamburg colleague, had integrated the classical equation of motion of an electron of mass \( m_e \), moving in the Coulomb field of a nucleus of charge \( Ze \), with the help of a vector quantity, **A**, defined as

\[
\mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{Ze^2 m_e} (\mathbf{M} \times \mathbf{p}) + \frac{\mathbf{r}}{r}, \qquad (191)
\]

where \( \mathbf{M} (= M_x, M_y, M_z) \) is the angular momentum vector, \( \mathbf{p} (= p_x, p_y, p_z) \) the linear momentum vector, \( \mathbf{r} (= x, y, z) \) the position vector of the electron relative to the nucleus (with \( r \) its absolute value), and the product on the right-hand side denotes the ‘cross’ or ‘vector’ product (i.e., \( (\mathbf{M} \times \mathbf{p})_x = M_y p_z - M_z p_y \), etc.). The

However, the information about the specific result was enough to stimulate Pauli to work out a theory of angular momentum in matrix mechanics for himself. He presented this theory in his published paper on the hydrogen atom (Pauli, 1926a, Section 3, pp. 348–349).

vector **A** is a conserved quantity in the classical Kepler problem and is related to \( W \), the energy of the system, by the equation

\[
1 - \mathbf{A}^2 = -\frac{2W}{Z^2 e^4 m_e} \mathbf{M}^2, \qquad (192)
\]

where \( \mathbf{M}^2 \) is the square of the total angular momentum of the electron. In the paper, in which Wilhelm Lenz presented his method, he had specifically remarked: ‘The emphasis must be placed on the fact that the quantum states are obtained here without applying the method of separation and altogether without immediate assistance of the concepts of action and angle variables’ (Lenz, 1924, p. 198). This was exactly what Pauli needed in quantum mechanics.

Several reasons may be thought of why Pauli considered using **A**, the ‘Lenz vector,’ in his treatment of the hydrogen atom.²¹⁷ First, he was familiar with Lenz’ method and had just recently discussed it in his *Handbuch* article on quantum theory (Pauli, 1926b, pp. 133–137, 159–162). Second, since Lenz had successfully employed the vector **A** in his treatment of the problem of the hydrogen atom in crossed electric and magnetic fields within the framework of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory (Lenz, 1924), Pauli expected to be able to do the same in matrix mechanics; then he could see whether the difficulties encountered previously would disappear or not. Probably a still deeper reason was the fact that, provided a proper re-interpretation of **A** existed in matrix language, the quantum-theoretical energy would be expressible in terms of observable quantities alone with the help of an equation which corresponds to the classical Eq. (192). In particular, no variables to which a physical significance could not be attached, such as the angle \( \phi \), would show up in intermediate steps of the calculation. Psychologically, quite another argument may have played an important role in Pauli’s decision to make use of the vector **A**: he could thereby afford to ignore all the learned algebraic tools—including infinite quadratic forms and what not—which Born had assembled. Pauli had only to keep in mind that the dynamical variables in quantum theory had to be represented by Hermitian matrices; with that knowledge alone he could play the game of ‘Knabenphysik,’

There he had stated that for the free atom (i.e., without a perturbing electric or magnetic field) the vector **A** is constant in time, as follows ‘from a little known, but easily sketched, method of integration of the equations of motion [of the electron in the hydrogen atom]’ (Lenz, 1924, p. 198), referring at the same time to Carl Runge’s book on *Vektoranalysis* (Runge, 1919, p. 68). Pauli, in his *Handbuch* article on quantum theory, referred to the use of the axial vector by Lenz (‘*Zu diesem Zweck bilden wir mit Lenz den Achsenvektor* **A** ...,’ Pauli, 1926b, p. 133).

The vector **A** had in fact been introduced a long time ago in connection with the integration of the motion of a celestial body in the gravitational field of the sun. While the earliest discussion may be found in the work of Jakob Hermann and Johann Bernoulli in 1710, Pierre Simon de Laplace presented in his *Traité de Mécanique Céleste*, Volume I (p. 165ff), the three constants of motion which make up the vector **A**. For a detailed account of the history of this vector quantity we refer to the articles of Herbert Goldstein (1975, 1976).

juggling suitably chosen classical dynamical relations until they fitted properly into matrix equations. In playing this young man’s game he would, of course, abide by the rules concerning the quantum-theoretical re-interpretation of classical mechanical quantities, which his friend Heisenberg had discovered.²¹⁸ Under these conditions the application of matrix methods to the problem of the hydrogen atom was going to be intellectual fun, which Pauli was willing to enjoy.

It took Pauli less than three weeks to derive the Balmer formula purely by means of the methods of matrix mechanics.²¹⁹ His quick success converted him completely to the scheme of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan. Pauli now became convinced that this theory constituted a ‘tremendous fundamental advance’ (‘*ungeheuren prinzipiellen Fortschritt*,’ Pauli to Bohr, 17 November 1925). This new feeling of progress stimulated his scientific work greatly. Dispelled suddenly from his mind was the desperation of a few months ago when physics had seemed to him ‘much too difficult’ that he wished he had chosen the occupation of a ‘film comedian’ (Pauli to Kronig, 21 May 1925). In the wake of ‘Heisenberg’s mechanics’ he had acquired ‘hope and joy of living’ (‘*Die Heisenbergsche Mechanik hat mir wieder Lebensfreude und Hoffnung gegeben*,’ Pauli to Kronig, 9 October 1925). The solution of the hydrogen problem had now proved the usefulness of ‘Göttingen’s deluge of [formal] learning’ (‘*Göttinger Gelehrsamkeitsschwall*’). For the time being, at least, Pauli’s heart had been captured by matrix mechanics; it appeared to him that only by means of this theory could one hope to make further progress in the understanding of atomic phenomena. Quantum theory had a future again.

## IV.5  The Solution of the Hydrogen Problem

In his lectures on problems of atomic dynamics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Max Born described the key to the solution of the hydrogen problem in matrix mechanics as follows: ‘In the classical theory of Keplerian motion it is customary to operate with polar coordinates. This process fails here because it does not seem possible to consider angular variables as matrices. Pauli avoided this difficulty by retaining rectangular coordinates and introducing an additional coordinate, the radius vector \( r \)’ (Born, 1926d, Lecture 18; 1970 reprint, p. 113). Born implied with this statement that he and his collaborators in Göttingen had not thought of using the quantity corresponding to the magnitude \( r \) of the radius vector in classical theory, although it occurs explicitly in the expression for the Hamiltonian \( H \) describing the hydrogen atom. For Pauli the

He was ultimately willing to accept Born’s mathematical scheme, the matrix mechanics, only to the extent it was necessary in order to formulate Heisenberg’s ideas about dynamical variables in a consistent mathematical language.

²¹⁹Pauli had not begun to treat the hydrogen problem until he received Heisenberg’s letter of 12 October. On 3 November Heisenberg acknowledged that he had received two letters from Pauli containing the solution (Heisenberg to Pauli, 3 November 1925).

necessity of introducing \( r \) into matrix mechanics was even greater because the expression for the vector **A** again involved it (see the right-hand side of Eq. (191)). Thus, the first step towards the solution of the hydrogen problem indeed consisted in defining the matrix \( r \), which involved, especially, the derivation of the commutation relations of \( r \) with the dynamical variables of the system.²²⁰

Pauli knew that if two independent constants of motion were found, he could integrate the equation of motion of the hydrogen atom. For these, he decided to choose the angular momentum, \( \mathbf{M} = (M_x, M_y, M_z) \), and **A**, the quantum-theoretical reformulation of the vector given by Eq. (191) in classical theory. He defined the angular momentum by the expression, \( m_e (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}) \), which involves the vector product of the vector matrices \( \mathbf{r} = (x, y, z) \) and \( \mathbf{v} = (\dot{x}, \dot{y}, \dot{z}) \).²²¹ Pauli proved that the components of the angular momentum commute with \( H \), the Hamiltonian matrix of the one-electron atom, hence they become constants of motion.²²² Then he wrote the classical vector **A** as the vector matrix **A**, where

\[
\mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{Ze^2 m_e} \cdot \frac{1}{2} \left[ (\mathbf{M} \times \mathbf{p}) - (\mathbf{p} \times \mathbf{M}) \right] + \frac{\mathbf{r}}{r}, \qquad (191a)
\]

and showed that its components, \( A_x \), \( A_y \) and \( A_z \), are constants of motion under the same condition as in classical theory, namely, that only central forces act on the electron.²²³ However, the nonclassical properties of vector matrix **A** may be recognized from the fact that the vector product, \( (\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{r}) \), is not the negative of the vector product, \( (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{A}) \), as in the case of the classical vectors **A** and **r**;

²²⁰Pauli defined \( r \) through the relation, \( r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \), where \( x \), \( y \) and \( z \) are the matrices describing the Cartesian coordinates of the electron. Then the matrix \( r \) commutes, of course, with all position coordinates, but not with the canonically conjugate momenta. Pauli wrote the commutation relations with the latter as (see Pauli, 1926a, p. 347, Eq. (34)): \( \mathbf{p}r - r\mathbf{p} = (h/2\pi i)(\mathbf{r}/r) \), where \( \mathbf{p} \) denotes the vector matrix of the momentum, i.e., \( \mathbf{p} = (p_x, p_y, p_z) \), and \( \mathbf{r} \) denotes the vector matrix of the position, i.e., \( \mathbf{r} = (x, y, z) \).

Therefore, he had to derive independently the results contained in Chapter 4 of the three-man paper. From the presentation of the angular momentum formalism in Pauli’s published paper (see Pauli, 1926a, Section 3), one finds that he occasionally emphasized different properties of the matrices \( M_x \), \( M_y \) and \( M_z \) (which he denoted by \( P_x \), \( P_y \) and \( P_z \)—see Pauli, 1926a, p. 348) than those mentioned in the paper of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan. In addition, Pauli reformulated in matrix language the two products of vector algebra, the scalar product and the vector product. He defined them in analogy with the classical definition: for instance, \( \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{M} = xM_x + yM_y + zM_z \), and \( \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} = (y\dot{z} - z\dot{y}, z\dot{x} - x\dot{z}, x\dot{y} - y\dot{x}) \). The definition of the vector product \( (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}) \) is not ambiguous, because \( (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})_x \) can be shown to commute with the matrix \( x \), \( (\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})_y \) can be shown to commute with \( y \), etc.

²²²The Hamiltonian matrix of the one-electron atom, whose nucleus bears the charge \( Ze \), is obviously given by the expression \( \mathbf{p}^2 / 2m_e - Ze^2 / r \). Note that the angular momentum components remain constants of motion if the second term in the Hamiltonian matrix is replaced by a central potential, i.e., by an arbitrary function of the matrix \( r \).

²²³In proving the time independence of the vector matrix **A**, defined by Eq. (191a), Pauli made use of the fact that the time derivative of the matrix quotient \( \mathbf{r}/r \) is given by the expression \( (2m_e)^{-1} [(\mathbf{M} \times \mathbf{r}/r^3) - (\mathbf{r}/r^3 \times \mathbf{M})] \). On the other hand, the time derivative of the first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (191a) becomes equal to \( (2Ze^2 m_e)^{-1} [(\mathbf{M} \times \dot{\mathbf{p}}) - (\dot{\mathbf{p}} \times \mathbf{M})] \) and, on substituting for \( \dot{\mathbf{p}} \) the expression \( -Ze^2 \mathbf{r}/r^3 \), one finds that \( \dot{\mathbf{A}} \) is indeed zero.

especially, the term in the square bracket can be rewritten as $2(\mathbf{M} \times \mathbf{p}) + 2(h/2\pi i)\mathbf{p}$, including an extra term, $(Ze^2 m_e)^{-1} \cdot (h/2\pi i)\mathbf{p}$, which is not contained in the classical expression, Eq. (191).$^{224}$

In spite of the differences between the classical and the quantum-theoretical variables, Pauli was convinced that the quantum-theoretical vector matrix, $\mathbf{A}$, together with the angular momentum matrix, $\mathbf{M}$, will provide the means for determining the energy eigenvalues of the hydrogen atom. He just went on to establish the commutation relations between these matrices, which, besides Eqs. (185), or

$$(\mathbf{M} \times \mathbf{M}) = -\frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{M}, \tag{193}$$

included the equations

$$(\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{M}) = -\frac{h}{2\pi i} \mathbf{A} \tag{194}$$

and

$$(\mathbf{A} \times \mathbf{A}) = \frac{h}{2\pi i} (Z^2 e^4 m_e)^{-1} 2\mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{M}, \tag{195}$$

where $\mathbf{H}$ is the Hamiltonian of the system. With the help of Eqs. (193)–(195) Pauli immediately obtained the matrix re-interpretation of Eq. (192), relating the axial vector matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and the energy eigenvalues of the one-electron atom, as

$$1 - \mathbf{A}^2 = -(Z^2 e^4 m_e)^{-1} 2\mathbf{H} \left( \mathbf{M}^2 + \frac{h^2}{4\pi^2} \mathbf{1} \right). \tag{192a}$$

(Here $\mathbf{A}^2 = (\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{A}) = \mathbf{A}_x^2 + \mathbf{A}_y^2 + \mathbf{A}_z^2$ and $\mathbf{M}^2 = (\mathbf{M} \cdot \mathbf{M}) = \mathbf{M}_x^2 + \mathbf{M}_y^2 + \mathbf{M}_z^2$.) Again, an extra term arose on the right-hand side of Eq. (192a) as compared to the classical equation (192).

In the set of matrix equations, Eqs. (193)–(195) and (192a), Pauli had formulated the rules of the game he was about to play. He would need all his skill to obtain his desired goal: a formula expressing the eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian of the one-electron atom in terms of the eigenstates of the matrices $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{M}$. The first difficulty arose already in the beginning of the calculation; it

In quantum theory this equation must be reformulated as $\frac{1}{2}[(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{r}) + (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{A})] = -(Ze^2 m_e)^{-1}(\mathbf{M}^2 + \frac{3}{2}(h^2/4\pi^2)\mathbf{1}) + r$. IV.5 The Solution of the Hydrogen Problem 177

had to do with the degeneracy of the system under investigation. Thus, Pauli remarked in his paper later on:

From the existence of the vector matrix $\mathbf{A}$, constant in time, we can infer that an atom with a single electron constitutes a degenerate system, even apart from the spatial orientation of the atom (a situation similar to the Kepler motion in classical mechanics). Namely, we can readily conclude from the relations derived above that in general $\mathbf{AM}^2 - \mathbf{M}^2\mathbf{A}$ cannot vanish. Since, on the other hand, $\mathbf{AH} - \mathbf{HA}$ vanishes, it is obvious that for a definite value of the energy $\mathbf{H}$ there is not just a single value of $\mathbf{M}^2$; the system is thus in fact degenerate. (Pauli, 1926a, p. 352)$^{225}$

Now Pauli was, of course, familiar with the trick of how to deal with degenerate systems in the Bohr–Sommerfeld atomic theory. All one had to do in that case was to add a small perturbation term to the original (unperturbed) Hamiltonian and to claim that all results calculated from the perturbed Hamiltonian, in which the degeneracy did not occur, will pass over smoothly into those of the unperturbed case. Born and Pauli (1922) had based their perturbation theory on this device, and Heisenberg had used it again when he calculated the polarization of radiation emitted by a degenerate system (Heisenberg, 1925a). The same procedure could be followed in matrix mechanics; in fact, it was also applied in Göttingen by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan just when Pauli faced the problem of degeneracy in his treatment of the hydrogen atom. At the time, however, Pauli did not know the details of their algebraic methods—nor would he have cared to use them had he been fully aware of them, for he had railed enough already against the Göttingen formalism.$^{226}$ In any case, he chose to avoid the problem of degeneracy completely as had been done in the previous treatments. Thus, he added an appropriate perturbing term to the Hamiltonian of the free one-electron atom on purely physical grounds. In this way he removed the degeneracy of the problem artificially in order to be able to perform the calculation; however, he also made sure that the perturbing term altered the energy spectrum of the free atom only by an amount which could be neglected for practical purposes.

Pauli introduced two kinds of perturbing forces: a non-Coulomb central force and the directed force of a constant external magnetic field. These forces contributed an additional energy to the time average of $\lambda\mathbf{H}_1$, the first-order perturbation term in the Hamiltonian. Pauli explained the action of the two perturbing forces as follows: 'If, in particular, the perturbing field is due to an

Further, the perturbation energy of a magnetic field in z-direction depends only on the momentum component $\mathbf{M}_z$, which is parallel to the field' (Pauli, 1926a, p. 353). These two perturbations thus completely remove the degeneracy of one-electron atoms and, as Pauli pointed out, they make it possible to discuss, at least in principle, certain more general questions which arise in the theory of these atoms: 'The requirement that $\mathbf{M}^2$ and $\mathbf{M}_z$ are to be diagonal matrices leads, therefore, to a special solution of Eqs. [(193)–(195), (192a)], adapted to the relativistic fine structure and to an additional weak magnetic field' (Pauli, 1926a, p. 353).$^{227}$ Although Pauli was not able to present the 'special solution' he had in mind in the published paper on the hydrogen atom, the fact, that the one-electron atoms can be perturbed in such a way that their degeneracy is removed and their energy eigenvalues are fully described by the eigenvalues of the matrices $\mathbf{M}^2$ and $\mathbf{M}_z$, played an important role in his calculation.$^{228}$

In the particular case when the matrices $\mathbf{M}^2$ and $\mathbf{M}_z$ for the hydrogen atom were diagonal, Pauli assumed that the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{M}_z$ were given by$^{229}$

$$M_z(j, m; j, m) = m \frac{h}{2\pi} \quad \text{where } -j \le m \le j. \tag{196}$$

It then followed from the commutation relation for the components of the angular momentum, contained in Eq. (193), that the matrices $\mathbf{M}_x$ and $\mathbf{M}_y$ could not be diagonal in the index $m$, the quantum number of $\mathbf{M}_z$. The only nonzero matrix elements of $\mathbf{M}_x$ and $\mathbf{M}_y$ were connected with transitions from the state $m$ (of $\mathbf{M}_z$) to states $m \pm 1$. Pauli was able to calculate the squares of these matrix elements and, with them, the eigenvalues of the matrix $\mathbf{M}^2$, obtaining the result $j(j + 1)(h/2\pi)^2$, in agreement with Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, Eq. (189).$^{230}$

After he had made the fullest use of Eq. (193), Pauli set out to exploit Eqs. (194) and (195) for the purpose of determining the vector matrix $\mathbf{A}$. This was a difficult task indeed and, in spite of his virtuosity in calculation, he might not

It should be noted that Pauli, in dealing with the hydrogen atom in matrix mechanics, came closer to the spirit of Sommerfeld’s discussion of the Balmer spectrum than to Bohr’s original approach of 1913. He had just recently reviewed in detail Sommerfeld’s theory, including the fine structure, in his *Handbuch* article (Pauli, 1926b, §§19–21). One may even say that his familiarity with *all* aspects of the earlier approaches—in short, Pauli’s erudition—contributed importantly to the quick success of his hydrogen calculation in matrix mechanics.

Kronig (1925) for the intensities of the Zeeman components. Since these intensities are characteristic of the squares of transition elements for an atomic system when a preferred direction, the z-axis, is given, their ratios should be identical to the ratios of the absolute squares of the corresponding matrix elements of $\mathbf{A}$. Hence Pauli assumed that

$$|A_x(j + 1, m; j, m \pm 1)|^2 = |A_y(j + 1, m; j, m \pm 1)|^2$$
$$= \frac{1}{4} C(j \mp m)(j \mp m + 1),$$
$$|A_x(j, m; j + 1, m \pm 1)|^2 = |A_y(j, m; j + 1, m \pm 1)|^2 \tag{197}$$
$$= \frac{1}{4} C(j \pm m + 1)(j \pm m + 2),$$
$$|A_z(j + 1, m; j, m)|^2 = C[(j + 1)^2 - m^2]$$

and discovered that these relations, together with the elements of the matrices, $\mathbf{M}_x$, $\mathbf{M}_y$ and $\mathbf{M}_z$, satisfied Eq. The matrix elements of $\mathbf{A}$, which do not occur in Eqs. (197), vanish; as, for instance, those in which the total angular momentum does not change (i.e., the transitions $j \to j$).$^{231}$

To determine the numerical value of the coefficients $C$ in Eqs. (197), Pauli referred to Eq. (195). This equation stated that the difference of matrix products, $A_x A_y - A_y A_x$, is a diagonal matrix in the indices or quantum numbers $j$ and $m$, and it yielded a relation involving two adjacent coefficients, $C_j$ and $C_{j+1}$, that is,

$$m[(2j - 1)C_j - (2j + 3)C_{j+1}] = m \frac{|W|h^2}{2\pi^2 Z^2 e^4 m_e}, \tag{198}$$

where $|W|$ is the absolute value of $H(j, m; j, m)$, the energy term.$^{232}$ Equation (198) was akin to a sum-rule, and Pauli made use of its contents by means of the following arguments. First of all, he looked for $j_{\text{min}}$, the smallest value of the angular momentum quantum number, which occurs for a given *finite* energy $W$

of the one-electron system. Evidently, the coefficient $C$ associated with $j_{\min}$ must be zero because $C_j$ is a factor connected with transitions $j \rightarrow j - 1$ and there is no state with $j_{\min} - 1$. By substituting $j = j_{\min}$ on the left-hand side of Eq. (198), one notices that it can be satisfied only by the specific value $m = 0$, else the two sides of the equation will assume different signs and will not match. Since, due to Eq. (196), $m$, the quantum number of $\mathbf{M}_z$, always ranges from $-j$ to $+j$, it follows that $j_{\min}$ must also be zero. However, by considering any energy value $W$ above $H(0, 0; 0, 0)$, the ground state, one obtains from Eq. (198) the coefficients $C_j$, with $j = 1, 2, \dots$, up to $j_{\max}$, the maximum value of the total angular momentum consistent with the energy $W$ under consideration. From this argument Pauli derived the important conclusion that $j$ and $m$ are ‘necessarily integral numbers’ (‘*Es sind demnach $j$ und $m$ notwendig ganzzahlig*,’ Pauli, 1926a, p. 356), and that for a general energy state $j$ runs from $j$ to $j_{\max}$. He was thus able to exclude half-integral angular momenta in the case of one-electron atoms.$^{233}$

In his calculation leading to Eqs. (196)–(198) Pauli had assumed that the degeneracy of the one-electron atom was removed by a small perturbation; on the other hand, in the discussion following Eq. (198), he associated different values of the total angular momentum, i.e., $j = 0, 1, 2, \dots, j_{\max}$, with a single value $W$ of the energy. Still the results did not contradict one another because the strength of the perturbing forces (which removed the degeneracy) did not enter anywhere in Eqs. (197) and (198); as a consequence the perturbation could be made arbitrarily small, and one was allowed to use Eqs. (196)–(198) in order to calculate the energy states of the one-electron atom from Eq. (192a). The left-hand side of the latter equation, taken for the matrix element denoted by $(j, m; j, m)$, reads$^{234}$

$$
1 - \mathbf{A}^2(j, m; j, m) = 1 - \frac{2 |H(j, m; j, m)|}{Z^2 e^4 m_e} \left( \frac{h}{2\pi} \right)^2 \left[ j_{\max}^2 - j_{\max} - j(j+1) \right].
$$

(199)

On the right-hand side of Eq. (192a), Pauli had just to substitute the value $j(j + 1)(h/2\pi)^2$ for the matrix $\mathbf{M}^2$; then it yielded the equation

$$
H(j, m; j, m) = \frac{2\pi^2 Z^2 e^4 m_e}{h^2 (j_{\max} + 1)^2}
$$

(200)

IV.5  The Solution of the Hydrogen Problem                                                          181

for the absolute value of the energy states of the one-electron atom. By identifying $(j_{\text{max}} + 1)$ with $n$ and denoting the energy value $H(j, m; j, m)$ appropriately by $W_n$, Pauli finally obtained Niels Bohr's formula of 1913, in which $n$ is usually called the principal quantum number. And he concluded: 'Herewith it has been demonstrated that the Balmer terms come out correctly from the new quantum mechanics' (Pauli, 1926a, p. 357).

Besides Heisenberg, it was Niels Bohr who first learned about the results of Pauli's hydrogen calculation. Hendrik Kramers, who spent a few days in Hamburg in early November, had informed Bohr about it. Bohr immediately wrote to Pauli: 'To my great joy I heard from Kramers that you have succeeded in deriving the Balmer formula' (Bohr to Pauli, 13 November 1925). In the same letter Bohr asked for further details of the calculation and Pauli obliged without delay. Bohr and the theoreticians close to him found Pauli's success striking. Convinced that it was indeed true, Bohr wrote to Pauli: 'Kramers, Kronig and I, who have just gone once again with the greatest pleasure through your beautiful calculation on the hydrogen spectrum, send you many friendly greetings from Tisvilde' (Bohr to Pauli, 5 December 1925).

The great satisfaction which Heisenberg and Bohr expressed on Pauli's achievement arose for a reason which could be appreciated nowhere better than in Göttingen and Copenhagen. At these places the conclusion had been reached during the past three years that Bohr's apparently-so-successful theory of atomic systems, including his celebrated derivation of the Balmer formula (Bohr, 1913b), possessed no rational theoretical foundation whatsoever. However, Pauli's admirable calculation of the hydrogen spectrum, performed on the basis of the matrix mechanics, which could be regarded as the complete logical and mathematical formulation of the quantum concepts developed in Copenhagen and Göttingen since 1923, now provided the necessary justification of the fundamental formula of Bohr's theory. It was natural to ask whether matrix mechanics would be able to resolve the difficulties which had occurred earlier in the treatment of multiply periodic systems, and Pauli provided the answer in his matrix treatment of hydrogen-like atoms.

One of the great successes of the theory of multiply periodic systems had been the calculation of the Zeeman effect (Sommerfeld, 1916d; Debye, 1916a) and Stark effect (Schwarzschild, 1916; Epstein, 1916a, c) of the hydrogen atom. A difficulty had arisen later when one had discussed, especially since 1923, the simultaneous action of electric and magnetic fields on the one-electron atom (O. Klein, 1924a, b; Lenz, 1924). The term, which had to be added to the energy state $W_n$ of the free atom in the case of the external fields, had been evaluated as

$$\Delta W_{n_1, n_2} = \left( \frac{n}{2} - n_1 \right) \omega_1 h + \left( \frac{n}{2} - n_2 \right) \omega_2 h, \qquad (201)$$

where $n_1$ and $n_2$ assume integral values between 0 and $n$, the principal quantum number. In Eq. (201), $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ denote frequencies, composed of the Larmor frequency $\nu_L$ and the precession frequency $\nu_s$ of the Stark effect: in the case of

IV.5 The Solution of the Hydrogen Problem 183

contains the scalar product of the vector matrix $\mathbf{M}$ and the magnetic field strength vector, $\mathbf{H}$, a classical quantity (because $\mathbf{H}$ describes an external macroscopic field); it may also be written as $2\pi(\boldsymbol{\nu}_L \cdot \mathbf{M})$, where $\boldsymbol{\nu}_L$ is the vector quantity $(= e\mathbf{H}/4\pi m_e c)$, whose absolute value is the Larmor frequency $\nu_L$. Evidently, the eigenvalues of the perturbation term could be expressed in terms of the eigenvalues of the matrix $\mathbf{M}_z$, i.e., the component of the angular momentum in the direction of the magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$; if these are $m\ h/2\pi$, then the eigenvalues of the matrix $2\pi(\boldsymbol{\nu}_L \cdot \mathbf{M})$ or $2\pi\nu_L\mathbf{M}_z$ are just given by $h\nu_L m$, where the ‘magnetic quantum number’ $m$ assumes the values $-(n-1), -(n-2), \dots, +(n-1)$, $n$ being the principal quantum number of the atom. Thus, Pauli obtained a normal Zeeman effect (because of the selection rule $m \rightarrow m \pm 1, m$), thereby reproducing quantum mechanically one of the results of the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory. The only difference from the older treatment was that, in agreement with Heisenberg’s statement, the value $m=0$ could not be excluded, and that $m$ did not assume the values $-n$ and $+n$.

Similarly, Pauli discussed the Stark effect of the one-electron atom in an external electric field of strength $\mathbf{E}$ by examining—in the approximation in which terms proportional to $\mathbf{E}^2$ can be neglected—the eigenvalues of the matrix, $\frac{3}{2} n(\mathbf{A} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nu}_s)$, where $\mathbf{A}$ is the Lenz axial vector matrix, and $\boldsymbol{\nu}_s$ a quantity proportional to $\mathbf{E}$ (i.e., $\boldsymbol{\nu}_s = (3nh/8\pi^2 m_e e Z)\mathbf{E}$) whose absolute value is the precession frequency $\nu_s$ of the Stark effect.$^{236}$ In order to determine the perturbation term of the energy in the electric field $\mathbf{E}$, Pauli had only to compute the eigenvalues of the component of the vector matrix $\mathbf{A}$, say $\mathbf{A}_z$, which is parallel to the electric field $\mathbf{E}$. He thus found the result$^{237}$

$$A_z(s, m; s, m) = \frac{s}{n} , \tag{203}$$

where $s$ assumes the integral values

$$s = -(j_{\max} - |m|), 2 - (j_{\max} - |m|), \dots, (j_{\max} - |m|). \tag{203a}$$

$^{236}$ To arrive at the above result, Pauli reformulated the classical expression, $\Delta W_n = e(\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}} \cdot \mathbf{E})$, for the perturbation term of the energy. The vector $\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}}$ denotes the average position of the electron, i.e., the position $\mathbf{r}$ averaged over a complete period of the (nonperturbed) orbit. (Bohr called $\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}}$ the position of the ‘electric centre’ of the atom: Bohr, 1918b, p. 70.) Lenz established the relation, $\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}} = \frac{3}{2} a_n \mathbf{A}$, between $\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}}$ and the axial vector $\mathbf{A}$, where $a_n$ is the semi-major axis of the Kepler ellipse having the quantum number $n$ (Lenz, 1924, p. 199, Eq. (4)). (For the free atom $a_n$ is given by the expression $\frac{1}{2} Ze^2 |W_n|^{-1}$, where $W_n$ is the energy of the atom in the state $n$.) Pauli demonstrated that in matrix mechanics the same relation holds between the corresponding matrices $\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}}$ and $\mathbf{A}$ as in the classical theory by proving two facts: first, $\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}}$ has the same commutation relations with the angular momentum matrices as the expression $\frac{3}{4} Ze^2 |W_n|^{-1}\mathbf{A}$; second, the matrix $(\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}} - \frac{3}{4} Ze^2 |W_n|^{-1}\mathbf{A})$ commutes with $\mathbf{A}$. (See Pauli, 1926a, pp. 253–254.) Hence he introduced the vector $\mathbf{A}$ instead of $\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}}$ in the perturbation term $e(\mathbf{r}_{\text{av}} \cdot \mathbf{E})$ and obtained $\frac{3}{4} Ze^3 |W_n|^{-1}(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{E})$, which he finally wrote as $\frac{3}{2} n(\mathbf{A} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nu}_s) \cdot h$, on substituting the expression for $\boldsymbol{\nu}_s$.

$^{237}$ Equation (203) for the matrix element $A_z(s, m; s, m)$ was suggested by the previous atomic theory. Pauli had just to show that in quantum mechanics the same equation held provided one introduced a new index $s$ which assumed the values given by Eq. (203a). In addition, he had also to calculate the elements of the matrices $\mathbf{M}$ and $\mathbf{A}_x$ and $\mathbf{A}_y$ in terms of the index pairs, $(s, s')$ and $(m, m')$ and to show that Eqs. (193)–(195) were satisfied. (See Pauli, 1926a, pp. 358–359.)

184 Chapter IV The Success of Matrix Mechanics

Again, there is a difference between the classical and the matrix calculations in the values admitted for the index $s$ characterizing the Stark effect. In the former theory, $s$ had assumed the values, $-(n - |m|), -(n(-|m| - 2), \dots, (n - |m|)$, with the subsidiary condition, $m \neq 0$; in quantum mechanics $s$ is automatically bounded by $(n - 1)$ because the maximum value of the angular momentum is not $nh/2\pi$ but $(n - 1)h/2\pi$. In addition, contrary to the classical situation, the state with zero eigenvalue of $\mathbf{M}_z$ would not be excluded.

Finally, turning to the case of crossed magnetic and electric fields, Pauli followed closely the classical treatment of Wilhelm Lenz. In this way he obtained a formula for the eigenvalues of the perturbation term, $\Delta H(n_1n_2; n_1n_2)$ or $\Delta W_{n_1,n_2}$, which has a structure very similar to the classical formula, Eq. (201), that is,

$$ \Delta W_{n_1,n_2} = \left( \frac{j_{\max}}{2} - n_1 \right) \omega_1 h - \left( \frac{j_{\max}}{2} - n_2 \right) \omega_2 h, \quad (204) $$

where $n_1$ and $n_2$ assume values between 0 and $j_{\max} (= n - 1)$, and $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ are the same combinations of the Larmor frequency $\nu_L$ (or the vector $\boldsymbol{\nu}_L$) and the precession frequency $\nu_s$ (or $\boldsymbol{\nu}_s$) of the Stark effect as in the previous theory.$^{238}$ The only difference from the classical formula (201) is the occurrence of $j_{\max}$ rather than $n$, the principal quantum number of the one-electron atom. The relations between the indices $m$ and $s$ and $n_1$ and $n_2$ in Eq. (204) were now given by

$$ m = j_{\max} - (n_1 + n_2) \quad \text{and} \quad s = n_2 - n_1 \quad \text{for} \quad \nu_L > \nu_s, \quad (204\text{a}) $$
$$ m = n_2 - n_1 \quad \text{and} \quad s = j_{\max} - (n_1 + n_2) \quad \text{for} \quad \nu_L > \nu_s. $$

Again, as in the case of the Zeeman or Stark effects, no specific value for $s$ or $n$ had to be excluded in the quantum-mechanical formula for the crossed-field problem.

In a long letter to Bohr, Pauli gave a detailed account of the status of atomic theory after the successful treatment of one-electron atoms in matrix mechanics. In it, he analyzed in particular the difficulty of the previous atomic theory, pointing out that

> the root of these difficulties is the arbitrary exclusion—from the point of view of the quantization rules—of pendulum orbits . . . This was the origin of all evil and the original sin of all considerations on the hydrogen atom, which rested on the

$^{238}$To prove Eq. (204), Pauli introduced the vector matrices, $\mathbf{J}_1$ and $\mathbf{J}_2$, defined by $2\mathbf{J}_1 = (2\pi/h) \cdot \mathbf{M} + n\mathbf{A}$ and $2\mathbf{J}_2 = (2\pi/h)\mathbf{M} - n\mathbf{A}$ (following the analogous treatments by Klein and Lenz in the classical theory), and derived the commutation relations for them. He found that the components of $\mathbf{J}_1$ and $\mathbf{J}_2$ satisfy similar commutation relations as the components of $\mathbf{M}$, and that $\mathbf{J}_1^2$ and $\mathbf{J}_2^2$ have the eigenvalues $(j_{\max}/2)(j_{\max}/2 + 1)$. As a result, the eigenvalues of the component of $\mathbf{J}_1$, parallel to the vector $\boldsymbol{\omega}_1$, can be labelled by $(j_{\max}/2 - n_1)$, and the eigenvalues of the component of $\mathbf{J}_2$, parallel to the vector $\boldsymbol{\omega}_2$, can be labelled by $(j_{\max}/2 - n_2)$, where $n_1$ and $n_2$ run from 0 to $j_{\max}$. (See Pauli, 1926a, pp. 359–360.)

quantization rules for periodicity systems. The exclusion of $m = 0$ was only the logically necessary consequence of this first ban, and the adiabatic processes in crossed fields represent only the specially noticeable bad consequences of the exclusion of $j = 0$ in the case of the fine structure, which was necessary on one hand to describe the phenomenon, and was theoretically completely unfounded on the other . . . And yet, nobody at that time had been able to avoid the original sin of the exclusion of the pendulum orbit, in which I see a limitation of the applicability of the theory of periodic systems, since redemption from it can be achieved for no smaller price than by renouncing the mechanical, space-time pictures of the stationary states of the hydrogen atom. [And he concluded:] Since in the new quantum mechanics of Heisenberg such additional bans do not occur in the case of hydrogen, the difficulties in crossed fields also disappear. (Pauli to Bohr, 17 November 1925)

# IV.6 The Problems of Intensities and the Diatomic Molecule

The calculation of the energy states of the hydrogen atom did more than convince Pauli about the correctness of matrix mechanics. He immediately began a serious search for new applications of the scheme. He knew that there were many questions concerning the hydrogen atom itself that still remained to be answered. For example, could one finally obtain intensities of the hydrogen lines? Or, could one calculate the relativistic corrections to the energy states given by Eq. (200)? On the other hand, as had happened before with Bohr’s theory of 1913, the new results on the spectrum of hydrogen stimulated the hope that one might be able to extend the matrix methods so as to deal with systems containing several electrons, especially the helium atom. In November 1925 the prospects for making rapid progress with the help of a consistent quantum theory of atomic structure appeared to be very bright, and Pauli, without losing any time, immediately attacked the problems facing him.

As for the problem of the intensities of hydrogen lines, there was some reason to be optimistic, because the treatment of the angular momentum in the hydrogen atom already implied the resolution of a difficulty, which had been described by Pauli in his *Handbuch* article on quantum theory. It did not concern the intensities of the spectral lines emitted by the free atom, but the intensities of the components into which a line is split after applying an axially symmetric field (Pauli, 1926b, pp. 164–165). In the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of multiply periodic systems, the transitions in one-electron atoms from states with the principal quantum number $n = 2$ to states with $n = 1$ occurred according to *Scheme* (a): If

$$m \rightarrow \quad -2 \quad -1 \quad 0 \quad 1 \quad 2$$
$$\text{.................. } n = 2$$
$$\text{.................. } n = 1$$

**Scheme (a)** Transition from the states with $n = 2$ to the states with $n = 1$.

no external field is present, all four transitions shown in *Scheme* (a) contribute to the same spectral line, which might appear as a resonance line. However, under the action of an axial field (say in *z*-direction), the transitions \((n, m) = (2, -2)\) to \((n, m) = (1, -1)\) and \((n, m) = (2, 2)\) to \((n, m) = (1, 1)\) give rise to two separated components, polarized circularly in opposite directions and shifted from the original line by the same distance, while the transitions \((n, m) = (2, -1)\) to \((n, m) = (1, -1)\) and \((n, m) = (2, 1)\) to \((n, m) = (1, 1)\) produce a linearly polarized, unshifted line component. The transition from the state \((n, m) = (2, 0)\) to the state \((n, m) = (1, 0)\) is, of course, excluded. Assuming that the emitted spectral line is unpolarized in the absence of the external field, Pauli had concluded from the above scheme that the intensity of each of the circularly polarized transition line components (with \(\Delta m = \pm 1\)) is as large as the sum of the intensities of the two linearly polarized transition line components (with \(\Delta m = 0\)). However, correspondence arguments demanded that the intensities of all transition lines should be the same. Since the two statements contradicted each other, Pauli had concluded that the transition *Scheme* (a) ‘does not correspond to reality, and that also in atoms with a single electron combinations via the middle [i.e., transitions from and to states with \(m = 0\)] might occur in reality’ (Pauli, 1926b, p. 165).

What Pauli had demanded earlier, now actually happened in matrix mechanics; i.e., the *Scheme* (a) had to be replaced by another scheme, *Scheme* (b), in which transitions occurred from the states \((n, m) = (2, \pm 1)\) and \((n, m) = (2, 0)\) to the ground state \((n, m) = (1, 0)\), and \(m = 0\) to \(m = 0\) transitions were especially not forbidden. In *Scheme* (b) all three components with \(\Delta m = 0, -1\) and \(+1\) have the same intensity, if the radiation was linearly polarized in the absence of the external field. And this was in full agreement with the correspondence arguments.

Much more involved than the intensity problem of the hydrogen lines appeared to be the problem of the structure of many-electron atoms. Pauli recognized this immediately from his calculation of the energy spectrum of the hydrogen atom. He had found, in particular, that the multiplicity of the energy state, \(W_n\), having the principal quantum number \(n\), was given by the sum of all states \((j, m)\) compatible with \(n\), that is,

$$
\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \sum_{m=-j}^{+j} m = \sum_{m=-j}^{n-1} (2j + 1) = n^2. \tag{205}
$$

IV.6  The Problem of Intensities and the Diatomic Molecule                     187

Hence it seemed to follow from quantum mechanics that the state with $n = 1$ could be assumed by only one electron, the state with $n = 2$ by four electrons, the state with $n = 3$ by nine electrons, etc. This result could not be correct in the light of atomic structure and, while reporting this matter to Bohr, Pauli wrote:

> However beautiful and closed [i.e., internally consistent] the result of applying Heisenberg's quantum mechanics to the hydrogen atom—which especially leads to the consequence that the ground state of the hydrogen atom should exhibit no magnetic moment—may be, I still do not consider it to be final. To be sure, it would be logically possible that the features of atomic structure, which you have summarized under the notation of "stress" ("Zwang"), first occur in atoms having several electrons. Nevertheless, I have the definite feeling (which I cannot prove by logical arguments) that the difference between the atoms with one electron and those with several electrons with respect to the existence of the stress has often been enormously exaggerated. In particular, I believe that one would, if one performed the experiment of deflecting hydrogen atomic beams in inhomogeneous magnetic fields (unfortunately, so far I could not convince Stern to carry it out), see the same thing as in the case of the Ag-atom, namely $\pm 1$ magneton and *not* non-magnetic atoms. In general I believe that reality deviates from the results, which can be derived from the present basis of Heisenberg's theory for the hydrogen atom, insofar as that for each orbital term $E_n = - Rh/n^2$ there exist instead of $n^2$ states in reality $2n^2$ states, such that for each energy value in the "stressless" ("zwanglosen") Heisenberg theory there arises in a magnetic field the additional term, $\pm 1$ times the Larmor frequency times $h$, thereby doubling the number of terms. (Pauli to Bohr, 17 November 1925)

These statements gave the outline of a systematic programme for developing the theory of atomic systems within the framework of matrix mechanics. An immediate task in this programme was to complete the discussion of the hydrogen atom including the intensity problem and the relativistic corrections. The next most obvious and 'elementary' task seemed to be to apply the methods worked out by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, and Pauli himself, to calculate the energy states of the helium atom. Pauli knew that for all these problems he needed an extension of the existing matrix scheme. For example, in the case of the helium atom there was no trick available—similar to the use of the axial (Lenz) vector in the hydrogen atom—which would help to avoid the use of action and angle variables. Moreover, he believed firmly that one had to bring into quantum mechanics the features described formerly by the notion of 'non-mechanical stress.' In November 1925, right after the calculation of the hydrogen states, he started to work hard on this programme. However, in spite of his efforts, in which he was soon joined by Heisenberg, progress could not be made as rapidly as he had hoped. In order to perform such tasks as the calculation of the relativistic hydrogen atom or even the helium atom, matrix mechanics had to be modified and extended considerably. Before that could be done, however, it was possible to treat only one other atomic problem: the diatomic molecule.
Just when Pauli became increasingly involved in treating the problems of atomic mechanics by using matrix formalism, Lucie Mensing, a former student¹

188 Chapter IV The Success of Matrix Mechanics

of Wilhelm Lenz’ from Hamburg, learned about the new quantum mechanics in Göttingen and became interested in applying it to calculate certain properties of the spectrum of diatomic molecules.$^{239}$ The motion of diatomic molecules could be described by means of very simple mechanical models: the rotator and the anharmonic oscillator. In order to treat these models in quantum mechanics one did not have to invent any new clever technique, such as the one Pauli had used for diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix of the hydrogen atom; all the necessary tools were already available in the papers of the Göttingen theoreticians (anharmonic oscillator: Born and Jordan, 1925b; rotator: Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926). Thus Mensing’s work on the diatomic molecule (Mensing, 1926a), apart from Pauli’s calculation of the spectrum of hydrogen, represented the earliest application of matrix mechanics to atomic problems.

The dynamical behaviour of a molecule consisting of two atoms (masses $m_1$ and $m_2$) may be described by a Hamiltonian matrix H, where

$$
\mathbf{H} = \frac{1}{2m_0} \left( \mathbf{p}_x^2 + \mathbf{p}_y^2 + \mathbf{p}_z^2 \right) + \mathrm{U(r)}, \tag{206}
$$

which is the matrix re-interpretation of the corresponding classical Hamiltonian. In Eq. (206), $m_0$ is the so-called reduced mass of the system, that is, the two atoms bound together in a molecule have been replaced by a single object having the effective mass $m_0$ (with $m_0^{-1} = m_1^{-1} + m_2^{-1}$, where $m_1$ and $m_2$ denote the masses of the two atoms, respectively); $\mathbf{p}_x$, $\mathbf{p}_y$ and $\mathbf{p}_z$ are the components of the momentum. The potential energy, U(r), analogous to its classical counterpart, $\mathrm{U(r)}$, is supposed to depend only on the matrix quantity $\mathbf{r} \left(= \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^2 + \mathbf{y}^2 + \mathbf{z}^2} \right)$, where $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ are the Cartesian coordinates of the effective mass). In the case of actual diatomic molecules, the potential energy had often to be expanded in a power series of the parameter $(r - a)$, where $a$ denotes the equilibrium distance of the effective mass in a state when no rotation occurs.$^{240}$ Now the matrix $\mathbf{a}$,

---

On our suggestion, she made an application, the first application of the new quantum mechanics, to—I think—a diatomic molecule’ (Jordan AHQP Interview, Second Session, 18 June 1963). This implied that Mensing had begun to work on the diatomic molecule before Pauli’s calculation of the hydrogen states became known in Göttingen. Her paper on this subject was received only much later, on 29 March 1926, by *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Mensing, 1926a); hence she could refer in it to certain results of Pauli’s paper (1926a).

Lucie Mensing, born in Hamburg on 11 March 1901, studied physics at the University of Hamburg, where Wilhelm Lenz became her supervisor. She submitted her first paper on an application of perturbation theory to problems of molecular structure as late as September 1925 (Mensing, 1925a), although she had obtained the results already in winter 1923–1924. In 1925 she received her doctorate at Hamburg with a thesis on the influence of electric fields on the widths of spectral lines (Mensing, 1925b). After that she spent some time in Göttingen and became interested in applying matrix mechanics to the problems of molecules. Later, in 1926, she continued the work of Heisenberg and Jordan (1926) on the anomalous Zeeman effects (Mensing, 1926b). Lucie Mensing married the physicist Wilhelm Schütz.

By applying the matrix method of treating the anharmonic oscillator with the help of the reformulated perturbation scheme, Mensing found that $W_{n,j}$, the energy states of the diatomic molecule belonging to a fixed angular momentum (characterized by the index $j$), were given by the equation

$$W_{n,j} = U_0 + \frac{h^2}{8\pi^2 m_0 a^2} j(j+1) + h\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)[\nu_0 + \beta j(j+1)]$$
$$+ \alpha h^2\left[n(n+1) + \frac{11}{30}\right] + \dots, \tag{207}$$

where $U_0$ is the diagonal element of the matrix $\mathbf{U}_0$ in Eq. (206a), $n$ the index characterizing the nuclear oscillations, and $\nu_0$, $\beta$ and $\alpha$ are constants for a given $j$.$^{244}$ The energy expression, Eq. (207), corresponded perfectly to the classical one. In the latter, the factor $j(j+1)$ in the second, the so-called rotational, term had been $j^2$; the third term had been $hn(\nu_0 + \beta j^2)$ and had been associated with the harmonic part of the oscillations of the nuclei and the mixed rotational-oscillational motion, respectively; and the fourth term, taking into account the anharmonicity of the oscillations, had been $h\alpha n^2$ (see, e.g., Born, 1925, p. 145, Eq. (12)). Thus, the result, Eq. (207), represented the quantum-theoretical formula describing all energy states of the diatomic molecule, except the excitations of the electrons.

Lucie Mensing did not stop at this point. She discovered further that only the transitions associated with the changes, $\Delta j = \pm 1$ of the rotational index $j$, and $\Delta n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$ of the vibrational index $n$, had finite intensities, while transitions with $\Delta j = 0$ in the free molecule could not be observed.$^{245}$ On the other hand, the matrix treatment of angular momentum required integral ‘quantum numbers’ $j$ and left no room for speculation about half-quanta. Both results, however, sufficed to remove a difficulty which had occurred in the previous theory of band spectra and had led to the introduction of half-integral values for the quantum number $j$.$^{246}$ Finally, Mensing noticed that in matrix theory the band lines of diatomic molecules should not exhibit a linear Stark effect—

$^{245}$ The reason for this lay in the fact that the diatomic molecule was treated as a one-body system; hence the matrix $\mathbf{z}$ of the coordinate perpendicular to the plane of motion had only zero elements, and consequently the intensities of the $\Delta j = 0$ transitions vanished.

$^{246}$ Mensing found, in particular, that the formula for the frequencies, $\nu(n, j; n', j-1)$ and $\nu(n, j-1; n', j)$, associated with finite intensities, can also be described by a classical formula involving half-integral rotational quantum numbers $j$ (Mensing, 1926a, p. 820). Then she showed that the intensities of the band lines symmetric to the ‘zero-intensity’ line, i.e., the intensities of the transitions $(n, j; n', j-1)$ and $(n, j-1; n', j)$ are approximately equal (Mensing, 1926, pp. 821–823).

These clear and straightforward conclusions pleased Pauli, who knew Lucie Mensing rather well—he had supervised her thesis during Wilhelm Lenz' illness—and he decided to collaborate with her on another problem of molecular physics: the calculation of the electric polarizability of diatomic molecules.

IV.6 The Problems of Intensities and the Diatomic Molecule

Although Pauli's earlier result had not yet been disproved empirically, Mensing and Pauli were convinced that the data would be represented correctly by the quantum-mechanical result.$^{250}$ They concluded: 'Hence it becomes obvious that here, as in some other cases, the new quantum mechanics comes—with respect to the statistical average values—closer to the results of classical mechanics than the erstwhile quantum theory' (Mensing and Pauli, 1926, p. 512).

Independently of Lucie Mensing and Wolfgang Pauli, the problem of treating the diatomic molecule according to the new quantum mechanics was taken up in 1926 by several authors in Europe and the United States. They not only worked out the energy states of the rotator in matrix mechanics (see, e.g., Tamm, 1926, and Landau, 1926), but also arrived at the above discussed formulae for the elements of the polarization matrix $\boldsymbol{\alpha}$ and the quantity $\overline{\overline{\mu}}_z$ in the limit of high temperatures (see, e.g., Van Vleck, 1926a; Kronig, 1926d).$^{251}$ Thus, the rotator became the standard system in which the theoreticians learned to use and appreciate the tools of matrix mechanics.

$^{250}$ In the previous atomic theory, Pauli had obtained the following expression for the elements $\overline{\mu}_z(j,m)$ (see Pauli, 1921a, p. 324, Eq. (17)):
$$\overline{\mu}_z(j,m) = \frac{8\pi^2 A \mu^2}{h^2} \cdot \frac{1}{4j^2} \left( 3 \frac{m^2}{j^2} - 1 \right).$$
The elements $\overline{\mu}_z(j,m)$—excluding the term with $j=0$—had contributed to $\overline{\overline{\mu}}_z$, in the limit of high temperatures $T$, the amount $1 \cdot 5367 kT \cdot |\mathbf{E}|$, rather than $\frac{1}{3} kT \cdot |\mathbf{E}|$ (Pauli, 1921a, p. 327, Eq. (26)).
In a review of recent data on the dielectric constant, Otto Blüh stated that they yielded only a lower limit for the constant $C$ in Debye's law, which was far below the classical value of $\frac{1}{3}$ (see Blüh, 1926, p. 235); hence one could not rule out the older result.
$^{251}$ The problem of determining the polarizability of diatomic molecules was taken up, shortly after Mensing and Pauli, by Charles Manneback in Zurich (Manneback, 1926). He applied the methods of wave mechanics, arriving at the same results as Mensing and Pauli had done with matrix methods. Thus, he contributed to demonstrating the equivalence of the two formulations of quantum mechanics.
