# Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

The fact that matrix methods were available for the task of formulating the ideas, which had emerged from the penultimate sharpening of the correspondence principle, must be considered to be fortuitous. It enabled Born and his collaborators to write down a scheme of the new quantum theory without having to invent new mathematical tools. However, the theory thus developed—matrix mechanics—did not satisfy the authors completely. Especially, when they investigated its physical applications they quickly realized that a wider, more general scheme was necessary in order to deal with problems in which nonlibrating variables played a crucial role. Fortunately for the further development of quantum mechanics such modifications were soon discovered, still before the end of the year 1925. Interestingly enough, the ideas leading to the generalization of matrix theory were brought in by outsiders: they were proposed by Cornelius Lanczos in Frankfurt and by Norbert Wiener at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. These outsiders knew certain mathematical methods which they considered to be superior to the matrix methods for handling the problems of atomic theory; their methods—the field-like formulation of quantum mechanics (Lanczos) and operator mechanics (Wiener)—would have led to far-reaching consequences if they had been properly pursued. However, these authors themselves did not possess the necessary knowledge of atomic physics in order to arrive at those consequences. The experts like Born, Pauli or Heisenberg, on the other hand, made use only of a small part of the possibilities offered by the different mathematical schemes. Born was primarily interested in treating the problem of uniform motion in a straight line, while Heisenberg and Pauli's minds were totally occupied by the efforts to introduce action and angle variables into matrix mechanics for the purpose of calculating such specific problems as the relativistic fine structure and the anomalous Zeeman effects.

In proceeding with their programmes, Heisenberg and Pauli discovered another important point. The existing quantum mechanics, even if generalized to allow for the representation of nonlibration coordinates, did not suffice to describe the atomic situation. The scheme had to be further extended to include a new concept—the spin of the electron—which had again been proposed by two outsiders: George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit in Leyden. But the incorporation of electron spin into the theory did not occur smoothly: in the beginning it seemed to create more difficulties than it removed. However, after a few months, following several careful analyses, the difficulties with electron spin disappeared and a satisfactory explanation of all atomic problems—with the exception of the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0199 -->

196 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

helium problem—could be reached. It took a further thorough examination of certain consequences of the quantum-mechanical scheme, especially a deeper look at the degenerate case leading to the recognition of an exchange phenomenon, until it became clear that the energy states of helium would also eventually come out correctly.

## V.1 Nonmechanical Stress versus Spin

The brilliant and successful application of matrix mechanics to the problem of calculating the energy states of the hydrogen atom raised great hopes that it might soon become possible to solve the outstanding problems of atomic structure. Two sets of atomic phenomena, which had become intimately connected with each other, required an explanation urgently: first, the anomalous Zeeman effects; second, the multiplet structure, in general, of spectral lines and, in particular, the doublet structure of hydrogen and alkali lines. Since Heisenberg and Pauli were intimately familiar with the problems which had arisen in dealing with these phenomena during the previous years and had now mastered the tools of matrix mechanics, they became involved in investigating these tricky aspects of atomic structure according to the new scheme.

The development began already before Pauli attacked the hydrogen problem. In a letter to Ralph Kronig, dated 9 October 1925, Pauli discussed the so-called intercombination lines, that is, the spectral lines arising from the combination of, say, the singlet and triplet terms in alkaline earth atoms, and he suggested that they might be explained on the basis of a heuristic ('*Ersatz*') mechanical model and the application of 'sharpened' correspondence arguments.$^{252}$ '*Ersatz* models' of atoms had been constructed, especially by Heisenberg and Pauli since fall 1924, in order to be able to deal with the 'classically non-describable duplicity' ('*klassisch nicht beschreibbare Art von Zweideutigkeit*,' Pauli 1925a, p. 385) of the states of the series electron in many-electron atoms. In spite of the successes achieved in this way in explaining the available wealth of spectroscopic data, Pauli noted:

> The substitute models really suffer from all the deficiencies [against] which I have always preached in the past years: 1. The "stress" ("*Zwang*") is not interpreted physically, but just described formally by reformulating the relativistic energy differences as such, which depend on the [relative] orientation of the [angular momentum] vectors and are characterized by the notorious double magnetism. 2. Hence one has here always two kinds of modification of the classical theory, which appear to be logically independent of each other. One may now characterize these as follows: (a) transition from the classical mechanics to Heisenberg's mechanics; (b) replacement of the classical Hamiltonian $H(p,q)$ by the one describing the substitute model. (Pauli to Kronig, 9 October 1925)

$^{252}$ The intercombination lines belonged to those phenomena which were the most difficult to explain on the basis of atomic models. In his *Handbuch* article, Pauli had discussed them twice (see Pauli, 1926b, Sections 36 and 44).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0200 -->

V.1 Nonmechanical Stress versus Spin 197

Thus, even though Pauli accepted the new quantum mechanics, which involved the reformulation of the classical Hamiltonian in terms of the corresponding quantum-theoretical quantities of matrices, he believed that the scheme developed so far could neither describe the anomalous Zeeman effects nor even the fact that the helium atom possessed singlet *and* triplet states. Moreover, he claimed, one had to incorporate certain essential features which had hitherto been expressed by the ‘*Ersatz*’ models.

Pauli had asked Kronig to show his letter to Heisenberg, who was also in Copenhagen at that time. Heisenberg, however, did not agree with the views Pauli had expressed, for he wrote in his next letter: ‘Further, I really do not believe any word anymore of your theory of stress (“*Zwang*”). Although it [the stress] also certainly exists in the case of hydrogen, nevertheless I don’t believe that it has the least bit to do with the nucleus; perhaps it is already present within the mould (“*Schimmel*”)’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 12 October 1925). Heisenberg tended to believe that the replacement of the mechanical models of atoms—which he and Pauli had designated as ‘*Schimmel*’ for a while—by the matrix representation might already be sufficient to account for the observed structure of spectral lines. He especially expected that some special feature of the quantum-mechanical scheme might prove to be helpful. Some indication was already provided by the fact that the Hamiltonian matrices describing the dynamical behaviour of atoms had both discrete *and* continuous energy eigenvalues. From this he concluded: ‘According to quantum mechanics, Larmor’s theorem, for instance, is not valid in general. For hydrogen, for example, there exists—even for the orbits in the ground state—a relatively large probability to pass over by absorption [of radiation] into free electrons, and for free electrons Larmor’s theorem certainly does not apply [because of the gyromagnetic ratio]’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 12 October 1925). Heisenberg was aware of the fact that Larmor’s theorem was valid in the matrix treatment of the harmonic and anharmonic oscillators, but in these cases only a discrete spectrum existed. For realistic atomic systems, however, there was a good chance that the theorem would break down and, as a result, the complex structure of spectra and the anomalous Zeeman effects might perhaps follow.

Within a few weeks of this exchange with Kronig and Heisenberg, Pauli arrived at two important conclusions, which emerged from his investigation of the hydrogen atom: first, by quantizing the total angular momentum one would not, at least in the case of the one-electron atom, obtain half-integral quantum numbers for the electron; second, it became inconceivable that Larmor’s theorem could be violated at all in quantum mechanics. Heisenberg immediately conceded to Pauli: ‘With your objection against introducing hyperbolic orbits for explaining the Zeeman effect, I surely agree. It also occurs to me fairly improbable that these hyperbolae [which describe the orbits of free electrons] would be sufficient to explain all the ugly features of the coupling [which gives rise to the anomalous Zeeman effects]’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 3 November 1925). However, Heisenberg was not yet convinced that his earlier speculation could be ruled out entirely, and he wrote again to Pauli: ‘I have also thought a bit about the “stress”’

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0201 -->

198 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

(“*Zwang*”), and I still have the hope again and again that it might come in only in the case of the coupling of two (or several) electrons (and, indeed, through your exclusion of the equivalent orbits)’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 16 November 1925). Pauli did not share Heisenberg’s opinion and, in writing to Bohr, stated quite emphatically:

I could join in the opinion that atoms with one electron are fundamentally different from atoms with several electrons only if one were able to establish a theory on a unified basis, from which would follow, on one hand, no stress (“*Zwang*”) for the hydrogen atom and, on the other, the empirically-obtained anomalous Zeeman effect correctly for the alkali atoms. In the present form of Heisenberg’s theory, however, this is not the case; it always leads to Larmor’s theorem, and I believe I can state with certainty that it [Heisenberg’s theory] will lead in the case of helium to one rather than two term systems. (Pauli to Bohr, 17 November 1925)

Pauli believed firmly that the occurrence of two term systems of the helium atom (i.e., ortho-helium and parhelium) was closely connected with the fact that already the ground state of the hydrogen atom (i.e., of a one-electron atom) in an external field was twofold. ‘In particular, I believe,’ he remarked to Bohr, ‘that one would, if one performed the experiment of deflecting hydrogen atomic beams in inhomogeneous magnetic fields ... , see the same thing as in the case of the Ag-atom, namely $\pm 1$ magneton and *not* non-magnetic atoms’ (Pauli to Bohr, 17 November 1925). In the matrix treatment of the hydrogen atom just performed, the ground state possessed the angular momentum zero (i.e., no angular momentum whatever), and there was no experiment available which contradicted this conclusion. Later, Erwin Wrede, a student of Otto Stern’s, began to work on a Stern–Gerlach experiment with atomic hydrogen. On 17 July 1926 he presented the results of his measurements in a talk entitled ‘Atomic Hydrogen Beams and their Magnetic Splitting’ (‘*Wasserstoffatomstrahlen und deren magnetische Aufspaltung*’) at the eleventh meeting of the *Gauverein Niedersachsen* (Lower Saxony Section) of the German Physical Society in Göttingen. He had found that under the action of an inhomogeneous magnetic field a beam of hydrogen atoms split up into two distinct parts, consistent with the fact that each atom possessed a magnetic moment of one Bohr magneton.$^{253}$ Then, however, this result, which confirmed Pauli’s earlier speculation, did not imply any difficulty concerning the theoretical understanding, for the spin of the electron had meanwhile been postulated and accepted as a fundamental property.

But in November 1925 the conceptual situation in this regard appeared to the pioneers of quantum mechanics to be quite unpleasant. As Heisenberg recalled: ‘We had this doubling [i.e., “two-valuedness”] and we really did not know what it meant. That was disagreeable. We were a bit unhappy, but then so many things

$^{253}$E. Wrede’s talk was listed among the talks given at the meeting (see *Verh. d. Deutsch. Phys. Ges.* (3) 7, p. 37). Wrede had reported his conclusions already earlier to Bohr (Wrede to Bohr, 6 July 1926). He obtained his doctorate with a thesis including the results of his hydrogen measurements (Wrede, 1927).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0202 -->

V.1 Nonmechanical Stress versus Spin 199

were still not understood that we thought, “Let’s wait and see what will come later.” Then the paper of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit came’ (Heisenberg, *Conversations*, p. 377).

On 17 October 1925, exactly a month before Pauli wrote to Bohr about his suspicion that the ground state of hydrogen ought to be twofold, George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit had signed their note for *Naturwissenschaften* in which they proposed to replace the hypothesis of the ‘non-mechanical stress’ (‘*unmechanischer Zwang*’) of an electron (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925). On the basis of a reanalysis of the existing models for explaining the spectroscopic data on multiplet structure and the anomalous Zeeman effects, they came to the conclusion that the entire empirical data—including relativistic and X-ray doublets—could be accounted for in a simple and satisfactory way by ascribing a ‘proper (i.e., intrinsic) rotation’ to the electron such that the angular momentum of this rotation assumed the value $\frac{1}{2}(h/2\pi)$. Heisenberg read Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit’s note immediately on its appearance in *Naturwissenschaften*—it came out in its issue No. 47 on 20 November—and wrote to Pauli about it on a postcard: ‘Since I have bothered you anyway with so many questions, a further one certainly does not matter; hence I would like to hear from you, as the master of criticism, what you think about [Uhlenbeck and] Goudsmit’s note in *Naturwissenschaften*.’ After mentioning a few difficulties arising from the intrinsic rotation hypothesis in atomic physics, he concluded: ‘It is funny that in the model of [Uhlenbeck and] Goudsmit [they] can indeed get the $Z^4$-law with the magnetic hypothesis; hence I am not *a priori* against [Uhlenbeck and] Goudsmit’s theory. However, I would like to hear your objections’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 21 November 1925).

With the ‘magnetic’ origin of the $Z^4$-law Heisenberg had in mind the idea proposed by Alfred Landé one and a half years previously. In discussing the origin of the so-called relativistic X-ray doublets, Landé had considered a magnetic coupling between the radiating electron and the atomic core of a many-electron atom. He assumed that there existed two different states of the atom, in which the core possessed the magnetic quantum numbers $m$ and $m + \Delta m$, respectively, in the direction of the magnetic field produced by the orbiting electron at the centre of the atom; then the energy difference of the two spectral terms associated with the quantum numbers $m$ and $m + \Delta m$ was given by $h\Delta\nu_{mag} = (const.)(Z^3\Delta m/n^3 k^2)$, $Z$ being the atomic number and $n$ the principal quantum number of the electron orbit. (See Landé, 1924a, p. 95; the constant factor has the value $8\pi^4 m_e e^8 h^{-4} c^{-2}$, where $m_e$ and $-e$ are the mass and charge of the electron, $h$ is Planck’s constant and $c$ is the velocity of light *in vacuo*.) Heisenberg now imitated Landé’s procedure; i.e., he considered a one-electron atom, having a nucleus with charge $Ze$, and he attributed to the electron, in accordance with Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit’s hypothesis, an ‘intrinsic’ angular momentum of $\frac{1}{2}(h/2\pi)$ and a magnetic moment of one Bohr magneton. Then, for terms with principal quantum number $n$ (and orbital angular momentum quantum number $k$ of the electron), he found for the energy difference according

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0203 -->

200 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

to the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory the expression

$$h\Delta\nu = \frac{8\pi^2 m_e e^8}{h^4 c^3} \cdot \frac{Z^4}{n^3 k^2} \cdot 2,$$ (211)

whose value, in the case of hydrogen and the helium ion, was twice as large as the one calculated from Sommerfeld’s relativistic theory (Sommerfeld, 1915c). ‘That $k^2$ occurs in the denominator instead of $k(k - 1)$,’ Heisenberg noted, ‘would not bother anybody, but I cannot get rid of the factor 2. If one could get rid of this factor 2, then the model [of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit] would agree indeed with your model 1925–10 [—this is how Heisenberg teasingly referred to Pauli’s *Ersatz* model, about which Pauli had reported to Kronig in the above-mentioned letter (Pauli to Kronig, 9 October 1925); there was obviously no dearth of such models—] and all difficulties would be removed with a magic wand (“*Zauberschlag*”)’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 21 November 1925). In his first reaction to the spin hypothesis, Heisenberg was quite positive. He thought that a quantum-mechanical treatment of an atomic system with intrinsic rotation might—besides yielding some ‘averaging’ over the angular momentum quantum number $k$—retain the essential features brought in by the new concept, especially the explanation of the multiplet structure of spectral terms. However, he noticed that besides the difficulty concerning the factor 2, there was another problem. ‘In addition one must however investigate,’ he remarked to Pauli, ‘where the really existing relativity disappears in the case of hydrogen’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 21 November 1925). Three days later, in his next letter to Pauli, Heisenberg was much more reserved; he had had time to reflect about certain implications of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit’s proposal and had found further difficulties which had to be removed before intrinsic rotation or spin—as it was to be called later—could be accepted in atomic theory. Thus he wrote:

Nevertheless, I myself do have very great reservations against the attempt of [Uhlenbeck and] Goudsmit to establish zoology [i.e., the term structure of many-electron atoms] in such a simple way: 1. Also the nucleus must [then] have angular momentum, and then the simplicity of the zoology could hardly be understood. 2. It would of course be simpler if the electron possessed only charge and mass, but no angular momentum; in principle, however, one cannot argue against the angular momentum, but the idea that the electron has a structure (in particular, that several types of electrons exist) appears to me to be detestable. 3. In the case of the alkaline-earth atoms the energy difference between singlet and triplet atoms having the *same* $l$ [in the erstwhile atomic theory the quantum number $l$ had been defined as $k - 1$, where $k$ was the quantum number of the orbital angular momentum (see, e.g., Pauli, 1926b, p. 219, Eq. (38)); $l$ assumed the values 0, 1, 2, etc., for the $s$-terms, $p$-terms, $d$-terms, etc.] should then arise only through different interactions of the magnets [i.e., magnetic moments] of the two electrons with each other. This yields a totally wrong order of magnitude. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 24 November 1925)

These three objections were certainly serious. Two of them, (1) and (3), arose from the analysis of the spectroscopic data, while (2) expressed the difficulty of

A week later Heisenberg informed Pauli that he might pass through Hamburg on 20 January in order to discuss the problem of evaluating the averages of the radial matrix quantities, $\overline{r^{-2}}$ and $\overline{r^{-3}}$, with the help of an action-angle formalism. On the same postcard he wrote: 'Herewith I am sending you the paper of Born and Wiener and a similar paper of Lanczos for [our] discussion on Wednesday' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 14 January 1926). The papers of Born and Wiener (1926b) and of Lanczos (1926a), to which Heisenberg referred, involved certain modifications of the matrix scheme; with these modifications one could try to establish a consistent quantum-mechanical scheme of action *and* angle variables, which seemed to be necessary in order to solve problems of relativistic fine structure and of the anomalous Zeeman effects.$^{256}$

**V.2 Field-Like Representation of Quantum Mechanics**

The new theory of quantum mechanics of Heisenberg, Born and Jordan, is related most closely with the theory of integral equations. The equations of motion and the quantum conditions can be written down in the form of integral equations. Thus there results a continuum interpretation, which must be placed side by side with the discontinuum interpretation [of Heisenberg, Born and Jordan] as having equal rights, since there exists a one-to-one relation between the two. For the fundamental interpretation of the theory, the integral formulation has the advantage that it is in immediate harmony with the usual field-like conceptions of physics. (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 812)

These programmatic lines constituted the abstract of the first paper on quantum mechanics that was written by a physicist outside the Göttingen and Copenhagen circles. It was entitled '*Über eine feldmäßige Darstellung der neuen Quantenmechanik*' ('On a Field-Like Representation of the New Quantum Mechanics') and its author was **Kornel** (or Cornelius, as he called himself later on) **Lanczos**, then an assistant at the Institute for Theoretical Physics of the University of Frankfurt-am-Main. Who was Cornelius Lanczos and how did he come to work on the new theory?
Lanczos was born on 2 February 1893 in Székesfehérvár, Hungary.$^{257}$ From

$^{256}$ Heisenberg had received from Born a copy of the paper of Born and Wiener and read it during the Christmas vacation; it was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 5 January 1926 and appeared in its issue No. 3 of 12 March 1926. On his return to Göttingen after the Christmas vacation he found a copy of Cornelius Lanczos' paper on a field-like representation of the new quantum mechanics (which, evidently, Lanczos had sent to Göttingen); this paper was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 22 December 1925 and later appeared in its issue No. 11/12 of 26 February 1926.
$^{257}$ Lanczos used the Hungarian spelling of his first name, Kornel (without the accent on e), in most of his German publications, changing in 1929 to Cornel and later to Cornelius. It is of interest to note that his family name, Lanczos, appeared in an early publication of 1923 as Lancius. Finally, it should be mentioned that his father's name was Carolus Loewy—'Lánczos' was the Hungarian translation of 'Loewy.'

1913 until 1921 he studied in Budapest at the Hungarian Royal Technical University, at the Technical University in Freiberg, and at the University of Budapest. From 1921 until 1924 he was a Privatdozent at the University of Frankfurt. In 1924 he went to Göttingen, where he worked for a year as an assistant at the Institute for Theoretical Physics under Max Born. During this period he wrote his first paper on quantum mechanics, which was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 22 December 1925.
In this paper Lanczos was concerned with the relationship between the matrix theory of Heisenberg, Born and Jordan and the theory of integral equations. He showed that the matrices of Heisenberg, Born and Jordan could be interpreted as the kernels of integral equations, and that the quantum conditions could be written in the form of integral equations. He also pointed out that this integral formulation had the advantage of being in harmony with the usual field-like conceptions of physics.$^{258}$
Lanczos' paper was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 22 December 1925 and appeared in its issue No. 11/12 of 26 February 1926.$^{259}$ It was read with great interest by Heisenberg, who had just returned from his Christmas vacation in Munich. In a letter to Pauli, dated 7 January 1926, Heisenberg wrote: 'I have used the railway travel from Munich to think a little about the famous average values. It is true that I have not arrived at any definite result, but perhaps you may be able to do something with the following idea' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 7 January 1926). Then he sketched a description of the electron's motion in the hydrogen atom in terms of polar coordinates. In particular, he proposed to introduce a quantum-theoretical angle $\phi$ through the reformulated classical relation

$$\phi = \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right), \tag{212}$$

where $x$ and $y$ were the Cartesian coordinate matrices. He added: 'That this quantity cannot be expanded in a [quantum-theoretical] Fourier series, is of no significance, according to a recent paper of Born and Wiener' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 7 January 1926).
A week later Heisenberg informed Pauli that he might pass through Hamburg on 20 January in order to discuss the problem of evaluating the averages of the radial matrix quantities, $\overline{r^{-2}}$ and $\overline{r^{-3}}$, with the help of an action-angle formalism. On the same postcard he wrote: 'Herewith I am sending you the paper of Born and Wiener and a similar paper of Lanczos for [our] discussion on Wednesday' (Heisenberg to Pauli, 14 January 1926).

The papers of Born and Wiener (1926b) and of Lanczos (1926a), to which Heisenberg referred, involved certain modifications of the matrix scheme; with these modifications one could try to establish a consistent quantum-mechanical scheme of action *and* angle variables, which seemed to be necessary in order to solve problems of relativistic fine structure and of the anomalous Zeeman effects.$^{260}$

**V.3 The Problem of Electron Spin and the Two-Body Problem**

In the course of 1925, the problem of the electron spin and the two-body problem had become more and more urgent. The spin hypothesis of Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck had been put forward in November 1925, and by the beginning of 1926 it was already causing great excitement in the physics community. The spin hypothesis provided a natural explanation for the anomalous Zeeman effect, but it also raised many new problems. One of the most serious of these was the problem of the factor 2 in the spin magnetic moment of the electron.
Pauli, who had been very skeptical about the spin hypothesis, finally accepted it in the spring of 1926. In a letter to Bohr, dated 21 February 1926, he wrote: 'I am now more or less convinced that the electron has an intrinsic angular momentum and an intrinsic magnetic moment. I am now convinced that this is the only way to explain the anomalous Zeeman effect' (Pauli to Bohr, 21 February 1926).$^{261}$
The acceptance of the spin hypothesis by Pauli was a great step forward, but it also meant that the problem of the factor 2 had to be solved. This factor was a consequence of the Dirac equation, which was not yet available in 1926. In the meantime, Heisenberg and Jordan tried to solve the problem by using matrix mechanics. In a paper submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 16 April 1926, they showed that the factor 2 could be obtained from the matrix theory of the electron, provided that one assumed that the electron had an intrinsic angular momentum of $\hbar/2$.$^{262}$
The work of Heisenberg and Jordan was a great achievement, but it also showed the limitations of matrix mechanics. The matrix theory of the electron was very complicated, and it was not easy to see how it could be applied to more complicated atoms. This was one of the reasons why Schrödinger developed his wave mechanics in the spring of 1926.

$^{260}$ See footnote 256.
$^{261}$ Pauli to Bohr, 21 February 1926, in *Niels Bohr: Collected Works*, Vol. 5, p. 213.
$^{262}$ Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926d.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0207 -->

207 V.3 The Problem of Electron Spin and the Two-Body Problem

The work of Heisenberg and Jordan on the electron spin was one of the last important contributions of matrix mechanics to the theory of the atom. By the middle of 1926, Schrödinger's wave mechanics had begun to replace matrix mechanics as the primary tool for atomic theory. The wave mechanics was much easier to use than matrix mechanics, and it also had the advantage of being more intuitive.
However, the matrix theory still had its advantages. It was more general than wave mechanics, and it could be applied to a wider range of problems. This was shown by Heisenberg in a paper published in *Zeitschrift für Physik* in 1927, in which he developed the matrix theory of the electromagnetic field.$^{263}$
The development of matrix mechanics from 1925 to 1926 was a very exciting time in the history of physics. It was a time of great creativity and of great confusion. Many different ideas were being put forward, and it was not clear which ones would survive. In the end, matrix mechanics was replaced by wave mechanics, but its influence can still be felt in many areas of modern physics.

$^{263}$ Heisenberg, 1927a.

1911 to 1916 he studied physics and mathematics at the University of Budapest, where his teachers were Loránd Eötvös and Lipot (Leopold) Fejér; Eötvös was known for his experimental researches connected with establishing the equivalence of gravitational and inertial masses and Fejér for his contributions to the theory of Fourier series. Upon graduation Lanczos became an assistant at the Polytechnical University of Budapest where, for the next four years, he worked on experimental physics. In 1921 he finally received his doctorate from the University of Szeged, which was also situated in Budapest at the time, with a thesis on 'The Function-Theoretic Behaviour of Maxwell's Vacuum Equations,' supervised by Rudolph Ortvay, a former student of Sommerfeld's. Adverse political circumstances prevailing in Hungary made it difficult for Lanczos to pursue his plans there upon completing his doctorate. Like many another young man at the time with an ambition to embark upon a career in scientific research, Lanczos went to Germany. He found a position at the Physics Institute of Freiburg-im-Breisgau and stayed there for three years.²⁵⁸ In fall 1924 he went to the University of Frankfurt, where the prospects for his scientific career seemed to be more promising.

In spite of the fact that he worked in places like Freiburg and Frankfurt, which did not count themselves among the principal centres of theoretical physics in Germany, Lanczos soon managed to achieve a good name for himself by his work on general relativity theory.²⁵⁹ During a visit to Berlin he had come under the spell of Albert Einstein, the founder of this theory. 'I had my first discussion with Einstein when I was in Germany in 1921,' Lanczos recalled forty-five years later. 'I had a chance to talk to him for a few minutes between two lectures. Of course, I had already had a tremendous admiration for him in my student days, and so I was in a great palpitation of heart when this opportunity came' (Lanczos in Whitrow, 1972, p. 48). Lanczos had at once admired the relativity theory because of its conceptual power and, as he expressed it in 1923 during a discussion, because of 'its logical consistency [Folgerichtigkeit], in that it takes the foundations of differential geometry—which

Thus, Lanczos, the former disciple of Eötvös, became a devoted researcher in general relativity theory during the following years, treating such topics as the equations of gravitation, the properties of de Sitter space, the problem of rotation, the theory of the perihelion shift of Mercury, and cosmology.²⁶⁰

It was while investigating the behaviour of weak fields in Einstein's theory of gravitation that Lanczos discovered an interesting fact (Lanczos, 1925a). He had to solve a differential equation for a tensor field with certain boundary conditions imposed on the solutions; he converted the differential equation into an integral equation and discovered that the latter was of the Fredholm type. This discovery pleased him very much, especially since he had arrived at the integral equation not by mathematical but by physical argumentation. Indeed, Lanczos did not know then that Hilbert had established the equivalence of differential equations (with boundary conditions) and integral equations nearly twenty years before.²⁶¹ It was perhaps a charming accident that Lanczos, who was well-trained mathematically, had not come across this result earlier; yet his rediscovery of the old methods of integral equations had a certain advantage which showed itself very soon in his work.

In fall 1924 Lanczos went to Frankfurt where Erwin Madelung, the Director of the Institute of Physics, was just preparing the second edition of his book, *Die mathematischen Hilfsmittel des Physikers*, a compendium of the mathematical tools of physics (Madelung, 1925). Madelung added a number of new topics, such as Green's functions, tensor analysis and general relativity theory in the new edition, and Lanczos helped him with their presentation.²⁶² In the course of this

²⁶⁰In the 1920s, when debates on relativity theory often took place in the discussions at physics meetings, Lanczos took a strong stand in favour of Einstein's theory. At the annual meeting of the Society in Bonn in September 1923, Lanczos expressed his opinion in support of relativity theory. Although the atmosphere then was less controversial than at the Bad Nauheim meeting three years earlier, some people still raised doubts about the validity of general relativity theory. New results, such as the measurement of the deflection of light in the gravitational field of the sun made by the *American Einstein Expedition* of 1922, seemed to be compatible with a different theoretical description than the one provided by Einstein's theory (Hopmann, 1923). Lanczos, however, argued that any numerical agreement obtained from a nonrelativistic theory had to be considered an extreme coincidence ('*kolossaler Zufall*,' Lanczos in Hopmann, 1923, p. 484).

V.2 Field-Like Representation of Quantum Mechanics 207

work for his new boss Lanczos had to study the mathematical literature, in particular the subjects treated in the book of Courant and Hilbert (1924), which had just been published and to which Madelung referred frequently. A short section on quantum theory was also included in the *Mathematische Hilfsmittel*, and it was more than a coincidence that, at about the same time as he assisted Madelung on the book, Lanczos began to address himself to an outstanding problem of quantum theory.

The current status of quantum theory had been reviewed recently, in September 1924, at the *Naturforscherversammlung* in Innsbruck, where Hendrik Kramers and Arnold Sommerfeld presented differing views concerning the structure of atoms. The most controversial question, as revealed by the discussions in which Einstein participated, was the status of the radiation problem. Two theories of radiation competed with each other at that time, each describing a certain set of phenomena adequately: one was the theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater, which had just been successful in accounting for the dispersion of light by atoms; the other was Einstein's old theory of light-quanta, which had recently been supplemented by the statistical method of the Indian physicist Satyendra Nath Bose. However, the two theories seemed to be completely at variance, and Lanczos became interested in the question whether general relativity theory might help in resolving the discrepancies. He hoped, especially, that perhaps some of the quantum features of radiation would follow by considering radiation in a closed universe.

Lanczos concerned himself with this question in the first half of 1925, making ample use of the methods of integral equations. The latter implied that the electromagnetic four-potential $\Phi_i$ ($i = 0, 1, 2, 3$; $\Phi_0$ denoting the electric potential, and $\Phi_1$, $\Phi_2$ and $\Phi_3$ forming the magnetic vector potential) satisfied an integral equation of the form

$$ \Phi_i = \int \sum_{j=0}^{3} K_{ij}(x, x') \Phi_j(x') \, dx', \quad i = 0, 1, 2, 3, \tag{213} $$

where $K_{ij}(x, x')$ is a kernel which depends on two points, $x$ and $x'$, of the four-dimensional space, and the path of integration extends over the entire universe. As a special case, Lanczos treated the situation in a spherical universe of finite, constant radius containing an atom at its origin (Lanczos, 1925b). The eigenfunctions solving Eqs. (213) in this example could be expressed as products of periodic functions in the spherical (spatial) coordinates (i.e., the distance from the origin and two angles). Every eigenfunction, $\Phi_i^{(n)}$, was then characterized by a number $\nu_n$, which Lanczos interpreted as the frequency of the 'standing ether waves' (Lanczos, 1925c, p. 129, p. 137). The 'ether waves' could be excited by an electron of the atom, which performs a periodic motion with frequency $\omega$. If integral multiples of $\omega$ coincide with the frequency of one of the ether oscillations, then the amplitude of the latter would become infinite according to the usual dynamical considerations (because the denominator, $\nu_n^2 - k^2 \omega^2$, is zero),

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0211 -->

208 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

unless one assumed zero coupling between the electron's motion and the ether-vibration. Lanczos now made this assumption and claimed that it provided an explanation for the stationary orbits of electrons in atoms as postulated by Bohr's theory in the following sense:

> Of all orbits, which are dynamically possible under the action of the Lorentz force, there exist only certain definite ones in which charge and current density possess such a distribution that they are in accord with the condition of stationarity [of the orbits]. Only on such orbits are permanent revolutions [of the electrons] possible, for then no transfer of energy to the ether occurs. In all other situations the electron emits radiation, probably not in the classical sense by the overflow of energy into space, but by the process that the amplitude of the forced ether vibrations increases steadily due to resonance [with the motion of the electron]. Because of the reaction of this radiation [i.e., of the ether vibrations] on the electron a new force, which is not of a conservative nature, arises in addition to the Lorentz force; and, as a consequence of this force, we have to understand [the fact] that the electron is always again driven back into the stationary orbits. (Lanczos, 1925c, pp. 140–141)²⁶³

Two types of radiation, had, therefore, to be distinguished in Lanczos' theory. The first, consisting of all the standing vibrations of the ether of constant amplitude, were described by the orthogonal and normalized eigenfunctions which were solutions of Eqs. (213). In the latter, the kernel $K_{ij}(x, x')$ took into account the motion of *all* charged particles (electrons and others) in the universe. Although Lanczos was aware of the fact that these 'eigenoscillations' of the ether had not been experimentally detected, he referred to the concept of 'virtual oscillator fields' in the theory of Bohr, Kramers and Slater (1924) as giving support to the existence of a permanent radiation of the ether. The second type of radiation was produced by the transitions of an electron from one stable orbit to another stable orbit. In this case, the energy of transition was regarded as being transferred completely to the ether, exciting in it a large number of eigenoscillations which interfered in such a way as to give rise to the monochromatic emission line of an atom.

With the help of these considerations, Lanczos reformulated the standard problem of describing the radiation emitted by atoms in a completely new manner. Instead of studying the mechanics of the atom one had now to investigate the excitation of the eigenoscillations in the ether (or the universe) by the motion of electrons in atoms. The fundamental difficulty of Lanczos' programme was how to construct the universal kernel function entering Eq. (213), and he therefore concluded: 'On the basis of this conception the solution of the quantum problem therefore appears to be reduced to the knowledge of a Hamiltonian principle, which for the time being still lies far in the dark, and its

²⁶³Lanczos proved himself again to be a follower of Albert Einstein's ideas about the origin of quantized electron orbits in quantum theory. Since many years Einstein had speculated that the stationary orbits may be obtained as specific solutions of some generalized field equations (see, in particular, Einstein, 1923d).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0212 -->

V.2 Field-Like Representation of Quantum Mechanics 209

connection with the eigenfunctions' (Lanczos, 1925c, p. 141). He suggested that the action principle of general relativity could possibly give a hint for finding the appropriate action principle in radiation theory. Realizing how difficult this task might be, Lanczos hoped to be able to throw new light on further details by a 'closer investigation of the powerful ("*weitgreifende*") "method of eigenfunctions," even without an explicit use of a Hamiltonian principle' (Lanczos, 1925c, p. 141).

While he was pondering about the continuation of this programme, Lanczos read the papers of Heisenberg (1925c) and Born and Jordan (1925b). He immediately grasped that these authors had made important progress and, in the introduction of his next paper, he noted:

> The far-reaching thoughts of Heisenberg might be of path-breaking importance for research in quantum theory. In a logical continuation of the new ideas, Born and Jordan succeeded in giving Heisenberg's conceptions an adequate mathematical expression by a large-scale generalization; thus they discovered the general formal foundations of the new theory. One arrives at a logically established discontinuum theory, for which the classical concepts are of importance merely through correspondence and as heuristic guidelines; however, the new theory proceeds from the very beginning along its own directions and associates with the old symbols a completely new meaning. The fundamental principles of quantum theory have thus obtained an unexpected deepening. (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 812)

To Lanczos the new development in quantum mechanics came as a big surprise, for it broke completely with the physical conceptions he had grown up with, especially the field theory of matter. However, he quickly saw that, in spite of the apparent differences in formulation, the Heisenberg–Born–Jordan quantum mechanics made some connection with his earlier work on relativity and quantum theories. And the key to this connection was provided by the method of integral equations which had become his favourite tool. Since Lanczos had become familiar with Hilbert's work, he knew perfectly about the equivalence of matrix equations, such as the ones that appeared in the paper of Born and Jordan, and integral equations, which he had used earlier. To exploit this mathematical equivalence now, in late 1925, became his goal. Within a few weeks he was able to accomplish this task, and before Christmas 1925 he submitted a paper on it to *Zeitschrift für Physik*.${}^{264}$ He summarized its content in the following words:

> In the following we wish to point to an extraordinarily simple and beautiful connection that can be established between the Heisenberg–Born–Jordan theory and the theory of integral equations. We shall see that all results of the theory may also be expressed in the form of integral equations; thus they obtain a formulation, which may appear more natural to the physicist—who is used to analytical methods

${}^{264}$ Born and Jordan's paper (1925b) on quantum mechanics was published in late November 1925. Lanczos' article on the field-like representation of quantum mechanics was received by *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 22 December 1925 (Lanczos, 1926a).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0213 -->

210 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

—than the matrix formulation. Simultaneously, there arises with it also a continuum interpretation, which, as far as the *description* of empirical facts is concerned, can stand with equal rights beside the discontinuum interpretation, since there exists a unique correspondence between the two interpretations. However, what concerns the *physical interpretation* of the facts, that is, the real nature of the quanta, it is not excluded that the integral formulation might even be superior to the matrix formulation; the reason is that it has the advantage of being immediately consistent with the field conceptions, in fact it is even built on them, while the concept of the field is apparently far removed from the discontinuum interpretation. (Lanczos, 1926a, pp. 812–813)

For the purpose of establishing the relation between matrix methods and the methods of integral equations, Lanczos introduced a finite, bounded mathematical space of arbitrary extension and dimensions, whose points he denoted by $s$ and $\sigma$. In this space he assumed a complete orthogonal set of eigenfunctions, $\phi^i(s)$ ($i = 1, 2, 3, \dots$), to be given; this set belongs to a *fundamental* kernel function, $K(s, \sigma)$, which is not specified for the moment. Thus, each eigenfunction, $\phi^i(s)$, solves an integral equation of the type of Eq. (213), i.e.,

$$\phi(s) = \lambda \int K(s, \sigma)\phi(\sigma) d\sigma, \qquad (214)$$

with a particular eigenvalue $\lambda_i$. Moreover, two different eigenfunctions, $\phi^i(s)$ and $\phi^k(s)$, with different eigenvalues (i.e., $\lambda_i \neq \lambda_k$), satisfy the orthogonality relations

$$\int \phi^i(s)\phi^k(s) ds = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } i = k \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \qquad (215)$$

(In Eqs. (214) and (215), the integrations extend over the entire space.) With the help of the functions $\phi^i(s)$ any given matrix, $(a_{ik})$, could be expressed in terms of a specific kernel function $f(s, \sigma)$—the latter being a function of the two variables $s$ and $\sigma$, which is at least piecewise continuous—by the equation

$$a_{ik} = \int f(s, \sigma)\phi^i(s)\phi^k(\sigma) ds d\sigma, \qquad i, k = 1, 2, \dots \qquad (216a)$$

Conversely, $f(s, \sigma)$ could be obtained from the elements of its associated matrix, $(a_{ik})$, as

$$f(s, \sigma) = \sum_{i, j=1}^{\infty} a_{ik} \phi^i(s)\phi^k(\sigma). \qquad (216b)$$

Equations (216a, b) established a one-to-one correspondence between the infinite matrices, $(a_{ik})$, and the piecewise continuous kernel functions, $f(s, \sigma)$. Lanczos was thus able to re-interpret without difficulty *all* the matrix operations and

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0214 -->

V.2 Field-Like Representation of Quantum Mechanics 211

equations, which Born and Jordan had used to establish quantum mechanics, by means of integral equations containing 'field-like' kernel functions.${}^{265}$

As the most important matrix operations to be translated, Lanczos considered the operations of taking the diagonal sum of a matrix, the product of two matrices, the differentiation of a matrix function with respect to one of its matrix variables, and the definition of the time derivative of a matrix. The first of these operations was easy to express because taking the diagonal sum of a matrix, $(a_{ik})$, was just equivalent to integrating the associated kernel for equal points, $s = \sigma$, over the entire space.${}^{266}$ The matrix product, on the other hand, was represented in Lanczos' formalism by folding the corresponding kernels, that is,

$$h(s, \sigma) = fg(s, \sigma) = \int f(s, \tau)g(\tau, \sigma) d\tau, \qquad (217)$$

where $h(s, \sigma)$ is defined as

$$h(s, \sigma) = \sum_m a_{im} b_{mk} \phi^i(s)\phi^k(\sigma), \qquad (217a)$$

and $f(s, \tau)$ and $g(\tau, \sigma)$ correspond to the matrices $(a_{im})$ and $(b_{mk})$. Also Born and Jordan's symbolic differentiation, i.e., the differentiation of a matrix function with respect to a matrix, Lanczos was able to translate properly (see Lanczos, 1926a, pp. 814–815). Finally, he turned his attention to the definition of the time derivative of a dynamical variable. In matrix mechanics, where a variable had been represented by a Hermitian matrix, the operation of taking the time derivative always produced a matrix whose elements were equal to the elements of the original matrix multiplied by the factor $2\pi i\nu(ik)$, where $\nu(ik)$ was the transition frequency (which was related to the difference of the energy terms, $W_i - W_k$). Lanczos claimed that in his field-like representation, where the quantum-mechanical dynamical variables were described by kernel functions, $f(s, \sigma)$, the time differentiation operation had to be expressed as

$$\dot{f}(s, \sigma) = (Kf - fK)(s, \sigma). \qquad (218)$$

Equation (218) again possessed the form of an integral equation due to the folding occurring on its right-hand side. It involves the fundamental kernel function, $K(s, \sigma)$, which determines the orthogonal set of eigenfunctions, $\phi^n(s)$, with the associated eigenvalues, $\lambda_n$. Evidently, the $\lambda_n$ must be related to the

${}^{265}$ In the case of Hermitian matrices with complex elements, one had to replace the products $\phi^i(s)\phi^k(\sigma)$ in Eq. (215) by the product $[\phi^i(s)]^*\phi^k(\sigma)$, and the same in Eq. (216a) and (216b). The kernel functions, such as $f(s, \sigma)$, would then be Hermitian, satisfying the relation $f(s, \sigma) = f^*(\sigma, s)$, where the asterisk denotes the complex conjugate. Since the consideration of Hermitian matrices leads only to this small formal modification, Lanczos carried out his proofs always for real matrices. We shall follow his treatment below.

${}^{266}$ The reason for this result is the validity of the orthogonality relation, Eq. (215), which ensures that $\int f(s, s) ds = \sum_{i, k} a_{ik} \int \phi^i(s)\phi^k(s) ds$ is equal to the diagonal sum $\sum a_{ii}$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0215 -->

212 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

energy terms $W_n$, the eigenvalues of the energy matrix of the system under investigation, through the equation${}^{267}$

$$\lambda_n^{-1} = \frac{2\pi i}{h} W_n. \qquad (219)$$

Hence the kernel $K(s, \sigma)$, apart from a constant factor, could replace the function $H(s, \sigma)$ representing the Hamiltonian in Lanczos' scheme. Equation (218) led to important consequences concerning the dynamical equations which had to be developed.

Lanczos did not have the slightest doubt that the dynamics in quantum theory had to be derived from a Hamiltonian principle. He was satisfied that the relevant Hamiltonian principle could be related to the fundamental integral equation (214) in the following way. He considered the special kernel function, $p\dot{q}(s, \sigma) - H(s, \sigma)$, which represented the Lagrangian in his scheme, and expressed the Hamiltonian principle by the equation

$$I = \int [p\dot{q}(s, s) - H(s, s)] ds = \int [(pKq - pqK)(s, s) - H(s, s)] ds = \text{extremum}, \qquad (220)$$

where $I$ is the action integral and $H(s, \sigma)$ denotes the Hamiltonian kernel function. This formulation implied, of course, that Lanczos now *identified the (so far) purely mathematical space of points $s$ with the physical space of four-dimensional (space-time) points $x$*. Then Eq. (220) was simply equivalent to the extremum principle, Eq. (88b), of Born and Jordan.${}^{268}$ Evidently, it is possible to derive the Hamiltonian equations of motion from the extremum principle, Eq. (220), by variation of the action-integral with respect to $p(s, \sigma)$ and $q(s, \sigma)$, the kernel functions representing the quantum-mechanical momentum and position variables. For this purpose, Lanczos had just to consider $H(s, \sigma)$ as a function of $p(s, \sigma)$ and $q(s, \sigma)$; then he obtained equations of motion which were equivalent to those in matrix mechanics.${}^{269}$

In varying the action-integral for obtaining the equations of motion the quantum conditions must be satisfied. Lanczos reformulated the Born–Jordan quantum condition, Eq. (67), as the integral equation

$$(pq - qp)(s, \sigma) = \frac{h}{2\pi i} E(s, \sigma), \qquad (221)$$

${}^{267}$ Lanczos omitted the factor $2\pi i$ (in Lanczos, 1926a, p. 816, Eq. (21)) because he defined $\dot{f}(s, \sigma) = (2\pi i)^{-1} \cdot df(s, \sigma)/dt$.

${}^{268}$ Since the diagonal sum of a matrix is replaced in Lanczos' scheme by the $s$-integral of the corresponding kernel function if taken for equal points $s = \sigma$, it follows that $D[p\dot{q} - H(p, q)]$ is equal to $(2\pi i/h) \int [(pKq - pqK)(s, s) - H(s, s)] ds$. Hence the two extremum principles, Eq. (220) and (88b), are equivalent.

${}^{269}$ Thus, for instance, the equation for $\partial H / \partial p$ was replaced by the equation $(\partial H / \partial p)(s, \sigma) = (Kq - qK)(s, \sigma)$, which agrees with the corresponding matrix equation if the relation between the eigenvalues of $K(s, \sigma)$ and $H(s, \sigma)$ is taken into account.
