214 & Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

corresponding to very high indices of the matrices do not occur in reality. All matrices, he concluded therefore, had to be finite and the regular function $U(s, \sigma)$ should always replace—up to a factor $2\pi i/h$—the unit kernel $E(s, \sigma)$ in Eq. (221).$^{273}$

Lanczos’ quantum-mechanical scheme may be summarized by two fundamental equations, the action principle and the quantum condition. Using the regular kernel $U(s, \sigma)$ in both instead of $E(s, \sigma)$, these equations assume the form

$$I = -\int \left[ KU(s, \sigma) + H(s, \sigma) \right] ds = \text{extremum} \tag{220a}$$

and

$$(pq - qp)(s, \sigma) = U(s, \sigma), \tag{221a}$$

where $K(s, \sigma)$, $U(s, \sigma)$ and $H(s, \sigma)$ have to be considered as functions that are given.$^{274}$ Disregarding, for the moment, the modification of the quantum condition envisaged by Lanczos, there existed a complete equivalence between his scheme and that of Born and Jordan. Thus, in principle, it did not matter whether quantum systems were described by means of equations involving matrices or integrals over field-like kernel functions. However, in practical cases the choice of one method or the other would depend upon the nature of the problem under investigation.

And yet, there was a considerable conceptual difference between the two formulations. In matrix mechanics a mechanical system was completely defined by its Hamiltonian matrix and the commutation relations for its dynamical variables. In Lanczos’ integral equation scheme one had to know the corresponding kernels $H(s, \sigma)$ and $U(s, \sigma)$ and, in addition, the fundamental kernel $K(s, \sigma)$. ‘For the matrix interpretation,’ Lanczos noted, ‘only the eigenvalues of this kernel are of importance, while the orthogonal system of eigenfunctions associated with it remains completely undetermined’ (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 820). Indeed, Eq. (219) meant only that the eigenvalues of the kernels $K(s, \sigma)$ and $H(s, \sigma)$ had to be, apart from a constant factor, exactly the same.$^{275}$ But from the mathematical theory it followed that different integral equations of the type of Eq. (214)—i.e., equations which have different kernels, $K(s, \sigma)$, $K'(s, \sigma)$, $K''(s, \sigma)$, ... , and a different set of eigenfunctions, $\phi^i(s)$, $\phi'^i(s)$, $\phi''^i(s)$, ... ,

---

$^{273}$In drawing the above conclusion, Lanczos thought of the harmonic oscillator as a typical system in quantum mechanics. There are other systems, however, such as the hydrogen atom, in which infinitely many states occur without $W_n$ going to infinity in the limit of large $n$.

Beginning with his earliest papers on general relativity theory, Lanczos had always argued in favour of nonsingular field solutions. His insistence on the regular solutions, $p(s, \sigma)$ and $q(s, \sigma)$, in quantum mechanics may be explained very well from this background.

$^{274}$Equation (220a) is obtained by rewriting the first term, $\int[pKq - pqK](s, s) ds$, as $\int[K(qp - pq)](s, s) ds$, which can be done if all factors in the products are regular (i.e. in that case, the factors in the products $pKq$ and $pqK$ can be cyclically permuted to give $Kqp$ and $Kpq$, respectively).

$^{275}$Note that in the integral equation approach the eigenvalues of $H(s, \sigma)$ are $W_n^{-1}$ rather than $W_n$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0218 -->

V.2 Field-Like Representation of Quantum Mechanics 215

may yield the same eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. If, however, the eigenvalues of different integral equations were identical, the associated sets of eigenfunctions, $\phi^i(s)$ and $\phi'^i(s) (i = 1, 2, \dots)$, would be connected by orthogonal transformations. Now it was clear why the eigenfunctions played no role in matrix mechanics because there two quantities related by orthogonal transformations had to be considered identical. Lanczos concluded: ‘Therefore one can never assert anything from matrix equations about the basis functions $\phi^i(s)$’ (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 820).

In a previous paper on the quantum problem, Lanczos had claimed that the eigenfunctions should have a physical meaning if the integral equation approach were to make any sense at all. This claim had grown out of his deeply felt scientific belief, for he had declared: ‘The author confesses his adherence to that Pythagorean view of the world, which sees in numbers more than just a formal and convenient tool for the purpose of describing [empirical] facts, which rather recognizes in mathematics an unavoidable symbolic language of nature, and which assumes that a certain harmony exists between mathematical aesthetics and Reality’ (Lanczos, 1925b, pp. 148–149). He was convinced that ‘the progress of mathematical knowledge is simultaneously accompanied by an increasingly more deeply penetrating knowledge of Reality’ (Lanczos, 1925b, p. 149). One of the most fundamental mathematical objects in the theory of integral equations was evidently the kernel, $K(s, \sigma)$, and the question arose whether nature provided any information about it beyond the eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. Lanczos now argued in his discussion of quantum mechanics:

> If all physical facts are of such a nature that they can always, in principle, only yield the coefficients of matrices, then the matrix representation deserves to be preferred (at least from the positivistic point of view!), for it does not introduce any fundamentally unrealizable element in the description of [empirical] facts. The situation changes, however, if the kernel possesses a physical meaning. In that case the field-like representation must be considered as the more adequate one, since the matrix formulation provides less information insofar as it can only furnish the eigenvalues of the kernel but leaves the system of eigenfunctions completely undetermined. (Lanczos, 1926a, pp. 820–821)

Evidently Lanczos, in agreement with his work on the electromagnetic radiation in a closed universe (Lanczos, 1925b, c), favoured the possibility that the kernel function $K(s, \sigma)$ occurring in his fundamental equation (214) had a physical significance and he made an effort to grasp it. He recalled the method he had employed earlier in general relativity theory for determining the kernel functions of the gravitational field (Lanczos, 1925a), and which he had later taken over in the case of the electromagnetic field (Lanczos, 1925c): it was to write down the differential equations for the fields, including all the source terms, and thereby constructing the kernels of the equivalent integral equations, which (i.e., the kernels) are identical to the Green’s functions of the problem. By analogy to these cases, the kernel $K(s, \sigma)$ of Lanczos’ field-formulation of quantum mechanics could be interpreted as a *universal* Green’s function of the theory; that is, the systems which it described embraced all the atomic systems

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0219 -->

216 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter V &nbsp; Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

existing in nature (each of which could be regarded as a subsystem in the approximation in which the interactions between the atoms were neglected). Hence $\lambda_i$, the eigenvalues of $K(s, \sigma)$, and the corresponding eigenfunctions $\phi^i(s)$ at once gave the energy states of all the atoms in mutual interaction.

Lanczos was further aware of the fact that, in constructing the fundamental kernel $K(s, \sigma)$ in quantum mechanics, one had to take into account the peculiar features of the quantum-theoretical fields, such as their dependence on two space variables, that were not common to classical fields. 'However, it must be noted,' Lanczos remarked, 'that the kernel functions $p(s, \sigma)$ and $q(s, \sigma)$ are associated with the system as the totality of all *possible* states, while a definite *real* quantum state is characterized by the usual field functions $p_i(s)$ and $q_i(s)$' (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 823, footnote 2). The latter could be obtained by a space integration over the fields as

$$p_i(s) = \int p(s, \sigma)\phi^i(\sigma) d\sigma,$$

$$q_i(s) = \int q(s, \sigma)\phi^i(\sigma) d\sigma. \qquad (222)$$

Thus, the variables in the actual quantum states, $p_i(s)$ and $q_i(s)$, were obtained by folding the field kernels $p(s, \sigma)$ and $q(s, \sigma)$ with $\phi^i(s)$, the eigenfunctions of the fundamental kernel $K(s, \sigma)$.

Another unusual situation occurred with respect to the description of the space coordinate, which appeared in Lanczos' theory in two ways: first, as a dynamical variable $q(s, \sigma)$; second as a geometrical variable $s$ or $\sigma$. Although this was a completely new, nonclassical feature of the theory that required proper interpretation, and although he could not yet provide any, Lanczos was not discouraged at all. Rather, he concluded his paper on the field-like representation of quantum mechanics with the words:

> This much, however, we do believe that we are allowed to conclude from the possibility of bringing the entire theory [quantum mechanics] in full accord with our field-like conceptions: that the modifications, which we must apply to our classical views in order to reach an understanding of the quantum problems, must lie in a totally different direction than could be characterized simply by the contrast between continuum and discontinuum; and that the solution of the quantum mystery should have hardly anything to do with a quantum-like re-interpretation of geometry or infinitesimal calculus. (Lanczos, 1926a, p. 823)

With this conclusion he stated clearly that the new development in quantum theory deviated from the line which it had taken during the previous years; not so much the discretization of the classical laws had to be achieved, but a more general modification which would *exhibit both discrete and continuous features*. Lanczos himself expected firmly to be able to contribute to the establishment of such a quantum mechanics.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0220 -->

V.2 Field-Like Representation of Quantum Mechanics
217

In his second paper on quantum mechanics, submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in the beginning of March 1926, Lanczos urgently pursued the problem of determining the fundamental kernel function $K(s, \sigma)$ or the fundamental, complete set of orthogonal eigenfunctions $\phi^i(s)$ (Lanczos, 1926b). He replaced this task by the equivalent one: If one starts out from the variational principle, Eq. (220a), in which $K(s, \sigma)$ only occurs folded with the kernel $U(s, \sigma)$, one may consider the fundamental set of eigenfunctions, $\phi^i(s)$, to be as much the solutions of the integral equation (214) as of a similar equation with $U(s, \sigma)$ as the kernel.$^{276}$ Lanczos, therefore, concluded: ‘It is not the energy function [i.e., $K(s, \sigma)$] which we must consider as the given basis kernel, but the quantum function [$U(s, \sigma)$], and it must yield that system according to which the other functions should be expanded’ (Lanczos, 1926b, p. 408).

The advantage of reformulating the problem as the determination of the fundamental set of eigenfunctions solving an integral equation with $U(s, \sigma)$ as the kernel function was evident. First it was the nonzero kernel, $U(s, \sigma)$, the so-called quantum function, which made the system under consideration, i.e., the universe, a quantum system; hence $U(s, \sigma)$ had to be treated as the primary concept in quantum mechanics. Second, unlike the energy function, which depends on the details of what constitutes the universe, the kernel $U(s, \sigma)$ was a global function, which was rather insensitive with respect to the specific properties of the systems constituting the universe.$^{277}$ Lanczos therefore believed that he had simplified the problem considerably. Moreover, the new situation agreed better with the principal idea which had guided his previous work on the quantum problem (Lanczos, 1925b, c): namely, the assumption that the structure of the universe, as expressed by the set of eigenfunctions $\phi^i(s)$, was responsible for the deviations from the classical description that were accounted for by the quantum functions $U(s, \sigma)$. As for the explicit determination of $U(s, \sigma)$ or $\phi^i(s)$, Lanczos was still not able to report any progress when he submitted his third paper on quantum mechanics to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in April 1926 (Lanczos, 1926c).$^{278}$

$^{276}$In matrix mechanics this situation is reflected by the fact that the matrices corresponding to the kernels $K(s, \sigma)$ and $U(s, \sigma)$ are simultaneously diagonal. Evidently, Lanczos took the kernel function $U(s, \sigma)$ as being different from the unit kernel, $E(s, \sigma)$, because the latter did not allow one to single out a fundamental set of eigenfunctions.

$^{277}$For example, the quantum function $U(s, \sigma)$ was the same for all systems having one degree of freedom. For systems having $f$ degrees of freedom, Lanczos proposed the same quantum function, i.e., $U(s, \sigma) = \sum_{k=1}^f (p_k q_k - q_k p_k)(s, \sigma)$. Born, Heisenberg and Jordan—as well as Kramers, Weyl and Pauli—had introduced the quantum condition for each degree of freedom; this corresponded to $U(s, \sigma) = (p_k q_k - q_k p_k)(s, \sigma)$, $k = 1, \dots, f$. Lanczos believed that his definition had to be preferred (Lanczos, 1926b, p. 407).

$^{278}$In this paper Lanczos investigated, especially, the possibility of representing the position and momentum variables in matrix mechanics by real matrices. he found that in this case the quantum function $U(s, \sigma)$ had positive and negative imaginary eigenvalues and its ‘diagonal sum,’ i.e., $\int U(s, s) ds$, was automatically zero. As a consequence, however, to each energy state $W_n$ there corresponded another energy state $-W_n$. This seemed to be at variance with the spectroscopic observation, since one would also expect term sums, $W_n + W_m$, besides term differences, $W_n - W_m$, determining the frequencies. In the example of the perturbed harmonic oscillator, Lanczos proved that the transition elements from states with positive energy to states with negative energy were zero; thus, he showed that in this case no contradictions to the observation followed.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0221 -->

218 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

By the time Lanczos realized that his programme on a modified formulation of quantum mechanics had become stuck, Erwin Schrödinger's first paper on 'Quantization as an Eigenvalue Problem' appeared in *Annalen der Physik* (Schrödinger, 1926c). In his paper Schrödinger proposed a treatment of atomic systems based on continuous field functions similar to those of Lanczos' integral equation scheme. By imposing a boundary condition, Schrödinger obtained the orthogonal set of eigenfunctions for a specific atomic problem, the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom, as solutions of a differential equation. In his further papers, which appeared in a rapid sequence, Schrödinger was able to treat other atomic systems as well by solving their particular differential equations (Schrödinger, 1926d, f). Schrödinger's differential equation method was found to be equivalent to Lanczos' integral equation method; especially, Eq. (214) could be rewritten as a Schrödinger equation *if the fundamental kernel $K(s, \sigma)$ were identified with the Hamiltonian function $H(s, \sigma)$*. Lanczos immediately recognized that by means of this step his own field-like representation of quantum mechanics was completed in some sense, and he refrained from further work on this theory. 'Afterwards it was too trivial,' he recalled several decades later. 'It was no longer of interest, because Schrödinger came along and he did it. As it often happens, it is the second man who hits the nail on the head and not the first one' (Lanczos in Mehra, 1973b, p. 287).

The Schrödinger-equation method completed Lanczos' integral-equation reformulation of quantum mechanics in the sense that it made a specific assumption about the nature of the fundamental kernel, $K(s, \sigma)$, which determines the orthogonal set of basic eigenfunctions $\phi^i(s)$ according to Eq. (214). That is, one now described different physical quantum systems by different sets of orthogonal, normalized eigenfunctions, $\psi^i_H(s)$, where the latter obeyed a Schrödinger equation involving a given Hamiltonian operator $H$ (the equivalent of Lanczos' Hamiltonian kernel function $H(s, \sigma)$). Thus, the Schrödinger functions, $\psi^i_H(s)$, characterize only the quantum states of a given system, like the hydrogen atom, provided it can be considered as being isolated from the rest of the universe. Since in our actual universe matter and energy are distributed very thinly, it was plausible to regard atomic systems as being isolated from the rest of the world to a certain extent. Therefore, the replacement of the kernel, $K(s, \sigma)$, by $H(s, \sigma)$, the Hamiltonian of the atomic system under investigation, in Eq. (214) provided a suitable description of the actual situation, and the success achieved by using the Schrödinger equation confirmed this assumption.

Lanczos, however, was not psychologically prepared to pursue his programme in this direction. For him the quantum problem had a cosmic dimension. In the beginning of 1925, in his search for a field theory unifying gravitation and electricity, he had concluded the existence of eigenoscillations in a closed universe as offering the explanation of certain quantum effects observed in electromagnetic radiation. Stimulated by the development of matrix mechanics in Göttingen he had then thought of formulating the quantum problem on the assumption that the universe as a whole was responsible for the behaviour of atomic systems. This explains why he chose to identify the kernel determining the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0222 -->

V.2 Field-Like Representation of Quantum Mechanics 219

basic set of eigenfunctions with a universal quantum function, $U(s, \sigma)$, rather than with specific Hamiltonian functions, $H(s, \sigma)$. Schrödinger's wave mechanics did not achieve the goal Lanczos had set himself: it offered no way of calculating $U(s, \sigma)$, and assumed it to be given instead.$^{279}$ Lanczos, on the other hand, did not entirely give up his plan and returned to it several years later.$^{280}$

Lanczos' work on quantum mechanics attracted Heisenberg's attention when he was looking for a way of dealing with the position variables that do not change periodically with time. But neither

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0223 -->

220 &emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp; **Chapter V &emsp; Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics**

beyond a mention in footnotes.<sup>281</sup> However, in the wider perspective of the development of quantum theory, Lanczos' was the first field-like approach to quantum mechanics; it raised many questions which, to some extent, were answered only later in the context of the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics and the systematic formulation of quantum field theory. In Lanczos' long scientific career, his concern with quantum mechanics remained a brief episode which lasted about one and a half years.<sup>282</sup> He first made use of the Schrödinger equation as late as 1930, when he applied it to calculate the effect of very strong electric fields on atoms; in this problem the usual perturbation methods failed and Lanczos developed an elegant mathematical method for obtaining an asymptotic solution (Lanczos, 1930).

# V.3 &emsp; The Operator Mechanics

At the end of October 1925 Max Born left Göttingen for the winter semester to give a series of lectures at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.<sup>283</sup> From 14 November 1925 to 22 January 1926 he

<sup>281</sup> For example, Schrödinger referred to him in his paper on the equivalence of matrix and wave mechanics (see Schrödinger, 1926e, p. 754, footnote 1). Note, however, that Schrödinger misunderstood Lanczos' approach, claiming that Lanczos' theory would lead to the wrong eigenvalues (i.e., to inverse energy eigenvalues). The same misunderstanding occurred when Pauli wrote to Jordan: 'As for Lanczos, my considerations [concerning the relation of wave mechanics to matrix mechanics] have only a few points of contact with his. He looks at a problem in which the energy values are the reciprocal eigenvalues, while here the energy values are the eigenvalues themselves. Further, in his treatment the functions, which like the Green's functions depend on two points, play an essential role; functions like that are not used here. I really believe that Lanczos' *Ansatz* is not of much use' (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926). Apparently, both Schrödinger and Pauli did not think of the fact that the eigenvalues of Hilbert's integral equations correspond to the inverse eigenvalues of the Schrödinger equation.

<sup>282</sup> Lanczos' later scientific career developed as follows. He became *Privatdozent* at the University of Frankfurt during the winter semester 1926–1927 and was appointed *Extraordinarius* for theoretical physics at the same place by the end of 1932. Being on leave of absence at that time, however, he did not return to Germany, but remained at Purdue University, Lafayette, Indiana, where he had been a professor of mathematics since 1931. Lanczos remained at Purdue until 1946, working on polynomials, Fourier analysis and mathematical methods. (In the year 1943–1944 he was on the staff of the National Bureau of Standards, contributing to the *Mathematical Tables Project*.) In 1946 he joined Boeing Aircraft Company in Seattle, Washington, as senior research engineer. From 1949 to 1952 he worked at the National Bureau of Standards' Institute for Numerical Analysis at the University of California, Los Angeles. During 1953–1954 he returned to industry as a specialist in computing with North American Aviation. Having spent the year 1952–1953 as a visiting professor at the Institute for Advanced Studies in Dublin, Ireland, he was offered a permanent position as a senior professor there in 1954. From then on he made his home in Ireland, marrying Ilse Hildebrand in 1954. (He had been married earlier to Maria Rupp from 1927 until her death in 1939; they had a son, Elmar, who was born in 1933.) From 1954 onwards he travelled frequently, lecturing at many places, especially in the United States and in Hungary, the land of his birth. He died in Budapest on 24 June 1974.

<sup>283</sup> Max Born had mentioned his plan of going to Boston as early as April 1924 in a letter to Niels Bohr. At that time Born expected that he 'probably will spend half of the winter semester [1924–1925] in America (Boston)' (Born to Bohr, 16 April 1924). The plan was finally realized a year later. In this

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0224 -->

224 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter V &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

Congress of Mathematicians in September 1920. He also presented a paper at the Congress dealing with a normed vector space (Wiener, 1921b); this paper became the first publication in a field that was later called Banach spaces.<sup>290</sup> In 1922, 1924 and 1925 Wiener again visited Europe, renewing his acquaintances and establishing new contacts with mathematicians in France and Germany. Thus, he obtained a reputation abroad, especially through some work on the boundary value problem in potential theory; and Leo Lichtenstein, in an addendum to his *Encyklopädie* article on recent developments in the theory of elliptical partial differential equations, remarked with respect to the boundary value problem: ‘With these problems . . . a series of papers by G. Bouligand as well as H. Lebesgue and, in particular, by N. Wiener is concerned’ (Lichtenstein, 1924, p. 1334).<sup>291</sup>

Besides potential theory Wiener became more and more involved in another mathematical problem that led to some of his more important work. The problem in question arose when the electrical engineers at M.I.T. wanted to have a proper mathematical foundation of communication theory, that is, of the

<sup>290</sup> The Polish mathematician Stefan Banach presented the idea of Banach spaces already in June 1920 in his doctoral thesis; however, he published his work only in 1922. Wiener, on the other hand, took up the problem shortly before the International Mathematical Congress at Strasbourg, at which he presented his results (Wiener, 1921b); he was stimulated to do this work by Maurice Fréchet’s postulational approach to topology. Wiener conceded later that Banach had slight priority in developing the concept. In 1920 the Banach spaces did not have any physical application; but later Wiener discovered that the differential space which describes Brownian motion was very closely related to them.

<sup>291</sup> On his visits to Europe Wiener got to know especially Henri Léon Lebesgue and George Louis Bouligand in France and Leo Lichtenstein, a distant cousin of his father, in Berlin. All three of them worked on potential theory in which Wiener had become interested. Wiener had noticed that the method of generalized integration, which had led him to work on Brownian motion, was also applicable to the problem of boundary conditions in potential theory. (For the origin of this work, see the story which Wiener told in his autobiography, Wiener, 1956, pp. 79–88, 90–93.) Lebesgue, however, already had studied the problem of boundary conditions in 1913. In December 1923 Bouligand submitted a note to the Academy of Sciences, Paris, on the solution of the Dirichlet problem, i.e., the problem of finding a solution of an elliptic differential equation with boundary values which connect continuously to the values in the interior of the domain (Bouligand, 1924a). Lebesgue took up the problem immediately and presented his own communication to the Paris Academy in its session of 21 January 1924, in which he pointed out the conditions under which the Dirichlet problem had no solution (Lebesgue, 1924a). In January 1924 Wiener also published a paper on potential theory (Wiener, 1924a) in the *Journal of Mathematics and Physics of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology* (which had been founded in 1922 and directed during its early years by Wiener and then by his friend Philip Franklin). When he saw the notes of the French mathematicians in print in the *Comptes Rendus*, Wiener knew that he had to hurry if he were to compete successfully in that field. Thus, he prepared a short note in French, assisted by a student who was better in French than he, and mailed it to Lebesgue for publication in *Comptes Rendus*. It arrived just in time, for Bouligand had meanwhile also obtained similar results and sent them to his former teacher Lebesgue. In keeping with the best traditions of the Paris Academy the two papers were presented at the same session of 24 March 1924 (Wiener, 1924b; Bouligand, 1924b), and Lebesgue added remarks on both notes (Lebesgue, 1924b). Unlike many other scientific competitions, this one ended with Wiener and Bouligand becoming friends and collaborators over many years. ‘Bouligand was even more prepared than I was to admit the somewhat greater completeness of my paper,’ Wiener noted thirty years later, ‘and we made arrangements to meet when I should come to France for a visit’ (Wiener, 1956, p. 93).

V.3 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Operator Mechanics &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 225

information contained in them was as uncertain as possible. This was the reason why they called the signals ‘noise’. This is not to be confused with the ‘white noise’ studied by Einstein in connection with Brownian motion.

When the theory was finally written up by Nyquist, it became possible, as Wiener later recalled, ‘to set up a complete set of technical specifications for telephone circuits which would be adequate to the needs of intelligible speech’ (Wiener, 1956, p. 124). It was the electrical engineers’ wish to find a mathematical tool for the analysis of these signals that led Wiener to develop a new type of integral. He began to work on this problem in 1924 and completed his investigations with a fundamental paper in 1926. This paper, which did not appear in print until 1930, established Wiener’s lasting reputation as a mathematician.<sup>292</sup>

<sup>292</sup> Wiener discussed the history of his own work on harmonic analysis in his autobiography (Wiener, 1956, pp. 124–128). See also the survey by Levinson, 1940. The latter author was a pupil of Wiener.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0226 -->

226 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Chapter V &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

the Fourier transforms of these time functions.

The new tools Wiener developed for this purpose were, as he later wrote, ‘at first more a heuristic aid than a precisely organized mathematical weapon’ (Wiener, 1956, p. 124). It was only after his visit to Göttingen in 1926 and his talks with Hilbert that he began to realize the full potential of his methods.

Hilbert was very much interested in the problems Wiener discussed. It was Hilbert who helped Wiener to formulate his work in a more rigorous mathematical framework. Hilbert’s own work on integral equations and quadratic forms in infinitely many variables provided the ideal mathematical setting for Wiener’s investigations. The collaboration between Hilbert and Wiener was very fruitful, even though it was brief.

Wiener’s work on harmonic analysis was based on the theory of generalized harmonic analysis, which he had developed earlier. In this theory, the functions to be analyzed are not necessarily periodic, but they possess a certain kind of statistical regularity. The Fourier transforms of these functions are not discrete, as in the case of periodic functions, but are continuous.

<sup>293</sup> For the history of the development of the theory of communication at M.I.T. see also the survey by Guillemin, 1957.

<sup>294</sup> Wiener’s paper on harmonic analysis was eventually published in 1930 under the title ‘Generalized Harmonic Analysis’. It appeared in *Acta Mathematica*, 55 (1930), pp. 117–258.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0227 -->

V.3 &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; The Operator Mechanics &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 227

it had been published in 1921 by Norbert Wiener as a

contribution to the theory of Banach spaces, but he did not publish the more general theory until 1926.

The new integral, which is now known as the ‘Wiener integral’, was a generalization of the Lebesgue integral. It was designed to deal with functions of infinite-dimensional spaces, which are the natural setting for the study of Brownian motion. The Wiener integral provided a powerful tool for the mathematical description of stochastic processes.

The theory of the Wiener integral was developed in several papers. In his autobiography, Wiener described the development of his ideas as follows: ‘I had found that the natural way to look at the space of all possible paths of a particle undergoing Brownian motion was as a generalization of the space of all possible paths of a particle undergoing ordinary motion’ (Wiener, 1956, p. 120).

The development of the Wiener integral was a major achievement, but it was only the beginning of Wiener’s work on stochastic processes. In the following years, Wiener developed a more general theory of stochastic processes, which is now known as the theory of random functions.

<sup>295</sup> The term ‘Wiener integral’ was coined by Paul Lévy. See Lévy, 1951, p. 129.

<sup>296</sup> For a survey of the theory of stochastic processes see the article by Cramér and Leadbetter, 1967.

V.3 The Operator Mechanics 225

theory describing the electrical oscillations which account for the transport of
messages along a telephone line, and Dugald C. Jackson, Chairman of the
Electrical Engineering Department at M.I.T., sought the help of his mathe-
matical colleagues. Until then the mathematical basis for dealing with this problem
had been the so-called harmonic analysis based on Fourier series and Fourier
integrals. It enabled one to deal *either* with strictly periodic oscillations *or* with
oscillations which had a very general structure, provided their amplitudes could
be regarded as being very small in the remote past and in remote future. The
electrical oscillations which occurred in a telephone line were of neither type;
hence it became Wiener’s task to extend harmonic analysis for that purpose.
Wiener knew that the engineers had previously used with considerable success
another method in the same context: *the operator calculus* of Oliver Heaviside.
Wiener now combined the two methods: he generalized harmonic analysis, and
with its help he put the Heaviside formalism on a more secure foundation.

In order to understand Wiener’s task we must briefly describe the operator
methods, especially those of Heaviside. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz and Joseph-
Louis Lagrange may be considered as the founders of operator methods.²⁹² Their
ideas were taken up and further developed in the late eighteenth and early
nineteenth centuries by numerous mathematicians; however, the lack of care in
handling the mathematical operations involved gave rise to many errors in these
early papers, and it became imperative to establish formal rules which were
satisfied by the specific operations in question. This was achieved during the first
half of the nineteenth century, principally by François Joseph Servois, Robert
Murphy and George Boole.²⁹³ As a particular example, the action of the *n*th
power of the operator $D (= d/dt)$, i.e., the differentiation with respect to the
variable parameter *t*, on a function $u(t)$ was considered, with *n* assuming both
positive and negative values or even rational values. It was this operator which
Heaviside used primarily in the electromagnetic theory with great success but, at

---
²⁹² Leibniz noted the resemblance between the formulae of the *n*-fold differentiation of the
product $x(t)y(t)$ of two functions, $x(t)$ and $y(t)$, with respect to the common variable *t*, on one hand,
and the *n*th power of the algebraic sum of $x$ and $y$, on the other (Leibniz, 1710). The observation of
the ‘modus operandi’ in $d^n(xy)$ is usually identified with the invention of operator calculus, although
its first explicit formulation is found in a much later paper of Lagrange (1772). Lagrange especially
proposed to use the calculus symbol in the same manner as an algebraic quantity.

²⁹³ While Servois studied the properties of the operations used (Servois, 1814), Murphy analyzed
the logical structure of the operator method (Murphy, 1837). In particular, Murphy distinguished
between what he called the ‘subject,’ i.e., the symbol on which a certain operation had to be
performed, the ‘operation’ itself represented by its own symbol, and the ‘result’ which may be
connected with the former two by the algebraic sign of equality. Thus, for example, in the algebraic
equation, $ab = c$, he considered the number $a$ to be the symbol of the subject, $b$ the symbol for the
operation of multiplication by the number $b$, giving rise to $c$ as the result. Murphy also noted that
some of the operations he had treated commuted with each other while others did not. Finally, Boole
not only turned operator methods into an effective tool for solving linear differential equations
(Boole, 1844), he also founded mathematical logic on them, thereby seeking to explain all of
mathematics on the basis of a few fundamental operations.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0229 -->

226 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

the same time, to the discomfort of his mathematically more rigorously oriented
contemporaries.²⁹⁴

Heaviside’s operator methods were as unusual as his education. Oliver Heavi-
side, a self-made scientist, had published a large number of papers on various
aspects of electromagnetic theory before he recognized the importance of opera-
tor calculus to the investigation of the transients and discussed the use of
‘operators in physical mathematics’ in detail in two papers published in *Proceed-
ings of the Royal Society* (Heaviside, 1893a, b).²⁹⁵ In the application of his
operator methods to solve problems in electrical circuit theory, Heaviside went
beyond everything which had been established in this field before him. The main
point was that in order to study the response to a given circuit having the
(complex) *impedance* $Z$,

$$
Z(i\omega) = R + i\omega L, \tag{223}
$$

where $R$ denotes the (real) *resistance*, $L$ the (real) *inductance* and $\omega$ the frequency
impressed upon the system ($i$ being the imaginary unit), he introduced the
step-function, $H(t)$, defined by

$$
H(t) = 
\begin{cases} 
0 & \text{for } t < 0 \\
1 & \text{for } t > 1, 
\end{cases} \tag{224}
$$

---
²⁹⁴ The history of operator calculus is discussed, for instance, in the *Encyklopädie* article of
Salvatore Pincherle, who contributed himself many papers on that subject (Pincherle, 1906). It should
be mentioned that the early work on operator methods was frequently motivated by the desire of
mathematicians to remove a metaphysical interpretation of the differential calculus, i.e., to avoid
talking about infinitely small quantities, such as the differential $dt$; this goal was certainly achieved
by treating, say, the symbols $dt$ and $d/dt$ like finite algebraic quantities.

The applications of operator methods, as discussed by Pincherle in his review article, were
confined to the theory of differential and difference equations and to selected problems of number
theory. If one operated with inverse powers of the differential operator $D (= d/dt)$, one could also
treat linear integral equations. Heaviside’s operator calculus was not mentioned by Pincherle.

²⁹⁵ Oliver Heaviside was born on 13 May 1850 in Camden Town, London, being the youngest son
of the artist Thomas Heaviside and his wife Rachel Elizabeth, *née* West. Rachel’s sister had married
the physicist and inventor Charles Wheatstone. However, Wheatstone did not influence his nephew’s
education, and young Oliver learned physics entirely on his own. After leaving school, Heaviside
served as a telegraph operator with the Great Northern Telegraph Company in Newcastle-on-Tyne,
but he retired from this appointment in 1874 because of increasing deafness. Supported by his
brother and later on by well-wishers and a pension from the Government, Heaviside lived in a seaside
cottage in Devonshire. Although he had not had the benefit of a formal higher education, he trained
himself in mathematical physics and played an important role in the development of Maxwell’s
electromagnetic theory and its practical applications. He published his first paper already in 1873 in
*Philosophical Magazine* and continued to contribute regularly in the following years. The value of his
work was only gradually appreciated by engineers and physicists—such as Lord Kelvin, who made
public some of Heaviside’s results in his Presidential Address to the Institution of Electrical Engineers
in 1889—but his reputation was firmly established after his papers were collected and published as
separate books.

Heaviside was elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 1891. The Institution of Electrical Engineers
made him Honorary Member in 1908 and awarded him the first Faraday Medal in 1921. He received
an honorary doctorate from the University of Göttingen. Heaviside became a legendary figure long
before he died in his seaside cottage at Torquay on 3 February 1925. His name has been attached to
one of the reflecting ionized layers (of the ionosphere) surrounding the earth, whose existence he had
predicted in 1902.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0230 -->

V.3 The Operator Mechanics 227

as a characteristic measure of action. That is, $H(t)$, the so-called ‘Heaviside
function,’ describes an external potential difference of one unit (volt), impressed
from the time $t = 0$ onwards. The response, $A(t)$, called the ‘indicial admittance’
—i.e., the current resulting in the circuit because of the unit action—is then given
by the solution of the linear differential equation

$$
Z(D)A(t) = H(t) \quad \text{with} \quad D = \frac{d}{dt}. \tag{225}
$$

The differential operator $Z(D)$ in Eq. (225) is obtained from the impedance
function $Z(i\omega)$, Eq. (223), by writing the operator $D$ instead of the variable $i\omega$.
Heaviside claimed that Eq. (225) could be replaced by the operator equation

$$
A(t) = \Omega H(t), \tag{226}
$$

where the operator $\Omega$ is just the inverse of the operator $Z(D)$, and he proposed
several rules for the practical solution of this equation. For example, if it is
possible to expand $\Omega$ into a negative power series in $D$, say as $\sum_{r=n}^{\infty} b_r D^{-r}$ (with
constant coefficients $b_r$), then one obtains as solution for $A(t)$ a positive power
series in the time variable $t$, i.e., $\sum_{r=n}^{\infty} (1/r!)b_r t^r$ for $t > 0$ (with the same
coefficients $b_r$). By carefully applying this rule and some others, Heaviside and
his followers were able to solve the differential equation (225) for almost every
electrical circuit under consideration.²⁹⁶

For a long time, Heaviside’s operator calculus remained suspect for the
mathematicians. One of the reasons was that the step-function $H(t)$ was not an
analytic function; hence the replacement of the differential equation (225) by the
operator equation (226) did not seem to be allowed under any conditions
whatsoever. Those who insisted on mathematical rigour, on clear definitions of
the operators and well-defined equations obeyed by them could not take Hea-
viside’s solutions seriously.²⁹⁷ Against these objections Heaviside held that
‘mathematics is an experimental science, and definitions do not come first, but
later on’ (Heaviside, 1893b, p. 121). He was completely vindicated, for soon after
his death in 1925 John Renshaw Carson and, independently, Norbert Wiener
provided a complete justification of his operator methods.²⁹⁸

---
²⁹⁶ Of course, in practical cases the observation helped that if $\Omega$ is a sum of two operators, $\Omega_1$ and
$\Omega_2$, and the solutions of Eq. (226) with these operators, namely, $A_1(t)$ and $A_2(t)$, are known, then the
response $A(t)$ may be obtained as the sum $A_1(t) + A_2(t)$.

²⁹⁷ By the turn of the century two methods had been developed to define operators in a rigorous
mathematical sense. First, linear operations of ‘subjects’ were considered as being similar to linear
transformations of a point in an $n$-dimensional (or even infinite-dimensional) space. Otherwise, one
used the method of ‘Laplace transforms.’ However, both methods were not applicable to deal with
Heaviside’s problem.

²⁹⁸ Carson (1887–1940), an engineer of the American Telegraph and Telephone Company, worked
mainly on transmission theory. In a series of papers, ending with a long memoir (Carson, 1925), he
proved the validity of Heaviside’s Eq. (226) by replacing it by the integral equation, $[Z(p)]^{-1}
= p\int_0^\infty A(t) \exp(-pt) dt$, with $p = i\omega$. (The equivalence of this equation with Eq. (226) is obtained by
observing that the integral $p\int_0^\infty H(t) \exp(-pt) dt$ is unity; furthermore, it is assumed that all
derivatives of $A(t)$ vanish at $t = 0$.) Then $[Z(p)]^{-1}$ represents a function similar to a Laplace
transform. With the help of the above equation Carson succeeded in establishing Heaviside’s rules.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0231 -->

228 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

The earliest attempts to establish Heaviside’s operator calculus rigorously was
based upon the use of integral transforms. It was found that, with certain
restrictions, the operator $\Omega$ in Eq. (226) could be replaced by a well-defined
integral, and from it the response function $A(t)$ could be obtained. For this
purpose the concept of the Laplace transform had to be extended in such a way
that it made sense to talk about the transform of the nonanalytic Heaviside
function.²⁹⁹ The possibility of an appropriate extension appeared to be likely in
the early 1920s, but a systematic mathematical theory had yet to be developed.
At this stage Norbert Wiener became interested in supplying the proof of
Heaviside’s methods and results. He decided to achieve his goal by making use
of harmonic analysis because, in principle, the Fourier integral allows one to deal
with nonanalytic functions. However, he noticed at once that ‘the functions to
which the Fourier integral applies are subject to severe restrictions at infinity’
and ‘these restrictions are much more severe than those to which Heaviside
applies his method’ (Wiener, 1926a, p. 560). He had, therefore, to *generalize*
harmonic analysis.

In seeking to formulate a consistent theory of electric circuits, Wiener had to
solve two problems: First, he had to extend the method of Fourier integrals in
such a way that all time-dependent functions (e.g., the external function $H(t)$
and the response function $A(t)$) could be represented as harmonic integrals, say
as $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(\omega)\exp(i\omega t) d\omega$; second, he had to define adequately the operators
occurring in the theory, especially the differential operator $Z(D)$ appearing in
Eq. (225). If the former task were achieved, the latter would be straightforward,
simply because the differential operator $D$ acts on a given harmonic component,
say $f(\omega)\exp(i\omega t)$, like a multiplicative factor $i\omega$. However, it is difficult to
understand that the inverse operator $[Z(D)]^{-1}$ (which is identical with $\Omega$), when
applied to the step-function $H(t)$, should yield results like the ones claimed by
Heaviside. The reason is that, for instance, the solution of Eq. (226) for $\Omega$—being
a series in inverse powers of $D$—involves integrals in which $[Z(i\omega)]^{-1}$ has to be
expanded over the entire range of $\omega$. In spite of this difficulty Wiener succeeded
in his task. In particular, he was able to generalize harmonic analysis in such a
way that it applied to all functions $f(t)$, which are integrable and square
integrable over any finite range of the variable $t$ and, for large $t$, do not grow
faster than a finite power of $t$.³⁰⁰ And he showed further that a well-defined
meaning could be given to the action of all the operators on the functions that
Heaviside had envisaged (Wiener, 1926a).

The main idea, which enabled Wiener to carry out his programme, was to
approximate any function $f(t)$ by functions $f_\lambda(t)$, whose expansion contained
only frequencies up to a given one, $\omega_\lambda$. The action of the operator $\Omega$ on $f_\lambda(t)$ was

---
²⁹⁹ See, e.g., the method of Carson described in footnote 298.

³⁰⁰ Evidently the step-function $H(t)$ is a function of this class since for large $t$ ($> 0$) it is constant
(and equal to unity).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0232 -->

then given by the equation (Wiener, 1926a, p. 565)

$$ \Omega f_{\lambda}(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{\lambda}(\tau) G(\tau - t, \lambda) d\tau, \tag{227} $$

where

$$ G(\tau - t, \lambda) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} F_{\lambda}(i\omega) \Omega(-i\omega) \exp[i\omega(\tau - t)] d\omega. \tag{227a} $$

V.3 The Operator Mechanics 229

(The function $\Omega(-i\omega)$ is obtained by replacing the operator $D$ in $\Omega$ by the variable $-i\omega$.) The function $F_{\lambda}(i\omega)$ restricts the absolute values of the limits of the frequency integration; $F_{\lambda}(i\omega)$ is basically unity for $|\omega| < \omega_{\lambda}$ and approaches zero in a smooth way for $|\omega| = \omega_{\lambda}$.$^{301}$ By substituting the appropriately approximated step-function for $f_{\lambda}(t)$, Wiener obtained the above-mentioned rule of Heaviside; that is, the application of the inverse powers of the operator $D$ could be justified and yielded the well-known result. A difficulty still remained if one wanted to have the operator $D$ acting directly on the step-function; this operation led to an object which, in those days, was considered as being ill-defined.$^{302}$ On the other hand, any positive noninteger power of $D$ could be applied to $H(t)$, yielding a well-defined function. Therefore, Wiener factorized any operator $\Omega$ containing a term proportional to $D$ as a product operator, $\Omega/\sqrt{D} \cdot \sqrt{D}$, and applied it to $H(t)$ in two steps: first, he calculated the result of the application of $\sqrt{D}$ on $H(t)$; then he expanded the operator $\Omega/\sqrt{D}$ in a Fourier series, finally obtaining the result (Wiener, 1926a, p. 579)

$$ \left( \frac{\Omega}{\sqrt{D}} \cdot \sqrt{D} \right) H(t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi t}} \left[ M(0) - \frac{1}{2} \frac{M'(0)}{t} + \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{3}{2} \frac{M''(0)}{t^2} - + \dots \right], \tag{228} $$

where

$$ M(i\omega) = \frac{\Omega(i\omega)}{\sqrt{i\omega}}. \tag{228a} $$

($M'(0)$ and $M''(0)$ denote the first and second derivatives of the function $M(i\omega)$ with respect to the variable $i\omega$ taken at the point zero.) From Eq. (228) Wiener concluded that the positive powers of $D$ always operate on the step-function to give a small response in the distant future (for $t$ very large), in agreement with an earlier assumption of Heaviside's.$^{303}$

$^{301}$ One may replace $F_{\lambda}(i\omega)$ in Eq. (227a) by the operator $F_{\lambda}(D)$. This operator played an important role in Wiener's considerations. For example, the action of the product operator $F_{\lambda}(D)D$ on an arbitrary function can always be shown to give a well-defined result.

$^{302}$ Paul Dirac later on identified such an object as the delta-function (Dirac, 1927a).

$^{303}$ Since the function $\sqrt{i\omega}$ possesses a cut on the axis of positive imaginary $i\omega$-values, Wiener distorted the path of the frequency-integration in Eq. (227a) slightly to the right of the cut, calling this procedure a 'backward' or 'retrospective' operation. He noticed that all operators $\Omega$, stemming from electrical circuits, were retrospective; that is, the corresponding functions $\Omega(i\omega)$ became analytic in the complex right-hand plane of the variable $(i\omega)$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0233 -->

230 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

After successfully applying his generalized harmonic analysis to establish Heaviside's operator calculus, Wiener continued to extend its use in different directions, both physically and mathematically. In this way he discovered, for example, that rather irregular functions, such as those which describe the time independence of noise in an electrical line, or the intensity of white light emitted by a continuous source, could be treated by means of the generalized harmonic analysis (Wiener, 1926b, c). Then, however, arose the problem of investigating the frequency spectrum of the function involved. In particular, Wiener became interested in the problem of describing a continuous spectrum, and he succeeded in doing so by again using the mathematical tool of Lebesgue's integral in a functional space of paths, the latter having properties similar to the space which he had introduced in the theory of Brownian motion (Wiener, 1926b, c). Not only was he able to examine in many cases the 'spectral intensity' of the functions $f(t)$, but he also showed how an essential *statistical feature* enters into the analysis of phenomena like white light.$^{304}$ Although the work on generalized harmonic analysis had a considerable impact on mathematical physics later on, it did not influence the development of quantum mechanics; only by helping Born to apply operator methods did Wiener contribute to the new theory in an important way. This was the more surprising as in summer 1925 when Wiener had passed through Göttingen and had presented there a seminar on his recent attempts at generalizing harmonic analysis it had seemed that this new mathematical tool might be appropriate for formulating quantum-theoretical problems.$^{305}$

$^{304}$ The problem of the analysis of white light in terms of the frequency spectrum had been studied already a long time before Wiener, especially by Lord Rayleigh and Arthur Schuster. A major difficulty had turned up when one wanted to explain why the intensities of two independent light sources added, despite the fact that in electromagnetic theory it is the amplitudes of the waves that add up. Lord Rayleigh had proposed that the reason was the following: different parts of a source emitting a continuous spectrum are not correlated in phase, hence the interference terms in the intensities drop out (Rayleigh, 1880). Schuster, on the other hand, had introduced special methods to perform the analysis of light and its intensities with the help of the so-called 'periodogram' (Schuster, 1894, 1897).
In 1926 Wiener finally put Schuster's intuitive procedure on a secure mathematical foundation. In agreement with Schuster's intent, he considered all Lebesgue measurable functions $f(t)$ which were square integrable and derived their spectral intensities.
$^{305}$ Wiener had revisited Göttingen, the place where he had studied in 1914, on his European trip in 1924. At that time he had found that his results on potential theory interested the Göttingen mathematicians, especially David Hilbert and Richard Courant. The interaction between Wiener and the Göttingen scientists became stronger a year later. As Wiener recalled: 'In 1925, after a little mountain climbing with [J. W.] Alexander, of Princeton, I again visited Göttingen, where my work on generalized harmonic analysis was beginning to attract real attention' (Wiener, 1956, pp. 95-96). Wiener gave a seminar on this subject. There is an interesting episode connected with this seminar. When, after the session, people gathered in *Café Rohn's* to have supper, Hilbert is reported to have said:

The speeches that are given nowadays are so much worse than they used to be. In my time there was an art to giving speeches. People thought a lot about what they wanted to say and their talks were good. But now the young people cannot give good talks any more. It is indeed exceptionally bad here in Göttingen. I guess the worst talks in the whole world are given in Göttingen. This year especially they have been very bad. There have been—no, I have heard no good talks at all. Recently it has been especially bad. But now, this afternoon, there was an exception . . . This afternoon's talk was the worst there ever has been. (Reid, 1970, pp. 169–170)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0234 -->

V.3 The Operator Mechanics 231

In fact, in the beginning of the summer semester of 1925 Max Born had already turned his attention to the treatment of those phenomena in which all the atomic motions could not be considered as being periodic. Especially, he had studied, together with Pascual Jordan, the action of aperiodic electric fields on an atom by reformulating the classical expressions for the resulting electric dipole moment in agreement with the correspondence principle (Born and Jordan, 1925a). In their work they had encountered the problem of representing the coordinates occurring in collision processes—in which the ingoing and outgoing electrons and atoms move along approximately straight-line trajectories—in terms of Fourier integrals. On hearing about Wiener's new mathematical theory, Born had thought that it might provide a general method which would allow the decomposition of all variables used for describing the motion of electrons in atomic systems, including the position variables of electrons colliding with atoms. Born, who was looking forward to visiting M.I.T. to give a series of lectures during the winter semester 1925–1926, had hoped that he would be able to carry on the work on aperiodic motion with the help of generalized harmonic analysis and the personal assistance of its expert, Norbert Wiener. However, by early November 1925, when Born arrived at M.I.T., the status of quantum theory had changed considerably from what it had been earlier that summer; he now brought along with him a new quantum theory, matrix mechanics, by means of which the problems of atomic physics were approached in a manner quite different from the one he had followed with Jordan just a few months previously. In making use of the results of the theory of infinite Hermitian matrices and quadratic forms, Born had recognized the possibility of being able to describe the continuous spectra emitted by atoms; yet, in formulating matrix mechanics in collaboration with Heisenberg and Jordan, he had not succeeded in developing a suitable method on which the calculation of continuous energy states could be based. An even more serious difficulty remained: the matrix methods failed completely in dealing with the problems of atomic collisions. Born still hoped that Wiener's mathematical technique, which the latter had presented in his Göttingen seminar, might provide the key for dealing with these questions, and he counted on Wiener's assistance during his stay at M.I.T. Norbert Wiener, who had just then become interested in quantum theory, felt enthusiastic about working with Born. He immediately recommended the use of operator methods, the intimate connection of which with generalized harmonic analysis he had already explored, as the appropriate tool for treating aperiodic motions.$^{306}$
Wiener had been led to discover the deeper mathematical justification of Heaviside's rules (in the operator theory of electrodynamics) by first recognizing

$^{306}$ When Wiener began to study operator methods he had in mind only the physical applications to problems of classical electrodynamics. (See the discussion in the introduction of Wiener, 1926a, pp. 557–562; the paper was submitted in April 1925.) Even when he stayed at Göttingen in summer 1925, he did not think of using his methods, whether of generalized harmonic analysis or of operator calculus, in quantum theory. As he recalled later in his autobiography: 'What I did not realize at that time was that my talk was closely keyed to the new ideas of physics which were about to burst into bloom at Göttingen in the form of what is now known as quantum mechanics' (Wiener, 1956, p. 97).

232 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

that it was possible to define more general operations than had been employed in the theory of integral equations up to that time. Now, in November 1925, he directed Born’s attention to the fact that the Hermitian matrices of matrix mechanics ‘could be regarded as operators, acting on vectors in a multidimensional space, and he suggested a generalization of matrix mechanics into a kind of operator mechanics’ (Born, 1978, p. 226).$^{307}$ Born was attracted at once by Wiener’s proposal because it connected well with the ideas he had developed in Chapter 3 of the three-man paper (BHJ, 1926). There he had discovered a considerable advantage in extending the matrix description of dynamical variables in such a way that the infinite matrix, say $(q_{mn})$ with $m, n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$, always occurred in equations of the type

$$y_m = \sum_{n=0}^\infty q_{mn} x_n, \quad m = 1, 2, 3 \dots \qquad (229)$$

That is, it acted like a linear operator, as the mathematicians would say, on a sequence of variables or on a vector, $(x_n)$, having an infinite number of components, in order to produce another such vector, $(y_m)$. From Hilbert’s theory of integral equations Born also knew that, if certain conditions were imposed upon the matrix elements, $q_{mn}$, and the vectors $(x_n)$ and $(y_m)$, Eq. (229) was equivalent to an integral equation; but the restrictions were very severe and the matrices used in matrix mechanics did not satisfy them. On the other hand, Wiener had just shown that operator equations could deal with physical problems of electrodynamics where the familiar integral equation methods failed (Wiener, 1926a). Born did not yet know much about operator methods. He somehow felt that the methods to be used had some resemblance to those of almost-periodic functions.$^{308}$ In any case, he entered into the collaboration with Wiener with optimism. They were soon able to establish an operator formulation of quantum mechanics which proved to be more powerful than the previous matrix methods, especially in dealing with such problems as those occurring in the description of atomic collisions. Before the end of the year they submitted papers on their results, both in English to the *M.I.T. Journal of Mathematics and Physics* and in German to *Zeitschrift für Physik*; these papers were identical in content and appeared a few months later in print (Born and Wiener, 1926a, b).

Their first task was to find the relation between Born’s algebraic equations (229) and the corresponding operator equation that would arise in Wiener’s formalism. In order to arrive quickly at the result, the authors turned to a system having only discrete eigenvalues, $W_n$ ($n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$). Then they claimed: ‘In

$^{307}$The idea to connect infinite matrices with operators had already occurred earlier in the mathematical theory of operators. As we have mentioned in footnote 297, the operators had been interpreted as causing linear transformations of points in a finite- or infinite-dimensional space; hence they could be described in principle by infinite quadratic matrices.

$^{308}$He expressed this feeling in a letter to Niels Bohr, where he remarked: ‘Please convey my greetings to your brother Harald, and tell him that Wiener and I are using methods which are closely related to his “almost periodic functions”’ (Born to Bohr, undated, probably early December 1925).

V.3 The Operator Mechanics                                                                         233

place of the transformation of an array of variables $x_1, x_2, \dots$, which lacks any
very obvious physical interpretation, we may consider transformations of func-
tions $x(t)$ of the time' (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 84).$^{309}$ The functions $x(t)$
were defined by the series

$$x(t) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} x_n \exp\left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} W_n t \right). \quad (230)$$

A conventional harmonic analysis into components of the frequency $\nu_n$
$(= W_n/h)$ could be carried out on $x(t)$, yielding the Fourier amplitudes $x_n$, due
to the relation

$$x_n = \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} x(t) \exp\left( -\frac{2\pi i}{h} W_n t \right) dt. \quad (231)$$

Similarly a function $y(t)$ was formed with the Fourier amplitudes $y_m$ (connected
with the frequencies $\nu_m = W_m/h$). With the help of these definitions Born and
Wiener translated Eqs. (229) into a single integral equation, that is,

$$y(t) = \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} q(t, s) x(s) ds, \quad (229')$$

where the 'kernel' function $q(t, s)$ was given by the expression

$$q(t, s) = \sum_{m, n=1}^{\infty} q_{mn} \exp\left[ \frac{2\pi i}{h} (W_m t - W_n s) \right], \quad (229'a)$$

in terms of the matrix elements $q_{mn}$ and the frequencies $W_m/h$ and $W_n/h$.
Equation (229') was finally interpreted as the operator equation

$$y(t) = qx(t), \quad (229'')$$

with the integral operator $q$ given by

$$q = \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} q(t, s) ds. \quad (229''a)$$

In Eq. (229'') the operator $q$ acts on the continuous function $x(t)$, transforming it
into the continuous function $y(t)$.

---
$^{309}$ In matrix mechanics the quantities or vectors $(x_n)$ or $(y_m)$ could not be related to a physical
quantity. One had just identified the $(x_n)$ as columns of the unitary transformation matrix which
brings the Hamiltonian matrix to diagonal form. (Note that in matrix mechanics the lowest value of
the indices $m$ or $n$ is 0 instead of 1.) Thus, the significance of the $(x_n)$ had remained ‘still very
obscure’ (Born, 1926d, p. 125). The German version of the above quote was even more definite, for
Born and Wiener remarked: ‘*In place of the transformation of any array of variables $x_1, x_2, \dots$, which
lack any obvious explanation, we may consider transformations of functions $x(t)$ of the time, which can
be interpreted in physics more easily*’ (Born and Wiener, 1926b, p. 174). They did not mean that the
quantity $x(t)$ had an obvious meaning; it expressed only the hope that a physical interpretation might
be easier to obtain.

234 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

With the help of this procedure a connection was established between the algebraic equations (229) and the operator equation (229") provided, of course, the expression on the right-hand side of Eq. (229'a) existed. However, for the matrices $(q_{mn})$, which were considered in matrix mechanics, that was not generally true; for example, if for the $q_{mn}$ one substituted the transition amplitudes of the harmonic oscillator, which grow with increasing indices ($m$ and $n = m \pm 1$), then the double sums in Eq. (229'a) would diverge. Therefore, Born and Wiener dropped the requirement that the kernel $q(t, s)$ should be represented by a trigonometric series as in Eq. (229'a). At first, they decided to admit all integral operators of the form (229"a), where the kernel $q(t, s)$ is an arbitrary function, compatible with the convergence of the integral on the right-hand side of Eq. (229'). But even this generalization did not reach far enough, for Wiener knew from previous experience that very important operations in physics (notably electrodynamics) could not be represented in this way. Hence he proposed to Born that Eq. (229), instead of being generalized into Eq. (229'), should be replaced right away by an operator equation of the type of Eq. (229"); however, the operator $q$ should be an *arbitrary linear operator*, which in general would not be written as in Eq. (229"a).$^{310}$

Although Eq. (229") admitted operators, which were much more general objects than the matrices which had been considered in matrix mechanics until then, Born and Wiener claimed that 'there corresponds to every operator a "matrix"' (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 86). In order to find the generalized matrix corresponding to a given operator, say $q$, they first generated the function $q(t, W)$ of time, $t$, and energy, $W$, by writing

$$q(t, W) = \exp \left( -\frac{2\pi i}{h} Wt \right) q \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} Wt \right). \tag{232}$$

The harmonic analysis of the function $q(t, W)$ was then made into components of the frequencies $(V - W)/h$; the corresponding amplitudes, $q(V, W)$, were given by

$$q(V, W) = \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} \exp \left( -\frac{2\pi i}{h} Vt \right) q \exp \left( \frac{2\pi i}{h} Wt \right) dt. \tag{233}$$

The significance of these generalized harmonic amplitudes is not difficult to recognize. If, in Eq. (233), the energy parameters, $V$ and $W$, assume only discrete values, $W_m$ and $W_n$, respectively, with $m, n = 1, 2, \ldots$, then $q(W_m, W_n)$ be-

---

$^{310}$A linear operator satisfies the equation, $q[c_1x_1(t) + c_2x_2(t)] = c_1qx_1(t) + c_2qx_2(t)$. Simple examples of linear operators are the multiplication by a constant or by a function $f(t)$.
That Eq. (229"), with $q$ a linear operator, generalizes Eq. (229) can be seen at once from the example of the unit operator (i.e., the operator which transforms the function $x(t)$ into itself). Evidently, it is a linear operator. On the other hand, when one seeks to represent this operation by the integral equation (229'), one recognizes that no kernel, $q(t, s)$, which is a function of both time variables, $t$ and $s$, in the conventional sense, can be used to describe it.

V.3  The Operator Mechanics  235

comes identical with the matrix element $q_{mn}$; hence all the values, which the function $q(V, W)$ can assume in this case, comprise the quantum-mechanical matrix $(q_{mn})$—or $(q(mn))$, as it was written in matrix mechanics—and the operator possesses a genuine matrix representation. The function $q(t, W)$ also has a straightforward meaning: its value for the particular energy parameter, $W = W_n$, becomes equal to the sum of elements in the $n$th column of the matrix $(q_{mn} \exp[(2\pi i/h)(W_m - W_n)])$. If, however, one or both energy parameters assume continuous values, the function $q(V, W)$ describes a matrix with (one or two) continuous indices, thus providing just the formalism which Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had searched for in vain a few months earlier. In this formalism the function $q(t, W)$—which Born and Wiener, in an obvious generalization of the case of discrete energy values, called ‘the sum of the line [i.e., column] of the “matrix” of $q$ corresponding to the value $W$ of the energy’ (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 87)—characterizes the system under consideration in the following manner: namely, $q(t, W)$ may be represented by a Fourier sum in case all energy states of the system are discrete; or by a Fourier integral when the energy spectrum is purely continuous; or by a sum of both when discrete and continuous energies occur.$^{311}$

The description in terms of operators could account for even more general quantum systems than the ones treated earlier by Born, Heisenberg and Jordan. However, the function $q(V, W)$, as calculated from Eq. (233), does not exist (in the conventional sense) for all linear operators even if the associated function $q(t, W)$, Eq. (232), is perfectly regular. An example of such an operator is the differential operator $D (= d/dt)$. Evidently, its associated function, $D(t, W) = (2\pi i/h)W$, is finite for all systems having finite energies; but its harmonic decomposition, $D(V, W)$, is not a conventional function.$^{312}$ Like $D$, many operators, describing dynamical variables of systems having continuous energy eigenvalues, have a ‘matrix’ which is singular in a manner similar to $D(V, W)$. As a result, conventional harmonic analysis, using either Fourier sums or Fourier integrals, cannot be applied to the differential operator $D$ or positive integer powers of it in such systems, and one has to use a procedure similar to the one proposed by Wiener for Heaviside’s operators (see Eqs. (227) and (227a)).

Before developing their operator formulation of quantum mechanics, Born and Wiener defined the Hermiticity property of operators. To begin with they noticed that any linear operator might be expressed as a sum of terms, each of

***

$^{312}$ Difficulties with the operator $D$ had been noticed by Wiener already in his attempts to justify Heaviside’s operator methods. In the present case one sees easily that the function, $(2\pi i/h) \cdot W \lim_{\tau \to \infty} (1/2\tau) \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} \exp[(2\pi i/h)(W - V)t] dt$, exhibits a peculiar structure when the system under consideration has continuous eigenvalues. (In the case of discrete eigenvalues $W_n, n = 1, 2, \dots$, $D(V, W)$ becomes identical with the original matrix, $((2\pi i/h)W_m \delta_{mn})$, which is a perfectly regular object.) The above function is zero everywhere except when $V$ sharply becomes the value $W$.

Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

which was a product of a function of time, $u_n(t)$, and a differential operator, $F_n(D)$, that is,$^{313}$

$$q = \sum_n u_n(t) F_n(D). \tag{234}$$

Then they showed that the transposed operator, $q^T$, was $\sum_n F_n(D)u_n(-t)$. Consequently the Hermitian conjugate of $q$ is $\sum_n F_n^*(D)u_n^*(-t)$. Thus, the authors stated the following condition of 'Hermitianness' (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 91, Eq. (24))$^{314}$:

$$\sum_n u_n(t) F_n(D) = \sum_n F_n^*(D) u_n^*(-t). \tag{235}$$

After these technical preliminaries Born and Wiener turned to the equations of quantum mechanics. They remarked: 'We represent a coordinate by a linear operator $q$ instead of by a matrix. This has the advantage of enabling us to treat cases where the matrix representation goes to pieces, even though we introduce the notion of a continuous matrix. We must seek for the meaning of the statement that an atom is represented by a number of operators in the fact that an atom is a mechanism the characteristic oscillations of which are in some way given when the coordinate operators are determined' (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 92). Similarly, they represented the momentum variable by an operator $p$ and required the quantum conditions to assume the form

$$pq - qp = \frac{h}{2\pi i} 1, \tag{236}$$

where 1 is the unit operator, i.e., the operator which when applied to a function yields the same function. In agreement with matrix mechanics Born and Wiener further assumed that all operators representing the dynamical variables of a quantum system were Hermitian.

With the above formulation, however, the description of mechanical systems was not yet complete because, as Eq. (229$''$) showed, the operators had always to be applied to the functions $x(t)$. Born and Wiener, therefore, associated with each system a set of functions ('zugehörige Funktionen,' Born and Wiener, 1926b, p. 182), $\{x(t)\}$, and required that this set be closed with respect to all linear operations occurring in the system. That is, if in Eq. (229$''$) one replaced the operator $q$ by any other Hermitian operator describing a dynamical variable of the same system, and applied it to any function $x(t)$ of the set $\{x(t)\}$, the resulting function $y(t)$ should also belong to $\{x(t)\}$.$^{315}$

---
$^{313}$ This situation is a generalization of the one in electrodynamics where the operators $Z$ and $\Omega$ are only functions of the differential operator.
$^{314}$ Evidently, the 'matrix elements' of a Hermitian operator $q$ must satisfy the condition $q(V, W) = q^*(W, V)$. Born and Wiener showed that this is so provided Eq. (235) holds (Born and Wiener, 1926a, pp. 90–91).
$^{315}$ The closure relation for $\{x(t)\}$ ensures that all operations for a given mechanical system can be defined in operator mechanics. As long as the physical significance of the functions $x(t)$ is not known, the closure relation remains the only requirement that can be imposed on them.
