V.3 The Operator Mechanics

Born and Wiener now *postulated* that the laws of quantum mechanics could be formulated in terms of the operators just as well as in terms of the matrices. In particular, the Hamiltonian equations of motion for each pair of variables, *q* and *p*, formulated as the operator equations,

$$\dot{q} = \frac{\partial H(p, q)}{\partial p} = \frac{2\pi i}{h}(Hq - qH),$$

$$\dot{p} = -\frac{\partial H(p, q)}{\partial q} = \frac{2\pi i}{h}(Hp - pH),$$

(237)

should determine the motion of a system whose Hamiltonian operator is *H*. Again, Eqs. (237) are a generalization of the corresponding matrix equations and, in agreement with matrix mechanics, *H* is *assumed to be an operator function of the dynamical variables, having the same functional dependence on the operators p and q as the classical Hamiltonian has on its dynamical variables*. In addition, the theory of canonical transformations and perturbation theory could be formulated as operator equations, being an obvious generalization of the corresponding matrix equations. Moreover, in analogy to matrix mechanics, the time derivative of any dynamical variable, say the operator *q*, might be replaced by the difference of operator products given by

$$\dot{q} = Dq - qD,$$

(238)

which was assumed to hold in all cases.<sup>316</sup> From Eq. (238) the frequency condition for the radiation emitted in the transitions between discrete states, in the transitions between discrete and continuous states, as well as in the transitions between continuous states, could be obtained. On the other hand, the conservation of energy followed from Eqs. (237) because the time derivative of the operator, $H(p, q)$, becomes identical to zero.

<sup>316</sup>When *q* describes a system having only discrete energy states, $W_n$, and the kernel of the operator, $q(t, s)$, is given by Eq. (229'a), Eq. (238) follows from the two equations

$$Dqx(t) = \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} \frac{\partial q(t, s)}{\partial t} x(s) \, ds$$

$$= \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} \sum_{m, n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2\pi i}{h} W_m q_{mn} \exp\!\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(W_m t - W_n s)\right] x(s) \, ds$$

and

$$qDx(t) = -\lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} \frac{\partial q(t, s)}{\partial s} x(s) \, ds$$

$$= \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} \sum_{m, n=1}^{\infty} \frac{2\pi i}{h} W_n \cdot q_{mn} \exp\!\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(W_m t - W_n s)\right] x(s) \, ds.$$

The second equation holds if there are no contributions to the integrand at $\tau = -\infty$ and $\tau = +\infty$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0241 -->

238

Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

In Born and Wiener's operator mechanics the Hamiltonian operator exhibited properties which had no direct analogue in matrix mechanics. For instance, because of the operator identity

$$H = \frac{h}{2\pi i} D,$$

(239)

*H* could be replaced in the operator equations by the operator *D* up to an additive constant.<sup>317</sup> Then, with the help of Eq. (233), it followed for the 'matrix elements' of *H* that

$$H(V, W) = W \lim_{\tau \to \infty} \frac{1}{2\tau} \int_{-\tau}^{+\tau} \exp\!\left[\frac{2\pi i}{h}(W - V)t\right] dt.$$

(240)

The expression on the right-hand side becomes equal to *W* for $V = W$ and zero otherwise. Hence, the 'matrix,' $H(V, W)$, associated with the Hamiltonian operator, is automatically diagonal. However, this fact alone did not contribute to the solution of the fundamental problem of operator mechanics, that is, to determine the energy eigenvalues of a system. The reason was that as long as $x(t)$, the associated functions of that system, were not known, the energy eigenfunctions could not be found by simply applying the differential operator, $(h/2\pi i)D$, to $x(t)$. Since Born and Wiener were not aware of any procedure for obtaining these functions, they were obliged to calculate the eigenvalues in the same way as Heisenberg had done in the case of the anharmonic oscillator (Heisenberg, 1925c): that is, for a given system (determined, for example, by its Hamiltonian $H(p, q)$ or the Newtonian equations of motion), they integrated the equations of motion, taking into account the restrictions imposed upon the variables by the Hermitian property and by the commutation relations. The operators occurring in these equations were tacitly assumed to act on the functions $x(t)$ or on their harmonic components, $x(\omega)\exp(i\omega t)$, where the frequencies $\omega$ were related to the energy eigenvalues of the system as $\omega = 2\pi W/h$. Thus, for a given operator equation, an ordinary equation was obtained involving the still unknown 'Fourier amplitudes' $x(\omega)$.

With the generalization of matrix mechanics into operator mechanics Born and Wiener hoped that those systems in which continuous eigenvalues occurred could now be treated. Before pursuing this matter they demonstrated that the new methods yielded the same result as matrix mechanics for the simple system of the harmonic oscillator. They observed that the operator equation of motion in this case,

$$D^2 q + \omega_0^2 q = 0,$$

(241)

with $\omega_0^2$ the force constant (the mass of the system having been assumed to be

$$q = \exp(i\omega_0 t)\phi(D) + \exp(-i\omega_0 t)\phi^*(D - i\omega_0),$$

(242)

where $\phi(D)$ satisfied the difference equation<sup>318</sup>

$$|\phi(D)|^2 - |\phi(D - i\omega_0)|^2 = \frac{h}{4\pi\omega_0} 1.$$

The last equation provides the complete solution of the problem, as can be seen from letting both sides operate on the function $\exp(i\omega t)$. Then the algebraic equation

$$|\phi(i\omega)|^2 - |\phi(i\omega - i\omega_0)|^2 = \frac{h}{4\pi\omega_0}$$

(242a')

follows, in which $\phi$ appears as a function of the variable $i\omega$. Equation (242a') states that the absolute square of $\phi$ assumes finite, positive values only for discrete values of $\omega$, i.e., $\omega_k = k\omega_0$, with $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. Hence *W*, the energy parameter of the harmonic oscillator, becomes restricted to the discrete values $W_k = (h/2\pi)\omega_0 k$, with $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$.<sup>319</sup> Finally, for these discrete *W*-values, the functions $\phi$ take on the values

$$\phi\!\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h} W_k\right) = \left(\frac{h}{4\pi\omega_0}\right)^{1/2} (k + 1)^{1/2} \exp(i\delta_{k+1}),$$

(243)

with the arbitrary phase $\delta_{k+1}$.

The result, expressed in Eq. (243), indicates that the operator *q* (and all other dynamical operators of the harmonic oscillator) have discrete eigenvalues. All these operators act on functions $x(t)$, which can be written as infinite Fourier sums of terms, $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} x(k\omega)\exp(ik\omega t)$. The set of functions, $\{x(t)\}$, is evidently complete because the application of the operators *p* and *q* on a term having the frequency $k\omega_0$ will produce terms with frequencies $(k\omega_0 \pm \omega_0)$, which, by assumption, occur already in the Fourier series.

The functions $x(t)$ had not appeared in matrix mechanics. To compare the results of the operator and matrix methods, Born and Wiener calculated the function $q(t, W_k)$, obtaining

$$q(t, W_k) = \left(\frac{h}{4\pi\omega_0}\right)^{1/2} \{(k + 1)^{1/2} \exp[i(\omega_0 t + \delta_{k+1})]$$
$$+ k^{1/2} \exp[-i(\omega_0 t + \delta_k)]\},$$

(244)

$$\mu D^2 q = 0,$$

$$q = t\phi_1(D) + \phi_2(D),$$

$$p = \mu\phi_1(D),$$

$$\phi_1(D) = \phi_1^*(D)$$

$$\phi_2(D) = \left[\frac{d\phi_1(D)}{dD} + \phi_2(D)\right]^*$$

(247b)

V.3 The Operator Mechanics 241

In the example of the harmonic oscillator, the commutation relation or quantum condition, Eq. (236), was responsible for the fact that the energy assumed discrete values. How would the commutation relation affect the motion in the present case? On substituting the expressions for $p$ and $q$, Eqs. (246) and (247), in Eq. (236), Born and Wiener arrived at an equation,

$$ \frac{d\phi_1}{dD} \phi_1(D) = \frac{h}{2\pi i \mu} 1, \quad (248) $$

for the operator $\phi_1(D).^{322}$ Thus, the operator $\phi_1(D)$ satisfied a differential equation rather than a difference equation like Eq. (242a), as in the case of the harmonic oscillator. Therefore, the operator solution of Eq. (248), that is,

$$ \phi_1(D) = \left( \frac{hD}{\pi i \mu} \right)^{1/2}, \quad (249) $$

depended on a continuous manner on the operator $D$.^{323}$ Substituting this result in Eq. (246a) and taking into account Eq. (247b), Born and Wiener finally obtained the position operator representing the uniform motion in quantum mechanics as

$$ q = t \left( \frac{hD}{\pi i \mu} \right)^{1/2} - \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{h}{\pi i \mu D} \right)^{1/2} + \psi(D), \quad (250) $$

where the operator function $\psi(D)$ denotes the real part of $\phi_2(D)$, which cannot be determined from the above dynamical relations.

The right-hand side follows because of the equation

$$ F(D)u(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k!} u^{(k)}(t) F^{(k)}(D), $$

with

$$ u^{(k)}(t) = \frac{d^k u(t)}{dt^k} \quad \text{and} \quad F^{(k)}(D) = \frac{d^k F(D)}{dD^k}, $$

which Born and Wiener called the 'Leibniz formula' ('*Leibnizsche Formel*,' Born and Wiener, 1926b, p. 179). Now one obtains the Hermitian conjugate by taking the complex conjugate of $q^T$. Since $\phi_1(D)$ is Hermitian, the equality of $(q^T)^*$ and $q$ yields Eq. (247b).

$^{322}$Since the operators $\phi_1(D)$ and $\phi_2(D)$ commute, the quantum condition (236) leads to the equation $(h/2\pi i)1 = \mu[\phi_1(D)t\phi_1(D) - t\phi_1(D)\phi_1(D)]$. The first term on the right-hand side may be rewritten with the help of the Leibniz formula, quoted in footnote 321, as $\mu[t\phi_1(D)\phi_1(D) + d\phi_1(D)/dD \cdot \phi_1(D)]$. Thus one term remains, which may be written as $\mu(d\phi_1(D)/dD) \cdot \phi_1(D)$ or $\mu\phi_1(D) \cdot (d\phi_1(D)/dD)$. Evidently, $d\phi_1(D)/dD$ is zero in the classical limit; consequently $\phi_1(D)$ is a constant then (independent of $D$) and $\phi_2(D)$ is a real function, due to Eq. (247b).

$^{323}$Equation (248) is equivalent to the operator equation, $(h/2\pi i) dD = d[\phi_1(D)]^2$, whose integration yields the solution, $(h/\pi i \mu) D = \phi_1^2(D) + \text{const}$. By dropping the constant and choosing the positive sign of the root, one arrives at Eq. (249).

242 &emsp; Chapter V &ensp; Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

From the operator solutions for $p$ and $q$ the authors calculated the functions, $q(t, W)$ and $p(t, W)$, obtaining

$$q(t, W) = t\left(\frac{2W}{\mu}\right)^{1/2} + i \frac{h}{4\pi(2\mu W)^{1/2}} + \psi\left(\frac{2\pi i}{h} W\right) \qquad (251a)$$

and

$$p(t, W) = (2\mu W)^{1/2}. \qquad (251b)$$

Both assumed real values, apart from a time-dependent imaginary part in $q(t, W)$, which, according to Born and Wiener, could be neglected because 'if $W$ is large, $h/4\pi(2\mu W)^{1/2}$ is small'; moreover, 'in this case the sum of the terms in a column really represents the motion' (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 98).<sup>324</sup> The 'matrix' $q(V, W)$ of the position operator is degenerate because, considered as a function of the variables $V$ and $W$, it is zero everywhere except when $V$ assumes sharply the value $W$. The function $q(t, W)$ cannot, therefore, be represented by a Fourier sum or integral, and the motion is free of any periodicity. Since the real parts of $q(t, W)$ and $p(t, W)$ showed the same dependence on time $t$ and energy $W$ as the corresponding classical variables of an accelerated particle, Born and Wiener considered them as the proper quantum-mechanical representations of position and momentum variables. They concluded that: 'Our representation is as close to the classical treatment as seems to be consistent with the foundations of quantum theory' (Born and Wiener, 1926a, p. 98).

The quantum-mechanical solution of the problem of uniform motion, notably Eqs. (251a) and (251b), which had been obtained by a straightforward application of the operator methods, cleared an important puzzle of the theory of atomic systems. This puzzle consisted in the observation that many features pertaining to moving electrons and atoms could be described perfectly by means of classical equations, though one expected that quantum theory would alter the description completely. Max Born, who was deeply concerned with these questions and had discussed them at length with Niels Bohr during the previous year, had good reason to be pleased with the results of his collaboration with Norbert Wiener; in particular, they had been able to demonstrate how, in spite of the restrictions imposed by quantum theory—especially, the commutation relations, Eqs. (236)—an unaccelerated mass-particle followed a classical trajectory. The position function, $q(t, W)$ in Eq. (251a), seemed to possess all the observed properties: in particular, it yielded the correct space-time interpretation, as can be seen by examining the structure of the 'kernel' function, $q(t, s)$, entering into the integral equation of the type of Eq. (229'). Born discussed this point in a letter to Niels

244 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

Wiener had not developed operator mechanics in the direction of wave mechanics. He remarked then: 'First we did the right thing. We expressed the energy as $d/dt$ and we wrote the commutation law for the energy and time as an identity by applying $(td/dt - dt/dt)$ to a function of $t$. It was absolutely the same as for $p$ and $q$, but we did not see that. I shall never forgive myself, because if we had done this, we would have had the whole wave mechanics at once, a few months before Schrödinger' (Born, Conversations, p. 16). Born even went on to blame Wiener for the clumsy parts of their formalism and lamented that: 'In one case he saw that it was a simple differential representation [i.e., for the energy in terms of $d/dt$], but in the other case [i.e., for the operators $p$ and $q$] he insisted on the very clumsy integral equation [Eq. (229')], which I did not quite understand. And we could understand only after having the wave theory [of Schrödinger]. Then we knew why the exponential factors [occurring, e.g., in the function $x(t)$] came into these integrals' (Born, Conversations, p. 17).

Though one may sympathize with Born and Wiener's failure to see, in November 1925, the connection between $p$, the momentum operator, and $d/dq$, the operator denoting the derivative with respect to the position operator, which plays an important role in wave mechanics, several reasons can be given for their failure. To begin with, one finds that nowhere in the Born–Wiener paper or in Born's letter to Niels Bohr of December 1925 was there any mention of a commutation relation between energy and time; Born and Wiener were therefore not likely to notice the analogy of this relation with the standard $pq$-commutation relations.$^{326}$ Second, in order to consider a relation between the momentum $p$ and $d/dq$ as being analogous to the relation between the energy $W$ and $d/dt$, one has to regard the position variable $q$ on the same footing as the time parameter $t$. To Born, such a treatment would have been unacceptable because it seemed to contradict the principle on which matrix mechanics had been founded; namely, the fundamental difference between dynamical variables and mere parameters. However, Schrödinger, who developed wave mechanics on the basis of concepts quite different from those of matrix mechanics, introduced the coordinate $q$ and the time $t$ on the same footing. In Schrödinger's theory, the ideas of de Broglie concerning matter waves played an important role. It is surprising that Born, who knew about the possibility that mass-particles might exhibit wave properties—e.g., from Einstein's work on quantum statistics (Einstein, 1925a), Louis de Broglie's thesis (1924e, 1925), and Walter Elsasser's explanation of the Ramsauer effect (Elsasser, 1925)—did not think of it when he dealt with the uniform motion of a particle in operator mechanics. Had he tried

(238) to obtain the relation, $Dt - tD = 1$. And, with the help of Eq. (239), the equation, $Ht - tH = (h/2\pi i)1$, would then have followed.

A commutation relation of energy and time was first considered by Wolfgang Pauli after he had learned the results of Born and Wiener (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926).

V.3 The Operator Mechanics 245

to incorporate the wave aspects into his formalism he might have been led to consider operators which could be applied to functions periodic in both the time and the position variables. However, in winter 1925–1926 de Broglie’s waves did not occupy his mind; in fact, he ignored a hint concerning them that had occurred in the solution, Eqs. (250) and (251), for the position variable of the uniform motion.$^{327}$

As for Wiener, he had only recently become interested in quantum theory and was not fully acquainted with its problems. The physical ideas involved in formulating operator mechanics came from Born; Wiener executed the mathematical parts of Born’s programme on the basis of his knowledge of operator methods.$^{328}$ The path to wave mechanics and the Schrödinger equation was thus not close to Wiener’s thinking. Moreover, in Heaviside’s electrodynamics it had not been necessary to introduce—in addition to the pair of operators $t$ and $D$—another pair consisting of the position operator $q$ and the differential operator $\partial / \partial q$. And the examples, which he treated in quantum mechanics with Born, did not require such an extension either. Wiener always remained pleased with the fact that, at the right historical moment, he had developed the mathematical methods by which matrices could be generalized, and that with their help he had assisted Born in solving an important physical problem in quantum mechanics. He was also happy with the fact that ‘operators have since remained an essential part of quantum theory’ (Wiener, 1956, p. 109). But in 1926 and 1927 when ‘quantum mechanics went into an active phase of growth in which young men like Heisenberg himself, Dirac, Wolfgang Pauli and John von Neumann were making new discoveries almost every day,’ he stayed out of it. He found that: ‘This feverish atmosphere is not one in which I function well, nor did I feel the need of intervening in a subject which was already so completely handled’ (Wiener, 1956, p. 109).$^{329}$

Nevertheless, it is surprising that in 1926, when the full power of operator methods began to be displayed in wave mechanics, Wiener’s name was no longer associated with the advances in quantum mechanics. Wiener did go to Göttingen in April 1926 and stayed there during the summer. Though this visit turned out to be less successful than Wiener and his hosts had hoped, he did have a fruitful

$^{327}$As mentioned above, Born and Wiener, in the position function, Eq. (251a), neglected the imaginary term, $(i/4\pi)(h/(2\mu W)^{1/2})$, because they considered it to be too small if $W$ was large. However, by introducing the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ ($= h/(2\mu W)^{1/2}$), the second factor in the imaginary term is recognized to be identical with it. Hence the uniform motion is described by a real position variable only when $\lambda$ can be neglected as being negligibly small.

$^{328}$Born recalled later that at M.I.T. he was kept very busy with his lectures and was involved in lots of discussions with other people, while Wiener spent much time in working out the results. Said Born: ‘He showed it to me and I made my remarks and suggestions’ (Born, Conversations, p. 16).

$^{329}$In spite of Wiener’s personal explanation, quoted above, it seems quite remarkable that Wiener, who had had the opportunity of contributing so early to the mathematical parts of quantum mechanics, and whose later work on harmonic analysis was closely connected with the foundation of the theory, left the field entirely to John von Neumann. The latter began to contribute to quantum mechanics only in spring 1927.

association with Born.$^{330}$ Born, who was just then treating another problem of aperiodic motion, the collision of atomic particles, though now with the methods of wave mechanics, again received Wiener’s assistance. He acknowledged it in a footnote in the extended paper on the statistical interpretation of Schrödinger’s wave function in the following words: ‘In the mathematical realization of this work I have been assisted most kindly by Professor N. Wiener of Cambridge, Mass.; I wish to thank him here and acknowledge that I would not have arrived at the goal without him’ (Born, 1926b, p. 805). This footnote of July 1926 described the actual role of Norbert Wiener in the formulation of quantum mechanics more adequately than the complaints which Born began to harbour against him later. At a time when just a few physicists struggled to develop a consistent theory of quantum mechanics, the Born–Wiener collaboration not only indicated the way for handling the problem of aperiodic motion but also contributed to the physical interpretation of the theory. Wiener himself had no reason to look back with regret on his work with Born, and he continued to return to the problems of quantum mechanics whenever his kind of mathematics seemed to offer an interesting and original application.$^{331}$

$^{330}$On Richard Courant’s suggestion, made in summer 1925, Wiener had applied for a fellowship of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation. Upon receiving the award of the fellowship for one year, he had planned to spend it entirely in Göttingen, where he expected a warm welcome. However, when he arrived, he found that Courant was ‘somewhat hostile’ towards him. In his autobiography, Wiener explained this change in Courant’s behaviour by the fact that, before leaving the United States, he had given an interview to an American newspaper, and Courant had learned about its contents as well as Leo Wiener’s anti-German activities during World War I. As Wiener recalled; ‘Courant scolded me for my newspaper publicity and was disposed to deny me the assistant and the complete official recognition he had promised to me . . . . Nevertheless he allowed me to continue in Göttingen in an unofficial way, and after some persuasion found an able young mathematician to aid in the preparation of my lectures, provided I should pay him out of my own pocket’ (Wiener, 1956, p. 114).
In addition to the difficulties with Courant, Wiener’s lectures were not successful at all. Born recalled: ‘When the students complained about his teaching, there was trouble between him and Courant, which I tried to smooth out’ (Born, 1978, p. 227). After the summer semester Wiener and his wife (whom he had married just before leaving the United States) left Göttingen for an extended honeymoon trip to Italy. They did not return to Göttingen; Wiener decided to spend the remaining months of his fellowship with Harald Bohr in Copenhagen. He received a warm welcome from both Harald and Niels Bohr.

$^{331}$Wiener kept up his interest in quantum mechanics for many years. For example, after his return to M.I.T. in 1927 he collaborated with a new colleague, the Dutch mathematician Dirk Jan Struik, applying the methods which the latter had used in differential geometry to differential equations, especially the Schrödinger equation (see, e.g., Struik and Wiener, 1927, and further papers). Wiener continued to publish papers on quantum theory occasionally, but then he stopped suddenly for more than twenty years. In 1953 he returned to the subject and tried to formulate, together with his student Armand Siegel, a new approach to the statistical interpretation of quantum mechanics, based on the mathematical concept of ‘differential space’ which he had used in the early 1920s to describe Brownian motion (Wiener and Siegel, 1953, and later papers).
Wiener spent many years of his career to extending harmonic analysis. He had numerous students and collaborators. For example, in 1932 he worked with the English mathematician R. E. A. C. Paley, and they wrote a book on complex Fourier transforms (Paley and Wiener, 1934). Wiener had another successful collaboration with Eberhard Hopf on certain specific integral equations, the so-called Wiener–Hopf equations. The latter played, together with harmonic analysis, an important role in the development of communication theory which occupied Wiener during the 1940s. This work not only

V.4 Action-Angle Variables and the Method of Complex Integration 247

**V.4 Multiply Periodic Systems: Action-Angle Variables and the Method of Complex Integration**

Born and Wiener’s paper on operator mechanics had an immediate impact on Heisenberg who saw it about the same time as it reached *Zeitschrift für Physik* on 5 January 1926.³³² Since November 1925 Heisenberg and Pauli had been trying unsuccessfully to calculate the energy states of the hydrogen atom, taking into account *relativistic* effects and perhaps the possibility that the electron possessed, as proposed by George Uhlenbeck and Samuel Goudsmit, an intrinsic magnetic moment. In order to achieve this goal, one had to compute the averages of certain negative powers of the radius variable of the electron, and this could be done only by introducing an angle variable $\phi$, as in classical theory. Pauli, in his matrix theory of the nonrelativistic hydrogen atom, had made use of the ‘Lenz vector’ just because it had not been possible to express an angle coordinate as a Hermitian matrix. Now Born and Wiener’s work suggested to Heisenberg that it might be possible to treat the angle, which is an aperiodic position variable, as an operator. He was very happy about it and he proposed immediately, in a letter written to Pauli on 7 January 1926, to treat the two-dimensional hydrogen atom in terms of polar coordinates, the radius $r$ and the angle $\phi$. While $r$ could be considered, in its quantum-theoretical reformulation, as a genuine matrix, like any other dynamical variable which had so far been used in matrix mechanics, the angle $\phi$ was certainly not a Hermitian matrix, although it could be defined, according to Eq. (212), as a function of the matrices representing the Cartesian coordinates of the electron (which, in classical theory, moves in a plane around the nucleus). Furthermore, Heisenberg defined the azimuthal momentum $p_\phi$, the canonically conjugate variable to the angle $\phi$, by the equation

$$p_\phi = x p_y - y p_x . \qquad (252)$$

The variable $p_\phi$ could, of course, be represented by a Hermitian matrix like the variables $x$, $p_x$, $y$ and $p_y$. But since he was dealing with a formalism, in which the variables (including the angle $\phi$) were represented by generalized matrices—

________________________

influenced the practical construction of computers, it also led Wiener to create a new mathematical field, ‘cybernetics,’ dealing with the problems of communication and control in artificial machines as well as in living organisms.

Wiener’s accomplishments received increasing recognition. In 1929 he was invited to lecture on his researches at Brown University. He spent the academic year 1931–1932 in Cambridge, England, where his former teacher G. H. Hardy asked him to give a course on Fourier integrals. During 1935–1936 he visited China, lecturing at the Tsing-Hua University in Peking. In 1951 he served as Fulbright Lecturer at the *Collège de France* in Paris and spent the academic year 1955–1956 as a guest professor at the Indian Statistical Institute in Calcutta. In 1933 Wiener received the Bôcher prize for analysis. Shortly before his death President Lyndon Baines Johnson awarded him the National Medal of Science. Norbert Wiener died in Stockholm on 18 March 1964.

notably the operators of the type which Born and Wiener had employed in their paper—Heisenberg dropped the matrix notation completely.³³³ From the matrix commutation relations for the variables, $x$ and $p_x$, $y$ and $p_y$, respectively, and using the formal expansion of the function defining $\phi$ in Eq. (212), Heisenberg obtained the commutation relation  

$$p_\phi \phi - \phi p_\phi = \frac{h}{2\pi i}, \tag{253}$$  

for $\phi$ and $p_\phi$. Equation (253), which had to be considered as an operator equation (including an operator 1 on the right-hand side), confirmed the correctness of the definition of $p_\phi$ through Eq. (252).  

With the help of these results, Heisenberg was able to proceed with the calculation of the average values of the negative powers of $r$ ($=\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$), the radius variable of the electron (for motions in a plane). He noted that $p_\phi$ could be replaced, as in classical theory, by the expression $m_e r^2 \dot{\phi}$, where $m_e$ is the mass of the electron. Assuming that $\dot{\phi}$, the time derivative of the angle, depends (again as in classical theory) only on the principal quantum number of the atom, he concluded that $\overline{r^{-2}}$, the average over a full period of the inverse square radius, depended on the orbital momentum quantum number $k$ in the same way as $(1/p_\phi)$. Since the values of $p_\phi$ were known from the spectroscopic data, the quantity $\overline{r^{-2}}$, which entered into the calculation of the relativistic correction to the hydrogen terms, could be evaluated. Heisenberg was very encouraged by this result and continued to work along the same lines. On 14 January 1926 he wrote again to Pauli, informing him about the progress he had made during the previous week. Heisenberg had accepted to give a talk on 19 January before the *Kegelklub* in Stade, close to Hamburg, and he planned to pass through Hamburg the following day before returning to Göttingen.³³⁴ ‘I hope,’ he wrote in anticipation of his intended meeting with Pauli, (on 20 January), ‘to spend many hours discussing physics with you’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 14 January 1926). One week after this meeting Heisenberg presented, in another letter to Pauli, a final report on what he had learned about ‘cyclical variables’ (‘das Kapitel “zyklische Variable”’) (Heisenberg to Pauli, 27 January 1926).  

In his letter Heisenberg outlined the treatment of the problem of periodic motion with one degree of freedom, which he formulated in terms of $J$, the action variable, and $w$, the angle variable, satisfying the commutation relation  

$$J w - w J = \frac{h}{2\pi i} . \tag{254}$$  

³³³ Born and Wiener used their quantum-mechanical operators to describe dynamical variables, employing the same symbols as were used in classical theory. By applying the operator methods the difference between the quantum-theoretical and the classical variables was so obvious that it did not have to be emphasized by a different notation. We shall follow the same procedure in the following sections and use the matrix notation only when absolutely necessary.  

³³⁴ See the letters from Heisenberg to Pauli, 24 December 1925 and 7 January 1926.

**V.4 Action-Angle Variables and the Method of Complex Integration**  
249  

Again Heisenberg considered the variables \( J \) and \( w \) in this equation as operators in the sense of Born and Wiener. If it is assumed that \( H \), the Hamiltonian operator, depends only on the action variable \( J \), then due to the equation of motion (i.e., \( \dot{w} = \partial H/\partial J \)) the time derivative of the angle \( w \) does not depend on time either. Thus, Heisenberg could write down the expression  
\[
w = t \cdot \omega(D) + w_1(D), \tag{255}
\]  
for \( w \), where the operator \( \omega(D) \) denotes the frequency of the atomic system (multiplied by \( 2\pi \)) and \( w_1(D) \), the angle at time \( t = 0 \), both quantities being independent of \( t \). The Cartesian coordinates, \( x \) and \( y \), representing the motion, as well as their conjugate momenta, \( p_x \) and \( p_y \), are periodic functions in time, being proportional to the exponential function \( \exp(iw\tau) \), where \( \tau ( = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots) \) is a positive or negative integer. The action variable \( J \) then assumes only the discrete values, \( J_n = \text{const.} + n(h/2\pi) \), \( n \) being a positive integer. By considering the time derivatives of the periodic variables, Heisenberg obtained the relation  
\[
\frac{d}{dt} [\exp(iw\tau)] = \frac{2\pi i}{h} \left[ H(J) - H\left(J - \tau \frac{h}{2\pi}\right) \right] \cdot \exp(iw\tau), \tag{256}
\]  
which includes, provided (\( \tau w \)) is interpreted as the transition frequency from the stationary state \( J \) to the state \( J - \tau h/2\pi \), Bohr’s frequency condition.\(^{335}\)  

Equation (256) and the fact that the action variable \( J \) assumes discrete values, separated by integral multiples of \( (h/2\pi) \), showed that an operator scheme of action-angle variables, as proposed by Heisenberg, would indeed yield the desired quantum-theoretical results for periodic systems. The important question still remained whether it was justified to regard the Hamiltonian operator as a function of the action variable only, that is, \( H = H(J) \). If the answer was affirmative, and Heisenberg had little doubt that it was, he could prove his earlier assumption concerning the average value of \( \dot{\phi} \) (namely, that it depended on the principal quantum number alone). Then he would be permitted to calculate the average values of \( r^{-2} \) and \( r^{-3} \) for the hydrogen atom as he had indicated in his letter to Pauli on 7 January.  

\(^{335}\) To prove Eq. (256), Heisenberg started from the expression  
\[
\frac{d}{dt} \exp(iw\tau) - \exp(iw\tau) \frac{d}{dt},
\]  
which according to Eq. (237), the equation of motion in operator mechanics, gives the time derivative of the variable \( \exp(iw\tau) \) (taking into account the operator identity, Eq. (239)). Then he expanded \( \exp(iw\tau) \) in powers of \( w \), and differentiated the powers of \( w \) with respect to time. Thus, he finally obtained for the above expression the result  
\[
\left[ i\tau \frac{\partial H}{\partial J} + \frac{h}{2\pi i} \frac{\tau^2}{2} \frac{\partial^2 H}{\partial J^2} - i\left( \frac{h}{2\pi i} \right)^2 \frac{\tau^3}{3!} \frac{\partial^3 H}{\partial J^3} + \dots \right] \exp(iw\tau),
\]  
which could be reformulated as the right-hand side of Eq. (256).

**Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics**  

In the meantime, Pauli, who shared Heisenberg’s interest in developing a complete theory of the hydrogen atom (that is, a relativistic hydrogen atom with or without electron spin), ‘had not remained idle’ (‘Ich war inzwischen auch nicht müβig,’ Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926). He had himself pursued a systematic formalism for treating action-angle variables. Unlike Heisenberg, he did not employ the operators of Born and Wiener. ‘The introduction of the “operators,”’ he commented in a letter to Heisenberg, ‘is at any rate superfluous for many purposes. They are related to the calculus with functions of “time” and energy—which I shall sketch in the following—just as the theory of principal-axes transformation [is related] to your matrix calculus. I am glad to have the operators behind me, and shall now happily go on with my calculations’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926).\(^{336}\)  

The principal idea involved in Pauli’s formulation was to represent the dynamical variables in quantum mechanics by functions of time \( t \) and energy \( W \); for instance, a position coordinate by \( q(t, W) \). Argued Pauli: ‘The only essential thing is that the quantities \( q(t, W) \) must be considered as continuous functions of the energy, as soon as one deals with non-periodic quantities besides periodic quantities’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926). Although the functions \( q(t, W) \) were formally identical with Born and Wiener’s generalized column-sums (which they had denoted by the same letters), Pauli gave them a quite different meaning. In particular, he remarked: ‘In general the “time” \( t \) has, however, no real physical significance, but only a formal one. For nonperiodic quantities \( q(t, W) \) the connection with observable phenomena remains an open question; there is no harm in this, if finally everything reduces again to periodic quantities \( x \), with the \( x(t, W) \) representing the sums of columns of matrices’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926). Pauli emphasized the different, formal significance of the ‘time’ variable in his scheme by *postulating the fundamental commutation relation*  
\[
Wt - tW = \frac{h}{2\pi i} 1 \tag{257}
\]  
between \( t \) and the energy \( W \). Pauli conceived Eq. (257) as a generalization of a matrix equation, as is evident from the use of the factor 1 (denoting something like a unit quantity) on the right-hand side. The energy variable, \( W \), embraces all possible energy values of the system. If it could be represented by a matrix, \( W \) would have to be identified with \( (W_m\delta_{mn}) \), the matrix obtained by diagonalizing the Hamiltonian matrix of the system, and Eq. (257) would be a genuine matrix equation.\(^{337}\)  

\(^{336}\) There is little doubt that Pauli thought that the operator formalism was again part of Born’s formal erudition. He believed that he could develop a method serving the same purpose (namely, to deal with aperiodic variables), but ‘simpler and better than that of Born and Wiener’ (Pauli to Bohr, 5 February 1926).  

\(^{337}\) Equation (257) can be derived in Born and Wiener’s operator mechanics from the commutation relation of \( t \) and \( D ( = d/dt) \) and the relation between the Hamiltonian operator \( H \) and \( D \), Eq. (239). The idea that the time variable \( t \) might enter into quantum mechanics in a more ‘formal’ manner than in classical mechanics occupied Pauli for some time. He mentioned it first in a letter to Niels

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0254 -->

**V.4 Action-Angle Variables and the Method of Complex Integration**  
251  

In contrast to Born and Wiener, who had embarked upon the formulation of a completely new mathematical scheme of quantum mechanics, Pauli wanted to stick as closely to matrix mechanics as the physical situation would allow, for he believed that the relations governing the dynamical variables, as represented by matrices, were well defined, and their interpretation in terms of empirical facts was clear. Thus, he proceeded to develop his formalism (or ‘Kalkül’) first for his description of a system which had the discrete energy eigenvalues \( W_n \), and whose position coordinate was represented by all possible matrix elements, \( q(n, n - \tau) \cdot \exp[2\pi i \nu(n, n - \tau)t] \), where \( \tau \) assumed positive and negative integral values. ‘In order also to be able to calculate with non-periodic quantities (as, for instance, polar angles), we must pay the price that the discontinuous index \( n \) is replaced by as many continuous variables as the number of degrees of freedom which the system possesses’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926). Restricting himself to systems of one degree of freedom, he replaced the discrete quantities, \( x(n, n - \tau) \) and \( \nu(n, n - \tau) \), denoting respectively, the amplitudes and transition frequencies in the matrix scheme, by \( x_\tau(W) \) and \( \nu_\tau(W) \), i.e., by functions of the (discrete and continuous) energy \( W \). Then he represented \( x \), say the position variable of the system, by the sum  
\[
x(t, W) = \sum_{\tau = -\infty}^{+\infty} x_\tau(W) \exp[2\pi i \nu_\tau(W)t], \tag{258}
\]  
where the underlined exponential function had the special properties  
\[
\frac{d}{dt} \{ \underline{\exp}[ f(W)t ] \} = f(W) \underline{\exp}[ f(W)t ] \tag{258a}
\]  
and  
\[
\frac{d}{dW} \{ \underline{\exp}[ f(W)t ] \} = \frac{df(W)}{dW} \underline{\exp}[ f(W)t ] \cdot t. \tag{258b}
\]  

Pauli emphasized that ‘only the \( x_\tau(W) \) possess physical significance via their transition probabilities,’ and he thought that \( t \) and \( \underline{\exp}[2\pi i \nu_\tau(W)t] \) were ‘for the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0255 -->

252  
**Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics**  

moment symbols without physical significance’ which just served to permit the multiplication of two quantities, \( x(t, W) \) and \( y(t, W) \). Making use of the commutation relation between \( W \) and \( t \), Eq. (257), he derived the multiplication law  
\[
xy(t, W) = \sum_\tau (xy)_\tau(W) \underline{\exp}[2\pi i \nu_\tau(W)t], \tag{259}
\]  
where the coefficient of the exponential factor was given by the equation  
\[
(xy)_\tau(W) = \sum_\sigma x_\sigma(W)y_{\tau - \sigma}(W - \nu_\sigma(W)h). \tag{259a}
\]  

Equation (259a) agreed perfectly with the multiplication law for the matrix amplitudes. In addition, the relation  
\[
\nu_{\sigma + \tau}(W) = \nu_\sigma(W) + \nu_\tau(W - \nu_\sigma(W)h), \tag{259b}
\]  
representing the frequency combination law, was valid.  

Having thus shown that his formalism, based on the functions \( x(t, W) \) provided a suitable extension of the matrix description of periodic variables, Pauli turned to the problem of introducing action-angle variables for periodic systems of one degree of freedom. Assuming that the energy of the system, following a canonical transformation of the variables, could be written as a function of \( J \), the action variable, alone, that is, \( W = W(J) \), he sought to represent the angle variable \( w \) by the equation  
\[
w = \omega(J) \cdot t + w_1(J), \tag{260}
\]  
where the factor \( \omega(J) \)—which, apart from a factor \( 2\pi \), is a frequency—is determined by the equation of motion  
\[
\omega(J) = \dot{w} = \frac{\partial W(J)}{\partial J}. \tag{261}
\]  

Equation (260) was completely equivalent to Heisenberg’s operator equation (255). Pauli also proved Heisenberg’s commutation relation between \( J \) and \( w \), Eq. (254), with the help of Eq. (257), his commutation relation between \( t \) and \( W \). Finally, he concluded that \( \nu_\tau(W) \), the frequencies occurring in Eq. (258), which in the case of a periodic system of one degree of freedom, depended on the action variable alone—that is, \( \nu_\tau(W) = \nu_\tau(J) \)—were the quantum-theoretical transition frequencies.  

Pauli’s formalism for treating action-angle variables was not yet complete, for he did not have a method that would allow him to transform the Hamiltonian of a given periodic system into a function \( W(J) \). However, it was important for him that ‘now the non-periodic coordinates have been stripped of their horror’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926). And he was anxious to apply the new methods to the hydrogen atom to see whether they would work in this case. For the actual

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0256 -->

V.4 Action-Angle Variables and the Method of Complex Integration 253

calculation, in particular to obtain the energy eigenvalues as functions of the action variable $J$, Pauli found it preferable to extend the perturbation scheme of matrix mechanics. Before, however, he was ready to publish any of his results, he came across a paper of Paul Dirac's dealing with the same problems (Dirac, 1926a). Pauli was disappointed. He had worked hard and fast enough to obtain an elegant formalism for treating action-angle variables, but Dirac had beaten him in the race. Pauli complained to Kramers: 'In the March issue of the *Proceedings of the Royal Society* there is a very beautiful paper of Dirac [Dirac, 1926a], which contains all the results that I have found since Christmas concerning the generalization of the matrix calculus to non-periodic quantities (e.g., polar angles). I regret that in this way I have lost so much time; I could well have done something else meanwhile' (Pauli to Kramers, 8 March 1926). Though Pauli felt that Dirac's paper had rendered most of his efforts on action-angle variables superfluous, he found that 'Dirac's calculations on the H-atom are, however, unnecessarily complicated. It can be done much more simply according to the methods of Wentzel and myself' (Pauli to Kramers, 8 March 1926).

Gregor Wentzel, to whose work Pauli referred to Kramers, spent the winter semester 1925–1926 at the University of Hamburg. He had been a member of Sommerfeld's Institute since 1920, staying on there after obtaining his doctorate in 1921, and had become a *Privatdozent* in 1922. He had worked mainly on the X-ray spectra of atoms, which had also been the subject of his thesis (Wentzel, 1921a), and he had become an expert in this aspect of atomic theory as well as in the theory of spectra of complex atoms.$^{338}$ For instance, in a paper submitted to *Annalen der Physik* in February 1925, Wentzel had thoroughly analyzed the difficulties arising from the current theoretical explanation of doublet spectra (Wentzel, 1925b), and his former teacher, Arnold Sommerfeld, had not hesitated to call this account 'the best that has been written on the *doublet-mystery* of optical and X-ray spectra' (Sommerfeld to Pauli, 18 June 1925). And Pauli, who, having just expounded his exclusion principle, was struggling with the same problem at the same time, had agreed with Sommerfeld (Pauli to Sommerfeld, 22 June 1925). In fall 1925, when Wentzel arrived in Hamburg, Pauli had completed the calculation of the energy states of the hydrogen atom with the help of matrix methods; he was very excited about the Göttingen scheme of quantum mechanics and hoped to exploit the possibility of extending it to deal with more complex atoms. The latter had been treated earlier by employing action-angle variables in the theory of multiply periodic systems. However, the difficulty of being able to represent angles in matrix theory seemed to prevent all progress. Wentzel was a witness when, after certain not very promising attempts of Heisenberg and Pauli, the important new hint as to how to proceed in the case of aperiodic position variables was provided by the operator methods of Born and Wiener and, as a result, Heisenberg and Pauli were able to envisage an action-angle formalism in quantum mechanics. The programme of developing a unified scheme, in which

$^{338}$Gregor Wentzel's background and his contributions to spectroscopy have been mentioned in Volume 1, Section III.4, and footnote 609.

254 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

both periodic and aperiodic motions could be treated, reminded Wentzel of an earlier work of his own on the same problem, a work in which he now discovered certain parallels to the new ideas of Born and Wiener and of Heisenberg and Pauli.

In a paper submitted to *Zeitschrift für Physik* in July 1924, Wentzel had attempted to calculate the properties of X-ray bremsstrahlung spectra, that is, the radiation emitted by electrons moving in hyperbolic orbits around the atomic core or nucleus in accordance with the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure (Wentzel, 1924d). In classical theory, the radiation from an accelerated atom could be obtained from the kinematics of the electron. Wentzel had proposed to take over the same formula into quantum theory, with the only change that the acceleration $\dot{\mathbf{v}}$ was replaced by a vector quantity $\mathbf{q}$.$^{339}$ He had found this quantity in the following way (see Wentzel, 1924d, appendix). For a system of $f$ degrees of freedom a ‘characteristic phase,’ $\phi$, is introduced as

$$\phi = -2\pi \left( \nu t + \sum_{k=1}^{f} j_k u_k \right). \tag{262}$$

In Eq. (262), $\nu$ is the frequency of the quantum transitions from the initial state with energy $W_i$ to the final state with energy $W_f$; the $u_k$, $k = 1, \ldots, f$, denote the averages of the position coordinates of the system between the same states, and the $j_k$ represent the changes in the canonically conjugate variables $I_k$. Then $\mathbf{q}$, the acceleration of the electron in quantum theory, is obtained from the equation

$$\mathbf{q} = \int \ldots \int \dot{\mathbf{v}}(u_k) \exp(-i\phi) dj_1 \ldots dj_f du_1 \ldots du_f, \tag{263}$$

involving the phase $\phi$, Eq. (262), and the classical acceleration $\dot{\mathbf{v}}$, taken as a function of the position coordinate $u_k$, $k = 1, \ldots, f$. All the $2f$ integrals in Eq. (263) extend from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$; that is, the right-hand side is a certain phase-space average of the classical acceleration vector $\dot{\mathbf{v}}$. Because of $\exp(-i\phi)$, the exponential weight function, $\mathbf{q}$ becomes identical with the values of $\dot{\mathbf{v}}$ at those coordinates $u_k$ which satisfy the condition

$$\sum_{k=1}^{f} j_k u_k = -2\pi \nu t. \tag{264}$$

It can be seen that the quantities $j_k$ determine the deviation from classical theory in the following sense: When the changes in the energy $W$ and all $j_k$ are small, $\mathbf{q}$ coincides with $\dot{\mathbf{v}}$, and the classical limit is achieved.$^{340}$ Hence for the

$^{339}$The classical equation expressing the electric field strength $\mathbf{E}$ at the point $\mathbf{r}$ (where $r$ is the distance from the electron's position to the point of observation) is $\mathbf{E} = (e/c^2r)[\hat{\mathbf{n}} \times (\hat{\mathbf{n}} \times \mathbf{v})]$, where $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the unit vector in direction of radiation.

$^{340}$In this limit the integral in Eq. (263) yields, for arbitrary $u_k$, the vector function $\dot{\mathbf{v}}(u_k)$ because condition (264) is automatically satisfied. The reason is that $\nu$ may be replaced by $-(2\pi)^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{f}\partial W/\partial I_k$; hence the right-hand side of Eq. (264) becomes identical with the left-hand side on account of the equations of motion $(\dot{u}_k = \partial W/\partial I_k, k = 1, \ldots, f)$ and the fact that the position variables $u_k$ are linear functions of $t$.

V.4 Action-Angle Variables and the Method of Complex Integration 
255

calculation of the soft (that is, long-wavelength) part of the bremsstrahlung spectra the classical equation may be used. For large values of $j_k$, however, Wentzel had found that this equation could not describe the observed data, but the agreement between theory and experiment was improved when $\dot{v}$ was replaced by $\mathbf{q}$, Eq. (263). On the other hand, by specializing to strictly periodic systems of $f$ degrees of freedom, Wentzel's $I_k$ became the action variables, $J_k$, each of which was quantized; hence the $j_k$ assumed integral values given by $\tau_k = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$ , and the position variables, $u_k$, were to be identified with the angle variables $w_k$. The energy, $W$, now depended only on the $J_k$, and conditions (264) now became

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{f} \tau_k w_k = \frac{1}{h} \left[ W(J_1, \ldots, J_f) - W\left(J_1 - \frac{\tau_1 h}{2\pi}, J_2 - \frac{\tau_2 h}{2\pi}, \ldots, J_f - \frac{\tau_f h}{2\pi}\right) \right] t. \tag{264'} $$

With the help of Eq. (264'), Wentzel's integral, Eq. (263), decomposed into an $f$-fold Fourier sum for $\mathbf{q}$, which could be written as

$$ \mathbf{q} = \sum_{\tau_k} \dot{v}(J_j) \exp(2\pi i \tau_k w_k), \tag{263'} $$

where the $\tau_k$, $k = 1, \ldots, f$, ran to all integral values and the quantum frequencies occurred explicitly in the exponentials because of Eq. (264').<sup>341</sup>

Though Eq. (263') had been derived on the basis of correspondence arguments long before matrix mechanics and operator mechanics made their appearance, it was entirely compatible with the spirit of quantum mechanics. It represented nothing less than a generalization of Pauli's expression (258) to nonperiodic systems of $f$ degrees of freedom. Because of this previous experience with aperiodic motions and his considerable skill in formal, complicated calculations, Wentzel was well prepared to enter into discussions with Pauli on action-angle variables in the beginning of 1926. He quickly mastered the new ideas of matrix and operator mechanics and began to build on Pauli's results on angle variables. He directed his attention primarily to those aspects of the theory which Heisenberg and Pauli had left out of their earlier discussions.<sup>342</sup> He developed a general theory of *multiply periodic* systems and answered, in particular, the question as to how to obtain the energy of these systems as a function depending on the action

---
<sup>341</sup> To calculate the bremsstrahlung intensities, Wentzel had studied the motion of an electron in an elliptical orbit, described by action and angle variables, $J$ and $w$. He had then taken over the equations expressing $J$ and $w$ in terms of the energy $W$ also for the hyperbolic motion, except that $W$ was always replaced by $-W$. With these results he had evaluated Eq. (263).

Note that Wentzel used as angle variables the angles divided by $2\pi$ and action variables multiplied by the same factor.

<sup>342</sup> Since Pauli and Heisenberg had developed their action-angle formalism towards the end of January 1926, and since Pauli was always concerned that nobody should interfere with Heisenberg's plans for quantum mechanics, Wentzel did not start his work on multiply periodic systems before early in February.

256    **Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics**

variable alone. The results pleased Pauli very much, and he wrote to Bohr on 26 February 1926: ‘By the way, Wentzel has performed a very beautiful investigation on the new quantum mechanics.’ A month later *Zeitschrift für Physik* received Wentzel’s paper, entitled ‘*Die mehrfach periodischen Systeme in der Quantenmechanik*’ (‘The Multiply Periodic Systems in Quantum Mechanics’), which was published in its issue of 22 May 1926 (Wentzel, 1926a).

The fundamental equations constituting the quantum theory of multiply periodic systems, described by $f$ angle variables $w_k$ and their canonically conjugate momenta, the $f$ action variables $J_k$, $k = 1, \dots, f$, are provided by the equations of motion

$$ \dot{w}_k = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (W w_k - w_k W) \tag{264a} $$

and

$$ \dot{J}_k = \frac{2\pi i}{h} (W J_k - J_k W), \tag{264b} $$

involving the energy $W$, and by the commutation relations between the dynamical variables, that is,

$$ J_k w_l - w_l J_k = \frac{h}{2\pi i} \delta_{kl} \quad \text{where } \delta_{kl} = 1 \text{ for } k = l, \text{ and } 0 \text{ otherwise,} $$
$$ w_k w_l - w_l w_k = J_k J_l - J_l J_k = 0, \quad k = 1, \dots, f. \tag{265} $$

Provided the energy depends only on the action variables, $J_l$, $l = 1, \dots, f$, every periodic variable—say, the Cartesian coordinates of the system or their conjugate momenta—can be expressed by means of an $f$-fold Fourier sum,

$$ q = \sum_{\tau_k} q_{\tau_k}(J_l) \exp\left[ 2\pi i \sum_k \tau_k w_k \right], \tag{266} $$

where the subscript $\tau_k$ in the sum denotes the set of numbers $(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_f)$. In the special case that $q$ is the acceleration vector $\mathbf{q}$, Eq. (266) becomes identical with Wentzel’s equation (263) of summer 1924. At the same time Eq. (266) generalizes Pauli’s *Ansatz*, Eq. (258), to systems of several degrees of freedom; that is, Pauli’s functions of energy and time have to be identified with Wentzel’s functions of action and angle variables. With the help of the commutation relations, Eqs. (265), Wentzel derived the result that by taking the time derivative of $q$ one reproduces a Fourier sum whose terms are identical with the terms on the right-hand side of Eq. (266)—i.e., the Fourier terms of $q$—multiplied by the factor $2\pi i \nu_{\tau_k} t$, where $\nu_{\tau_k}$ are the quantum frequencies satisfying the equations

$$ \nu_{\tau_k} = \frac{1}{h} \left[ W(J_k) - W\left( J_k - \frac{\tau_k h}{2\pi} \right) \right], \quad \tau_k = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots \tag{267} $$

V.4 Action-Angle Variables and the Method of Complex Integration 257

Again Eq. (267) generalizes Pauli’s result for periodic systems of one degree of freedom.³⁴³ From it Wentzel concluded: ‘If one requires, in addition, that the $J$’s form a “closed set,” it follows at once that they assume discrete values, separated from each other by integral multiples of $h/2\pi$’ (Wentzel, 1926a, p. 82).³⁴⁴ Finally, again under the assumption that the energy is a function of the action variables alone, i.e., $W = W(J_k)$, and with the help of the commutation relations, Eqs. (265), Wentzel showed that the variables $q$ obey Heisenberg’s multiplication rule for quantum variables.³⁴⁵

One question still remained open in this scheme of action-angle variables: Could general methods be established that would allow for the determination of energy $W$ as a function of the action variables for a given multiply periodic system described by the variables $q_k$ and $p_k$, $k = 1, \dots, f$? The same method would then yield directly, via Eq. (267), the transition frequencies of the system. This question had not been answered thus far in quantum mechanics, not even by Heisenberg and Pauli. Hence Wentzel noted in the introduction of his paper: ‘In Heisenberg’s quantum mechanics [as also in the operator mechanics of Born and Wiener] there still is not available a general procedure for calculating the frequencies of spectral lines independently of their intensities’ (Wentzel, 1926a, p. 80). However, after the introduction of action and angle variables the quantum-mechanical theory of multiply periodic systems showed a great similarity with the previous Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic systems. It now occurred to Wentzel that: ‘Since only the frequencies were determined in the previous quantum theory, one should ask the question: could somehow the old methods not be translated in the language of matrices so that the terms [i.e., energies] can be determined directly in the new theory as well?’ (Wentzel, 1926a, p. 80).

In the classical theory of multiply periodic systems the problem of obtaining the energy, say of a system of $f$ (periodic) degrees of freedom, as a function of the

³⁴³ In order to prove the results, Wentzel started from the equation of motion for the variable $q$, i.e., $\dot{q} = (2\pi i/h)(Wq - qW)$, and took into account that $W = W(J_l)$. Then he proved the validity of the equation $\exp[2\pi i \tau_k w_k] W(J_1, \dots, J_f) = W(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J_k - \tau_k h/2\pi, J_{k+1}, \dots, J_f)$. By substituting it into the right-hand side of the equation of motion, he obtained the result $Wq - qW = (2\pi i/h)[W(J_k) - W(J_k - \tau_k h/2\pi)]q$. Since the left-hand side may be identified with $2\pi i \nu_{\tau_k}$, Eq. (267) follows.

³⁴⁴ The postulate that all values, which an action variable $J_k$ can assume, form a ‘closed set’ was, of course, a consequence of Born and Wiener’s postulate stating that the set of functions, $\{x(t)\}$, associated with quantum-mechanical operators, was closed. This postulate then allowed one to determine the values of $J_k$ up to a constant, i.e., $J_k = \tau_k h/2\pi + \text{const.}$, where the constant had to be determined from the properties of the system under investigation. (For instance, it could be calculated from the boundary conditions imposed on the system.)
Note that Wentzel, in his paper, took action variables which were $2\pi$-times our variables $J_k$; thus, his discrete $J_k$ were separated by integral multiples of $h$ rather than of $h/2\pi$. As a result, Wentzel’s angular variables, $w_k$, were $2\pi$-times smaller than the ones used above. We have not followed his choice in order to keep the notation of action-angle variables uniform throughout this chapter.

³⁴⁵ For example, the square of a variable $q$ is represented by the $f$-fold Fourier sum, $q^2 = \sum_{\tau_k} q^2_{\tau_k}(J_l) \exp[2\pi i \sum \tau_k w_k]$, where the coefficient $q^2_{\tau_k}(J_l)$ is given by the expression

$$q^2_{\tau_k}(J_l) = \sum_{\sigma_k} q_{\sigma_k}(J_l) q_{\tau_k-\sigma_k} \left( J_1 - \frac{\sigma_1 h}{2\pi}, J_2 - \frac{\sigma_2 h}{2\pi}, \dots, J_f - \frac{\sigma_f h}{2\pi} \right).$$

258 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

action variable $J_k$ alone, is solved with the help of the Hamiltonian–Jacobi partial differential equation for the action function $S$. (See Eq. (129) for systems having one degree of freedom.) This function depends on the original position variables $q_k$ and the transformed momentum variables, $J_k$, $k = 1, \dots, f$, and may be defined by the equation

$$dS = \sum_{k=1}^{f} p_k dq_k + \sum_{k=1}^{f} w_k dJ_k, \quad\quad (268)$$

expressing the total differential of $S$ by sums of terms, $p_k dq_k$ and $w_k dJ_k$, where the $p_k$ are considered to be functions of the $q_k$ and $J_k$. The action function $S$ provides a canonical transformation from the original set of dynamical variables, $p_k$ and $q_k$, to the action-angle variables, $J_k$ and $w_k$. Expressed in terms of the action-angle variables, the Hamiltonian will depend only on the $J_k$, which are constants of motion; hence the energy of the system will be given in terms of the values of the action variables. Thus, the energy of a classical system can be obtained, and it was this procedure which Wentzel wanted to reformulate in quantum theory.

In quantum theory all canonical transformations from one complete set of dynamical variables of a given system into another complete set—according to the investigations of Born, Heisenberg and Jordan (1926, Chapter 1, Section 4)—were unitary transformations. Since the angle variables did not admit of a matrix representation, Wentzel reformulated the classical action function not as a unitary matrix but as a more general object, say of the type of a unitary operator in the language of Born and Wiener (i.e., an operator which when multiplied by its Hermitian conjugate yields the unit operator), or of Pauli's functions of energy and time, or as the $q$-number objects of Paul Dirac.$^{346}$ By referring to the analogy argument, according to which the differential expressions of classical mechanics are always replaced by the differences of products in quantum mechanics, Wentzel suggested that the quantum-mechanical action function satisfies the following two sets of equations:

$$SJ_k - J_kS = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{l=1}^{f} [p_l(q_l J_k - J_k q_l) + (q_l J_k - J_k q_l)p_l] \quad\quad (269a)$$

and

$$Sq_k - q_kS = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{l=1}^{f} [w_l(J_l q_k - q_k J_l) + (J_l q_k - q_k J_l)w_l], \quad\quad (269b)$$

$^{346}$Wentzel, in his published paper (Wentzel, 1926a), did not at all refer to the article of Born and Wiener (1926) from which Pauli's considerations on action-angle variable had taken their point of departure. Rather, he quoted the work of Dirac (1926a), which dealt with action-angle variables in the $q$-number scheme. Dirac's methods were indeed closer to Wentzel's own thinking than the operator methods of Born and Wiener. It should be emphasized, however, that Wentzel had obtained his results concerning the calculation of the energy states of multiply periodic systems already at the end of February (see Pauli to Bohr, 26 February 1926), i.e., before he had seen Dirac's paper.

**Figure 1**  Sommerfeld's Complex Phase-Integral Evaluation.

of the degrees of freedom of the atomic system under investigation, the radial momentum $p_r$ always assumed the form

$$p_r = \left( A + \frac{2B}{r} + \frac{C}{r^2} \right)^{1/2}, \tag{272}$$

with $A$, $B$ and $C$ the constants of integration, depending on the angular momentum and the energy. The functions (272) were not analytic on the real axis, where they possessed, for instance, a cut extending from $r_{\text{min}}$ to $r_{\text{max}}$. Therefore, the closed path in the integral on the right-hand side of Eq. (271) could not be carried out on the real axis, but had to pass from the first branching point, $r_{\text{min}}$, into the complex plane of $r$ on one Riemannian sheet, that is, a little below the real axis, until the second branching point, $r_{\text{max}}$, was reached; then the path returned from $r_{\text{max}}$ on the other Riemannian sheet of the square-root function, that is, a little above the real axis to $r_{\text{min}}$. This path is denoted by (I) in Fig. 1. Sommerfeld had proposed to evaluate the integral (271) according to the rules of complex integration as follows. He turned the original path (I) into a large circle (C), within which all singularities were contained. Then the integral along the path (C) contributed nothing to the right-hand side of Eq. (271). But this was not the entire result of the integration; there still remained integrations to be carried out along the paths (II') and (II''), which encircled the point singularities of the integral $p_r$, Eq. (272), lying at $r = 0$ and $r = \infty$, in the opposite sense of the original path (I). Their contribution was obtained from the residue formula (i.e., according to Cauchy's integral theorem) as

$$\Delta S_r = -2\pi i [\text{Res}(0) + \text{Res}(\infty)], \tag{273}$$

where $\text{Res}(0)$ denotes the residue of $p_r$ at $r = 0$ and $\text{Res}(\infty)$ the residue at $r = \infty$, which are the coefficients multiplying the first inverse power in the Laurent series for $p_r$ around the points $r = 0$ and $r = \infty$, respectively.
