Wentzel recognized that a similar situation arose in his theory of multiply
periodic systems (Wentzel, 1926a, §3). When the quantum system is separable in
the quantum variables, \( p_k \) and \( q_k \), such that each \( p_k \) becomes a function of the
conjugate variable \( q_k \) only, then the quantum-mechanical action function also
becomes a sum of individual terms, \( S_k \), \( k = 1, \ldots, f \). Every \( S_k \) satisfies the \( f \)
equations,

\[ S_k J_l - J_l S_k = \frac{1}{2} [ p_k(q_k J_l - J_l q_k) + (q_k J_l - J_l q_k) p_k ], \quad l = 1, \ldots, f, \quad (274) \]

which follow from Eq. (269a) and the commutation relations between \( p_k \) and \( q_k \).
Since the dependence of the momentum \( p_k \) on the coordinate \( q_k \) of a separable
system in quantum mechanics is the same as in the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory, \( p_k \)
may be expressed as a square root of a function of \( q_k \) similar to Eq. (272). Hence
one has to take into account the cut in the complex plane associated with the
quantum variable \( q_k \) when evaluating the periodicity modulus \( \Delta S \), Eq. (270).
Wentzel assumed that in the complex plane associated with the quantum variable
\( q_k \) a theorem similar to Cauchy’s integral theorem would be valid; that is, the
function \( S_k \), defined by Eq. (274), returns to its initial value when the \( q_k \)-path is a
closed curve in the complex plane within whose interior there is no singularity of
the function \( p_k(q_k) \), but it will change its value when the closed \( q_k \)-path encircles
a pole or a cut of the same function. In particular, Wentzel expected that: ‘One
can, therefore, obtain the periodicity modulus of \( S \), defined above, in the
following way. Instead of taking the path around the branch-cut one goes around
the poles of \( p \) in one of the Riemannian sheets, exactly as in Sommerfeld’s
procedure of evaluating the phase-integrals \( \int p \, dq \)’ (Wentzel, 1926a, p. 84).
With this idea in mind, Wentzel first calculated the energy eigenvalues in two
cases in which the results were well known from previous matrix calculations: the
harmonic oscillator (Heisenberg, 1925c; Born and Jordan, 1925b) and the
nonrelativistic hydrogen atom (Pauli, 1926a). Both calculations provided a wel-
come check upon his methods. However, Wentzel was particularly interested in
treating the problem of the relativistic hydrogen atom, in which Pauli had not
gotten anywhere with matrix methods. Wentzel succeeded brilliantly in demon-
strating in this example the power of the action-angle scheme and, especially, of
the reformulated method of complex integration. We shall now turn to it and
present the principal steps of his solution.
In the relativistic hydrogen atom an electron, of rest mass \( m_e \) and charge \( -e \),
moves in a planar orbit (say, in the \( xy \)-plane) around the proton, whose charge is
\( +e \) and whose mass is so much larger than \( m_e \) that its motion can be neglected.
The Hamiltonian, \( H \), of the system is given as a function of the Cartesian
coordinates, \( x \) and \( y \), and their conjugate momenta, \( p_x \) and \( p_y \), by means of the
equation

\[ p_x^2 + p_y^2 = 2m_e \left( H + \frac{e^2}{r} \right) + \frac{1}{c^2} \left( H + \frac{e^2}{r} \right)^2, \quad (275) \]

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0265 -->

where \( r = (x^2 + y^2)^{1/2} \) and \( c \) is the velocity of light *in vacuo*.³⁴⁹ The separation of
the variables had been achieved previously by transforming the Cartesian coordi-
nates and momenta into spherical coordinates, \( r \) and \( \phi \), and momenta, \( p_r \) and \( p_\phi \).
In quantum mechanics the Hamiltonian and the Cartesian dynamical variables
are related formally in the same way as in classical theory; hence Eq. (275) is also
valid for the corresponding quantum variables, \( x \), \( y \), \( p_x \), \( p_y \) and \( H \). Again, one
can introduce spherical variables—the angle \( \phi \) and the angular momentum \( p_\phi \),
defined by Eqs. (212) and (252), respectively, and \( r \) and \( p_r \)—but one has to make
sure that in doing so the commutation relations are satisfied. After carrying out
the transformation to spherical variables one observes two facts: First, the
transformed Hamiltonian does not depend on the angle \( \phi \), as in classical theory;
hence \( p_\phi \) is a *constant of motion*. Second, the quantum-mechanical relativistic
hydrogen atom becomes a separable system in the new variables, in which \( p_r \), the
radial momentum, is given as a function of the radial coordinate \( r \) by the
equation

\[ p_r^2 = A + r^{-1}B + Br^{-1} + \left( C + \frac{1}{4} \frac{h^2}{4\pi^2} \right) r^{-2}, \quad (272') \]

where the coefficients, \( A \), \( B \) and \( C \), depend on \( W \), the energy of the electron
(which replaces \( H \), the Hamiltonian in Eq. (275), and \( p_\phi \), the angular momen-
tum) as³⁵⁰

\[ A = 2m_e W + \frac{W^2}{c^2}, \quad (272'a) \]
\[ B = m_e e^2 \left( 1 + \frac{W}{m_e c^2} \right), \quad (272'b) \]
\[ C = -p_\phi^2 + \frac{e^4}{c^2}. \quad (272'c) \]

Then, with the help of Eqs. (274), Wentzel proceeded to calculate the two
terms, \( S_\phi \) and \( S_r \), of the action function, or, more accurately, the periodicity
moduli of \( S_\phi \) and \( S_r \). With the help of Eq. (270), the expressions for \( J_\phi \) and \( J_r \),
the action variables, are then obtained, which, via the coefficients \( A \) and \( B \)—Eqs.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0266 -->

(272'a) and (272'b)—involve the energy \( W \). From these expressions, finally, \( W \)
can be calculated as a function of the action variables, and the problem is solved.
The first part of this programme, the evaluation of the expression for \( J_\phi \),
presented no difficulty: Wentzel simply found that \( J_\phi \) was equal to the angular
momentum \( p_\phi \).³⁵¹ The action function \( S_r \), on the other hand, has to be deter-
mined from the equation³⁵²

\[ S_r J_r - J_r S_r = \frac{1}{2} [ p_r(r J_r - J_r r) + (r J_r - J_r r) p_r ]. \quad (274a) \]

To solve this equation Wentzel used the analytic properties of the momentum \( p_r \)
as a function of \( r \), following from Eq. (272'). Evidently, this function exhibits a
cut starting from one branch point, \( r = r_{\min} \), to the other, \( r = r_{\max} \), where \( r_{\min} \)
and \( r_{\max} \) are the extremal values assumed by the radial variable \( r \) for a given \( W \)
and a given angular momentum \( p_\phi \). The situation corresponds exactly to the one
in the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure, where \( p_r \) is expressed by the
right-hand side of Eq. (272). And, just as in the classical case, the quantum-
mechanical function \( p_r \), Eq. (272'), possesses poles for the values \( 0 \) and \( \infty \) of the
variable \( r \). Hence, in the evaluation of the quantum-mechanical function only the
singularities at \( r = 0 \) and \( r = \infty \) will play a role.
The nature of these singularities is recognized from an expansion of \( p_r \) in a
‘quantum mechanical Laurent series,’ that is, a series of terms \( P_n r^n \) or a series of
terms \( r^n P'_n \), where \( n \) assumes positive and negative integral values, and the
coefficients \( P_n \) and \( P'_n \) will depend on expressions \( A \), \( B \) and \( C \), Eqs. (272'a, b, c).
By substituting the Laurent series for \( p_r \) in Eq. (274a), \( S_r \) is obtained as a function
of the radial variable \( r \), the action variable \( J_r \), and the \( P_n \) and \( P'_n \), which may
contain the action variable \( J_\phi (= p_\phi) \) via the coefficient \( C \). This \( S_r \) can also be
expanded in a Laurent series; however, apart from the power terms in the radial
variable, terms proportional to \( \ln r \) have to be added in all those cases in which
the coefficients \( P_{-1} \) and \( P'_{-1} \), multiplying the first inverse power of \( r \) in the
Laurent series for \( p_r \), are not zero. Hence \( S_r \) will assume the form

\[ S_r = \frac{1}{2} ( P_{-1} \ln r + \ln r P'_{-1} + \ldots ), \quad (276) \]

where the dots denote the power terms in \( r \).³⁵³ Now the latter do not contribute

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0267 -->

to the change of the action function \( S_r \) when the variable \( r \) goes through a full
period, while the logarithmic terms give \( \Delta S_r \), that is,

\[ \Delta S_r = \pm \pi i (P_{-1} + P'_{-1}). \quad (273') \]

Equation (273'), when applied to all poles of the function \( p_r \), Eq. (272'), represents
the quantum-mechanical analogue of the classical Eq. (273); it states that the
periodicity modulus, \( \Delta S_r \), can be obtained with the help of the same ideas that
were contained in Sommerfeld’s evaluation by the complex integration method of
the phase integral (271) with the momentum \( p_r \), Eq. (272). The sign of \( \Delta S_r \) has to
be chosen in agreement with the classical limit, as will be seen below.
In the case of the relativistic hydrogen atom there are two singularities or
poles of the function \( p_r(r) \), at \( r = 0 \) and \( r = \infty \), and the terms \( n = -1 \) (the
‘residue’ terms) in the quantum-mechanical Laurent series are found to be

\[ P_{-1} = \sqrt{C} - \frac{1}{2} \frac{h}{2\pi i}, \quad P'_{-1} = \sqrt{C} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{h}{2\pi i} \quad (277a) \]

for the pole at \( r = 0 \), and

\[ P_{-1} = P'_{-1} = + \frac{B}{\sqrt{A}} \quad (277b) \]

for the pole at \( r = \infty \). Hence the periodicity modulus of \( S_r \) is given by the
equation³⁵⁴

\[ \Delta S_r = 2\pi J_r = 2\pi \left( \frac{B}{\sqrt{-A}} \right) - (\sqrt{-C}). \quad (273'a) \]

Wentzel noted that: ‘This, together with Eqs. [(272'a, b, c)], is exactly the formula
from which Sommerfeld derived the fine structure of the Balmer series. It is true
that we have been able to substantiate this formula here only in the first
relativistic approximation; the higher approximations should, according to this
method, be calculable only with great computational work’ (Wentzel, 1926a,
p. 94).³⁵⁵ All one had to do to obtain the fine-structure formula was, of course, to

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0268 -->

268 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

evaluate consistently (in quantum mechanics) the averages, $\overline{r^{-2}}$ and $\overline{r^{-3}}$, occurring in Eqs. (279b) and (279c). This task involved an extension of the matrix scheme to include also a treatment of aperiodic variables, such as the angle variables. During January 1926 Heisenberg and Pauli, following the hints from Born and Wiener’s operator scheme, had been able to develop the quantum-mechanical action-angle theory far enough that they could apply it for the purpose of calculating the desired average values. In particular, for a one-electron atom (with atomic number $Z$) whose electron had the angular momentum $p_\phi$, they had obtained the results

$$ \left( \overline{\frac{1}{r^2}} \right) = m_e \frac{\overline{\dot{\phi}}}{p_\phi} , \quad \text{and} \quad \left( \overline{\frac{1}{r^3}} \right) = \left( \overline{\frac{1}{r^2}} \right) \frac{e^2 Z m_e}{p_\phi^2 - \frac{1}{4}(h/2\pi)^2} , \quad (281) $$

where $\overline{\dot{\phi}}$ denoted the average over a full period (of the unperturbed motion of the electron) of the time derivative of the angle $\phi$ (the canonically conjugate variable to the angular momentum $p_\phi$). The value of $\overline{\dot{\phi}}$ was given by the time derivative of the variable $w$, the canonically conjugate variable to the action variable $J (= nh)$ of the unperturbed atom, that is,

$$ \overline{\dot{\phi}} = \dot{w} = - \frac{\partial H_0}{\partial J} = + \frac{4\pi R Z^2}{n^3} , \quad (282) $$

where $R = 2\pi^2 e^4 m_e / h^3$ is Rydberg’s constant (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 27 January 1926). Since $\overline{\dot{\phi}}$ was thus found to be independent of the angular momentum $\mathbf{k}$ of the atom, a difficulty arose with the magnetic perturbation term, Eq. (279b), in the lowest state of the atoms; namely, in the $s$-state the denominator $p_\phi^2 - \frac{1}{4}(h/2\pi)^2$—which is equal to $k(k+1)(h/2\pi)^2$, with $k$ the quantum number of the angular momentum $\mathbf{k}$ of the electron—in the expression for $\overline{r^{-3}}$ becomes zero and $H_2$ consequently infinite. ‘For the [Uhlenbeck–] Goudsmit theory, however, this result is very sad,’ Heisenberg commented on it in a letter to Pauli. ‘If you have an idea, do please write to me; I don’t know what to do with the Zeeman effects without Goudsmit [i.e., without the spin hypothesis]’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 27 January 1926).

Pauli agreed with Heisenberg’s calculations and the conclusions he had drawn from them. ‘Therefrom it follows,’ he wrote back, ‘first, that the numbers for the sum $E_{\text{rel}} + E_{\text{mag}}$ [Pauli’s $E_{\text{rel}}$ and $E_{\text{mag}}$ were the quantum-mechanical terms $H_2$ and $H_3$, Eqs. (279b) and (279c), respectively] following from our equations are certainly completely inconsistent with the observations ... Hence it appears that on the basis of quantum mechanics the fine structure does not come out correctly either with the [Uhlenbeck–] Goudsmit electrons or with point electrons [i.e., the electrons without “proper” rotation and intrinsic magnetic moment]!’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926).

A few days later, in a letter to Niels Bohr, Pauli reported ‘of the great catastrophe, to which the new quantum mechanics leads concerning the fine

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0269 -->

269 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

structure’ of the hydrogen atom (Pauli to Bohr, 1 February 1926). Pauli’s ‘catastrophe’ was the fact that, in his letter to Bohr of 3 February 1926, he wrote: ‘it follows from our equations, as far as one can see, that in no case does the fine-structure formula come out correctly ... with $\alpha = 1$ one would obtain the formula for point electrons and with $\alpha = 2$ one would obtain the formula for electrons with magnetic moment $\mu = e/2m_e c$’ (Pauli to Bohr, 3 February 1926). The fine-structure formula in question, which can be derived from Eqs. (279b) and (279c), is given by

$$ E^{(1)} = \frac{W^2}{2m_e c^2} \left( -\frac{1}{n^4} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{n^3 \left( k + \frac{1}{2} \right)} \right) \qquad \text{for } \alpha = 1 \text{ or } 2, \tag{283} $$

where $W$ is the energy of the unperturbed hydrogen atom. Since, as Pauli remarked, neither value for $\alpha$ produced the observed fine structure, Pauli concluded that ‘on the basis of quantum mechanics the fine structure does not come out correctly either with the [Uhlenbeck–] Goudsmit electrons or with point electrons [i.e., the electrons without “proper” rotation and intrinsic magnetic moment]!’

The solution of this problem was found by L. H. Thomas in March 1926 (Thomas, 1926; see also Pauli to Bohr, 17 April 1926). Thomas, starting from a relativistic kinematics of the electron, showed that the spin of the electron, which rotates with respect to a fixed coordinate system, would precess even in a fixed (e.g., central) field; this precession of the spin vector $\mathbf{s}$ with respect to the orbital motion of the electron is caused by the fact that the coordinate system attached to the moving electron is not an inertial system. Thus, the electron possesses a magnetic moment $\mu$, which undergoes a precession in the internal magnetic field of the atom; this Thomas-Wigner precession contributes to the fine-structure splitting an amount which is just half of the splitting given by Eq. (279b). This means that the magnetic contribution to the fine-structure splitting is reduced by a factor of 2, thus making the value of $\alpha$ in Eq. (283) equal to $3/2$, in perfect agreement with the observation (see also Goudsmit, (1925) and Breit, (1928)). The Thomas precession is a purely kinematic effect and was already known in classical mechanics (Thomas, 1926; Wigner, 1939; see also Pauli, 1948, p. 71 and note 22). In his 1926 paper, Thomas, who did not refer to Goudsmit’s work, derived his precession formula by an explicit calculation; the effect, however, had already been taken into account by Goudsmit in his 1925 thesis, although he did not derive it explicitly (see also Breit and Condon, 1933).

The fact that the electron possesses an intrinsic magnetic moment $\mu$ means that it also has an anomalous magnetic moment in a magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$. This anomaly was first suggested by Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck in their 1925 paper (see Breit, 1928).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0270 -->

270 V.5 The Electron Spin, Fine Structure and Anomalous Zeeman Effects

In a letter to Bohr of 24 February 1926, Pauli expressed the hope that ‘the doublet structure is just due to the magnetic field of the electron itself’ (Pauli to Bohr, 24 February 1926). This hope was fulfilled by Landé, who suggested that the doublet structure of the alkali spectra is due to the interaction of the spin magnetic moment of the electron with its own orbital motion, which, however, would not be given by the magnetic fine-structure term $H_2$ of Eq. (279b), but by an interaction term which, in Landé’s notation, would be proportional to $(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{s})/r^3$. The fine-structure splitting given by this new mechanism would be

$$ E_{\text{mag}} + E_{\text{rel}} = 2m_e c^2 \left( - \frac{1}{n^2} + \frac{1}{n \left( k + \frac{1}{2} \right)} \right) \qquad \text{for } k = 1, 2, \dots, n. \tag{284} $$

This result, as Pauli wrote in his letter to Bohr of 1 March 1926, ‘agrees with the observations, at least in the alkali spectra’ (Pauli to Bohr, 1 March 1926). As for the Zeeman effect, Pauli wrote to Bohr that ‘Goudsmit’s theory’—as he called it— ‘is now in a position to predict also the Zeeman effects, provided that one makes the assumptions ... that the magnetic moment of the electron is $\mu = e/m_e c \cdot \mathbf{s}$ and that it is not the magnetic field of the nucleus that acts on the magnetic moment of the electron, but only that part of it that is due to the orbital motion of the electron’ (Pauli to Bohr, 1 March 1926). Pauli, however, was still bothered by the fact that, according to the Thomas-Wigner precession, the magnetic contribution to the fine-structure splitting would be reduced by a factor of 2, thus making the total fine-structure splitting proportional to $(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{s})$ rather than $(\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{s})/r^3$. This difficulty was finally resolved by the development of Dirac’s relativistic wave equation of the electron (Dirac, 1928), which, as Pauli later wrote, was able to explain both the Thomas precession and the Landé factor of the electron (Pauli, 1948, p. 21).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0271 -->

271 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

In 1928, Breit derived the fine-structure formula (284) by taking into account the spin of the electron and the Thomas precession (Breit, 1928). Breit’s derivation was based on the interaction of the spin of the electron with its own orbital motion, as suggested by Landé. The resulting fine-structure splitting, in Breit’s notation, is given by

$$ E^{(1)} = - \frac{m_e e^4 Z^4}{2 \hbar^2 n^2} \qquad \text{for } n = 1, 2, \dots \tag{285} $$

and

$$ E^{(2)} = - \frac{m_e e^4 Z^4}{2 \hbar^2 c^2 n^3} \left[ \frac{1}{k + \frac{1}{2}} - \frac{3}{4n} \right] \qquad \text{for } n = 1, 2, \dots \text{ and } k = 1, 2, \dots, n, \tag{286} $$

where the first term $E^{(1)}$ is the nonrelativistic energy and the second term $E^{(2)}$ is the fine-structure correction. The total energy is $E = E^{(1)} + E^{(2)}$. The formula (286) is in perfect agreement with the observations of the hydrogen atom.

As for the anomaly in the Zeeman effect, Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck, in their 1925 paper, had already suggested that the magnetic moment of the electron should be twice as large as the value expected from classical orbital motion. This suggestion was based on the fact that the magnetic moment $\mu$ of the electron should be given by

$$ \mu = \frac{e}{2m_e c} (\mathbf{k} + 2\mathbf{s}) \tag{287} $$

where $\mathbf{k}$ is the orbital angular momentum and $\mathbf{s}$ is the spin angular momentum. The factor of 2 in front of $\mathbf{s}$ is the $g$-factor of the electron spin, which was found to be approximately 2. This result was later confirmed by the Dirac theory (Dirac, 1928), which predicted a $g$-factor of exactly 2 for the electron spin (see also Breit and Condon, 1933).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0272 -->

# V.5 The Electron Spin, Fine Structure and Anomalous Zeeman Effects 269

structure of the hydrogen spectrum' (Pauli to Bohr, 5 February 1926).$^{356}$ He listed in detail the various difficulties which arose in explaining the fine structure in quantum mechanics, both with a point-like electron and an Uhlenbeck-Goudsmit (i.e., spinning) electron, and claimed that neither model accounted for the empirical data; while the point-electron led, in connection with the observed selection rules, to a theoretical inconsistency, the electron with spin yielded quantitatively wrong results. 'The "moral of the story,"' he concluded, 'seems to be in the following: *It is true that one can try to associate with the electron a preferred axis with angular momentum and magnetism; the interaction energy of such an electron with a nucleus, as well as the interaction energy of two such electrons—so far as it deviates from that of point electrons and depends on the orientation of the electron axes—cannot, however, be simply and only represented by magnetic dipoles*' (Pauli to Bohr, 5 February 1926, Pauli's emphasis). In Pauli's view these difficulties—which also included the problems of explaining the singlet-triplet structure of the spectra of helium and alkaline-earth elements quantitatively, as well as the exclusion of several equivalent electrons in atoms—had to do with a problem, noted already by Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, namely, whether an intrinsic angular momentum of the electron of the order of $h/4\pi$ and the small mass of the electron were mutually compatible at all (Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1925, p. 954, second column, footnote 2). Hence he expected that only a treatment of the electron theory on a deeper level would give a satisfactory answer to these questions.

And yet, a more fundamental level of atomic and electron theory, which Pauli envisaged in February 1926, was really not necessary in order to remove the difficulties in the calculation of the fine structure of hydrogen spectral lines. Remarkably enough, Pauli had already indicated the solution of the problem in his letter to Heisenberg at the end of January, when he made what he called 'a totally stupid remark' ('*eine ganz dumme Bemerkung*'): namely, if one assumed the magnetic term arising from the action of the internal field, $H_2$, to have only one-half of the value given in Eq. (279b), then the diagonalization of the matrix replacing the sum $H_2 + H_3$, where $H_3$ is taken from Eq. (279c), would exactly reproduce Sommerfeld's fine-structure formula. But where would one possibly find the necessary factor of $\frac{1}{2}$? 'Therefore: "A half, a half, a kingdom for the factor $\frac{1}{2}$,"' Pauli exclaimed, paraphrasing King Richard's desperate appeal ('*Also: "Ein halb, ein halb, ein Königreich für den Faktor $\frac{1}{2}$,"*' Pauli to Heisenberg, 31 January 1926).

$^{356}$As we have mentioned in Section V.1, Pauli had discussed the spin problem very often with Bohr, both in letters and conversations. Bohr had tried to convince him of the correctness of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit's hypothesis and also suggested certain guesses for the quantum-theoretical values of $H_3$ and $H_2$, notably (see Bohr to Pauli, 24 December 1925) $E_{\text{mag}} = C [\pm \frac{1}{2}/k(k+1)]$ and $E_{\text{rel}} = C(k+\frac{1}{2})/k(k+1)$, with $C = 8\pi^2 Z^2 e^4 m_e / n^3 h^4 c^2$. Pauli, in his reply, had rejected these formulae because of several reasons (Pauli to Bohr, 30 December 1925). First, he argued that the angular momentum quantum number $k$ was zero in an $s$-state and, therefore, the fine-structure splitting would be infinite; second, he insisted on a derivation of the terms $H_2$ and $H_3$ from a quantum-mechanical calculation.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0273 -->

270 # Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

Pauli saw no possibility of getting the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ from the theory, but Llewellyn Hilleth Thomas, a young visitor to Bohr's Institute from Cambridge, England, soon found it.$^{357}$ By a systematic relativistic discussion of the motion of an electron around the atomic nucleus, Thomas noticed that in calculating the internal magnetic field $\mathbf{H}_i$, one was not allowed to substitute, as Heisenberg had done in deriving Eq. (280), simply the nucleus-electron relative velocity $\mathbf{v}$. Rather, the rotational character of the electron's motion had to be taken into account. Thus, Thomas found that the rest frames of the electron (orbiting with velocity $\mathbf{v}$ around the nucleus) at two infinitesimally neighbouring times, $t$ and $t + dt$, could be related to each other by an infinitesimal Lorentz transformation with velocity $d\mathbf{v} = \dot{\mathbf{v}} dt$ plus an infinitesimal rotation described by the axial vector $d\mathbf{w} = (1/2c)(\dot{\mathbf{v}} \times \mathbf{v})dt$ (Thomas, 1926; see also Frenkel, 1926). The field, acting on $\boldsymbol{\mu}$, the intrinsic magnetic moment of the electron, was, therefore, not given by the expression on the right-hand side of Eq. (280), but the term $(m_e c/e)(d\mathbf{w}/dt)$ had to be subtracted from it; that is, the effective internal field was only one-half of the field given by Eq. (280). Consequently, Eq. (279b) for the perturbation term $H_2$ had to be replaced by the equation

$$H_2 = \frac{1}{2} \frac{Ze^2}{m_e^2 c^2} \left( \frac{\overline{1}}{r^3} \right) (\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{s}), \qquad (279b')$$

and the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ that Pauli had searched for in vain was provided.$^{358}$

Niels Bohr, the advocate of the electron spin hypothesis for several months, was extremely happy with Thomas' result and he immediately informed Pauli about it. Thus, on the same day that Thomas completed his note and sent it to *Nature*, Bohr wrote to Pauli:

> Now, however, comes the surprise for the learned relativity theoretician and the scientist laden-with-responsibility [in Danish: "*laerde Relativitetsteoretikere og ansvarsyngeede Videnskabsmaend*," that is, Pauli]. A young Englishman [Llewellyn Hilleth] Thomas, who spent the past half year here, has recently found that the entire problem of the unfortunate factor 2 rests probably exclusively on an error in the calculation of the relativistic motion of the electron and of the nucleus. He has tried to give an elementary presentation of his consideration in a note, which he intends to send to *Nature*, and I enclose a copy of it with the request for severe criticism. (Bohr to Pauli, 20 February 1926)

Pauli studied Thomas' note, but he was not satisfied at all. He especially criticized two facts: that Thomas had not calculated the expression for the energy

$^{357}$L. H. Thomas, born on 21 October 1903 in London, became a student at Cambridge in 1921, obtaining there his B.A. in 1924 and his doctorate in 1927. During winter 1925-1926 he spent several months in Copenhagen as Isaac Newton Student; there he found the general relativistic argument in favour of electron spin. In 1929 he joined Ohio State University as an assistant professor; he was promoted to associate professor in 1930 and made a full professor in 1936. In 1946 he joined the Watson Scientific Computing Center in New York City, and in 1950 became a professor of physics at Columbia University. In his later scientific career, Thomas worked especially on electron distribution in atoms and molecules and on the use of computing machines in solving scientific problems.

$^{358}$Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit had also come across the difficulty concerning the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in connection with the quantitative application of Eq. (279b). (See Bohr to Pauli, 20 February 1926.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0274 -->

# V.5 The Electron Spin, Fine Structure and Anomalous Zeeman Effects 271

term arising from the interaction of the electron's magnetic moment with the internal field explicitly, but only the change of the angular momentum of the electron; and that he had discussed the situation only in frames moving with the electron and not in the frame where the nucleus is at rest. He came to the judgment: 'I hold Thomas' conclusion that, "The difficulty of explaining at the same time the spectral structures *therefore* disappears," to be wrong or at least not to be sufficiently justified ... In any case, I regard the publication of the present note by Thomas in *Nature* as a mistake, and would be glad if you [i.e., Bohr] would prevent it or achieve a substantial change in the text of the note' (Pauli to Bohr, 26 February 1926).

The reason for Pauli's strong verdict was that he did not believe that any kinematical investigation could resolve the difficulty. He emphasized this belief very clearly in his letter to Bohr by saying: 'But I have the strong feeling that in this case absolutely nothing will be achieved by formal learning ("*formaler Gelehrsamkeit*") and that, if the assumption of the magnetic electron really strikes at the truth, a more detailed investigation of the structure of the electron and especially a theory of the electron-mass (eventually by taking into account gravitational fields) will be necessary' (Pauli to Bohr, 26 February 1926). Pauli admitted at the same time that he did not yet have the courage to undertake a study of these profound problems, though he did not consider it an '*a priori* hopeless undertaking' ('*ein von vornherein hoffnungsloses Unternehmen*,' Pauli to Bohr, 26 February 1926). Evidently, Pauli divided the problem connected with the role of the electron's properties in the explanation of atomic spectra into two classes: the *fundamental* problems included the theory of the electron's mass, the basic idea for the calculation of the separation of singlet and triplet terms in the helium spectra, and the physical reasons for the existence of the exclusion principle; a more *modest* task seemed to be to derive the fine structure of the hydrogen atom and the anomalous Zeeman effects from the same unified assumptions concerning the properties of the electron. (See Pauli to Bohr, 5 March 1926.)

Niels Bohr, though he sympathized with Pauli's opinions, nevertheless tried to convince him that Thomas' calculations were correct and had solved the problem of the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ satisfactorily. In particular, he argued that the use of the coordinate reference frames moving with the electron was justified (Bohr to Pauli, 3 March 1926). Still Pauli did not give in; in his letter to Bohr, dated 5 March 1926, he again repeated his objections against Thomas' kinematic treatment, claiming that the transformation of the results from the moving frames of reference to the coordinate system in which the nucleus was at rest might lead back to the old difficulties about the factor $\frac{1}{2}$. A few days later, on 8 March, Samuel Goudsmit, who had spent several weeks in Copenhagen, passed through Hamburg; he brought news about the details of Thomas' calculations for the purpose of finally converting the nonbelieving Pauli. But his efforts failed completely, and Pauli immediately sent a letter to Copenhagen, addressing it this time to Kramers. 'Today Mr. Goudsmit was here and I was very happy to see him,' Pauli wrote. 'What he told me about Thomas' calculations and Thomas'

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0275 -->

272 # Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

manuscripts, which he had brought along, have strengthened my opinion most strongly that I am perfectly right in the arguments, which I have tried to formulate in my last two letters to Professor Bohr' (Pauli to Kramers, 8 March 1926). Even in greater detail than he had written previously to Bohr, he discussed the question of the different coordinate systems, appealing to Kramers' thorough knowledge of relativity theory and requesting him to check the details. 'This time it cannot, I believe,' he wrote, 'be difficult at all to reach an agreement, because we are not dealing with a religious or political matter, indeed not even with a quantum-theoretical question, but rather with a problem of classical physics' (Pauli to Kramers, 8 March 1926).

The last remark was correct: the decision whether Thomas' calculation gave the correct answer or not was based on a classical argument. Pauli also did not have to wait until Kramers replied. The answer was already contained in a letter which Bohr had written soon after receiving Pauli's letter of 5 March. In particular, Bohr had drawn attention to one fact: namely, that the goal of the calculation had been to obtain the average value of the internal magnetic field $H_i$ or the associated perturbation energy; hence it should not matter what specific frame of reference one used, 'for the only thing, about which one can talk by the very nature of the problem, is the change of the orientation of the electron's [angular momentum] vector after one revolution in the electron orbit, where the velocity relative to the nucleus is the same as before [the revolution]' (Bohr to Pauli, 9 March 1926). Then, finally, Pauli gave in:

> Many thanks for your letter of 9 [March] and the enclosed remarks of Thomas [he replied]. Now all that remains for me is to *capitulate completely*! ... In any case, I must now answer both questions of your letter in the sense you desired: 1. Thomas' calculation of the secular change of the electron's axis [i.e., of the electron's angular momentum] is correct in the approximation he considered. 2. Of course, I always had the opinion that the magnitude of this change is decisive for the fine structure. The corresponding energy change of the atom basically states nothing else physically; it must, I believe, always result formally automatically, if one describes the associated secular perturbation by equations of motion of the canonical type. (Pauli to Bohr, 12 March 1926)

The same day Pauli wrote a letter to Kramers, and on 13 March a postcard to Goudsmit, in which he withdrew his reservations against the electron spin hypothesis and acknowledged the correctness of the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in Eq. (279b').

With Pauli's capitulation the path was clear to solve what Bohr and Pauli had called the 'modest' part of the electron problem; namely, to perform quantum-mechanical calculations of the anomalous Zeeman effects and the fine structure of the hydrogen lines. In fact, Heisenberg had reported about these calculations, which he had carried out together with Pascual Jordan, on 15 February 1926 at the meeting of the Lower Saxony Section (*Gauverein Niedersachsen*) of the German Physical Society in Braunschweig.$^{359}$ All one had to do now was to bring

$^{359}$See the announcement of Heisenberg's talk, entitled '*Über die Anwendung der Quantenmechanik auf das Problem der anomalen Zeemaneffekte*' ('On the Application of Quantum Mechanics to the Problem of the Anomalous Zeeman Effects'), in *Verh. d. Deutsch. Phys. Ges.* (3) **7** (1926), p. 13.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0276 -->

in the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ obtained by Thomas. This was done by Jordan, for Heisenberg had left Göttingen after the end of the winter semester for an extended vacation, and a few days after 12 March, the date of Pauli’s capitulation, he (Jordan) sent the joint paper on the anomalous Zeeman effects—which also included the fine structure of hydrogen lines—to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, where it was published three months later (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926).$^{360}$

The main theoretical task, which Heisenberg wanted to achieve in the paper with Jordan, was to calculate the eigenvalues of the quantum-theoretical formulation of the Hamiltonian $H$, Eq. (279), with the perturbation terms given by Eqs. (279a), (279b′) and (279c), and to obtain from them the anomalous Zeeman effects and fine structure of spectral lines. To achieve this goal, the authors proceeded in several steps. First, they studied the question of whether the well-known selection and intensity rules, which had been obtained from the analysis of the anomalous Zeeman effect data, could be derived from the matrix mechanical treatment of the problem. The calculation of the amount of magnetic splitting turned out to be strenuous work, involving as it did the exact evaluation of certain inverse powers of the matrix of the radial variable for realistic three-dimensional atoms. With the extension of the matrix scheme to include angle variables, such as the one developed by Heisenberg and Pauli in January 1926, the authors succeeded in obtaining the desired results, which they summarized in the abstract of their paper in the following words: ‘For explaining the anomalous Zeeman effect, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit have applied Compton’s hypothesis of the rotating electron. In the present paper [we] investigate the quantum mechanical behaviour of the atomic model characterized by this hypothesis. The result is that the Zeeman effects and the fine structures of the doublet spectra can be explained completely by the said hypothesis’ (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926, p. 263).$^{361}$

The actual calculations of Heisenberg and Jordan were straightforward, for they followed exactly the pattern of matrix methods which had been developed

$^{360}$Since Heisenberg was on vacation, he did not immediately receive the news about developments concerning the problem of electron spin. Thus, he did not witness Pauli’s withdrawal of objections against Thomas’ calculation. On 4 April 1926 Heisenberg wrote to Jordan from Munich: ‘Since the day before yesterday I am again back in Germany [probably from a skiing trip to Austria], [and I am] filled with the best will to begin a new life and to understand again something of physics. Could you be so kind as to write to me what you have done with our unhappy work [on the anomalous Zeeman effects], whether you believe in the factor 2 [in the denominator of Eq. (279b′)], and whether you have meanwhile brought into order the radiation theory and all quantum theory of the world?’ Jordan sent him the desired information immediately, especially a copy of the finished manuscript on the anomalous Zeeman effects (which he had already submitted for publication three weeks earlier), and Heisenberg wrote back: ‘I admire your industry in rewriting our clumsy piece of work’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 9 April 1926). Thus, he agreed with Jordan’s final version of the joint paper. Still, he wanted to know more details about the story of the factor 2, for he added: ‘That you do not write to me why Thomas is right with the damned factor 2 is a shrieking scandal’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 9 April 1926).

$^{361}$Heisenberg and Jordan referred here to the fact that already Arthur H. Compton had introduced the idea of a rotating electron in August 1921 (Compton, 1921d). Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit took note of this fact in their later papers (Goudsmit and Uhlenbeck, 1926, p. 625, footnote 2; Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit, 1926, p. 264).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0277 -->

in the three-man paper and in Pauli’s treatment of the hydrogen atom. In order to diagonalize the quantum-mechanical Hamiltonian corresponding to Eqs. (279), (279a), (279b′) and (279c) with the help of perturbation theory, the authors had first to determine the degree of degeneracy of the unperturbed Hamiltonian $H_0$.$^{362}$ Although $H_0$ is degenerate with respect to $\mathbf{k}$, the angular momentum of the electron, that is, the same energy eigenvalues $W_n$ arise for different values of the quantum number $k$ (which runs from $0, 1, 2, \ldots$ to $k_{\text{max}}$, with $k_{\text{max}} = n - 1$, where $n$ is the principal quantum number—see Pauli’s treatment of the hydrogen atom in Section IV.5), for the purpose of calculating the anomalous Zeeman effect one may assume that it is a diagonal matrix in $H_0$. The reason why this assumption can be made is that $H_1$ and $H_2$, the perturbation terms given by Eqs. (279a) and (279b′), respectively, depend only on $\mathbf{k}$ but not on its conjugate (angle) variable; hence already infinitesimally small perturbations of the type $H_1$ or $H_2$ will remove the degeneracy of $H_0$ with respect to the values of $k$ without changing the other properties of the system. $H_0$ is also degenerate with respect to both the values of the spin $\mathbf{s}$ and the values of the total angular momentum $\mathbf{M}$ (composed of $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{s}$). Both of these degeneracies are removed if an infinitely small external magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ is applied in the $z$-direction.

There is, however, still one coordinate of the system with respect to which $H_0$ remains degenerate, as can be seen from Eq. (279b′) for the perturbation term due to the interaction of the spinning electron with the internal field. The expression for $H_2$ contains both $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{s}$ but not their conjugate angle variables. The only angle which occurs is the one between $\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{s}$, due to the scalar product of these vectors; hence one of the angle variables will not be determined, and $H_0$ must be considered degenerate with respect to the degree of freedom described by it. Heisenberg and Jordan chose this angle variable in such a way that $H_0$ became degenerate with respect to the values of $s_z$, the $z$-component of the spin $\mathbf{s}$. Moreover, they observed that since the spin did not occur in the perturbation term $H_3$, Eq. (279c), the perturbation calculation had to be carried out only with the terms $H_1$ and $H_2$, Eqs. (279a) and (279b′). The relativity term $H_3$ thus contributed merely an additive constant to the final result, depending, of course, on the values of $n$ (the so-called principal quantum number) and $k$ which the state under investigation assumed.

Heisenberg and Jordan now turned to the evaluation of $H_1 + H_2$, the sum of the perturbation terms, Eqs. (279a) and (279b′), writing it as

\[
H_1 + H_2 = \mu \frac{2\pi}{h} (k_z + 2 s_z) + \lambda \left( \frac{2\pi}{h} \right)^2 \left[ k_z s_z + \frac{1}{2} (k_x + i k_y)(s_x - i s_y) + \frac{1}{2} (k_x - i k_y)(s_x + i s_y) \right], \tag{283}
\]

$^{362}$In agreement with Heisenberg and Jordan we drop the explicit matrix notation in the present section. Any quantum-theoretical variable which can be represented by a matrix is then assumed to be a matrix without being explicitly identified as such. On the other hand, the quantum-mechanical variables which are not periodic, such as angles, etc., will be written as they normally are; they just do not have proper matrix elements. (See Sections V.3 and V.4.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0278 -->

where

\[
\mu = \frac{h e |\mathbf{H}|}{4\pi m_e c} \quad \text{and} \quad \lambda = \frac{Z e^2 h^2}{8\pi^2 m_e^2 c^2} \left( \frac{\overline{1}}{r^3} \right). \tag{283a}
\]

That is, they assumed the magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ (with the absolute value $|\mathbf{H}|$) to be in $z$-direction and took into account only those transitions which occurred for constant values of the orbital angular momentum $\mathbf{k}$, the spin momentum $\mathbf{s}$ and $M_z$, the $z$-component of the total angular momentum $\mathbf{M}$ ($= \mathbf{k} + \mathbf{s}$), respectively.$^{363}$ The latter values were denoted by $k$ (obtained from $\mathbf{k}^2 = (h/2\pi)^2 k(k + 1)$), by $s$ (obtained from $\mathbf{s}^2 = (h/2\pi)^2 s(s + 1)$) and by $j$ (obtained from $\mathbf{M}^2 = (h/2\pi)^2 j(j + 1)$). Thus, the matrix $\lambda$, which depends on $n$ and $k$, i.e., $\lambda = \lambda(n, k)$, could be replaced by a constant in the following calculations.

According to the angular momentum formalism, the only matrix elements which do not vanish are $k_z(k, m_k; k, m_k)$, $(k_x + i k_y)(k, m_k; k, m_k + 1)$ and $(k_x - i k_y)(k, m_k; k, m_k - 1)$, and $s_z(s, m_s; s, m_s)$, $(s_x + i s_y)(s, m_s; s, m_s + 1)$ and $(s_x - i s_y)(s, m_s; s, m_s - 1)$. Here $m_k$ and $m_s$ denote, respectively, the quantum numbers of $z$-components of the orbital angular momentum (i.e., $k_z = (h/2\pi)m_k$) and of the spin angular momentum (i.e., $s_z = (h/2\pi)m_s$); moreover, one can add $m_k$ and $m_s$ to give $m (= m_k + m_s)$, the quantum number of the total angular momentum. For constant values of $k$, $s$, $j$ and $m$, one obtains the following elements of the perturbation matrix:

\[
(H_1 + H_2)(m_s, m_s) = \mu(m + m_s) + \lambda m_s(m - m_s), \tag{284a}
\]

\[
(H_1 + H_2)(m_s, m_s - 1) = (H_1 + H_2)(m_s - 1, m_s) = \frac{1}{2} \lambda \{ [s(s + 1) - m_s(m_s - 1)] [k(k + 1) - (m - m_s)(m - m_s + 1)] \}^{1/2}. \tag{284b}
\]

For a given set of quantum numbers $k$, $s$ and $m$, the $z$-component of the spin, $s_z$, assumes values $m_s(h/2\pi)$ such that $k + m \geq m_s \geq -k + m$. For instance, if $s = \frac{1}{2}$ (which applies only when one electron is considered) and $m = k + \frac{1}{2}$, with $k$ arbitrary, $m_s$ will assume only the value $\frac{1}{2}$ (because the condition, $-s \leq s_z \leq +s$, also holds), and no degeneracy will arise in this case; the same is true for $m = -k - \frac{1}{2}$. However, when $m$ lies between $-k - \frac{1}{2}$ and $k + \frac{1}{2}$, $m_s$ will always have exactly two values, $+\frac{1}{2}$ and $-\frac{1}{2}$.

In order to calculate the energy contributed to a given state by the interaction of the spinning electron with the magnetic fields, external and internal, Heisenberg and Jordan made use of the perturbation theory of degenerate systems, especially of Eq. (154) derived in the three-man paper. The submatrix of

$^{363}$Note that we have, in agreement with the authors, introduced the notation $\mathbf{M}$ for the total angular momentum.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0279 -->

$H_1 + H_2$, which has to be substituted in Eq. (154), is a $(2 \times 2)$-matrix in the case of $s = \frac{1}{2}$, i.e., for doublet spectra. Hence, with Eqs. (284a) and (284b), one obtains the secular or characteristic equation,

\[
\det \begin{vmatrix}
W - \mu\left(m - \frac{1}{2}\right) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\left(m + \frac{1}{2}\right) & - \frac{\lambda}{2} \left[ k(k + 1) - \left(m + \frac{1}{2}\right)\left(m - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right]^{1/2} \\
- \frac{\lambda}{2} \left[ k(k + 1) - \left(m + \frac{1}{2}\right)\left(m - \frac{1}{2}\right) \right]^{1/2} & W - \mu\left(m + \frac{1}{2}\right) - \frac{\lambda}{2}\left(m - \frac{1}{2}\right)
\end{vmatrix} = 0, \tag{285}
\]

which has the two solutions,

\[
W_m = \mu \left[ m - \frac{v}{4(k + \frac{1}{2})} \pm \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 + 2 \frac{m}{k + \frac{1}{2}} v + v^2 \right)^{1/2} \right], \tag{286}
\]

where

\[
v = \frac{\lambda}{\mu} \left( k + \frac{1}{2} \right), \tag{286a}
\]

provided $m$ does not assume the extremum values $\pm(k + \frac{1}{2})$. If it does, the degeneracy is automatically removed, and the submatrix of $(H_1 + H_2)$ for the states characterized by the quantum numbers $k$, $s = \frac{1}{2}$ and $m = \pm(k + \frac{1}{2})$ contains only one (diagonal) element given by

\[
W_{m = \pm(k + 1/2)} = \mu \left[ \pm(k + 1) + \frac{v}{2} \left( \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{(k + \frac{1}{2})} \right) \right]. \tag{287}
\]

These formulae were identical with the ones obtained by Sommerfeld when he re-interpreted Woldemar Voigt’s equations for the anomalous Zeeman effects in accordance with the Bohr–Sommerfeld theory of atomic structure (Sommerfeld, 1922a; see also Heisenberg, 1922a, p. 284, Eq. (18)).$^{364}$ The theoretical understanding of the anomalous Zeeman effects in the old approach (which we discussed in Volume 1, Chapter IV) was, however, fundamentally different from the present calculation based on quantum mechanics; the coincidence of the results obtained by so different means was, therefore, deemed fortunate. Heisenberg was really ‘excited and enthusiastic about the fact that the old formulae of Voigt actually did come out of quantum mechanics’ (Heisenberg, *Conversations*).

The difference between the methods used by Sommerfeld, on the one hand, and by Heisenberg and Jordan, on the other, showed up in particular in the calculation of the intensities of the Zeeman lines. Voigt had discussed the

$^{364}$In the paper of Heisenberg and Jordan (1926), the first equation (p. 270, Eq. (23)) contained a few errors; for instance, in the denominator of the second term in the bracket one had to insert a factor 4, and the square had to be multiplied by a factor $\frac{1}{2}$.

V.5 The Electron Spin, Fine Structure and Anomalous Zeeman Effects 277

question of line intensities on the basis of the classical electromagnetic theory of emission of light by bound charges, and Sommerfeld had not changed this aspect in his treatment of 1922. In Heisenberg and Jordan's calculation the intensities had to be obtained from the matrix elements of $\mathbf{q}$, the position vector matrix of the orbiting electron. The amplitudes of the radiation emitted from a rotating electron in an unperturbed atom, when a state having the angular momentum $kh/2\pi$ passes into a state of angular momentum $(k-1)h/2\pi$, were proportional to the quantities

$|q_z^0(k, m, m_s; k-1, m, m_s)|^2$, $|(q_x^0 + iq_y^0)(k, m-1, m_s; k-1, m, m_s)|^2$

and

$|(q_x^0 - iq_y^0)(k, m, m_s; k-1, m-1, m_s)|^2$,

respectively. These quantities had been calculated in the three-man paper and could be taken over now (see BHJ, 1926, p. 604, Eqs. (31)–(33)).$^{365}$ The perturbations due to the magnetic fields transform the position matrices from $\mathbf{q}^0$ to $\mathbf{q}$, and also give rise to transitions in which $m_s$ changes by $0, \pm 1$. The matrix $S$, which generates this transformation of the position matrices, especially the particular submatrices of $S$ belonging to a given set of values, $k, s$ and $m$, can be calculated from the perturbation theory of degenerate systems.$^{366}$ Thus, for the transition $k=1$ to $k=0$, $m=\frac{1}{2}$ to $m=\frac{1}{2}$, $m_s=\pm\frac{1}{2}$ to $m_s=\frac{1}{2}$, Heisenberg and Jordan obtained the result (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926, p. 272, Eq. (30))

$$ \left|q_z\left(1, \frac{1}{2}, \pm \frac{1}{2} ; 0, \frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)\right|^2 = \frac{1}{2} |A(1)|^2 \left[ 1 \pm \frac{\mu^2 + \frac{1}{2}\lambda}{\left(\mu^2 + \lambda\mu + \frac{9}{4}\lambda^2\right)^{1/2}} \right], \quad (288) $$

$^{365}$Note that $m$ in the three-man paper (BHJ, 1926, p. 604, Eqs. (31)–(33)) has to be replaced by $m_k = m - m_s$.
$^{366}$For example, Heisenberg and Jordan calculated the submatrix of the transformation matrix $S$, by means of which the submatrix of $(H_1 + H_2)$, associated with a given set of quantum numbers $k, m$ and $s = \frac{1}{2}$, was diagonalized. They then obtained for the matrix elements the result (see Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926, p. 271, Eqs. (26))

$$ S_{-1/2, -1/2} = C_{-1/2} \frac{\lambda}{2} \left[ k(k+1) - \left(m^2 - \frac{1}{4}\right) \right]^{1/4}, $$

$$ S_{-1/2, +1/2} = C_{+1/2} \frac{\lambda}{2} \left[ k(k+1) - \left(m^2 - \frac{1}{4}\right) \right]^{1/2}, $$

$$ S_{+1/2, -1/2} = \frac{1}{2} C_{-1/2} \left\{ \mu + \lambda m - \left[ \mu^2 + 2\lambda\mu m + \lambda^2\left(k + \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \right]^{1/2} \right\}, $$

$$ S_{+1/2, +1/2} = \frac{1}{2} C_{+1/2} \left\{ \mu + \lambda m + \left[ \mu^2 + 2\lambda\mu m + \lambda^2\left(k + \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \right]^{1/2} \right\}, $$

where the coefficients $C_{-1/2}$ and $C_{+1/2}$ depend only on $k$ and $m$. (Evidently, the suffixes $\pm \frac{1}{2}$ denote the matrix indices associated with the values of the spin quantum numbers $m_s$, i.e., the submatrix $S$ is written as $(S_{m_s, m_s})$.)

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0281 -->

278 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

where $A(1)$ is a factor characteristic of the state with angular momentum $k=1$. The intensity of the corresponding transition line (parallel to the external field $\mathbf{H}$) is proportional to expression (288), which again agreed completely with Sommerfeld's earlier result (Sommerfeld, 1922a, p. 266).
Heisenberg and Jordan's matrix calculation, in the case of $s = \frac{1}{2}$, accounted perfectly for the observations of the anomalous Zeeman effect in alkali doublets, and all the expressions obtained were equivalent to Sommerfeld's successful formulae of 1922. The new theory described equally well the situation for the spectra of alkaline earths. The latter have series of singlet and triplet spectral lines when no external magnetic field is present, which may be readily explained by assuming that the spin angular momenta of the two outer electrons (responsible for the radiation) either subtract from each other to give $s=0$ or add up to give $s=1.$^{367}$ It is not difficult to show that the application of the matrix mechanical perturbation scheme to the triplet system leads, in general, to a cubic characteristic equation for the eigenvalues of $W_m$, the magnetic perturbation energy; that is, each set of states denoted by the quantum numbers, $k, m$ and $s$ (where $s$ assumes the value 1), is normally split by the perturbation into three states according to the three different values of $m_s$ ($= -1, 0, +1$). Similar considerations apply to the higher multiplets. In the case of the singlet, however, one may disregard the spin altogether.
Heisenberg was also happy to derive another result, a 'summation principle' ('*Summationsprinzip*'), from the equations of perturbation theory. Let $m_1$ be the smallest and $m_2$ the largest value of $m_s$ admitted for a state described by the set of quantum numbers, $k, s$ and $m$, then it follows from the corresponding characteristic equation that the sum of the energy terms is given by the equation$^{368}$

$$ \sum_{m_s=m_1}^{m_2} W_{m_s} = \sum_{m_s=m_1}^{m_2} \left[ \mu(m_s + m_1) + \lambda m_s(m - m_s) \right]. \quad (289) $$

The right-hand side of this equation depends linearly on $\mathbf{H}$, the field strength of the external field. Heisenberg had already arrived at this 'summation principle' in the special case of doublets and triplets in his very first treatment of the anomalous Zeeman effects (Heisenberg, 1922a).
Heisenberg and Jordan drew further conclusions applicable to all multiplets, that is, independent of the specific system under investigation, by considering perturbation Hamiltonians, Eq. (283), in cases when either $\lambda \ll \mu$ or $\lambda \gg \mu$. In the

$^{367}$Evidently, the model assumed to describe the empirical situation is one in which the two spin vectors, $\mathbf{s}_1$ and $\mathbf{s}_2$, add up to $\mathbf{s}_1 + \mathbf{s}_2$, and the two orbital angular momenta, $\mathbf{k}_1$ and $\mathbf{k}_2$ add up to $\mathbf{k}_1 + \mathbf{k}_2$; thus, the total angular momentum $\mathbf{M}$ is obtained by adding $(\mathbf{s}_1 + \mathbf{s}_2)$ to $(\mathbf{k}_1 + \mathbf{k}_2)$. The case of the so-called ($j-j$)-coupling (where spin and angular momentum of each electron contribute to the momenta, i.e., $\mathbf{M}_1 = \mathbf{s}_1 + \mathbf{k}_1$ and $\mathbf{M}_2 = \mathbf{s}_2 + \mathbf{k}_2$, and $\mathbf{M}_1$ and $\mathbf{M}_2$ have finally to be added up in order to give the total angular momentum of the two-electron system) has to be treated differently.
$^{368}$We have corrected an obvious error in Eq. (17) of Heisenberg and Jordan (1926, p. 269); in the second term on the right-hand side of this equation $m_1$ must be replaced by $m_s$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0282 -->

V.5 The Electron Spin, Fine Structure and Anomalous Zeeman Effects 279

first case, the external magnetic field exerts a much stronger influence on the spectral lines than the internal field and the perturbation matrix $(H_1 + H_2)$ becomes diagonal, up to the order $\lambda^2$, in the quantum number $m_s$. Since, in this case, there are no transitions with $\Delta m_s \neq 0$, each spectral line will only split into a (normal) Zeeman triplet under the action of a magnetic field because of the change $\Delta m_k = 0, \pm 1$ of the $z$-component of the orbital angular momentum, in agreement with the Paschen-Back effect.
The other extreme situation, i.e., the case $\lambda \gg \mu$, occurs when the splitting due to the external magnetic field $\mathbf{H}$ is small compared with the natural line splitting (i.e., the distances between the components of a multiplet). When $\mathbf{H}$ is zero, the perturbation is given only by the term $H_2$ in Eq. (283), which may be rewritten as $\frac{1}{2}\lambda(2\pi/h)^2[\mathbf{M}^2 - \mathbf{k}^2 - \mathbf{s}^2]$, where $\mathbf{M} = (\mathbf{k} + \mathbf{s})$. Hence $H_2$ becomes a diagonal matrix in $j$, the quantum number of the total angular momentum $\mathbf{M}$, having the elements

$$ H_2(j, k, s; j, k, s) = \frac{1}{2}\lambda \left[ j(j+1) - k(k+1) - s(s+1) \right]. \quad (290\text{a}) $$

In the language of a classical mechanical model, the direction of the total angular momentum $\mathbf{M}$ serves as the axis of precession. When the magnetic field is switched on, it gives rise to separate precessions of the orbital angular momentum $\mathbf{k}$ and the spin angular momentum $\mathbf{s}$; however, their components perpendicular to the axis of precession (the direction of $\mathbf{M}$) do not contribute to $\overline{H}_1$, the average of the (classical) perturbation energy over a complete orbit. This argument could be taken over into quantum theory, as the matrices in question commute in the approximation $\mu \ll \lambda$. Hence $\overline{H}_1$ was also given there by the components parallel to $\mathbf{M}$, that is,

$$ \overline{H}_1 = \left( \frac{2\pi}{h} \right) \mu \frac{(\mathbf{H} \cdot \mathbf{M})}{|\mathbf{H}|} \left[ 1 + \frac{(\mathbf{M} \cdot \mathbf{s})}{\mathbf{M}^2} \right]. \quad (290\text{b}) $$

The matrix elements of the total perturbation energy can be obtained by adding $H_2$ and $\overline{H}_1$ as

$$ (\overline{H}_1 + H_2)(j, k, s; j, k, s) = \mu m \left[ 1 + \frac{j(j+1) - k(k+1) + s(s+1)}{2j(j+1)} \right] + \frac{1}{2}\lambda \left[ j(j+1) - k(k+1) - s(s+1) \right] \quad (291) $$

for $\mu \ll \lambda = \lambda(k)$. The factor within square brackets in the first term on the right-hand side of Eq. (291) is identical with the well-known $g$-factor, while the second term expresses the 'interval rule,' both discovered by Alfred Landé in 1923 from an analysis of Back's data on the anomalous Zeeman effects (Landé, 1923a).

The final section (Section 5) of Heisenberg and Jordan's paper was devoted to a calculation of the fine structure in the case of the one-electron atom, where $s = \frac{1}{2}$. The authors evaluated the average values of the inverse powers of the radial matrices $r$ carefully and found for $H_2 + H_3$, the sum of the internal field and the fine-structure field terms, the result

$$ (H_2 + H_3)(n, j; n, j) = \frac{2R^2 h^2 Z^4}{m_e c^2 n^3} \left[ \frac{3}{4n} - \frac{1}{j + \frac{1}{2}} \right], \quad (292) $$

for an atom with atomic number $Z$ in a state characterized by the principal quantum number $n$ and the total angular momentum quantum number $j$ (also $R = \text{Rydberg constant} = 2\pi^2 e^4 m_e / h^3$).$^{369}$ For hydrogen, one has only to put $Z=1$ and Sommerfeld's well-known fine-structure formula follows.
From Eq. (292) it also becomes evident that a difficulty, which had been noted by Heisenberg and Pauli during the early stages of their discussion on fine structure, disappeared: this was the fact that the expression for the magnetic energy seemed to become infinite because of the factor $r^{-3}$. (See the second Eq. (281) with the denominator $p_\phi^2 - \frac{1}{4}(h/2\pi)^2$ being equal to $k(k+1)$.) The reason is that in this case the other factors in $H_2$ cancel this infinity; for zero angular momentum there is no magnetic energy at all.
Equation (292), though derived strictly for only one-electron atoms, could be applied approximately also to non-hydrogen-like atoms, for example to alkali atoms, where the spectral lines are emitted by the valence electron in the outermost shell. Then, of course, the atomic number $Z$ had to be replaced by an effective number $Z_{\text{eff}}$, which is smaller than the atomic number but larger than unity.$^{370}$ Therefore, the separation of the alkali doublets is much larger than the splitting of the hydrogen lines. Furthermore, Eq. (292) accounted for the X-ray doublets, for, as Heisenberg and Jordan noted: 'In particular, it follows from the absence of $k$ in Eq. [(292)] that the "screening doublets" can be explained by the hypothesis of Compton, Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit [i.e., the hypothesis of rotating

$^{369}$By inserting the expression for $\overline{r^{-1}}$ ($= 1/e^2 \cdot (2RhZ/n^2)$) (from Pauli's theory of hydrogen atom and for $\overline{r^{-2}}$ ($= (m((h/2\pi)(k + \frac{1}{2}))^{-1}) \cdot (4\pi RZ^2/n^3)$) from Eq. (281) into Eq. (279c), and adding it to Eq. (279b'), the result followed that

$$ (H_2 + H_3)(j, k, s; j, k, s) = \frac{2Rh^2 Z^4}{m_e c^2 n^3} \left[ \frac{j(j+1) - k(k+1) - s(s+1)}{2k(k + \frac{1}{2})(k+1)} - \frac{1}{k + \frac{1}{2}} + \frac{3}{4n} \right]. $$

For doublets having $s = \frac{1}{2}$ and $j = k \pm \frac{1}{2}$ this reduced to Eq. (292). In this equation we have replaced the variables, $j, k$ and $s$, on the left-hand side by $n$ and $j$, because $s$ is fixed and $k$ does not enter on the right-hand side anymore.
$^{370}$The actual calculation of $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is rather complicated. However, from a classical consideration, one can see that $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is larger than unity. Assume that the orbits of the valence electron move partly outside the core of the alkali atom and partly inside. Then one has to replace the factor $(Z/r^3)$ in Eq. (279b') by a sum, i.e., $(Z/r^3)_{\text{ext}} + (Z/r^3)_{\text{int}}$ where the subscripts 'ext' and 'int' refer to the orbits outside and within the core, respectively. Evidently, the internal term is much larger than the external term, in which $Z=1$; hence $Z_{\text{eff}}$ is larger than 1.

## Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

spite of the fact that he knew that Schrödinger was calculating similar things and he had to hurry.376 He did not have to worry long about the question of publication. Schrödinger had included some preliminary results of his own calculation on the intensities of Balmer lines in a communication which he submitted to *Annalen der Physik* in the beginning of May (Schrödinger, 1926f, p. 476); Pauli informed Schrödinger about his results, and Schrödinger, in a postscript added in proof to his paper, gave the full intensity formulae of the hydrogen lines obtained by Pauli (Schrödinger, 1926f, pp. 489–490).
The continuing concern with the intensities of the hydrogen lines prevented Pauli from working on other important problems of the day. After the question of electron spin had been settled, and the formulae describing the fine structure of the hydrogen lines and the empirically observed anomalous Zeeman effects had been derived from a systematic application of the quantum-mechanical scheme, one of the few remaining questions which concerned the complex structure of spectral lines was the problem of explaining the helium spectra. Pauli had hoped that Bohr and Goudsmit, who had been collaborating together in Copenhagen earlier in 1926, would find a solution.377 However, no progress came out of these efforts. As Goudsmit recalled later on about his discussions with Bohr:

> That was a complete fiasco. Bohr knew what the next problem was, [but] I did not understand it; it was not [up] my alley. By looking at the helium spectrum Bohr understood right away that [if] you turned over one of the two spins [of the electrons in the helium atom] the energy suddenly would be entirely different. We got together every day in the hope that his talking to me would put some idea in my mind which would solve the problem. It didn't. So after five or six weeks he gave me a first class ticket back to Holland on a sleeper ... with the admonition that I had to get off at Hamburg and tell Pauli about the Thomas factor 2. (Goudsmit, AHQP Interview, 7 December 1963, p. 25)

## V.6 Key to the Helium Problem

It might seem rather surprising that Pauli, who had been concerned so much with the programme of extending the matrix methods to include action-angle variables and with the problem of explaining the fine structure of hydrogen, was not at least co-author of one of the two papers, i.e., Wentzel's paper on the multiply periodic systems (Wentzel, 1926a) or Heisenberg and Jordan's paper on the complex structure and anomalous Zeeman effects (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926). Being unhappy with the course of events, he just stayed away from any publication. Indeed, in March 1926 Pauli had several reasons to be dissatisfied with the progress of his scientific work. During the previous few months he had wasted much time on arguments against the electron spin hypothesis until he finally withdrew, in his letter to Niels Bohr (dated 12 March 1926), his objections against the relativistic calculations of L. H. Thomas. Thus, an important conceptual aspect of the theory of atomic structure, to which Pauli had devoted himself since fall 1922, had been established by a graduate student from Cambridge, England, in spite of his authoritarian criticism. At the same time, Paul Dirac, another Cambridge research student, had developed the quantum-mechanical scheme of action-angle variables much faster than Pauli, although a number of the fundamental ideas from which both of them departed had been the same. The explanation of this failure of such a seasoned theoretical physicist as Pauli to compete with practically unknown graduate students like Thomas and Dirac may be sought to a large extent in Pauli's attitude towards atomic physics in general and the priorities he had set up for himself in approaching specific problems.
Early in 1926 Pauli, more than anybody else working on quantum mechanics, still believed the theory to be only in a preliminary stage of development. Therefore, he still adhered to the cautious procedure he had learned from Niels Bohr several years earlier when the previous atomic theory had run into serious contradictions with certain empirical facts: namely, to look with suspicion at every result obtained from theory and not accept it until it had been fully established by agreement with experiment. It was in this spirit that he had

attacked, in October 1925, the problem of calculating the energy states of the hydrogen atom with the help of matrix mechanics. Afterwards, since he was convinced of the correctness of Sommerfeld's fine-structure formula of 1916, he gave priority to extending matrix methods in such a way that the energy states of the relativistic hydrogen atom could be obtained.373 When the puzzle with the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ had been solved in favour of Thomas' calculation, the quantum-mechanical derivation of the fine-structure formula became trivial and Pauli left it to Heisenberg and Jordan to publish it in their paper on the anomalous Zeeman effects (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926). Another theoretical problem of this kind—i.e., one in which the results could be tested by comparison with the empirical data—was to calculate the intensities of the hydrogen spectral lines, and Pauli had thought about it in particular since December 1925.374 In the beginning of February 1926 this problem still concerned him, for he wrote to Niels Bohr: 'At the moment I am occupied with carrying further the solutions of the matrix equations for the hydrogen atom in order also to arrive at the final formulae for the intensities' (Pauli to Bohr, 5 February 1926). During March and April he continued his attempt but, even though he made use of the method of action-angle variables, he did not achieve his goal.375
Pauli had been anxious to exploit matrix methods as far as possible, rather than make use of a new formalism which might be more adequate to deal with the intensity problem. Thus, he had not really examined the possibilities that were offered in this respect by the operator scheme of Born and Wiener. Erwin Schrödinger's first paper on wave mechanics (Schrödinger, 1926c) took him, therefore, by surprise, for he had not expected that the operator methods would lead to anything useful in practice. The set of functions, which Born and Wiener had associated with the quantum-mechanical system under consideration (Born and Wiener, 1926, §2), and which Pauli had scrupulously avoided in his formalism dealing with angle variables, now reappeared triumphantly as Schrödinger's eigenfunctions. However, Pauli made use of the new approach very soon; after proving the equivalence of the wave and matrix methods, he was 'occupied with the problem of computing from the eigenfunctions—calculated by Schrödinger—the transition probabilities for hydrogen' (Pauli to Jordan, 12 April 1926). Though he obtained certain results on the intensities of Balmer lines, he did not publish them immediately, but rather waited for an experimental verification, in

In Hamburg, Goudsmit did not succeed in persuading Pauli of the correctness of Thomas’ calculation.378 Moreover, Pauli was ‘not very pleased to hear from Goudsmit that he had not made the slightest progress in the two most important problems [of spectroscopy], which are still unsolved; namely, the calculation of the separation of singlet and triplet terms (e.g., ortho- and parhelium) and the physical foundation of the formal exclusion rules for equivalent orbits’ (Pauli to Kramers, 8 March 1926). As Goudsmit recalled, he was out of his depth in dealing with these questions:

> I invented all kinds of magnetic interactions [to explain the large energy differences between the corresponding singlet and triplet terms of the helium atom, i.e., terms having identical quantum numbers $n$ and $k$ but different spin quantum number $s$], and I have a letter from Bohr in which he tells me that I am all wet. But still I wrote [to Bohr] about it later; I kept on thinking about it. Then he called [upon] Heisenberg who indeed found the solution—the antisymmetric wave functions and so on. That was *way beyond* me. I would never have been able to guess anything like it. (Goudsmit, AHQP Interview, 7 December 1963, p. 25)379

From mid-November to mid-March 1926 Heisenberg did not submit any paper for publication that dealt with new methods in or applications of matrix mechanics. This, for Heisenberg, was an unusually long time, and he later tried to explain the reason for his silence as follows: ‘It was partly due to the absence of Born [who was in America], partly due to the teaching which I had to do, and partly also a kind of exhaustion. I felt, “Well, now let’s wait for a time”’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 302).380 Though Heisenberg’s work with Jordan on the treatment of anomalous Zeeman effects had been in progress for some time, he did not wait around for the question of spin to be settled in favour of Uhlenbeck and Goudsmit by Thomas’ calculation; as soon as his teaching obligations for the winter semester 1925–1926 were over, Heisenberg left Göt-

Bohr, in his reply, stated: ‘I must point out, however, that it is very difficult to see in your considerations a sufficient mechanical justification’ (Bohr to Goudsmit, 17 April 1926). Having turned down the offer of an associate professorship [or *Extraordinariat*] at the University of Leipzig, he arrived in Copenhagen towards the end of April, refreshed in body and spirit and full of new ideas and ambition.$^{382}$

In Copenhagen, Heisenberg plunged immediately into one of the outstanding problems being discussed there: the calculation of the energy states of the helium atom. No progress had been made in it since about the middle of March when Pauli had withdrawn his serious objections against the electron spin hypothesis and written to Bohr: ‘Now I only hope that my gibes about the “new heresy” (“*neue Irrlehre*”) [i.e., the electron spin hypothesis] would have the result that your zeal would be so incited that you would be able to finish off soon the remaining points of the programme (helium spectrum, separation of the singlet-triplet system, equivalent orbits)!’ (Pauli to Bohr, 12 March 1926).$^{383}$ Heisenberg took his assignment very seriously and, within a few days of his arrival in Copenhagen, reported to Pauli about his initial progress:

> Then I want to write to you that we have found a rather decisive argument that your exclusion of equivalent orbits [i.e., of the electron orbits in helium denoted by the same values of the four quantum numbers *n*, *j*, *k* and *m$_s$*] is connected with the singlet-triplet separation. Consider the energy written as a function of the transition probabilities. Then a large difference results, if one—at the energy of H-atoms—has transitions to *1S*, or if, according to your ban [exclusion principle], one puts them equal to zero. That is, par- and ortho-[helium] do have different energies, independently of the interaction between the magnets. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 May 1926)

V.6 Key to the Helium Problem | 287
:--- | ---

And, just three weeks later, Heisenberg could write to Max Born who had meanwhile returned from the United States: ‘Since coming here I have very seriously worked on [the problem of] the helium spectrum, and I believe that now all the essential things are all right; however, I have not yet completed the quantitative calculation’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

There were several reasons for Heisenberg’s rapid progress in dealing with the problem of the helium atom in quantum mechanics. First, he was evidently more qualified to work on quantum mechanics than both Goudsmit and Bohr who had tackled this problem earlier. Goudsmit’s abilities, in any case, lay in the analysis of empirical data, while Bohr did not have enough experience in applying the complicated formalism of matrix mechanics, without which no progress could be made. Second, Heisenberg had had a long personal association with the helium problem ever since he had attempted, in fall 1922, to account for the observed energy states of helium by using half-quantum numbers in the theory of multiply periodic systems. While the half-quantum numbers had been discarded in 1923 as being in contradiction with the principles of the then quantum theory (see, for instance, Born and Heisenberg, 1923b, p. 243), they had returned in fall 1925 in the guise of electron spin. After Heisenberg had accepted the spin hypothesis he could also reasonably expect that a repetition of his old, unpublished calculations within the scheme of matrix mechanics would yield results in agreement with the observed data.$^{384}$

However, before being able to calculate the energy states of helium, Heisenberg had to handle two difficulties which he stated in a letter to Max Born: ‘1. Because of the equivalent orbits and Pauli’s ban [exclusion principle], quantum mechanics did not seem to be applicable to the problem of several-electron atoms. 2. The large separation between the singlet and triplet systems could not be explained by a magnetic interaction of the rotating electrons; one had therefore to assume with Hund a large force of unknown origin between the magnets’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).$^{385}$

***

$^{384}$ Heisenberg had reported about his calculation of the helium atom with half-integral quantum numbers in letters to his teacher Arnold Sommerfeld during winter 1922–1923 (Heisenberg to Sommerfeld, 28 October, 4 December 1922, 4 and 15 January 1923). At that time he had tried to obtain the ionization potential of helium, and by assuming the angular momentum values of the electron orbits in the ground state to be $\frac{1}{2} h / 2 \pi$ and $-\frac{1}{2} h / 2 \pi$, respectively, he had obtained a result very close to the empirical value of 24.5 V. (See Volume 2, Section II.3.)

$^{385}$ A calculation of the usual (electromagnetic) interaction *between* the magnetic moments of the two electrons yielded a splitting which was smaller than the splitting *within* a given multiplet due to the interaction of the magnetic moment of one electron with the internal field $\mathbf{H}_{i}$, Eq. (279b'). (See, e.g., Hund, 1927, pp. 123–124.) This result had been noticed by Heisenberg soon after he learned about the electron spin hypothesis. ‘I myself have very great reservations against Goudsmit’s attempt to establish zoology [i.e., the spectroscopic terms] in such a simple way,’ he had written to Pauli, and added: ‘For the alkaline-earth atoms the energy difference between singlet and triplet terms with equal $k$ must result only from the different interaction of the electron magnets upon each other. This yields a completely wrong order of magnitude’ (Heisenberg to Pauli, 24 November 1925). Therefore, if one wanted to keep up the magnetic origin of the singlet–triplet splitting, one had to assume a strong, so-far-unknown interaction between the magnetic moments of the electrons in the helium atom.

289 V.6 Key to the Helium Problem

irregular in the case of real alkaline-earth elements Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, in which the distance between singlet and triplet terms is large compared to the distance of triplet terms from each other’ (Pauli, 1926b, p. 218). This situation showed up most prominently in the spectrum of helium, the purest two-electron system in nature: consistent with the fact that the ratio of the component splitting in ortho-helium to the average distance of the ortho-helium multiplet from the corresponding parhelium singlet is much smaller than in the alkaline-earth atoms, the intercombination lines in helium were found to be particularly weak.$^{386}$

All these empirical facts suggested strongly that, in order to understand two-electron systems, one had first to establish a proper theory of helium spectra, and the most important task of this theory was to determine the energy difference between the ortho-helium and parhelium terms *from the Coulomb repulsion of the electrons*. That is, from the Coulomb repulsion of the electrons a new strong force had to arise that would explain the large singlet-triplet splitting. At this point Heisenberg was able to exploit his earlier acquaintance with the helium problem. Especially, he could refer to an idea which had been emphasized by Born and himself several years previously (Born and Heisenberg, 1923a). They had then discovered that, in atomic systems having two or more electrons, the phases between the motions of the electrons assumed fixed values when the perturbation—i.e., the electron–electron interaction—was switched on; for these systems, which they had called ‘accidentally degenerate,’ they had developed a proper perturbation scheme.$^{387}$ The phase relations gave rise to a certain resonance effect which had been discussed in Göttingen quite frequently in connection with a mechanical example. As Heisenberg recalled: ‘There is the old classical experiment which is shown in every lecture course: two pendula being coupled by a piece of rubber. It was natural to study this system in quantum theory, and we certainly discussed it already very early in the period before quantum mechanics, especially in connection with dispersion theory’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 362).

In the dispersion approach, which had been used especially since Kramers’ work in 1924, the motions of electrons in atoms were represented by harmonic
