It should be mentioned at this point that the triplet structure of ortho-helium lines had not yet been (experimentally) settled in 1926 when Heisenberg developed the theory of the helium spectrum. Thus, in one of the best known tables in those days the ortho-helium lines were listed as ‘doublets’; however, it was also indicated that the Zeeman effect of the ‘helium’ doublet lines had a character different from those of the alkali-doublets (see Paschen and Götze, 1922, p. 28, especially footnote 3). This empirical situation did not prevent Pauli from writing in his *Handbuch* article: ‘Nevertheless it is obvious to compare, apart from the complex structure, *both* term systems of helium with the two term systems of alkaline earths, since, at any rate, one is dealing with a two-electron system in the case of helium as well.’ (Pauli, 1926b, p. 218)

oscillations of given frequencies. Thus, the coupling of the valence-electrons in an atom could be described by the following simplified model: two identical oscillators, each having the same mass $m$ and frequency $\nu$ ($= \omega/2\pi$), were coupled by an (in general small) interaction term, $m\lambda q_1q_2$, where $q_1$ and $q_2$ denote the position variables of the oscillators 1 and 2. In classical mechanics, the system will develop a resonance and a beat frequency will interfere with the original frequency giving rise to two new, shifted frequencies. This effect may be demonstrated easily by performing a canonical transformation of the variables, the momenta $p_1$ and $p_2$ and the position coordinates $q_1$ and $q_2$. The Hamiltonian, $H$, of the system—i.e., $H = (1/2m)(p_1^2 + m^2\omega^2q_1^2) + (1/2m)(p_2^2 + m^2\omega^2q_2^2) + m\lambda q_1q_2$—assumes the form

$$H = \frac{1}{2m}\left(p_1'^2 + m^2\omega_1'^2q_1'^2\right) + \frac{1}{2m}\left(p_2'^2 + m^2\omega_2'^2q_2'^2\right), \tag{293}$$

where the new position variables are given by the equations

$$q_1' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(q_1 + q_2) \quad \text{and} \quad q_2' = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(q_1 - q_2), \tag{293a}$$

and the new frequencies, $\nu_1'$ and $\nu_2'$, by the equations

$$2\pi\nu_1' = \omega_1' = \sqrt{\omega^2 + \lambda} \quad \text{and} \quad 2\pi\nu_2' = \omega_2' = \sqrt{\omega^2 - \lambda} \; . \tag{293b}$$

Hence, there arise two specific motions, one with frequency $\nu_1$ in which the two oscillators vibrate in phase, and the other with lower frequency $\nu_2$ in which they vibrate with an opposite phase.

Heisenberg quickly recognized that the reformulation of the classical example of coupled oscillators in quantum mechanics would yield an analogous result. That is, if one considered two identical oscillators which were coupled by a small perturbation term, $m\lambda q_1q_2$, where $q_1$ and $q_2$ are the position variables of the individual oscillators, then exactly the same coordinate transformation as in the classical theory, Eq. (293a), could be made. Again, the transformation leads to a Hamiltonian having the form given by Eq. (293), and the eigenvalues of this Hamiltonian are

$$W_{n_1'n_2'} = \left(n_1' + \frac{1}{2}\right)h\nu_1' + \left(n_2' + \frac{1}{2}\right)h\nu_2', \tag{294}$$

where $n_1'$ and $n_2'$ assume integral values, $0, 1, 2, \dots$, etc., and $\nu_1'$ and $\nu_2'$ denote the two frequencies given by Eq. (293b).

In the three-man paper, where a universal algebraic formalism of perturbation theory applicable to arbitrary quantum-mechanical systems had been developed, Born, Heisenberg and Jordan had mentioned explicitly the fact that now ‘two originally identical, non-degenerate systems (where all the frequencies of the individual system should be different) coupled by arbitrary forces,’ could be treated (BHJ, 1926, p. 589). The authors had, however, not treated any example,

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0294 -->

291 V.6 Key to the Helium Problem

although the two coupled harmonic oscillators did have exactly the properties which they mentioned.$^{388}$ The algebraic perturbation theory was first used by Heisenberg and Jordan in their calculations of the anomalous Zeeman effects, where they considered an atomic system whose Hamiltonian (including the terms $H_1$ and $H_2$, Eqs. (279a) and (279b’), due to magnetic interaction) was degenerate in the $z$-component of the electron spin (Heisenberg and Jordan, 1926, Section 3). The perturbation calculation then yielded multiplets which were separated (for small magnetic field strengths) by magnitudes of the same order as the fine-structure terms that arose both from magnetic interactions and relativistic corrections. It was the result of this calculation which convinced Heisenberg that the interaction arising from the addition of electron spin alone to the existing mechanical description of atoms would not be sufficient to explain the differences between the terms of different sequences in the spectrum of helium. Such a large difference, he was certain, would only be caused by a perturbation term containing the Coulomb repulsion between the two electrons. That was the basic idea which Heisenberg followed and tried to formulate mathematically, and it indeed provided the key to the solution of the helium problem.

Between 5 May, when he wrote to Pauli about his initial thoughts, and 26 May, when he sketched the scheme in his letter to Born, Heisenberg developed the method for calculating the energy states of the helium atom. He began by considering a system consisting of two electrons moving around a (heavy) nucleus. In zeroth approximation, the influence of the electrons on each other and effects due to spin were neglected and the Hamiltonian, $H_0$, was assumed to be made up of two terms, $H^a$ and $H^b$, each referring to the motion of one electron (denoted by the indices $a$ and $b$, respectively). He assumed, in agreement with the earlier discussions of many-electron atoms, that in this approximation the second electron just altered the effective charge of the nucleus; that is, the effective charge took on values between $e$ and $2e$, depending upon whether the second electron moved inside or outside the orbit of the other electron. Thus, the Hamiltonians of the two electrons, i.e., $H^a$ and $H^b$, were identical, and, as a result, there existed a peculiar degeneracy of the Hamiltonian $H^0$. The reason for this was that any eigenvalue $W_{nm}^0$ of $H^0$, in which the electrons $a$ and $b$ were not in equivalent orbits, that is,

$$W_{nm}^0 = W_n^a + W_m^b \quad \text{with} \quad W_n^a \neq W_m^b, \tag{295}$$

$^{388}$One may naturally ask the question why Born, Heisenberg and Jordan, in fall 1925, did not illustrate the use of their general perturbation scheme by treating a few, obvious examples. ‘When we wrote that paper,’ Heisenberg recalled, ‘our general situation was this: We saw that we had entered a new field where one could pick up new things wherever one went. Therefore, we just took what came our way but without following it further, because we realized that to follow it further would take some time and we would have to do some work’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 363). Surely, the application of the abstract formalism of degenerate systems, as developed by Max Born in the three-man paper (BHJ, 1926, Chapter 3), to calculate something as practical as the states of helium did not seem to be the most pressing problem. ‘But it may be that we discussed it among ourselves,’ Heisenberg remarked later. ‘We had already in mind that when we had finished the paper [i.e., BHJ, 1926] then, sooner or later, we must try the helium problem and the problem of two equal [i.e., identical] coupled systems’ (Heisenberg, Conversations, p. 364).

292 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

was twofold degenerate, for an exchange of the motions of the two electrons, indicated here by an exchange of the two quantum numbers $n$ and $m$ of the partial systems, did not alter $W_{nm}^0$.$^{389}$ This degeneracy was removed by the Coulomb repulsion of the electrons.

Heisenberg informed Born: ‘The line of thought is totally linked with your calculation for two originally identical systems in ‘Quantum Mechanics II’ [i.e., in BHJ, 1926, Chapter 3]. Your result was that for two similar systems *both* the states, which emerge by exchanging the electrons between each other, split into two separate terms; only for originally *equivalent* orbits does there remains *one* state’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926). In the case of the two-electron system, described by a degenerate Hamiltonian $H^0$ and an interaction term $H^1$, one obtains—with the help of Born’s scheme—two equations to determine $W^1$, the perturbation energy, namely,

$$\left[ W^1 - H^1(nm, nm) \right] x_{nm} - H^1(nm, mn)x_{mn} = 0 \tag{296a}$$

and

$$- H^1(mn, nm)x_{nm} + \left[ W^1 - H^1(mn, mn) \right] x_{mn} = 0, \tag{296b}$$

which have to be satisfied simultaneously for any pair $(n, m)$ with $n \neq m$. The $H^1(nm, nm)$, etc., are the corresponding elements of $\overline{H^1}$, the time average of the perturbation matrix $H^1$; the matrix $\overline{H^1}$ contains all those elements of $H^1$ whose transition frequencies in the unperturbed system (described by $H^0$) are zero. The $x_{nm}$ and $x_{mn}$ form the columns of the $2 \times 2$-submatrix of a transformation matrix which is supposed to diagonalize the perturbation Hamiltonian $H^1$.$^{390}$ Equations (296) yield, similar to the classical problem of two coupled oscillators, two solutions, which are denoted by $\bullet$ and $\times$, respectively, that is

$$W_{nm}^{1\bullet} = H^1(nm, nm) + H^1(nm, mn), \tag{297a}$$
$$x_{nm}^{\bullet} = S_{nm, nm} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\;, \qquad x_{mn}^{\bullet} = S_{mn, nm} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\;, $$

and

$$W_{mn}^{1\times} = H^1(nm, nm) - H^1(nm, mn), \tag{297b}$$
$$x_{nm}^{\times} = S_{nm, mn} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\;, \qquad x_{mn}^{\times} = S_{mn, mn} = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\;, $$

$^{389}$Heisenberg had already used this kind of exchange energy in a letter to Sommerfeld, dated 28 October 1922. There he had treated a system of two elliptic orbits, each occupied by an electron ($a$ or $b$), whose planes made an angle of 60$^{\circ}$, and had argued that the exchange of two orbits (which he described as ‘slipping through’ (*Hindurchschlüpfen*) of the electrons) accounted for the relativistic corrections to the helium ground state.

$^{390}$The corresponding quantum-theoretical equation is $W^1 = S^{-1}\overline{H^1}S$.

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0296 -->

296 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

model, which he mentioned as items two and three in his letter to Born. He began by describing a second model as: ‘2. If one now puts arbitrary magnets on the electrons [i.e., the electrons are associated with a magnet having a magnetic moment $\mu$ in a fixed direction, say along the $z$-axis], then the picture I of the terms [see Fig. 3] remains exactly the same, but now the electrons are in general not equivalent anymore, hence weak inter-combinations occur’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926). That is, if the interaction between the electrons’ magnetic moments (in a fixed direction in space) and the internal magnetic field $\mathbf{H}_i$ (caused by the helium core at the position of the electrons—see Section V.5) is considered, then the energy of a given orbit (i.e., the average energy of the electron moving in an orbit, neglecting the Coulomb repulsion between the electrons) depends on the relative orientation of the magnetic moment $\mu$ (and, therefore, also of the spin $s$, according to Eq. (278)) with respect to the plane of the orbit. Although this magnetic energy (whose strength is equal to the scalar product $\mu \cdot \mathbf{H}_i$) is comparatively small, it removes the initial degeneracy of the two-electron system. The perturbation calculation, including the Coulomb term and the magnetic term, then leads more or less to the same spectra as shown in Fig. 2 or Fig. 3. However, each term ($nm$) gets slightly shifted and transitions between the dotted ($\bullet$) and crossed ($\times$) sequences begin to take place; their intensities are determined by the magnetic interaction and are, therefore, small.

Though model 2 represented more features of the helium atom than the spinless model, Heisenberg was not yet satisfied. In particular, this model did not quite explain the structure of the helium spectra, for, with a fixed direction of the spin, both terms would be singlets. Moreover, it was difficult to understand how nature would create a preferred direction of electron spin. Heisenberg, therefore, proceeded to deal with a third model, which he described to Born as follows: ‘3. If one puts the right [Uhlenbeck–] Goudsmit magnet *without* a given direction on each electron, then the electrons are again equivalent. But the separation [after the Coulomb repulsion term $H^1$ is switched on] into the two systems is different from the previous one. To begin with, for each term of I, four positions of the magnet must occur, hence four new terms will result [instead of one in I]’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926). Indeed, Heisenberg knew from his earlier considerations of the magnetic interaction (e.g., from the discussion of the anomalous Zeeman effects) that the spins of two electrons might add up to produce either a singlet (total spin 0) or a triplet (total spin 1) having three separate states. This term scheme, to a good approximation, is represented by Fig. 4, which Heisenberg drew in his letter to Born, calling it system II: in it the spin singlet term and the middle term of the spin triplet (i.e., the term of the spin triplet with zero component of the spin in the direction of the internal magnetic field) coincided. Now it seemed that the division into two term sequences lost its meaning: on the one hand, each quadruplet could be divided into a singlet and a triplet system representing qualitatively both term spectra of helium; on the other, weak transitions between all terms appeared to be possible. However, the last conclusion was wrong, for there occurred a new, different separation of term sequences, which was denoted again by dots ($\bullet$) and crosses ($\times$) in Fig. 4.

V.6 Key to the Helium Problem 293

where use has been made of the symmetry of the matrix $\overline{H^1}$ with respect to the electrons (i.e., $H^1(nm, nm) = H^1(mn, mn)$ and $H^1(nm, mn) = H^1(mn, nm)$, respectively).

Heisenberg did not write down the above equations in his letter to Born because he assumed that Born would immediately make the simple calculation himself, but he pointed out their consequence:$^{391}$ ‘For all following considerations the decisive result now is this: The term system can be divided into two separate parts ($\bullet$ and $\times$), such that transitions occur only within the $\bullet$ system or within the $\times$ system, but never from the $\bullet$ system to the $\times$ system.’ And he drew a figure to illustrate this (see Fig. 2). Heisenberg then explained: ‘The transitions from [the states] $\bullet$ to [the states] $\times$ vanish not only in the dipole radiation, but also in the quadrupole radiation and in all higher approximations, provided only that the two [unperturbed] systems are really totally equivalent, as for instance two electrons revolving around *one* nucleus. One can also never induce transitions by collisions from one system to the other. You will be able to verify this easily’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

Heisenberg found the results of these simple considerations so important that, about two weeks after he had written the letter to Born, he submitted a paper entitled. *Mehrkörperproblem und Resonanz in der Quantenmechanik* (‘Many-Body Problem and Resonance in Quantum Mechanics’) to *Zeitschrift für Physik* (Heisenberg, 1926b), in which he gave a full discussion of the points he had mentioned to Born. Especially, he proved there the statement that no transitions occur from the terms denoted by $\bullet$ to terms denoted by $\times$ in the following way. The radiation amplitudes, $f_{n_1m_1, n_2m_2}$, of the unperturbed system are symmetric with respect to an exchange of the electrons $a$ and $b$ (i.e., $f_{n_1m_1, n_2m_2} = f_{m_1n_1, m_2n_2}$). Heisenberg then computed the special amplitudes of the perturbed system with the help of the tranformation matrix $S$, whose elements were given by Eqs. (297a) and (297b).$^{392}$ Thus, for example, in the case of the specific transition between two states of the term sequence denoted by $\bullet$ (as in Fig. 2), say ($n_1m$) and ($n_2m$) with $n_1, n_2 < m$, he obtained the transition amplitude,

$$f'_{n_1m, n_2m} = f_{n_1m, n_2m} + f_{n_1m, mn_2}. \tag{298a}$$

The right-hand side of Eq. (298a) is different from zero unless the two unperturbed amplitudes vanish. On the other hand, if he took transitions between states belonging to different term sequences, say ($n_1m$) and ($mn_2$) with $n_1, n_2 < m$, where the first one belongs to the sequence denoted by $\bullet$ and the second to the sequence denoted by $\times$, he found the amplitude to be

$$f'_{n_1m, mn_2} = f_{n_1m, n_2m} - f_{mn_1, mn_2}, \tag{298b}$$

$^{391}$ Equations (296a, b) and (297a, b) can be found, however, in Heisenberg’s paper on the many-body problem and resonance in quantum mechanics, which grew out of the general considerations on coupled systems. (See Heisenberg, 1926b, p. 418, Eqs. (10), (11) and (12).)

$^{392}$ The elements, other than the ones given by Eqs. (297a) and (297b), are zero.

**Figure 3** Term Spectrum of Helium without Spin. The Energy Increases from Left to Right.

The results contained in Eqs. (298a–d) encouraged Heisenberg to treat the helium atom as a system showing what he called the ‘resonance effect,’ i.e., a behaviour characterizing systems which can approximately be separated into two partial systems such that ‘the absorption frequency of one system coincides with the emission frequency of the other system, and *vice versa*’ (Heisenberg, 1926b, p. 416). The helium spectra indeed possessed many features similar to the one derived in the case of two coupled linear oscillators (of the same frequency) which Heisenberg had discussed in his letter to Born and, in more detail, in the above-mentioned paper on the many-body problem and resonance. Thus, he explained, for example, in his letter to Born:

> Now the application to helium is as follows: 1. We assume that the electrons have no magnets [i.e., are spinless]. Then the term spectrum evidently looks like [Fig. 3] and the two systems, in which the term spectrum separates, are parhelium [denoted by the dots (●), in agreement with Fig. [2]] and ortho-helium [denoted by the crosses (×)]. With this explanation one understands immediately, first, that the separation between par- and ortho-helium is of the order of magnitude of the Rydberg correction; second, that no combinations occur between the two systems in this approximation; and third, that the 1s-term [i.e., the term denoted by (11) in Fig. [2] or the first dot (●) in the first row of Fig. [3]] in the ortho-system is missing.
> (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926)

Indeed, the singlet–triplet difference of corresponding terms—as, for instance, of (12) and (21) or of (24) and (42) in Fig. 2—is obtained from Eqs. (297a) and (297b) as

$$\Delta_{nm} = 2H^1(nm, mn), \quad (299)$$

where $H^1(nm, mn)$ may be interpreted physically as the difference of the perturbation energies which the Coulomb repulsion between the electrons adds to the energies, $W_n^a$ and $W_m^b$, of the single electron orbits. The same Coulomb repulsion was also responsible for the so-called Rydberg correction in the empirical helium term formula; hence Eq. (299) provided a qualitative understanding of the helium spectra. And, as Heisenberg wrote to Born: ‘Quantitatively I have computed the singlet–triplet separation for *p*-terms; this agrees rather well [with the data] for He and Li$^+$’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

This coarse model for treating the helium atom did not, of course, solve all the problems which Heisenberg had set for himself. It did not account for effects due to electron spin, nor did it make any use of the exclusion principle (whose role in atoms having several electrons had become well established). In order to approach these problems, Heisenberg developed modifications of his simplified

Heisenberg reported to Born: ‘The one system (• in II) has the singlets in parhelium and the triplets in ortho-helium, while the other (×) has the triplets in parhelium and the singlets in ortho-helium. The two systems, which are thus characterized [that is, the terms of the two sequences • and ×] *cannot* now combine at all; on the other hand, weak inter-combinations between parhelium and ortho-helium [states] are now possible within one system [• or ×]([they have the] order of magnitude of [the ratio of] magnetic interaction to singlet–triplet [energy difference])’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

The above claims rested on two observations which Heisenberg discussed in some detail in his published paper on the spectra of atoms with two electrons (Heisenberg, 1926c, Part II, § 1). First, it is evident from Fig. 4 that in each of the quadruplets of the first and second row the two states (having the same component, $m_s$, of the total spin in the direction of the inner field $\mathbf{H}_i$) are degenerate if one neglects the mutual interaction between $\boldsymbol{\mu}_a$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_b$, the magnetic moments of the two electrons $a$ and $b$. However, taking into account the latter interaction—which again is considerably smaller than the interaction between the internal magnetic field of the atom and the electrons’ magnetic moments—one may repeat a perturbation calculation by using a scheme similar to the one given in Eqs. (296), but with a different perturbation Hamiltonian. As a result the two degenerate states of each quadruplet, which have zero $m_s$-value, will split into a separate pair with an energy difference of the order of the interaction energy between the magnetic moments $\boldsymbol{\mu}_a$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_b$. The higher term of each pair of states with zero $m_s$ may then be grouped together with the two remaining states of the quadruplet, to which both electrons contribute the total $m_s$-value, either $+1$ or $-1$; the remaining lower state of each pair, however, becomes an isolated state. Thus, each quadruplet is ordered into a singlet (with total spin momentum zero) and a triplet (with total spin momentum $h/2\pi$ and the components $m_s = +1, 0, -1$). Moreover, no singlet of the upper term sequence in Fig. 4 will combine with any triplet state of the same sequence; similarly there will be no singlet–triplet transitions among the terms of the lower sequence in Fig 4. Strong transitions occur between different states of singlets and between different states of triplets in the same term sequence.

The second important point to be noted is that the singlet terms of the lower sequence (denoted by ×) show a special symmetry when the two electrons of the

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0301 -->

298 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

atom exchange their orbits *and* their spin components (i.e., $m_s^a$ and $m_s^b$) in the direction of the internal field. As a result, nonvanishing transition amplitudes might be obtained between the triplet states of the upper sequence and the singlet states of the lower sequence (in Fig 4), whose magnitude is determined by the interaction between the two magnetic moments. Similarly, transitions are to be expected between the singlet states of the upper sequence and the triplet states of the lower sequence. The calculation of the transition amplitudes, which included the spin degrees of freedom, confirmed these possibilities. It also showed that transitions between the triplets of the upper series and the triplets of the lower series were forbidden, as were the transitions between the singlet states of the upper and the singlet states of the lower sequence.$^{394}$

At one point the model 3 in Heisenberg’s letter to Born was not correct; it turned out to be *too rich in so far as it provided two ortho- and two parhelium term sequences*. In order to reproduce the empirical facts which implied one term sequence for each (ortho- or par-) helium spectrum, Heisenberg proposed the following hypotheses: ‘The system • [in Fig. 4] represents the helium spectrum and [the system] × does not exist at all.’ This hypothesis, he argued in his letter to Born, would not contradict the purely quantum-mechanical calculation ‘since all the probabilities of transition to the other system vanish anyway; the term spectrum is “complete” (“vollständig”) in your sense.’$^{395}$ The exclusion of one of

$^{394}$The reason is that the transformation matrix $S$, whose elements enter into the matrix equation $f' = S^{-1}fS$ (where $f$ describes the matrix of the amplitudes of the unperturbed system—which is degenerate both in the orbital and spin angular momentum quantum numbers), is now a product of two transformation matrices, $S'$ and $S''$. $S'$ refers to the transformation matrix which has been introduced in connection with the perturbation term $H^1$ stemming from the Coulomb repulsion of the electron. (This perturbation term removes the orbital degeneracy of the electrons.) $S''$ removes the degeneracy in $m_s$, i.e., it has been introduced in connection with the perturbation term stemming from the interaction of the two magnetic moments of the electrons. Now, for instance, if one calculates the amplitude of transition between a triplet state of the upper sequence and a singlet state of the lower sequence, all the elements of the matrix $S^{-1}$—which multiply $f$ from the left-hand side—are identical and equal to $1/\sqrt{2}$. On the other hand, the elements of the matrix $S$ on the right-hand side stem from the second columns of the matrices $S'$ and $S''$. Both are antisymmetric with respect to the quantum number involved, as can be seen from Eq. (297b). However, if both the orbital *and* the spin quantum numbers are exchanged, the two minus signs in the matrix elements $S_{mn, mn}$ (in the second Eq. (297b)) cancel. Hence all the matrix elements under consideration again become identical and equal to $1/\sqrt{2}$, and finite transition amplitudes are obtained.

It should be mentioned that it is also possible to prove that transitions which are not allowed according to the above results can also not be excited by collisions of atoms. Heisenberg proved this by replacing the two-electron system by a system of coupled oscillators in which nonlinear terms (in the oscillator coordinates $q_1$ and $q_2$) are taken into account. Again he found that the separation between the two term sequences is strictly maintained. Since the effect of collisions between atoms can be described in terms of these nonlinear couplings, no new transitions emerge in two-electron systems even if collisions occur between them (Heisenberg, 1926b, pp. 415–416).

$^{395}$In the joint paper with Norbert Wiener, Born had postulated the existence of a closed set of functions associated with each operator in quantum mechanics (Born and Wiener, 1926, p. 92); in particular, this set had been defined by the fact that any operator of a mechanical system applied to a function leads to another function of the set. The functions may be chosen to have the form $\exp(2\pi i \nu t)$, where the $\nu$ are the quantum-mechanical frequencies. Now if only transitions between states of one term sequence occur, no frequencies other than those given by the equation $h\nu = W_n - W_m$, where $W_n$ and $W_m$ are the terms of the sequence, arise. Hence this term sequence leads to a closed and *complete* set of functions, $\{\exp(2\pi i \nu t)\}$, as postulated by Born and Wiener.

V.6 Key to the Helium Problem 299

the term sequences was not only possible, to Heisenberg it even seemed to be a necessary requirement because it ‘agrees with the Bose statistics, which reduces the statistical weights by a factor of two and automatically yields Pauli’s ban [exclusion of equivalent orbits]’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

Thus, Heisenberg finally brought in the exclusion principle which was known to play an important role in atomic systems containing several electrons. He had also demonstrated, as he had mentioned three weeks earlier to Pauli (Heisenberg to Pauli, 5 May 1926), how the exclusion of equivalent orbits, that is, orbits which have all of their quantum numbers (including $m_s$) identical, was connected with the singlet–triplet energy difference in helium. Moreover, he had made a move in the direction of realizing Pauli’s programme of a deeper understanding of the exclusion principle, for, as he noted: ‘If only one (•) of the two systems occurs in nature, then it yields, on one hand, a reduction of the statistical weights, just in the sense proposed by Bose; on the other hand, Pauli’s exclusion of equivalent orbits is automatically satisfied for the correct choice of the system’ (Heisenberg, 1926b, p. 422). By generalizing this consideration to the case of atomic systems containing $n$ electrons, in which he proposed to retain only that one of the $n!$ noncombining sequences (arising from the perturbation calculations) which contained no equivalent orbits, Heisenberg concluded that ‘Pauli’s exclusion prescription and Bose’s rule are the same, that they do not contradict quantum mechanics, and that one can calculate the energy values and all other quantities in quantum mechanics’ (Heisenberg to Born, 26 May 1926).

In relating together Pauli’s exclusion principle and the Bose statistics [for light-quanta] Heisenberg, who was hardly an expert in statistical mechanics, had been particularly misled by the observation that Bose’s counting method consisted in reducing $n!$, the statistical weight of a state containing $n$ identical particles (equal to 2 in the case of a two-electron system), to unity. Enrico Fermi had already discovered a little earlier that there was another counting method which, obeying Pauli’s exclusion principle, would also reduce the statistical weight in the same way, but that it was different from the method proposed by Bose for light-quanta and applied by Einstein to a monatomic ideal gas (Fermi, 1926a). Although Fermi’s work was also published in an issue of *Zeitschrift für Physik* before the end of May (Fermi, 1926b), Heisenberg did not sense the connection between Fermi’s ideas and his own investigations on two-electron atoms.$^{396}$

Pauli, who, in June 1926, received from Heisenberg a copy of the manuscript

$^{396}$Paul Dirac, like Heisenberg, made use of Schrödinger’s wave mechanical approach in treating quantum systems of several particles; without taking notice of Fermi’s papers, he rediscovered Fermi (–Dirac) statistics a few months later (Dirac, 1926f). Even more remarkable, Pauli, who, based on his record at that time, was a greater expert on statistical mechanics than either Heisenberg or Dirac, did not at all recognize the connection established by Fermi and Dirac between the statistics of identical particles, the many-electron problem and the exclusion principle. At first, Pauli maintained that it (the Fermi–Dirac statistics) was all wrong, but several months later, after he had carefully studied the fluctuation term in gases, he wrote to Heisenberg: ‘I now think much more kindly about the Fermi–Dirac statistics, and several arguments appear to me to speak in its favour’ (Pauli to Heisenberg, 19 October 1926).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0303 -->

300 Chapter V Modifications and Extensions of Matrix Mechanics

on the helium problem (see Heisenberg to Pauli, 8 June 1926), was not satisfied with Heisenberg’s attempt at a deeper justification of the exclusion principle by applying ‘unattractive additional constraints’ (‘*unschöne Zusatzverbote*,’ Pauli to Wentzel, 5 July 1926) to the quantum-mechanical equations. He hoped for a better argument; but since, for the time being he was unable to find it, Heisenberg went ahead with his helium calculation and eventually submitted a paper on the spectra of two-electron systems towards the end of July (Heisenberg, 1926c). In this paper he simplified some of his previous arguments by applying a different method: Schrödinger’s wave mechanics. Thus, for example, he easily obtained the result that in the case of electrons with spin (i.e., the model 3 in his letter to Born) the resulting term systems denoted by dots (•) and crosses (×), respectively, would not combine; the reason was that the crossed terms had to be described by Schrödinger functions, which were antisymmetric in both the space and spin coordinates of the electrons, while the dotted terms had to be described by totally symmetric Schrödinger functions, and no transitions occurred between any symmetric and antisymmetric states. The second, and for Heisenberg the more important, point, was a practical one: by the end of May he was well prepared to embark upon the detailed computation of helium states. In principle, the tools of matrix mechanics had already been extended—by Cornelius Lanczos, Born and Norbert Wiener, Pauli and Heisenberg himself, and by Gregor Wentzel and Paul Dirac—to the extent that the two-electron system could be treated. However, at the same time Erwin Schrödinger’s method of the wave equation had also been published (Schrödinger, 1926c), and Heisenberg did not hesitate using it (rather than the clumsier matrix methods) to obtain the elements of perturbation matrices occurring in equations of the type of Eqs. (296) for the energy states of the helium atom.$^{397}$ Thus, a calculation which was considered as a climactic proof of the validity of matrix mechanics, provided an immediate triumph of the alternative scheme of wave mechanics.

However, the key to the helium problem—the resonance effect in coupled equivalent quantum systems—had been found within the Göttingen formulation of quantum mechanics. This resonance effect would play a crucial role in the solution of two outstanding problems of atomic theory: the problem of covalent binding of molecules, such as the hydrogen molecule, and the problem of understanding the origin of ferromagnetism. While the hydrogen molecule was first treated by Walter Heitler and Fritz London, who associated the covalent

$^{397}$Heisenberg knew from Pauli that Schrödinger’s scheme was equivalent to the extended matrix formalism and could be used, especially, to calculate matrix elements elegantly. In his paper on the two-electron atoms, Heisenberg stuck to matrix methods and considerations as far as principles were concerned; however, when it came to calculate the matrix elements of the perturbation terms in the Hamiltonian, he remarked simply: ‘The calculation of the quantities is performed in the simplest way according to Schrödinger’s method of eigenfunctions’ (Heisenberg, 1926c, p. 503).

Let us add here in passing that Gregor Wentzel, who had discussed the Stark effect (including that of the second order in the electric field strength) at the joint meeting of the *Gauverein Württemberg, Baden und Bayern* of the German Physical Society on 16 May 1926 in Stuttgart, did not publish his results in contrast to his announcement (see, *Verh. d. Deutsch. Phys. Ges.* (3) 7, p. 26, (1926)). The obvious reason was that meanwhile Schrödinger had come out with his calculations of the Stark effect by means of the wave mechanical methods (Schrödinger, 1926f).

<!-- source-page: hdqt_v03 p0304 -->

V.6 Key to the Helium Problem 301

binding with the exchange forces arising from the resonance effect (Heitler and London, 1927), Heisenberg himself attacked the problem of ferromagnetism beginning in fall 1926. There one had to cope with a similar difficulty as in the helium problem, namely, how only the weak spin–spin interactions (i.e., the interactions between the magnetic moments arising from the spin due to Eq. (278)) can create the ‘strong molecular field’ introduced by Pierre Weiss many years earlier (Weiss, 1907). Heisenberg discovered that in the phenomenon of ferromagnetism it was again the Coulomb forces between the electrons that gave rise to the molecular field, whereas the mutual interaction of electron spins only created the empirically observed regular alignments of the magnetic moments of the atoms in the solid state (Heisenberg, 1928).$^{398}$

Thus, in spite of the fact that Pauli’s question concerning the physical explanation of the exclusion principle could not yet be answered, the helium calculation opened the path towards an understanding of complex atomic systems.$^{399}$ In any case, Heisenberg was very optimistic. ‘I am convinced,’ he wrote to Jordan a few days after submitting his paper on helium spectra to *Zeitschrift für Physik*, ‘that the spectra of all chemical elements can be obtained (apart from the satellite structure [i.e., those caused by a magnetic moment of the nucleus, as in Pauli’s treatment of the hyperfine structure (Pauli, 1924c)]) from quantum mechanics in a unique manner without physics [i.e., additional physical assumptions] by bone-headed calculation’ (Heisenberg to Jordan, 28 July 1926).

---

$^{398}$Heisenberg first suggested his ideas about solving the problem of ferromagnetism in a letter to Pauli. He wrote:

I have myself thought a little about the theory of ferromagnetism, superconductivity, and similar obscenities (“Schweinerein”). The idea is this: In order to use Langevin’s theory of ferromagnetism, one has to assume a large coupling force between the spinning electrons (only these truly rotate). As in the case of helium, this force should be provided indirectly by the resonance. I believe that one can prove in general that the smallest energy results when the spin-vectors are parallel to each other. The energy differences in question are of the electrical order of magnitude, but they vanish very fast with increasing distance [between the atoms]. I have the feeling (without knowing the matter in the least) that this might suffice in principle for an interpretation of ferromagnetism. In order to decide the question why most materials are not ferromagnetic, but some are, one must of course calculate quantitatively; one could perhaps make it plausible that in the case of Fe, Co and Ni the situation [for ferromagnetism] is most favourable. It is the same for conductivity; here the resonance migration of electrons à la Hund may explain the situation. (Heisenberg to Pauli, 4 November 1926)

$^{399}$In trying to approach the problem of explaining the exclusion principle, Pauli, in fall 1926, turned to fluctuation considerations. Since the fluctuation formula for particles obeying Fermi statistics (which corresponds to Einstein’s formula, Eq. (181)) contains a wave-like term with a negative sign, Pauli speculated: ‘Perhaps this behaviour might be interpreted by assuming phase relations between the different de Broglie eigenvibrations; this might give a hint for a future physical explanation of the fundamental basis of Fermi-statistics and therewith also of the “equivalence rule” [i.e., the exclusion principle]’ (Pauli, 1927, pp. 95–96). Pauli continued to study the problems connected with spin and statistics over many years, returning to them time and again during the following three decades, before a more satisfactory ‘explanation’ of the exclusion principle from general quantum-theoretical considerations could be given; this was the so-called spin-statistics theorem. (See, e.g., Pauli, 1955.)

Interestingly enough, in fall 1926 Heisenberg also concerned himself with the treatment of fluctuations in quantum-mechanical systems (Heisenberg, 1926e). However, Heisenberg’s work dealt with the connection between the concepts of matrix mechanics and wave mechanics. In pursuing this question further, Heisenberg arrived at the uncertainty relations, which constituted a fundamental step in the physical interpretation of quantum mechanics (Heisenberg, 1927b).
